How is JSON different from a JavaScript object?
What does JSON.parse do?
What does JSON.stringify do?
Why is JSON commonly used in web APIs?
What are some syntax rules that make JSON stricter than JavaScript object syntax?
Where do parsing and stringifying occur in an API data flow?

title: HTTP Status Codes
description: Learn to read HTTP status codes as meaningful signals about the outcome of a request, with emphasis on the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx response classes.
mastery: The learner can explain the purpose of HTTP status codes, identify the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx classes, interpret common examples, and avoid treating every response containing data as a successful request.
learningObjectives: Explain why HTTP responses include status codes.
Distinguish the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx status-code classes.
Interpret common success, redirection, client-error, and server-error responses.
Use the status code as part of the decision about whether a request succeeded.
Explain why a response body alone does not determine whether an HTTP request succeeded.
Recognize when a frontend should display success, failure, or another state based on the response outcome.

sections.text: The Number at the Top of the Response Matters
In the previous lesson, you learned how data can arrive as JSON. Now add another piece of information to the response: the HTTP status code.
The status is a compact signal about what happened to the request.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Read the status code as the response's outcome category before you decide what to do with the response body.
The Four Classes You Need First

sections.title: Status-code classes
sections.code:
2xx
→ successful

3xx
→ redirection

4xx
→ client/request problem

5xx
→ server problem

sections.text: The first digit gives you the broad class. You will learn individual status codes by seeing them in context rather than memorizing a giant list.
2xx: The Request Succeeded

sections.title: Common 2xx examples
sections.code:
200 OK
→ request succeeded and a normal response may be returned

201 Created
→ a resource was successfully created

204 No Content
→ request succeeded but there is no response body

sections.text: The exact meaning depends on the status code and the API contract, but the 2xx class indicates a successful request. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
3xx: The Client Is Being Redirected

sections.title: Redirection class
sections.code:
3xx
→ further action is involved in completing the request
→ commonly associated with redirection or cached/conditional behavior

sections.text: For frontend application code, you will often encounter redirects through browser and HTTP behavior rather than manually handling every 3xx status yourself. The important foundation is recognizing that 3xx is its own response class, not automatically a server failure.
4xx: The Request Could Not Be Fulfilled as Sent

sections.title: Common 4xx examples
sections.code:
400 Bad Request
→ request is invalid or cannot be understood

401 Unauthorized
→ authentication is required or has not been accepted

403 Forbidden
→ server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it

404 Not Found
→ requested resource was not found

sections.text: The 4xx class indicates a client-side/request-side problem in the HTTP interaction. The exact cause still comes from the individual code and API contract. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
5xx: The Server Could Not Fulfill the Request

sections.title: Common 5xx examples
sections.code:
500 Internal Server Error
→ unexpected server-side failure

503 Service Unavailable
→ server is currently unable to handle the request

sections.text: A 5xx response tells the client that the failure is on the server side or within the server's ability to fulfill the request. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not call every non-empty response a success. A 404 or 500 response can contain perfectly useful JSON while still representing a failed HTTP operation.
The Body and Status Tell Different Stories

sections.title: Error with useful JSON

sections.text: The response body gives useful information about the failure. The 404 status tells you how the HTTP operation itself should be classified.
200 Does Not Mean 'The User Got What They Wanted'
A successful HTTP transport-level response does not automatically mean the application's business goal was successful.

sections.title: Two layers of success
sections.code:
HTTP success
→ the HTTP operation completed successfully

Application outcome
→ the returned data may still represent an empty result,
   a business-level failure, or a state that needs special UI handling

sections.text: This distinction becomes especially important when the API returns valid data representing an empty result. The HTTP request can succeed while the interface still needs to show an empty state.
Interactive Practice: Status Classifier

sections.title: HTTP Status Classifier
sections.instructions: Read each response and classify it as success, redirect, client error, or server error. Then identify the likely frontend response to the status before reading the explanation.

sections.text: Drill 1: Stop Treating Every Response as Success

sections.title: Status-Aware UI Decision Drill
sections.instructions: The frontend currently checks only whether response data exists. Replace that reasoning with a status-aware decision. For each response, choose the appropriate UI state and explain why.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
Status: 200
Body: { "lessons": [] }

Scenario B
Status: 404
Body: { "error": "Lesson not found" }

Scenario C
Status: 401
Body: { "error": "Login required" }

Scenario D
Status: 503
Body: { "error": "Service unavailable" }

Possible UI decisions:
- Show lesson data
- Show empty state
- Ask user to authenticate
- Show a not-found state
- Show a temporary service error

Task:
Match each status to the most appropriate UI decision.

sections.text: A Status Code Is Not the Whole Error Model
The status gives you an important category, but frontend code still needs to consider the actual API contract and the application state.

sections.title: Think in layers
sections.code:
Status
→ What happened at the HTTP level?

Response body
→ What additional information did the server provide?

Application state
→ What should the interface do now?

sections.text: This layered reasoning prevents status-code handling from becoming a collection of hardcoded messages with no connection to the actual user experience.
Example: Authentication

sections.title: 401 vs 403
sections.code:
401 Unauthorized
→ the client needs valid authentication credentials

403 Forbidden
→ the server understood who/what is making the request,
   but access is not allowed

sections.text: These codes can lead to different UI behavior. A 401 may lead to a sign-in flow, while a 403 may require showing that the authenticated user lacks permission.
Example: Not Found

sections.title: 404 is a state, not necessarily a crash
sections.code:
GET /api/lessons/999

404 Not Found

Frontend could show:
'We couldn't find that lesson.'

sections.text: A 404 does not necessarily mean the entire application is broken. It identifies a specific request outcome that the interface can handle appropriately.
Example: Server Failure

sections.title: 503 can suggest retry behavior
sections.code:
GET /api/lessons

503 Service Unavailable

Frontend might show:
'Lessons are temporarily unavailable. Please try again.'

sections.text: Whether retrying is appropriate depends on the product and API behavior. The key is to distinguish a temporary server problem from a malformed client request.
Do Not Memorize Fifty Codes Yet
You will encounter many HTTP status codes in real work. At this stage, the most valuable skill is recognizing the classes and understanding a small set of common codes in context.

sections.title: Foundation set
sections.code:
200 → OK
201 → Created
204 → No Content
301/302 → Redirect family
400 → Bad Request
401 → Unauthorized
403 → Forbidden
404 → Not Found
500 → Internal Server Error
503 → Service Unavailable

sections.text: As you encounter APIs in projects, read the documentation for the statuses that API actually uses rather than trying to memorize the entire HTTP specification.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lessons will connect HTTP status to HTTP method semantics, then to actual frontend loading/error/empty states and Fetch.
More specialized statuses and protocol behavior are intentionally deferred. This lesson is about building a reliable first classification system.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Status codes tell you what happened at the HTTP level. They do not automatically define the exact UI. Your frontend still needs to interpret that outcome within the API contract and product context.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What do the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx classes mean?' A strong answer is: '2xx indicates successful responses, 3xx indicates redirection or further action, 4xx indicates a problem with the request or client-side conditions, and 5xx indicates a server-side failure.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Does a response body mean the request succeeded?' No. Error responses can contain useful JSON bodies, so the status must also be checked.

Another follow-up is: 'What's the difference between 401 and 403?' In practical terms, 401 indicates that valid authentication is required or was not accepted, while 403 indicates that the request is understood but access is not allowed.
Reflect
Imagine a dashboard receives a 503. What should the user see? What information might a developer need? What would be different if the same request returned 404?
Treat the status as evidence about what happened, not as an excuse to show a generic 'Something went wrong' message for every situation.

sections.label: Correctly classify the supplied HTTP status examples, distinguish successful, redirected, client-error, and server-error responses, and pass the status-aware UI decision exercise without relying on response-body content alone.
sections.hint: Read the status class first. Then use the body and API contract to decide what the interface should do.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

HTTP status codes communicate the outcome class of a response: 2xx successful, 3xx redirection, 4xx client/request problem, and 5xx server problem. Common foundation codes include 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500, and 503. A response body can contain useful data even when the HTTP operation failed, so frontend code should interpret status and body together rather than treating any non-empty response as success.

exercises.title: HTTP Status Classifier
exercises.brief: Classify common HTTP responses by status class and explain what each outcome means.

exercises.title: Status-Aware UI Decision Drill
exercises.brief: Map different HTTP outcomes to appropriate frontend states instead of checking only whether response data exists.

quiz.question: What does a 2xx response indicate?
options: A successful HTTP operation.
A client error.
A server error.
A redirect only.
quiz.explanation: 2xx status codes indicate successful responses.

quiz.question: What does a 4xx response generally indicate?
options: A successful request.
A redirection.
A problem with the request or client-side conditions.
A server crash in every case.
quiz.explanation: 4xx status codes indicate a client/request-side problem in the HTTP interaction.

quiz.question: What does a 5xx response generally indicate?
options: A server-side failure.
A successful creation.
A browser rendering issue only.
A normal redirect.
quiz.explanation: 5xx status codes indicate server-side failure.

quiz.question: Why is this reasoning incorrect: 'The response has JSON, so the request succeeded'?
options: JSON can only appear in successful responses.
Error responses can also contain useful JSON, so the HTTP status must be considered.
JSON is not allowed in HTTP.
Only 200 responses can contain bodies.
quiz.explanation: The presence of a response body does not determine the HTTP outcome.

quiz.question: What is the practical distinction between 401 and 403?
options: 401 generally indicates authentication is required or not accepted; 403 indicates access is not allowed.
401 means the server crashed; 403 means the browser crashed.
They always mean exactly the same thing.
403 means the resource does not exist.
quiz.explanation: 401 and 403 communicate different access-related outcomes.

summary: HTTP status codes provide a compact signal about request outcomes. The foundation classes are 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client/request problems, and 5xx server problems. Common codes such as 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500, and 503 are useful starting points. Frontend developers should read status and response body together because error responses can still contain useful structured data.

What are common 2xx status codes?

Can an error response contain JSON?
Why should frontend code inspect the status rather than only the response body?

title: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
description: Understand the intended semantics of the main HTTP methods and practice choosing the appropriate method for reading, creating, replacing, partially updating, and deleting resources.
mastery: The learner can select an appropriate HTTP method for common API operations, explain the difference between PUT and PATCH, construct simple request examples, and recognize when using GET for a state-changing action violates the API's intended contract.
learningObjectives: Explain the intended role of GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
Map common CRUD-style operations to appropriate HTTP methods.
Distinguish replacing a resource with PUT from partially updating it with PATCH.
Recognize that the exact behavior of a method is determined by HTTP semantics plus the API contract.
Construct simple method/path/body examples.
Choose an appropriate HTTP method from a written API requirement.
Explain why state-changing operations should not be hidden inside GET requests.

sections.text: The Method Is Part of the Meaning
You now know that an HTTP request has a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body. The method is not decorative. It communicates the intended kind of operation.
When you look at an API request, the path tells you what resource is involved, while the method helps tell you what the client intends to do with it.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of the method as the action word of the request: retrieve, create/process, replace, partially update, or delete.
GET: Retrieve

sections.title: Read lessons
sections.code:
GET /api/lessons HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

sections.text: GET is used to retrieve a representation of a resource. Its semantics are intended to be safe: a GET request is not supposed to ask the server to change application state just because it was made. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
POST: Submit Data for Processing

sections.title: Create a lesson

sections.text: POST asks the target resource to process the submitted representation according to the API contract. A common use is creating a new resource in a collection. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/POST?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
PUT: Replace the Target Representation

sections.title: Replace a lesson
sections.code:
PUT /api/lessons/12 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "title": "HTTP Methods",
  "duration": 40,
  "completed": true
}

sections.text: PUT is used to create or replace the target resource representation, depending on the API and current resource state. The important beginner distinction is that PUT represents replacement of the target representation rather than a small patch to one field. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/PUT?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
PATCH: Partial Update

sections.title: Update one field

sections.text: PATCH is intended for partial modification of a resource. Instead of representing the complete replacement, the request describes the modification to apply according to the API's patch semantics. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/PATCH?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

sections.title: PUT vs PATCH
sections.text: A useful beginner model is: PUT says 'make the target representation this.' PATCH says 'apply this partial modification.' The exact API contract still determines what fields are required and how updates are interpreted.
DELETE: Remove

sections.title: Delete a lesson
sections.code: DELETE /api/lessons/12 HTTP/1.1

sections.text: DELETE asks the server to delete the specified resource according to the API's rules. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/DELETE?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
The Core Comparison

sections.title: Method → typical intent
sections.code:
GET
→ retrieve

POST
→ submit data for processing / commonly create

PUT
→ create or replace the target representation

PATCH
→ partially modify

DELETE
→ remove

sections.text: These are useful working meanings, not a license to ignore the API documentation. Real APIs can impose additional constraints on fields, responses, authorization, and resource behavior.
Interactive Practice: Choose the Method

sections.title: HTTP Method Matcher
sections.instructions: Choose the best HTTP method for each API requirement before checking the answer. Explain what resource is involved and whether the operation reads, creates, replaces, partially updates, or removes it.
sections.initialCode:
Requirement A
Get the list of all lessons.

Requirement B
Create a new lesson with title and duration.

Requirement C
Replace all fields of lesson 12 with the supplied representation.

Requirement D
Change only lesson 12's completed field.

Requirement E
Remove lesson 12.

For each requirement:
1. Choose GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.
2. Write a sample path.
3. Say whether a request body is needed.

sections.text: Drill 1: GET or State Change?

sections.title: Method Semantics Drill
sections.instructions: The API below has endpoints for loading and changing learner progress. Decide which requests should use GET and which should use a state-changing method. Explain why putting the action in a GET URL is a poor design.
sections.initialCode:
API requirements:

GET /api/learners/42/progress
→ read learner 42's progress

POST /api/learners/42/progress
→ record a new progress event

Bad idea:
GET /api/learners/42/progress?markLessonComplete=12

Questions:
1. Which request reads data?
2. Which request changes state?
3. Why should the state-changing action not be hidden inside GET?
4. What method would better represent the state-changing operation?

sections.text: GET has safe semantics: clients can retrieve information without intending to mutate server state. Using GET for a state-changing action makes caching, prefetching, crawling, retries, and other infrastructure behavior much harder to reason about. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not use GET because it is convenient when the operation actually changes server state. Method semantics communicate intent, and infrastructure may treat GET as safe to retrieve or prefetch.
PUT and PATCH: A Closer Comparison

sections.title: Suppose lesson 12 currently is
PUT example
sections.code:
PUT /api/lessons/12

{
  "id": 12,
  "title": "Closures",
  "duration": 45,
  "completed": true
}

sections.title: PATCH example

sections.text: The first represents a complete replacement-style payload. The second describes a partial modification. Again, the actual API documentation determines exactly which representation and fields are accepted.
Drill 2: Repair the API Client

sections.title: HTTP Method Debugger
sections.instructions: Several frontend functions use the wrong HTTP method. Repair them according to the API contract. Do not change the endpoint unless the contract requires it.
sections.initialCode: Each function currently uses the WRONG HTTP method for its action. Fix them in the code panel to match REST convention (GET to read, POST to create, PUT to fully replace, DELETE to remove).

sections.text: Method Semantics and Idempotence

You may hear the word idempotent when discussing HTTP methods. At a practical level, an idempotent method is defined so that making the same request multiple times has the same intended effect as making it once, assuming the same conditions and request semantics.

sections.title: Foundation view
sections.code:
GET
→ safe and idempotent

PUT
→ idempotent

DELETE
→ idempotent by HTTP semantics

POST
→ not generally idempotent

PATCH
→ may or may not be idempotent depending on the patch semantics

sections.text: Do not reduce idempotence to 'the response is identical every time.' It is about the intended effect of repeating the same request, and the server can still return different metadata or timestamps.
Why Method Semantics Matter to Frontend Developers
The method affects more than readability. Browsers, caches, proxies, clients, and API tooling can make assumptions based on HTTP semantics.

sections.title: Good semantic communication
sections.code:
GET
→ safe retrieval

POST
→ submit/create/process

PUT
→ replace

PATCH
→ partially modify

DELETE
→ remove

sections.text: Correct semantics make the system easier for other developers and infrastructure to reason about.
What's Being Deferred?
Authentication, authorization, request retries, caching headers, optimistic UI, and more detailed REST design are deliberately deferred.
The current goal is narrower: look at an API requirement and choose the method that best expresses the intended operation.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Do not turn this into a CRUD memorization exercise. HTTP method semantics matter because they communicate intent and interact with the broader HTTP ecosystem.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'When do you use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE?' A strong answer is: 'GET retrieves a resource, POST submits data for processing and is commonly used to create resources, PUT represents replacement of a target resource, PATCH represents partial modification, and DELETE requests removal.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What's the difference between PUT and PATCH?' Put represents replacement of the target representation, while PATCH applies a partial modification according to the API's patch semantics.

Another follow-up is: 'Why shouldn't you use GET for a state-changing action?' GET is defined with safe retrieval semantics, and clients/infrastructure can rely on that expectation. Hiding a state change inside GET creates surprising behavior and can cause unintended mutations when requests are retried or prefetched. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
Reflect

Take five actions a learning application might perform: load lessons, create a note, replace a profile, update a completion flag, and delete a note. For each, choose a method and explain what the method communicates.

sections.label: Complete the method-matching, GET-vs-state-change, and API-client debugging exercises. The learner must choose the appropriate HTTP method and explain the semantic reason rather than relying only on CRUD memorization.
sections.hint: Retrieve → GET. Submit/create → POST. Replace → PUT. Partial modification → PATCH. Remove → DELETE.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

HTTP methods communicate intended operations. GET retrieves, POST submits data for processing and is commonly used to create resources, PUT represents replacement, PATCH represents partial modification, and DELETE requests removal. Method semantics are part of the API contract and the wider HTTP system, so do not hide state-changing actions behind GET simply because the URL is convenient.

options: GET
POST
PATCH
DELETE

quiz.question: Which method is commonly used to create a new resource in a collection?
options: GET
POST
DELETE
PATCH

quiz.question: What is the beginner-friendly distinction between PUT and PATCH?
options: PUT retrieves; PATCH deletes.
PUT represents replacement; PATCH represents partial modification.
PUT is always read-only; PATCH is always read-only.
They are identical in all situations.
quiz.explanation: PUT is used for replacement semantics, while PATCH is intended for partial modification.

quiz.question:
Why is this endpoint design problematic?
GET /api/lessons/12?markComplete=true
options: GET URLs cannot contain numbers.
It hides a server-side state change inside a method intended to have safe retrieval semantics.
GET can only return HTML.
Query parameters are never allowed.
quiz.explanation: GET has safe semantics and should not be used to request a state-changing action. ([developer.mozilla.org](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

quiz.question: Which method asks the server to remove a resource?
options: POST
PUT
DELETE
GET
quiz.explanation: DELETE requests removal of the target resource.

summary: HTTP methods communicate intended operations as part of an API contract. GET retrieves, POST submits data for processing and is commonly used for creation, PUT represents replacement, PATCH represents partial modification, and DELETE requests removal. Choosing the correct method is more than CRUD memorization: safe and idempotent semantics affect how clients and infrastructure can reason about requests, which is why state-changing actions should not be hidden inside GET.

title: Loading, Error, and Empty States
description: Design and implement explicit loading, error, and empty states so data-driven interfaces remain understandable when data is delayed, unavailable, or simply absent.
mastery: The learner can distinguish loading, error, and empty states, implement each state in a data-driven interface, transition between them deliberately, and avoid treating every non-data condition as either a blank screen or a generic error.
learningObjectives: Explain why asynchronous interfaces need explicit loading, error, and empty states.
Distinguish loading, error, empty, and success states.
Render a meaningful loading state while data is being requested.
Render a meaningful error state when the request fails.
Render a meaningful empty state when the request succeeds but contains no usable items.
Transition cleanly between loading, success, error, and empty states.
Choose UI messaging that tells the learner what is happening and what they can do next.
Recognize why a blank interface is not an adequate loading or empty state.

sections.text: The Data Is Not Always There Yet
A static page can assume the content exists when the browser renders it. A data-driven interface cannot make that assumption.
When your frontend requests lessons, there is a period when the answer has not arrived. The request can also fail. And sometimes it succeeds perfectly but there simply are no lessons to display.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A data-driven UI should represent the state of the data request honestly. Loading means we are waiting. Error means the operation failed. Empty means the operation succeeded but there is nothing to show. Success means usable data is available.
The Four States

sections.title: Think in explicit UI states
sections.code:
loading
→ request is in progress

success
→ data arrived and can be displayed

empty
→ request succeeded, but there is no data to display

error
→ request failed

sections.text: These states are different. A good interface gives each one an appropriate visual and behavioral response.
Loading Is Not 'Nothing'
A blank screen during a network request gives the learner no information. They cannot tell whether the page is loading, broken, or simply empty.

sections.title: Weak loading state
sections.code: [completely blank area]

sections.title: Useful loading state
sections.code:
Loading lessons…

or

[lesson-card skeletons]

sections.text: The exact UI depends on the product, but the state should be visible enough that the user understands the application is doing work.
Error Is Not Empty

sections.title: Two very different situations
sections.code:
Error:
'We couldn't load your lessons. Try again.'

Empty:
'You have no lessons here yet.'

sections.text: The first means the application could not obtain the data. The second means the application successfully obtained the data and discovered that the result contains zero items.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not render an empty result as an error, and do not render a failed request as an empty list. Those states imply different causes and require different user actions.
A Simple State Model

sections.title: Represent the state explicitly

sections.text: The exact state architecture can vary, but the important idea is that your UI should have enough information to know which state it is currently representing.
Interactive Practice: Live State Switcher

sections.title: Loading / Error / Empty State Playground
sections.instructions: Change the request state live and observe how the interface should change. Test loading, success with data, success with no data, and failure. For each state, predict the UI before switching it.
sections.initialCode: Current status: loading

sections.text: Success With Data vs Success With No Data

sections.title: Same successful request, different UI

sections.text: An empty state is usually a branch inside the successful data state. The request succeeded; the collection simply contains nothing.
Empty Can Be Normal
A newly created account may have no saved lessons. A search may return no matches. A learner may have completed all available work. None of those conditions necessarily means something broke.

sections.title: Different empty-state contexts
sections.code:
New account:
'You haven't saved any lessons yet.'

Search:
'No lessons match "closures".'

Completed filter:
'You have no incomplete lessons.'

sections.text: A good empty state often explains why the area is empty and gives the user a useful next action.
Error States Should Help Users Recover

sections.title: Weak error
sections.code: Error.

sections.title: More useful error
sections.code:
We couldn't load your lessons.

[Try again]

sections.text: The exact recovery action depends on the failure. A retry button may make sense for a temporary network or service problem; asking the learner to sign in may make more sense for an authentication failure.
Loading Can Preserve Context

A loading state does not always need to replace the entire page. When refreshing an already visible list, a small progress indicator or disabled action may communicate the state while preserving useful context.

sections.title: Initial load vs refresh
sections.code:
Initial load:
[page-level loading state]

Refresh existing data:
[existing lessons remain visible]
[small 'Refreshing…' indicator]

sections.text: The product decision depends on the interaction. The principle stays the same: make the current request state understandable.
Drill 1: Diagnose the Blank Screen

sections.title: State Diagnosis Drill
sections.instructions: A lesson dashboard currently shows a blank area whenever the list is not rendered. Determine which state each scenario represents and choose the appropriate UI state and message.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
The request is still waiting for the server.

Scenario B
The request failed with a 503.

Scenario C
The request succeeded with lessons: [].

Scenario D
The request succeeded with three lesson objects.

Current UI behavior:
if (!lessons) {
  return null;
}

Task:
1. Explain why this implementation is insufficient.
2. Name the missing state distinctions.
3. Propose a UI response for each scenario.

sections.text: Retry Does Not Mean 'Pretend Nothing Happened'
A retry action should normally put the UI back into a loading state while the new request is in progress.

sections.title: Retry transition
sections.code:
error
  ↓ user selects Try again
loading
  ↓ request succeeds
success

or

loading
  ↓ request fails again
error

sections.text: Making the transition explicit prevents stale error messages from remaining on screen while a new request is running.
Drill 2: Repair the State Machine

sections.title: State Transition Debugger
sections.instructions: Repair the request flow so retry changes the interface to loading, success with data shows the list, success with no data shows an empty state, and failure shows an error with a retry action.

sections.text: Avoid State Contradictions

A poorly designed state object can contain contradictory information such as status: 'error' while also showing a successful lesson list. The exact state architecture varies, but mutually exclusive request states should be represented clearly.

sections.title: Contradictory state
sections.code:
status: 'error'
lessons: [five lessons]
error: 'Request failed'

sections.text: Now the UI has to guess which field to trust. A cleaner design makes the active state clear and keeps stale information from creating contradictory output.
A Useful State Table

sections.title: Map data conditions to UI
sections.code:
loading
→ progress indicator / skeleton

success + data
→ render content

success + empty
→ empty-state message and useful next action

error
→ failure message and possible recovery action

sections.text: This table is often enough to expose missing UI states before you write the component.
Frontend Debugging Connection
When a data-driven component looks blank, ask what state it is actually in before changing CSS.

sections.title: Debug in this order
sections.code:
Is the request still loading?

Did it fail?

Did it succeed with zero items?

Did it succeed with data?

Is the data shape what the component expects?

sections.text: This is especially important because a blank screen can be caused by several completely different problems.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson introduces Fetch and connects these state ideas to real browser network requests. More advanced topics such as skeleton design systems, stale-while-revalidate strategies, optimistic updates, and sophisticated query-cache state machines come later.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: You do not need a state-management library to understand these states. First make the state model explicit with ordinary JavaScript and UI conditions.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why do loading, error, and empty states matter?' A strong answer is: 'Asynchronous data is not immediately available and can fail or return no items. Explicit states keep the UI truthful and give users useful feedback instead of leaving a blank or ambiguous interface.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What's the difference between empty and error?' Empty means the request succeeded but there is no data to display. Error means the request or operation failed.

Another follow-up is: 'What should happen when the user retries after an error?' The UI should normally transition back to loading while the new request is in progress, then move to success or error based on the result.
Reflect
Choose a data-driven feature you have built or seen. List all states it can realistically enter before, during, and after a request. Which state is easiest to forget?

sections.title: A blank screen is a state too—but a terrible one

sections.text: When the UI has no explicit loading, error, or empty representation, the user is forced to guess. Your job as a frontend developer is to remove that guesswork.

sections.label: Complete the live state-switcher exercise and both state diagnosis/debugging drills. The learner must correctly distinguish loading, success with data, success with no data, and error, and implement the appropriate UI response for each.
sections.hint: Loading, error, empty, and success are different states. Do not collapse them into 'data exists' versus 'data does not exist.'

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Data-driven interfaces should explicitly represent loading, success, empty, and error states. Loading means the request is in progress; error means it failed; empty means it succeeded with no usable items; success with data means content can be rendered. These distinctions make interfaces more understandable, help users recover from failures, and prevent blank screens from hiding the true state of the application.

exercises.title: Loading / Error / Empty State Playground
exercises.brief: Change the live request state and predict the correct UI for loading, success with data, success with no data, and error.

exercises.title: State Diagnosis Drill
exercises.brief: Diagnose a blank data area and distinguish the underlying loading, error, empty, and success conditions.

quiz.question: What does a loading state represent?
options: The request is still in progress.
The request failed.
The request succeeded with zero items.
The request succeeded and all content is ready.
quiz.explanation: Loading means the application is still waiting for the requested data or operation to complete.

quiz.question: What is an empty state?
options: A failed request with no error message.
A successful request that produces no items or usable content for the current context.
A request that is still loading.
A server crash.
quiz.explanation: An empty state represents a successful data operation with nothing to display.

quiz.question: Why is rendering a blank screen during loading a poor experience?
options: Because blank screens always consume more memory.
Because the user cannot tell whether the interface is loading, empty, or broken.
Because loading states must always use animations.
Because browsers cannot render blank elements.
quiz.explanation: An explicit loading state communicates what the application is currently doing.

quiz.question: What should normally happen when a user retries after an error?
options: Leave the old error state visible while silently requesting data.
Transition to loading, then to success or error based on the new result.
Immediately show success.
Clear the entire application state permanently.
quiz.explanation: Retry begins a new request, so the UI should represent that request as loading before showing its result.

quiz.question: Why should empty and error states be separate?
options: They always use different colors.
Empty means the request succeeded with no data, while error means the operation failed.
Errors always contain arrays and empty states never do.
There is no meaningful difference.
quiz.explanation: They represent different causes and therefore can require different messaging and recovery actions.

summary: Data-driven interfaces need explicit states for loading, success, empty results, and errors. Loading tells the user the request is still in progress, error communicates failure and potential recovery, empty communicates that the request succeeded but there is nothing to show, and success with data renders the content. Explicit state modeling prevents blank or contradictory interfaces and gives the frontend a truthful model of what is happening.
interviewQuestions: Why do data-driven UIs need explicit loading, error, and empty states?
What's the difference between an empty state and an error state?
What should a loading state communicate?
How should a retry interaction affect UI state?
Why is a blank data region a poor state representation?
How would you model loading, success, empty, and error state in a component?
What bugs can contradictory state data create?

title: Working with Fetch
description: Use fetch() to make HTTP requests from JavaScript, inspect the response, handle JSON data, and deliberately handle HTTP failures instead of assuming a rejected Promise means every failed HTTP status.
mastery: The learner can use fetch() for a GET request, inspect response.ok and response.status, convert a JSON response into JavaScript data, handle network and HTTP failures deliberately, and explain why fetch does not automatically reject for 4xx or 5xx responses.
learningObjectives: Use fetch() to make a browser HTTP request.
Explain that fetch() returns a Promise.
Use the Response object to inspect status information.
Use response.ok to distinguish successful HTTP responses from unsuccessful ones.
Read JSON response data with response.json().
Handle HTTP errors and network failures as different failure cases.
Use async/await consistently when working with fetch().
Explain why fetch() does not reject its Promise merely because the server returned a 4xx or 5xx status.
Update application state according to the actual request outcome.

sections.text: Now Make the Request for Real

You have already learned what APIs are, how HTTP requests and responses work, how JSON crosses the network boundary, what status codes mean, which methods to use, and how a UI should represent loading, error, empty, and success states.
fetch() is the browser API that connects those ideas to actual JavaScript code.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: fetch() starts an HTTP request and gives you a Promise for the response. You then inspect the Response, decide whether the HTTP result is acceptable, and parse the response body when appropriate.
The Smallest Fetch Example

sections.title: Make a GET request

sections.text: fetch() returns a Promise. When the browser receives an HTTP response, that Promise fulfills with a Response object.
The Response Is Not the JSON Yet

sections.title: Read the JSON body

sections.text: The first then receives the Response object. response.json() reads the body and asynchronously parses it into a JavaScript value.

sections.title: Two stages
sections.text: fetch() gives you the HTTP response. response.json() gives you the parsed JSON data. Do not confuse the Response object with the application's data.
The Modern Style: async/await

sections.title: Fetch with async/await

sections.text: This is easier to read because it follows the same Promise model you learned earlier, just with sequential-looking syntax.
The Critical fetch() Rule
There is a subtle behavior that surprises many beginners: fetch() does not reject its Promise merely because the server returns an HTTP error status such as 404 or 500.

sections.title: The dangerous assumption

sections.text: If the server returns a normal HTTP response with status 404, the fetch Promise can still fulfill. The catch block is not automatically triggered just because the HTTP status is unsuccessful.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: fetch() rejects for problems such as a network failure, but HTTP 4xx and 5xx responses do not automatically reject the fetch Promise. You must inspect the Response, commonly with response.ok or response.status.
response.ok

sections.title: Check HTTP success explicitly

sections.text: response.ok provides a simple success check for the HTTP response. If the response is not considered successful, your application can deliberately enter its error path.
Why This Connects Directly to the Previous Lesson

sections.title: Fetch plus explicit UI state
sections.code:
Start request
→ loading

fetch succeeds + response.ok
→ parse data
→ success or empty

fetch succeeds + !response.ok
→ error

fetch rejects because the request cannot be completed
→ error

sections.text: This is the complete state discipline you built in the previous lesson, now connected to a real HTTP request.

sections.title: Inspect the exact status

You Can Handle Different HTTP Errors Differently

sections.title: Status-aware handling

sections.text: The correct level of detail depends on the application. Sometimes every unsuccessful response can use one generic error path. Sometimes particular statuses require different user actions.

sections.text: Fetch Can Take Request Options

sections.title: POST with JSON

sections.text: This combines the earlier lessons: method semantics, headers, JSON.stringify, Promise-based asynchronous behavior, and explicit HTTP-error handling.
The Fetch Recipe

sections.title: A reusable mental recipe
sections.code:
1. Start loading state.

2. await fetch(...).

3. Inspect response.ok / response.status.

4. If unsuccessful, enter the error path.

5. Parse the body when appropriate.

6. Distinguish data from an empty result.

7. Render success state.

sections.text: This pattern should become familiar enough that you can adapt it to different APIs without forgetting the important status check.
Network Failure vs HTTP Failure

sections.title: Two different failure paths
sections.code:
Network-level failure
→ fetch Promise rejects
→ catch can handle it

HTTP-level failure
→ fetch Promise may fulfill
→ response.ok is false
→ your code must handle it

sections.text: That distinction is the single most important thing to remember from this lesson.
A catch block alone does not prove your HTTP error handling is correct. You still need to inspect the Response for unsuccessful HTTP statuses.
Debug Fetch With the Network Panel

sections.title: Evidence-driven debugging
sections.code:
Request URL?
→ Is the endpoint correct?

Method?
→ Does it match the API contract?

Request headers/body?
→ Is the request shaped correctly?

Status?
→ What HTTP outcome occurred?

Response body?
→ What data or error details came back?

sections.text: This connects directly to the Network-panel skill from lesson-2-4-2. fetch gives the application the programmatic side of the request; the Network panel gives you a visual record of the actual exchange.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson is the API Integration Project. It will combine the whole module: real API data, loading/error/empty handling, request semantics, JSON, status codes, and fetch into one working feature.
More advanced Fetch topics such as AbortController, streaming responses, request cancellation, retries, and sophisticated caching are intentionally deferred.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: The goal here is not to memorize every fetch option. It is to reliably complete the request → inspect response → handle failure → parse data → update UI cycle.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How does fetch work?' A strong answer is: 'fetch returns a Promise for a Response. I inspect the response status, check response.ok, then read the body, for example with response.json(). I handle rejected network requests with catch or try/catch, and I handle unsuccessful HTTP statuses explicitly because fetch does not reject just because the server returned 4xx or 5xx.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is response.json()?' It reads the response body and asynchronously parses JSON into a JavaScript value.
Another follow-up is: 'Why check response.ok?' Because fetch can resolve with an HTTP error response. response.ok lets the application explicitly detect that unsuccessful HTTP outcome.
Reflect
Imagine a fetch request returns 404 with a JSON error body. What will your JavaScript receive at the first await? What do you need to check before treating the response as successful data?
Never let 'fetch succeeded' and 'HTTP request succeeded' become the same mental statement. The Promise can fulfill while the HTTP operation is unsuccessful.

sections.label: Complete the Fetch Playground and both drills. The learner must make a fetch request, inspect response.ok/status, parse JSON, handle HTTP and network failures, and connect the result to loading/success/empty/error UI states.
sections.hint: fetch Promise fulfillment gives you a Response. Then inspect response.ok/status before trusting the body as successful data.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

fetch() makes HTTP requests from JavaScript and returns a Promise for a Response. response.json() reads and parses a JSON response body. The most important Fetch rule is that HTTP 4xx/5xx responses do not automatically reject the fetch Promise, so frontend code must inspect response.ok or response.status and enter an error path explicitly. A reliable fetch flow is loading → fetch → inspect response → handle unsuccessful HTTP result → parse data → distinguish empty from success → update the UI.

quiz.question: What does fetch() return?
options: The parsed JSON object immediately.
A Promise for a Response.
An HTTP status number.
The rendered DOM.
quiz.explanation: fetch returns a Promise that fulfills with a Response object when the HTTP response is available.

quiz.question: What does response.json() do?
options: Changes the HTTP method to JSON.
Reads and asynchronously parses JSON from the response body.
Checks whether the status is 200.
Sends the request again.
quiz.explanation: response.json() reads the body and parses its JSON content into a JavaScript value.

quiz.question: What happens when fetch receives a normal HTTP 404 response?
options: fetch always rejects immediately.
fetch can still fulfill with a Response whose ok property is false.
The browser automatically converts the 404 into an empty array.
response.json() automatically retries the request.
quiz.explanation: HTTP error statuses do not by themselves cause fetch to reject; application code should inspect response.ok or response.status.

quiz.question:
Why should this code check response.ok?

const response = await fetch('/api/lessons');
options: Because response.ok tells whether the HTTP response is successful.
Because fetch never returns a Response otherwise.
Because ok contains the JSON body.
Because ok is the request URL.
quiz.explanation: response.ok provides a boolean indication that the HTTP response is in the successful range.

quiz.question: Which sequence best represents a robust basic Fetch flow?
options: fetch → assume success → render
fetch → inspect response → handle unsuccessful status → parse body → update UI
render → fetch → ignore response
catch → always show success
quiz.explanation: The response must be inspected before the body is trusted as successful application data.

summary: fetch() connects JavaScript to real HTTP requests. It returns a Promise for a Response, and response.json() asynchronously parses a JSON body. The critical behavior is that fetch does not automatically reject merely because the server returned a 4xx or 5xx HTTP status. Frontend code should inspect response.ok or response.status, handle unsuccessful responses deliberately, parse the body when appropriate, and update loading, success, empty, and error UI states based on the actual outcome.

title: API Integration Project
description: Build a working frontend feature that consumes a real API and handles loading, success, empty, and error states without hardcoding an ideal response shape.
mastery: The learner can integrate a real API into a working frontend feature, inspect and adapt to the actual response shape, handle loading/error/empty/success states, use fetch correctly, and explain the decisions made around the API contract and UI state.
learningObjectives: Integrate a real web API into a working frontend feature.
Read the API documentation before implementing the request.
Use fetch with explicit HTTP-success checking.
Parse and use the actual response data rather than assuming an ideal structure.
Represent loading, success, empty, and error states explicitly.
Handle realistic API failures without showing false success.
Adapt the UI to the actual response shape.
Use Network-panel evidence to diagnose integration problems.
Explain the complete request-to-UI data flow.

sections.text: This Time, There Is No Perfectly Prepared Answer
You have spent the module learning the individual pieces of API work: contracts, HTTP requests and responses, JSON, status codes, methods, UI states, and fetch.
Now you have to use them together.

The project intentionally does not give you a fake response object that perfectly matches your first assumption. You need to inspect the API, understand what it actually returns, and build the feature around the real contract.

sections.title: The capstone rule
sections.text: Do not invent the API response shape and then force the real endpoint into that shape. Read the actual contract, inspect the actual response, and adapt your client to reality.
Project Brief
Build a Lesson Explorer feature for Forge Academy. The feature should retrieve lesson data from a real web API and allow the learner to browse the returned results.

sections.title: Required behavior
sections.code:
1. Request data from a real API.
2. Show an explicit loading state while the request is running.
3. Show useful content when the request succeeds with data.
4. Show a deliberate empty state when the request succeeds with no usable results.
5. Show a useful error state when the request fails.
6. Check the HTTP response before treating it as success.
7. Adapt to the actual response shape.
8. Provide a retry path when appropriate.
9. Keep the implementation understandable and explainable.

Deliberately cause the request to fail. Temporarily change the endpoint to a nonexistent path, use a testable invalid request, or use the API's documented failure mechanism when available.

request → success → content

sections.text: A project that works only while the network behaves perfectly is not finished.
Debugging With Evidence

sections.title: When something breaks
sections.code:
1. Open the Network panel.
2. Find the request.
3. Check the URL and method.
4. Check request parameters/body.
5. Check status code.
6. Inspect response body.
7. Compare actual shape with your code.
8. Fix the layer where the mismatch occurs.
9. Retest the complete state flow.

sections.text: Do not immediately rewrite the component because the list is blank. The blank list could come from a failed request, a wrong response path, a normalization bug, or a rendering condition.

When debugging an API feature, follow the data from the network response to the JavaScript value to the state object to the rendered UI. Find the first point where reality diverges from your assumption.
Architecture Review

sections.title: Can you explain these boundaries?
sections.code:
API layer
→ knows how to request data

Normalization layer
→ adapts external data when needed

UI state
→ knows whether the feature is loading, successful, empty, or failed

Presentation
→ renders the appropriate state

sections.text: The project does not require this exact file structure. It requires you to understand the responsibilities and avoid mixing every concern into one opaque function.
Code Quality Requirements

sections.title: Review before submission
sections.code:
□ The API endpoint is documented or clearly identified.
□ The request method matches the contract.
□ response.ok or equivalent status handling is present.
□ JSON is parsed correctly.
□ The actual response shape is handled.
□ Loading is visible.
□ Error is visible and useful.
□ Empty is distinct from error.
□ Retry behaves correctly.
□ No hardcoded 'ideal' response is hiding the real API.
□ No debug console output remains without purpose.
□ The implementation is understandable.

sections.text: Product Thinking

A technically correct API integration can still provide a poor user experience. Ask whether the messages make sense, whether the retry action is useful, whether the empty state explains what happened, and whether the loading state preserves enough context.
Root-Cause Reflection
Use the debugging approach from earlier lessons. The strongest submission is not simply one where the UI works; it is one where you can explain why the implementation works.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Walk me through your API integration.' A strong answer is: 'I start by reading the API contract, make the request with fetch, inspect the response status, parse the documented response data, normalize it only if useful, and update explicit loading, success, empty, and error states. I verify the actual request and response in the Network panel rather than assuming the API behaves as expected.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What happens if the API response shape changes?' A good answer is: 'The client should rely on the documented contract, validate or normalize the incoming shape where appropriate, and avoid scattering assumptions throughout the UI.'

Another follow-up is: 'How do you know whether a failure is frontend or backend?' The first step is evidence: inspect the actual request, response status, response body, and the point where the application transforms the data. That identifies which layer is failing instead of guessing.
Submission Checklist

sections.title: Before you call it finished
sections.code:
FUNCTIONAL
□ Real API request works.
□ Data renders from the actual response.
□ Loading works.
□ Success works.
□ Empty works.
□ Error works.
□ Retry works.

HTTP
□ Method is correct.
□ Status is checked.
□ JSON is parsed correctly.

QUALITY
□ No idealized fake response assumptions.
□ No unnecessary complexity.
□ Code responsibilities are clear.
□ Debugging evidence was used.
□ You can explain the data flow.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The purpose of this project is to turn API knowledge into a working frontend feature. A reliable integration follows the real contract, inspects the actual network response, checks HTTP success explicitly, parses the real data shape, and gives the UI honest loading, success, empty, and error states. The capstone is successful when the learner can explain not only that the feature works, but why each part of the integration is structured the way it is.

quiz.question: Why should you inspect the real API response before finalizing the UI mapping?
options: Because APIs always return different data every time.
Because your initial assumption about the response shape may be wrong, and the UI must follow the actual contract and response.
Because JSON cannot be parsed.
Because fetch does not return a Response.

quiz.question: What should happen before the application treats fetched data as successful?
options: Only check whether response.json exists.
Inspect the HTTP response and explicitly handle unsuccessful statuses.
Assume any fulfilled fetch Promise means 200.
Render immediately and check later.

quiz.question: Which sequence best describes a robust API-driven UI?

Request → loading → inspect response → parse data → distinguish empty/success → render, or enter error state.
Request → immediately render an empty list regardless of response.
Request → always show success.

quiz.question: Why is hardcoding one 'ideal' response shape risky?
options: It can make the client fail or display incorrect data when the real API response differs.
Hardcoded objects cannot be used in JavaScript.
APIs never return JSON.
It automatically creates a network error.
quiz.explanation: The client should adapt to the documented and actual data contract rather than assumptions.

quiz.question: When debugging an API integration, why is the Network panel valuable?

It automatically changes the API contract.
