4. Name meaningful sections.
5. Build a component tree.
6. Check which data must flow between branches.
7. Only then begin implementation.

sections.text: This sequence prevents implementation details from determining the architecture too early.
The Component Tree Is Not the DOM Tree

A component tree and a DOM tree are related, but they do not have to be identical. A component can return several nested DOM elements, and a component boundary can represent behavior or responsibility rather than a single visual element.

sections.title: Component vs DOM
sections.code:
LessonCard component
└── article
    ├── h2
    ├── p
    ├── button
    └── p

sections.text: The component gives the group a meaningful identity in the React architecture.
Use Design Repetition as Evidence
If a UI pattern appears repeatedly, that is evidence that the repeated structure may deserve a component. But the component should still represent a coherent concept.
Use Behavior as Evidence
A part of the UI with its own interaction often makes a natural component boundary. Search boxes, dialogs, tabs, and interactive cards are common examples.
Use Change as Evidence

Another useful question is: which parts are likely to change independently? If navigation changes frequently while the lesson list changes for different reasons, separating them can make those changes easier to manage.

sections.title: Three signals
sections.code:
Repeated
or
Interactive
or
Conceptually independent

→ candidate component boundary

sections.text: The Tree Should Help You Answer Ownership Questions
A good hierarchy makes later questions easier: where should the state live, which component should receive the data, and which child needs a callback?

sections.title: Architecture leads to data flow
sections.code:
Parent
↓ props
Child
↓ callback
Parent

The exact ownership decision comes next,
but the component tree gives you the map.

sections.text: Drill 2: Plan Before Code

sections.title: UI Planning Drill
sections.instructions: Before writing JSX, design a component hierarchy for the given feature. Include the likely data each component receives, but do not implement state or effects yet.
sections.initialCode:
Feature:
A course page contains:
- course title
- instructor information
- search box
- category filter
- list of lessons
- each lesson has a title, duration, progress state, and expand/collapse details
- a progress summary appears above the list

Your plan:

Component tree:
____________________________
____________________________
____________________________

Repeated components:
____________________________

Independent interactions:
____________________________

Likely shared data:
____________________________

One boundary you deliberately would not create:
____________________________

sections.text: What This Prevents

sections.title: Without planning
sections.code:
Start coding
→ component grows
→ state gets added
→ more conditions appear
→ repeated markup appears
→ props become tangled
→ refactoring becomes necessary

sections.title: With planning
sections.code:
Inspect UI
→ identify concepts
→ define component tree
→ decide data relationships
→ implement smaller pieces

sections.text: Planning does not eliminate refactoring. It gives you a deliberate starting architecture instead of discovering the entire architecture through accidental complexity.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lessons focus on the specific architecture questions that emerge from this tree: what belongs in props versus state, and how to lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.
This lesson deliberately avoids solving every state-ownership question. First build the hierarchy; then reason about data flow.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Component architecture starts with decomposition. Do not jump into state management, context, or abstractions before you understand the UI tree you are trying to build.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer gives you a dashboard mockup and says, 'How would you build this in React?' A strong first step is not immediately writing JSX. Say: 'I'd first decompose the UI into a component hierarchy, identify repeated and independently interactive pieces, and determine which parts need to communicate.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you decide whether something should become a component?' Explain that repetition, independent interaction, meaningful conceptual boundaries, and independent change are useful signals.

Another follow-up is: 'Why not make every visual section a component?' Because component boundaries should improve clarity or reuse; arbitrary fragmentation can make the architecture harder to understand.
Reflect

Take the React Interaction Challenge from the previous module. Before looking at your implementation, draw the component tree you think the feature should have. Then compare it with your code. Where did implementation choices force the architecture instead of the UI requirements determining it?

sections.title: Design the tree before the branches

sections.text: A component tree is a reasoning tool. It lets you discuss responsibilities and data flow before syntax, hooks, and implementation details make the design harder to change.

sections.label: Complete the component-tree Playground and both planning drills. The learner must decompose the supplied UI into meaningful components, identify repeated and interactive boundaries, and justify at least one boundary they deliberately do not create.
sections.hint: Start from the UI: visible regions → repetition → interaction → meaningful concepts → component tree.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Thinking in Components means decomposing a UI into a meaningful component hierarchy before writing detailed React code. Use repetition, independent interaction, conceptual responsibility, and likely independent change as signals for boundaries. Avoid both one giant component and arbitrary fragmentation. The component tree is the architectural map that makes later props, state, and data-flow decisions easier.

options: Immediately create one giant component.
Decompose the UI into a meaningful component hierarchy.
Add a global state library.
Create a component for every DOM element.
quiz.explanation: Thinking in Components begins with decomposing the UI into meaningful boundaries before implementation.

quiz.question: Which is a useful signal that something might deserve its own component?
options: It is always exactly ten lines of code.
It is repeated, independently interactive, or conceptually meaningful as a unit.
It contains a div.
It has a CSS class.
quiz.explanation: Repetition, interaction, and meaningful responsibility are useful component-boundary signals.

quiz.question: Why can over-decomposition be harmful?
options: React cannot render many components.
Arbitrary tiny components can add indirection without creating a useful responsibility boundary.
Components cannot be nested.

quiz.explanation: A component should provide a useful conceptual, behavioral, or reusable boundary rather than merely increase file count.

summary: Thinking in Components means planning a component hierarchy from the UI before writing detailed implementation code. Identify visible concepts, repeated patterns, independent interactions, and responsibilities that may change independently. Then create meaningful component boundaries while avoiding both a single monolithic component and unnecessary fragmentation. This hierarchy becomes the map for later decisions about props, state, and shared data.

title: Props vs State
description: Learn to distinguish parent-provided props from component-owned state, decide which values belong in each, and use ownership to make React data flow predictable.
mastery: The learner can identify whether a value should be a prop or local state, explain who owns each value, and recognize when incorrectly storing parent-owned or derived information as local state creates synchronization problems.
learningObjectives: Explain props as parent-provided inputs used to configure a child.
Explain state as component-owned changing information.
Identify the owner of a value in a component tree.
Decide whether a value should be a prop, local state, or a derived value.
Explain why a child should not duplicate parent-owned state unnecessarily.
Recognize synchronization bugs caused by copying props into state without a clear reason.

sections.text: The Same UI Can Use Both Props and State
You already know both concepts individually. Props let a parent provide data. State lets a component remember changing information.
The architecture question is now: which values belong where?

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Props flow down from a parent for configuration and input. State belongs to the component that owns and changes that information. The key question is always: who owns this value?
A Simple Example

sections.title: Props plus local state
Ownership
sections.code:
title
→ parent provides it
→ prop

expanded
→ LessonCard owns and changes it
→ state

sections.text: The distinction is about ownership, not about whether a value changes visually.
Props Configure the Component

sections.title: Same component, different inputs
sections.code:
<LessonCard title="JSX" />
<LessonCard title="Props" />
<LessonCard title="State" />

sections.text: The component does not decide its title. Its parent configures that aspect through props.
State Represents Local Memory

sections.title: Local interaction state
sections.code: const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);

sections.text: The parent does not need to know whether this particular card is expanded unless some other part of the application depends on that information.
The Three-Way Decision

sections.title: Ask which category fits
sections.code:
Parent-owned input
→ prop

Component-owned changing information
→ state

Value calculated from existing values
→ derived during render

sections.text: That third category matters. Not every value needs to become state.

sections.title: Derived value

sections.text: percentage is derived from props. Creating separate state for it would introduce another value that can become out of sync.
The Common Anti-Pattern: Copying Props Into State

sections.title: Usually unnecessary

sections.text: Now the component has two values representing the lesson title: title from the parent and localTitle inside the child. If the parent changes title later, localTitle does not automatically follow.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not copy props into state just because you want to use the value inside the child. That creates two potential sources of truth. Use the prop directly unless the child intentionally needs an independent local draft or snapshot.
When a Local Copy Can Be Legitimate

sections.title: Editable draft

sections.text: Here the local state has a distinct purpose: it represents an editable draft that can temporarily differ from the parent value. The distinction should be intentional and documented by the interaction.
Interactive Practice: Classify the Values

sections.title: Props or State Playground
sections.instructions: For each value, decide whether it should be a prop, local state, or derived value. Then modify the example so the ownership matches your decision.
sections.initialCode:
Component: LessonCard

Value A
lesson.title
→ parent already owns the lesson
Decision: __________________

Value B
expanded
→ changes when the user clicks Show details
Decision: __________________

Value C
progressPercentage
→ calculated from completed and total
Decision: __________________

Value D
draftTitle
→ user edits locally before pressing Save
Decision: __________________

Value E
lessonId
→ parent identifies which lesson is being rendered
Decision: __________________

sections.text: Drill 1: Repair the Duplicate Source of Truth

sections.title: Props/State Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The child duplicates parent-owned lesson data in local state. Repair the component so the title remains driven by props while preserving local state only for the editable draft interaction.

sections.text: Ask Who Needs the Value

sections.title: Ownership questions
sections.code:
Who creates this value?
Who changes it?
Who needs to read it?
Would another component need to stay synchronized with it?
Can it be derived from existing props/state?

sections.text: These questions often reveal where the value should live.
A Shared Value Usually Needs a Common Owner

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
LessonDashboard
├── SearchBox
└── LessonList

Both depend on:
searchQuery

A later lesson will ask:
Where should searchQuery live?

sections.text: If two siblings need to stay synchronized around one changing value, local state in only one sibling may not be enough. That problem leads directly to lifting state up.
Props Are Not 'Lower-Level State'
A prop and state can both hold ordinary JavaScript values. Their difference is ownership and data flow, not the type of the value.

sections.title: Same value type, different role
sections.code:
string prop
→ parent owns the string

string state
→ component owns the changing string

sections.text: Drill 2: Ownership Decisions

sections.title: State Ownership Drill
sections.instructions: For each scenario, identify the best owner and whether the value should be a prop, state, or derived value. Explain what would become difficult if you put the value in the wrong place.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A LessonCard receives a lesson object from LessonList.
Who owns lesson?
____________________________

Scenario B
The card has a Show details button that only affects that card.
Who owns expanded?
____________________________

Scenario C
ProgressSummary calculates completed / total.
Does percentage need state?
____________________________

Scenario D
SearchBox and LessonList both need the same search query.
Where should that changing query eventually live?
____________________________

Scenario E
An editor lets the user change a draft before saving it.
Why might draftTitle be local state even though initialTitle is a prop?
____________________________

sections.text: A Helpful Rule: One Source of Truth
When multiple pieces of code can independently change or represent the same conceptual value, synchronization becomes harder.

sections.title: Prefer one owner
sections.code:
One conceptual value
        ↓
One clear owner
        ↓
Other components receive it through props
or receive callbacks to request changes

sections.text: This is not a rule that every value must exist in exactly one variable. It is a design principle: avoid accidental duplicate sources of truth.
Debugging Props vs State

sections.title: When a value is stale
sections.code:
1. Where is the value originally created?
2. Who is supposed to own it?
3. Is it being duplicated in local state?
4. Is it derived from another value?
5. Are multiple components trying to change their own copies?

sections.text: Many React synchronization bugs are ownership bugs in disguise.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson takes the shared-state case and solves it directly with lifting state up. Composition and more advanced state architecture follow later.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is about recognizing ownership. The next lesson is about moving shared state to the closest common ancestor when siblings need synchronized access.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between props and state?' A strong answer is: 'Props are inputs provided by a parent and treated as read-only by the child. State is information owned and changed by the component. The decision is fundamentally about ownership and data flow.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Should you copy props into state?' Usually no. Copying creates two sources of truth and can make the local value stale when the parent changes. An explicit editable draft or snapshot can justify local state.
Another follow-up is: 'What if two siblings need the same changing value?' That is a signal that the value may need to move to their closest common parent, which is the lifting-state-up pattern.
Reflect

Take the Lesson Search project. Which values are user-editable local state? Which values are inputs to child components? Which values can be derived? Which value would become problematic if both SearchForm and SearchResults owned their own copies?
When React code feels confusing, stop and ask who owns each piece of changing information. Once ownership is clear, props, state, and callbacks become much easier to place.

sections.label: Complete the Props/State classification Playground and both ownership drills. The learner must correctly classify values as props, state, or derived values and explain why duplicating parent-owned props in state can create synchronization problems.
sections.hint: Prop = parent-owned input. State = component-owned changing value. Derived = calculated from values you already have.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Props and state are different primarily because of ownership. Props flow from a parent into a child as configurable input. State belongs to the component that owns and changes the information. Values that can be calculated from existing props or state should usually remain derived rather than becoming additional state. Avoid copying props into state unless you intentionally need an independent local draft or snapshot, because duplicate sources of truth can become unsynchronized.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between props and state?
options: Props are always strings and state is always numbers.
Props are parent-provided inputs; state is component-owned changing information.
Props are mutable and state is read-only.
They are exactly the same mechanism.
quiz.explanation: Ownership and data flow distinguish props from state.

quiz.question: Why is copying a prop into state usually risky?
options: The child may end up with two values representing the same concept that can become out of sync.
React does not allow strings in state.
Props cannot be read by child components.
State cannot be updated.
quiz.explanation: Duplicated sources of truth can diverge when the parent prop changes.

quiz.question: Which value is most likely derived rather than state?
options: A toggle controlled by a button.
A user's draft text.
A percentage calculated from completed and total.
A selected tab that the user can change.
quiz.explanation: The percentage can be calculated from existing values and does not need independent state.

quiz.question: Two sibling components need to stay synchronized around one changing value. What is the likely architectural signal?
options: Give each sibling an independent copy.
Move the shared value toward their closest common parent.
Put the value in a random child.
Convert the value into a constant.
quiz.explanation: Shared state often belongs in the closest common ancestor, which leads to lifting state up.

summary: Props versus state is an ownership question. Props are parent-provided inputs that configure a child; state is information owned and changed by a component. Derived values should usually be calculated rather than stored as another state variable. Copying props into state is usually unnecessary and can create two sources of truth, though an intentional editable draft or snapshot is a legitimate use case.

title: Lifting State Up
description: Learn how to move shared state to the closest common ancestor so sibling components can stay synchronized through props and callbacks.
mastery: The learner can recognize when sibling components need shared state, move that state to their closest common ancestor, pass the value down through props, and pass callbacks down so children can request updates.
learningObjectives: Recognize when two or more components need synchronized access to the same changing value.
Explain why independent copies of shared state can drift apart.
Move shared state to the closest common ancestor.
Pass shared state down through props.
Pass callbacks down so children can request state changes.
Keep local-only UI state in the component that actually needs it.
Explain one-way data flow in a lifted-state architecture.

sections.text: The Sibling Problem
Suppose a dashboard has a SearchBox and a LessonList. The SearchBox needs to know what the user typed, and the LessonList needs the same value to determine which lessons to display.
Neither sibling should maintain an independent copy if they need to stay synchronized. There needs to be one shared owner.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: When sibling components need the same changing information, move that state to their closest common ancestor. The parent owns the state, passes the value down, and gives children callbacks to request updates.
The Problem With Two Copies

sections.title: Two independent states

sections.text: Both components now have a value called query, but they are not the same state. One can change without the other knowing.

sections.title: The synchronization problem
sections.code:
SearchBox query = "react"

LessonList query = ""

The UI disagrees with itself.

sections.text: Move State Up

sections.title: Common owner

sections.text: Now there is exactly one query state. The dashboard owns it, and both children receive the information they need.
Data Flows Down

sections.title: Shared state architecture
sections.code:
LessonDashboard
      │
      ├── query ─────────→ SearchBox
      │
      └── query ─────────→ LessonList

sections.text: The value flows down through props. The parent remains the source of truth.
Actions Flow Back Up

sections.title: Callback flow
sections.code:
SearchBox
   │
   │ onQueryChange(nextQuery)
   ↓
LessonDashboard
   │
   │ setQuery(nextQuery)
   ↓
query changes
   ↓
SearchBox + LessonList render from the same value

sections.text: The child does not directly change the parent's state. It calls the callback supplied by the parent, and the parent performs the update.
The Complete Pattern

sections.title: Parent owns the shared state

sections.text: Interactive Practice: Synchronize Two Siblings

sections.title: Lifting State Up Playground
sections.instructions: The SearchBox and LessonList must stay synchronized around one search query. Start with the supplied architecture, then change it so the parent owns the query and both children receive the correct props.

sections.text: Drill 1: Lift the Filter State

sections.title: Shared State Repair Drill
sections.instructions: Repair the dashboard so SearchBox and LessonList use one shared query state. Keep SearchBox responsible for the input UI and LessonList responsible for filtering and displaying results.

sections.text: The Closest Common Ancestor Rule

sections.title: Where should shared state live?
sections.code:
SearchBox
     \ 
      LessonDashboard
     /
LessonList

→ Put query in LessonDashboard.

sections.text: The closest common ancestor is a useful default because it gives every consumer access without moving the state unnecessarily high in the component tree.
Do Not Lift State Higher Than Necessary

sections.title: Too high
sections.code:
App
└── huge shared state object
    └── unrelated page-specific components

sections.text: Lifting state means moving it to a common owner, not automatically moving all state to the top of the application.
Keep Local State Local

sections.title: Not everything needs lifting
sections.code:
LessonDashboard
├── SearchBox
│   └── query → shared
│
└── LessonCard
    └── expanded → local

sections.text: If only one LessonCard needs to know whether its details are expanded, there is no reason to lift that state into the dashboard.
Shared State Changes the Component Contract

sections.title: Before
After lifting

sections.text: The SearchBox is now a controlled child. Its parent owns the query and controls the value.

sections.title: Lift or Keep Local?
sections.instructions: For each state value, decide whether it should stay local or move upward. Explain which components need it and whether they need to stay synchronized.
sections.initialCode:
Component tree:
Dashboard
├── SearchBox
├── FilterBar
├── LessonList
│   └── LessonCard
└── ProgressSummary

A
Search query
Consumers: SearchBox, LessonList
Decision: __________________

B
Whether one LessonCard's details are expanded
Consumers: one LessonCard
Decision: __________________

C
Selected category filter
Consumers: FilterBar, LessonList
Decision: __________________

D
Hovered state for one button
Consumers: one button
Decision: __________________

E
Completed lesson collection
Consumers: LessonList, ProgressSummary
Decision: __________________

sections.text: Lifting State Creates a Predictable Loop

sections.title: One-way flow
sections.code:
Parent state
    ↓
props to children
    ↓
child event
    ↓
callback to parent
    ↓
parent updates state
    ↓
new props
    ↓
children render again

sections.text: This loop may feel indirect at first, but the benefit is predictability: one owner controls the shared value.
Why This Is Better Than Direct Sibling Communication
React's basic data flow is parent to child. Siblings do not normally reach into one another's state. They communicate through their shared parent.

sections.title: Avoid
sections.code:
SearchBox
↕ directly changes
LessonList

sections.title: Prefer
sections.code:
SearchBox
   ↓ callback
Parent
   ↓ prop
LessonList

sections.text: Debugging Lifted State

sections.title: When siblings disagree
sections.code:
1. Where is the shared value owned?
2. Is there only one source of truth?
3. Does the parent pass the current value to every consumer?
4. Does the child call the correct callback?
5. Is one child maintaining a duplicate local copy?

sections.text: If two siblings show different versions of the same conceptual value, inspect the ownership boundary first.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses on component composition and how to build reusable components by combining specialized children without unnecessary prop plumbing.
Context and global state are intentionally deferred. First master the simplest shared-state mechanism: a common ancestor.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Lifting state up solves shared state for related components. It does not mean every piece of state belongs in the highest component or that a global store is required.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What does lifting state up mean?' A strong answer is: 'When multiple components need to stay synchronized around the same changing value, I move that state to their closest common ancestor and pass the value down with props and update functions down through callbacks.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why the closest common ancestor?' It provides a shared owner to all consumers without moving the state higher in the tree than necessary.
Another follow-up is: 'Should all state be lifted?' No. State that only affects one component should usually remain local to that component.
Reflect

Look at your Lesson Search challenge. Which values had multiple consumers? Which values belonged only to one component? What would happen if SearchForm and SearchResults each kept their own query state?

sections.title: One shared value, one clear owner

sections.text: When siblings need synchronized state, give that value one owner and let the component tree carry the data and callbacks.

sections.label: Complete the Lifting State Up Playground and both decision/repair drills. The learner must move shared state to the closest common ancestor, pass the value down, and pass callbacks up without unnecessarily lifting local-only state.
sections.hint: Shared by siblings → common parent. Used by one component → keep it local. Data goes down; actions come back through callbacks.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Lifting state up is the basic React pattern for synchronizing sibling components. Move the shared changing value to the closest common ancestor, pass the current value down through props, and pass callbacks down so children can request updates. Keep state local when only one component needs it. The goal is one clear source of truth with predictable parent-to-child data flow.

quiz.question: When should you usually lift state up?
options: Whenever any component uses state.
When multiple components need to stay synchronized around the same changing value.
Only when a component has more than 100 lines.
Whenever a value is a string.
quiz.explanation: Shared state belongs in a common owner so sibling consumers can stay synchronized.

quiz.question: Where should shared state generally live?
options: Inside the first child that needs it.
In the closest common ancestor of the components that need it.
Always at the root App component.
Inside a random utility function.
quiz.explanation: The closest common ancestor is the usual owner that can provide the shared state to all consumers.

quiz.question: How does a child request a shared-state update?
options: By directly mutating its sibling's state.
By calling a callback passed down from the parent.
By changing the DOM.
By editing the parent's local variable.
quiz.explanation: Callbacks let children communicate requested updates back to the component that owns the shared state.

quiz.question: Which state should usually remain local?
options: A search query needed by two siblings.
A lesson collection needed by a list and progress summary.
Whether one individual card's details are expanded.
A selected category shared by filter and result components.
quiz.explanation: If only one component needs the value, lifting it adds unnecessary coordination.

summary: Lifting state up moves shared state to the closest common ancestor of the components that need to stay synchronized. The parent becomes the single source of truth, passes the value down through props, and passes callbacks down so children can request changes. State that is only relevant to one component should remain local. This pattern keeps sibling components synchronized without introducing global state.

title: Composition
description: Learn to build flexible React components by composing smaller components through children and other props, rather than creating rigid components packed with special-case branches.
mastery: The learner can use composition to build flexible component structures, pass nested JSX through children, distinguish composition from unnecessary inheritance-style abstractions, and choose component boundaries that remain reusable as the interface grows.
learningObjectives: Explain composition as building larger UI from smaller components.
Use the children prop to create flexible wrapper components.
Pass JSX or components into another component when customization is needed.
Distinguish composition from hardcoding specific child structures.
Identify when a component should accept children instead of knowing its exact contents.
Avoid creating rigid components with many special-case props.
Explain why composition can make component APIs easier to reuse.

sections.text: A Parent Does Not Always Need to Know the Exact Child UI

Lifting state up taught you how data can move between components. Composition addresses a different architectural question: how can a component provide a reusable structure without hardcoding exactly what appears inside it?

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Composition means building a component from other components or JSX supplied by its consumer. The wrapper owns the structure; the consumer supplies the content or specialized pieces.
Start With a Rigid Component

sections.title: Hardcoded panel

sections.text: This panel only knows one piece of content. Reusing it for a different kind of message would require adding more special-case props or branches.
Let the Consumer Supply the Contents

sections.title: Composition with children

sections.text: The Panel owns the reusable container structure while the parent decides what belongs inside it.
The children Prop

sections.title: Nested JSX becomes children

sections.text: Anything placed between the opening and closing tags of a component is available through its children prop.

sections.title: Think of children as a slot
sections.code:
<Card>
  ???

sections.text: Composition Can Be More Flexible Than Many Props

sections.title: Rigid API

sections.text: A component with many props that exist mainly to support unrelated combinations can become difficult to understand.

sections.title: Composition API

sections.text: Composition can move variation into the content supplied by the consumer rather than encoding every possible variation into the wrapper's API.

Composition and Props Solve Different Problems

The Common Anti-Pattern: Conditional Mega-Components

sections.text: Composition and Component Architecture

Thinking in Components identifies boundaries. Props define data contracts. Lifting state up defines shared ownership. Composition defines how components can expose flexible structure without knowing every concrete child.

sections.title: The architecture toolkit so far
sections.code:
Components
→ meaningful UI boundaries

Props
→ parent-to-child data/configuration

State
→ component-owned changing information

Lifting state up
→ shared state ownership

Composition
→ flexible child structure/content

sections.text: Avoid Premature Abstraction
Composition is useful because it creates flexibility, but do not abstract a component before you understand the repeated structure it is actually solving.

sections.title: Useful abstraction
sections.code:
Two or more consumers share a real structural pattern
→ extract the common shell

sections.title: Premature abstraction
sections.code:
One consumer
+ hypothetical future use cases
→ elaborate generic component

sections.text: A component API should solve today's known design problem without making the code unnecessarily abstract.
What's Being Deferred?

The following lessons move into more advanced component architecture and state patterns. Context, reusable custom hooks, and broader application state are intentionally not introduced through this lesson.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Composition is about flexible component structure. It does not replace props or state, and it does not require a global state system.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is component composition?' A strong answer is: 'Composition means building a reusable component around a common structure while allowing the consumer to supply the inner content or specialized pieces, often through children or JSX props.'
A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use children instead of many props?' Use children when the wrapper owns the structure but the consumer needs freedom over what appears inside it.
Another follow-up is: 'Why is composition useful?' It prevents reusable components from needing to predict every possible content variation through special-case props and conditional branches.
Reflect
Look at your previous projects. Can you identify a component whose API grew because it tried to support too many specialized layouts? Which part could instead be supplied through children?

sections.title: Own the shell, compose the contents

sections.text: When a component has a stable outer structure but variable inner content, composition is often a cleaner boundary than a growing list of special-case props.

sections.label: Complete the Composition Playground and both architecture drills. The learner must build a reusable wrapper with children, replace an over-specialized component with composition, and correctly choose between props and composition.
sections.hint: Stable outer structure + variable inner content → composition. Data/configuration → props.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Composition lets a reusable component own a stable structural shell while its consumer supplies variable content or specialized UI, commonly through children. It is especially useful when a component would otherwise accumulate many special-case props and conditional branches. Composition complements props and state rather than replacing them: props provide data and configuration, while composition provides flexible child structure.

exercises.title: Composition Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Replace a rigid, prop-heavy Notice component with a reusable container that receives variable content through composition.

exercises.title: Architecture Choice Drill
exercises.brief: Choose between normal props, children composition, or a combination for several component-design scenarios.

quiz.question: What is component composition?
options: Building larger components from smaller components and supplied JSX.
Storing all application state globally.
Copying props into local state.
Replacing every component with one generic component.
quiz.explanation: Composition allows a component to provide reusable structure while consuming components supply content or specialized pieces.

quiz.question: What does the children prop contain?
options: Only strings passed through normal props.
The JSX/content placed between a component's opening and closing tags.
The component's state.
The React event object.
quiz.explanation: Nested JSX supplied by the consumer is available through the children prop.

quiz.question: When is composition especially useful?
options: When the component's outer structure is stable but its inner content varies.
When every value is a number.
When a component has no JSX.
Only when using global state.
quiz.explanation: Composition lets consumers provide variable inner structure without requiring many special-case props.

quiz.question: What is a warning sign that a component may be too rigid?
options: It accepts many special-case boolean and variant props to support unrelated layouts.
It accepts children.
It renders a semantic element.
It receives a title prop.
quiz.explanation: A growing matrix of special-case props can indicate that the variable UI should instead be composed by the consumer.

summary: Composition lets components expose reusable structure while allowing their consumers to supply variable contents. The children prop is the simplest composition mechanism: the wrapper owns the shell, while the consumer supplies nested JSX. Composition can prevent rigid components from accumulating many special-case props and branches. It works alongside props and state rather than replacing them.

title: Reusable UI Patterns
description: Practice extracting repeated UI into reusable, parameterized components such as cards, modals, and list items, using props and composition instead of copy-pasting similar implementations.
mastery: The learner can identify repeated UI, extract a reusable component, parameterize its variable data through props, reuse it in multiple contexts, and avoid duplicating nearly identical components.
learningObjectives: Recognize repeated UI patterns that should become reusable components.
Extract a reusable component from duplicated JSX.
Parameterize variable content with props.
Reuse one component across multiple data items or contexts.
Combine reusable components with list rendering.
Use composition when repeated structure contains variable inner content.
Avoid copy-pasting similar components with small differences.
Explain why a reusable component is preferable to duplicated UI code.

prerequisites.note: Inferred from lesson order; not asserted in YAML.

sections.text: This Lesson Is Practice, Not New Theory
You already learned component boundaries, props, lifting state, and composition. Now apply those ideas to a very common frontend problem: the same UI structure appears in multiple places.

sections.title: The practice rule
sections.text: When the same UI structure appears repeatedly, extract one reusable component and configure the differences with props rather than maintaining several copied versions.
Spot the Duplication

sections.title: Two nearly identical cards

sections.text: The data differs, but the structure is almost identical. This is a strong signal that the shared structure belongs in a reusable component.
Extract the Shared Structure

sections.title: Reusable LessonCard

sections.text: Now there is one implementation of the card structure. Changes to the card presentation can happen in one place.
Parameterize the Differences

sections.title: Stable structure vs variable data
sections.code:
Stable
→ article structure
→ title position
→ duration position
→ status position

Variable
→ title
→ duration
→ status

sections.text: Props define the component's variable inputs. The reusable component owns the shared presentation structure.
Pattern 1: Reusable Cards

sections.title: Card pattern

sections.text: A single object prop can also be useful when the component conceptually represents one domain object.
Pattern 2: Reusable List Items

sections.title: Compose with map

sections.text: The component becomes reusable across every item in the collection. The list owns collection structure; LessonCard owns one item's presentation.
Pattern 3: Reusable Modal Shells

sections.title: Modal shell with composition

sections.text: A modal shell can be reused for different content because the outer structure stays stable while children provide the variable body.
The Key Skill: Extract, Then Configure

sections.title: Reusable component workflow
sections.code:
Repeated JSX
    ↓
Identify stable structure
    ↓
Identify variable data/content
    ↓
Create component
    ↓
Expose variable parts as props/children
    ↓
Replace copies with the reusable component

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Don't copy-paste similar components
sections.text: If two components have almost the same markup and differ only in data, creating two separate implementations usually creates duplicate maintenance work.
The goal is not to make every component generic. The goal is to remove genuine duplication while preserving a clear component API.
Practice 1: Extract the Lesson Card

sections.title: Reusable Card Drill
sections.instructions: The dashboard contains three copied lesson-card implementations. Extract one reusable LessonCard and replace all three copies with it. Then change the shared card styling or markup once and verify every card updates.

sections.text: Practice 2: Configure One Component Across Contexts

sections.title: Reusable Component Drill
sections.instructions: Build one reusable StatusCard that can represent progress, a warning, or a completion message using props. Do not create separate ProgressCard, WarningCard, and CompletionCard implementations.

sections.text: Practice 3: Reusable List + Card

sections.title: List Pattern Drill
sections.instructions: Create a reusable LessonCard and render it from LessonList with map and stable keys. Then add a second list that uses the same LessonCard component with different data.

sections.text: Avoid the Wrong Abstraction

sections.title: Too generic

sections.text: A reusable component is not automatically good because it has many configuration options. Excessive configuration can simply move duplication into a harder-to-understand API.
Good Reuse Has a Clear Concept

sections.title: Good
sections.code:
LessonCard
→ represents one lesson
→ title/duration/status vary

Modal
→ represents a dialog shell
→ title/body/actions vary

sections.title: Suspicious
sections.code:
UniversalBox
→ represents whatever the caller needs

sections.text: The reusable component should still communicate a domain or UI concept. Reuse is a consequence of a good abstraction, not the only definition of one.
When Props Are Enough

sections.title: Data changes, structure stays the same
sections.code:
<LessonCard
  title="Composition"
  duration={35}
  status="In progress"
/>

sections.text: Use normal props when the variation is data or simple configuration.
When Composition Is Better

sections.title: Structure itself varies
sections.code:
Progress

Warning

Network unavailable.

sections.text: Use composition when the inner structure varies substantially while the outer shell remains shared.
Reusable Components and Lists Work Together

sections.title: One definition, many instances
sections.code:
LessonCard definition
       ↓
   ┌───┼───┐
   ↓   ↓   ↓
  JSX Props State

sections.text: A reusable component is still one component implementation even when it appears many times in the UI. Each instance receives its own props and can have its own local state.
A Reusable Component Can Own Local State

sections.title: Reusable card with local interaction

sections.text: Each rendered LessonCard instance has its own expanded state. Reuse does not mean instances share state automatically.
A Practical Extraction Checklist

sections.title: Before extracting
sections.code:
□ Is the structure genuinely repeated?
□ What parts are stable?
□ What parts vary?
□ Are the variations simple data or arbitrary content?
□ Does the resulting component have a clear name?
□ Will changing the shared UI benefit from one implementation?
□ Am I creating a generic abstraction just to avoid a few lines of duplication?

sections.text: Refactor Without Changing Behavior
A good reuse exercise should preserve the visible behavior first. Extract the component, replace the copies, and then verify the UI still works before making additional design changes.

sections.title: Safe refactoring sequence
sections.code:
Existing duplicated UI
        ↓
Extract shared structure
        ↓
Parameterize differences
        ↓
Replace copies
        ↓
Run existing behavior checks
        ↓
Only then improve the abstraction further

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson is the module's capstone: a Component Architecture Challenge where you refactor or redesign a small application using composition and lifted state.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is about applying reusable-component patterns. Advanced abstraction techniques, custom hooks, compound components, and broader application architecture come later.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you identify reusable UI?' A strong answer is: 'I look for repeated structure with meaningful stable and variable parts. I extract the stable structure into a component and expose the variable parts through props or composition.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you avoid over-abstraction?' Explain that the component should represent a clear concept and solve real repeated structure rather than becoming a universal component with dozens of configuration flags.
Another follow-up is: 'When would you use children instead of props?' Use props when the variation is data/configuration; use children or composition when the inner UI structure itself needs to vary.
Reflect
Look back through the React features you built earlier. Find one place where you copied JSX that could have been parameterized. What would be the stable structure, and what would become props?

sections.title: Extract the pattern, not the accident

sections.text: Good reuse captures a real repeated concept. Do not abstract arbitrary similarities that happen to appear once or twice without a meaningful shared responsibility.

sections.label: Complete all reusable UI Playground drills correctly without hints. The learner must extract duplicated UI, parameterize it, reuse it across multiple contexts, and avoid creating separate copied components for each variation.
sections.hint: Stable structure stays inside the reusable component. Data differences become props; substantial inner-structure differences can use composition.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Reusable UI patterns turn repeated structures into one clear implementation configured by props or composition. Cards, list items, modals, and similar UI patterns should generally be built once and reused rather than copied into multiple nearly identical components. Good reuse captures a meaningful concept without becoming a giant generic abstraction. This lesson is intentionally practice-focused: the goal is to recognize and apply the pattern repeatedly.

exercises.title: Reusable Card Drill
exercises.brief: Extract three duplicated lesson cards into one reusable LessonCard component and verify that a shared change updates all instances.

exercises.title: Reusable Component Drill
exercises.brief: Build one configurable StatusCard instead of separate components for progress, warning, and completion states.

exercises.title: List Pattern Drill
exercises.brief: Combine a reusable LessonCard with LessonList and stable keys, then reuse the same components across two different collections.

quiz.question: When should repeated JSX usually be extracted into a reusable component?
options: When it represents a genuine repeated UI concept or structure.
Whenever two lines happen to look similar.
Only when the component needs state.
Only when there are exactly ten copies.
quiz.explanation: Reuse is valuable when it captures a meaningful repeated UI concept.

quiz.question: What should usually become props in a reusable component?
options: The stable component structure.
The variable data or simple configuration.
Every DOM element.
The component name.
quiz.explanation: Props parameterize the parts that vary while the reusable component owns the stable structure.

quiz.question: What is a warning sign of over-abstraction?
options: A clear LessonCard with title and duration props.
A component with many unrelated boolean and variant props controlling dozens of branches.
A reusable modal shell with children.
A list rendering the same card component for each item.
quiz.explanation: A large matrix of configuration flags can indicate that the abstraction is too generic and difficult to reason about.

quiz.question: When is composition preferable to simple data props?
options: When the inner UI structure itself varies substantially while the outer shell remains shared.
Whenever a component receives a string.
Only when rendering a list.
When you want every child to share the same state.
quiz.explanation: Composition lets the consumer supply variable inner structure while the wrapper owns the shared shell.

summary: Reusable UI Patterns is an applied practice lesson. Extract repeated UI into a meaningful reusable component, keep its stable structure inside the component, and parameterize variable data through props. When the inner structure varies substantially, use composition. Avoid both copy-pasting nearly identical components and creating overly generic components with large matrices of special-case configuration.

title: Component Architecture Challenge
description: Refactor or design a small React application by applying the component-architecture patterns from this module: deliberate component boundaries, correct state ownership, lifting shared state, composition, and reusable UI patterns.
mastery: The learner can produce a working refactor or design that uses meaningful component boundaries, one clear owner for shared state, composition where appropriate, and reusable components, then justify the architecture according to data flow and responsibility rather than visual appearance alone.
learningObjectives: Apply component decomposition to an existing or supplied React feature.
Identify where shared state should live based on data flow.
Lift duplicated sibling state into a common parent when necessary.
Use props and callbacks to preserve one-way data flow.
Use composition when variable child structure should remain under consumer control.
Extract genuinely repeated UI into reusable components.
Evaluate a component hierarchy by responsibility and data flow.
Explain the tradeoffs behind the resulting architecture.

sections.text: The Module Capstone

This challenge does not introduce another React architecture pattern. Everything you need has already been taught: thinking in components, props vs state, lifting state up, composition, and reusable UI patterns.
Your job is to apply those ideas to a small application where the component structure is not given to you.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: Refactor or design a small React app's component hierarchy using composition and lifted state. Your architecture should follow the data flow and responsibilities of the feature, not merely the way the screen happens to look.
Project Scenario: Lesson Workspace
You are given a small lesson workspace. It displays a collection of lessons, lets the learner search/filter them, shows progress, and allows an individual lesson to reveal additional details.

sections.title: Feature requirements
sections.code:
The application must provide:

• A lesson collection.
• A search/filter interaction.
• A progress summary.
• Reusable lesson cards.
• Expand/collapse details on individual lessons.
• A clear empty state when no lessons match.
• A consistent outer panel/card structure where appropriate.

Architecture must demonstrate:
• Meaningful component boundaries.
• One owner for shared search/filter state.
• Props flowing downward.
• Callbacks flowing upward.
• Composition where inner structure varies.
• Reusable UI instead of copied markup.

sections.text: Starting Data

sections.title: Lesson data

sections.text: First: Sketch the Architecture
Do not start by converting every visible rectangle into a component. Sketch the feature's responsibilities first.

sections.title: Possible starting tree
sections.code:
App
└── LessonWorkspace
    ├── SearchControls
    ├── ProgressSummary
    └── LessonResults
        └── LessonCard

sections.text: This is only a starting point. You may alter the hierarchy when the data flow reveals a better boundary.
Architecture Question 1: Who Owns Search?

sections.title: Search state
sections.code:
SearchControls
→ needs the current query

LessonResults
→ needs the current query

Therefore:
query should have one shared owner
that can provide it to both.

sections.text: The closest common ancestor is a natural candidate. SearchControls can receive the current value and an update callback, while LessonResults receives the current query and filters the collection.
Architecture Question 2: Who Owns Expansion?

sections.title: Local interaction
sections.code:
LessonCard
→ only this card needs to know
  whether its own details are expanded.

Therefore:
expanded can remain local to LessonCard.

sections.text: Do not lift state merely because another component is above the card. Lift it when another part of the application actually needs to coordinate around that value.
Architecture Question 3: What Should Be Reusable?

sections.title: Repeated UI
sections.code:
LessonCard
→ one implementation
→ many lesson instances

LessonResults
→ maps lesson data
→ supplies stable keys
→ renders LessonCard

sections.text: Architecture Question 4: Where Does Composition Help?

sections.title: Stable shell, variable content
sections.code:
Panel
└── children

Possible uses:
Progress content
Search controls
Empty state
Lesson details

sections.text: A reusable shell can expose a stable layout while the consuming feature supplies the inner JSX. Use this only where the outer structure really is shared.
The Core Misconception

sections.title: Don't design the hierarchy from appearance alone
sections.text: Two things can look close together on the screen but belong to different responsibilities. Two things can look visually unrelated but need to share state or belong to the same data-flow boundary.
The architecture should follow responsibility and data flow. Visual grouping is useful evidence, but it is not the final authority.

sections.text: Implementation Challenge

sections.title: Component Architecture Challenge
sections.instructions: Implement the Lesson Workspace from your architecture plan. Your solution must have one clear owner for shared search state, a reusable LessonCard, local expansion state, stable parent-to-child data flow, callback-based updates where needed, and at least one appropriate use of composition. Test the empty filter case and explain your architecture after the implementation works.

sections.text: Minimum Architecture Requirements

sections.title: Required
sections.code:
COMPONENTS
□ More than one meaningful component boundary.
□ One reusable LessonCard implementation.
□ No duplicated lesson-card markup.

STATE
□ Search query has one shared owner.
□ LessonCard expansion state remains local.
□ No unnecessary duplicate derived state.

DATA FLOW
□ Shared query flows down through props.
□ SearchControls updates it through a callback.
□ LessonResults consumes the current query.

COMPOSITION
□ At least one meaningful use of children/composition.
□ Composition is used because structure varies, not just for novelty.

LISTS
□ Lessons are rendered from data.
□ Stable keys identify list items.

UI
□ Empty search result state is handled.
□ Existing lesson information remains understandable.

sections.text: Required Test Cases

sections.title: Behavior checks
sections.code:
1. Initial page
→ all lessons appear.

2. Type "Props"
→ results narrow to the matching lesson.

3. Clear the search
→ all lessons return.

4. Search for a nonexistent lesson
→ empty state appears.

5. Expand one lesson
→ its details appear.

6. Expand another lesson
→ each card maintains its own local UI state.

7. Change the shared query
→ SearchControls and LessonResults remain synchronized.

sections.text: A correct solution is not simply the one with the most components. You should be able to explain why each boundary improves responsibility, reuse, or data flow.
Refactor Test
Imagine the product owner asks for a different search UI while keeping lesson results unchanged. Which component should change?
Now imagine every lesson card needs a visual redesign. Which component should change?
Finally, imagine another sibling feature needs the current search query. Which ownership decision would need reconsideration?
Red Flags

sections.code:

AND parent owns query
→ duplicate source of truth

Every LessonCard receives expanded from parent
→ unnecessary lifted state

Three different card components share 90% of their markup
→ missed reuse opportunity

→ suspicious abstraction

→ data-flow problem may be hidden

sections.text: What Counts as a Strong Submission?

sections.title: Strong submission
sections.code:
Working feature
+
Clear component boundaries
+
Single owner for shared state
+
Intentional local state
+
Reusable UI
+
Appropriate composition
+
Correct data flow
+
Clear explanation of architecture

sections.text: The project is manually/rubric graded. Functionality matters, but code quality and the reasoning behind the architecture matter too.
Reflection

Which architecture decision was hardest to make? Was it deciding where query belongs, deciding what to keep local, identifying a reusable pattern, or choosing composition? Explain the competing options and why you selected one.
You have now practiced the core component-architecture toolkit: planning a hierarchy, distinguishing props from state, lifting shared state, composing flexible UI, and extracting reusable patterns.

sections.label: Submit the Component Architecture Challenge for manual/rubric grading. The project must demonstrate functional behavior plus meaningful component boundaries, correct shared-state ownership, composition, reusable UI, and coherent data flow.
sections.hint: Design from data flow first: one owner for shared state, props down, callbacks up, local state kept local, repeated UI extracted once, and composition where the inner structure genuinely varies.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Component architecture is not about choosing a particular number of files. It is about organizing responsibility and data flow so the application remains understandable and changeable. A strong architecture gives shared state one clear owner, keeps local UI state local, passes data down through props, communicates updates through callbacks, composes flexible structure, and extracts genuine repetition into reusable components.

The architecture is evaluated by both functionality and code quality, with particular attention to whether the hierarchy follows actual responsibilities and data flow instead of merely mirroring the screen's visual arrangement.

title: Why Applications Need Routing
description: Understand why multi-view React applications need real client-side routes, how URLs map to views without a full page reload, and why toggling components with local state is not a substitute for routing.
mastery: The learner can explain what client-side routing provides, distinguish route changes from local UI toggles, and explain why URLs, browser history, back/forward navigation, refresh behavior, and shareable links matter in a multi-view application.
learningObjectives: Explain why multi-view applications need routing.
Explain client-side routing as mapping URLs to application views without a full page reload.
Distinguish a route from a local UI state toggle.
Explain why meaningful URLs matter for navigation and sharing.
Explain how browser back and forward behavior depends on navigation history.
Recognize when an application should use routes instead of conditional component state.
Explain the role of a router at a conceptual level without implementing route configuration yet.

prerequisites.note: The Plan Book specifies completion of Module 3-3 as the prerequisite for this lesson.

sections.text: A Bigger React App Has More Than One View

The component-architecture module focused on building and organizing a single application interface. Real applications often have several distinct views: a dashboard, a lesson detail page, settings, an account page, and so on.
The application now needs a way to connect those views to URLs.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Routing maps a URL to a view. In a client-side React application, the router can change which view is rendered without requiring the browser to load an entirely new document for every navigation.
Why Not Just Use State?

sections.title: A tempting approach

sections.text: This can switch views, but the current view only exists as component state. The browser URL does not necessarily describe where the user is.
The Problems With State-Only Pages

sections.title: State-only navigation
sections.code:
User clicks Settings
        ↓
page = 'settings'
        ↓
Settings renders

But the URL may still be:
/dashboard

sections.text: Now the visible application state and the address bar disagree.
URLs Are Part of the Application's State

sections.title: Meaningful URL
sections.code:
/dashboard
→ Dashboard view

/lessons
→ Lesson list

/lessons/42
→ Lesson 42

/settings
→ Settings

sections.text: A meaningful URL lets the application represent the current location in a way the browser, user, and other systems can understand.
The Back Button Matters

sections.title: Navigation history
sections.code:
/dashboard
    ↓
/lessons
    ↓
/lessons/42

Browser Back
    ↓
/lessons

Browser Back
    ↓
/dashboard

sections.text: A routing system integrates navigation with browser history so the back and forward controls correspond to the user's navigation through views.
Shareable URLs
A route gives a view an address that can be copied, bookmarked, opened in a new tab, or shared with someone else.

sections.title: State-only view
sections.code:
Copy this:
https://example.com

Recipient may only see the default view.

sections.title: Routed view
sections.code:
Copy this:
https://example.com/lessons/42

The URL itself identifies the requested view.

sections.text: Client-Side Routing vs Full Page Navigation

Traditional browser navigation can request a new document from the server. Client-side routing allows a JavaScript application to respond to navigation and render the appropriate view without rebuilding the entire document for every internal route transition.

sections.title: Conceptual difference
sections.code:
Traditional document navigation
URL change
→ server/document request
→ new document
→ browser loads page

Client-side route transition
URL change
→ router identifies route
→ React renders matching view
→ existing application remains active

sections.text: The key idea is not that the server disappears. The important distinction is how an already-running application handles internal navigation.
A Router Creates the Mapping

sections.title: Conceptual route table
sections.code:
URL pattern          View
────────────────────────────
/                    Home
/dashboard            Dashboard
/lessons              LessonList
/settings             Settings

sections.text: A router turns this conceptual mapping into application behavior. Later lessons will implement the actual route configuration and navigation APIs.
A Route Is Not the Same as a Component
A component defines a reusable UI unit. A route defines how a URL maps to a view in the application.

sections.title: Different concerns
sections.code:
Component
→ UI architecture
→ reusable boundaries

Route
→ URL → view mapping
→ navigation structure

sections.text: A Route Can Render a Component Tree

sections.title: Route to hierarchy
sections.code:
/lessons
    ↓
LessonPage
├── SearchControls
├── LessonList
└── ProgressSummary

sections.text: Routing determines which top-level view is active. The component architecture inside that view still follows the patterns from Module 3-3.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Don't build multiple pages as toggled state
sections.text: Switching between Dashboard and Settings with local component state does not give you real route semantics. Without routing, the URL, browser history, refresh behavior, and shareable location can become disconnected from the visible view.
When a Toggle Is Still the Right Tool

sections.title: Local UI state
sections.code:
Accordion open/closed
Modal visible/hidden
Card expanded/collapsed
Dropdown open/closed

These are UI states, not application routes.

sections.text: Routing should not replace ordinary component state. Use local state for UI conditions that do not need their own navigable URL.
A Useful Decision Test

sections.title: Ask this question
sections.code:
Should this view have its own meaningful URL
that a user could bookmark, share, refresh, or revisit?

Yes
→ likely a route

No
→ likely local UI state

sections.text: Examples

sections.title: Likely routes
sections.code:
Account settings
Course overview
Lesson detail
Search results
Admin dashboard

sections.title: Likely local state
sections.code:
Show details
Open modal
Selected tab inside a self-contained widget
Expanded card
Temporary tooltip

sections.text: Think About Refresh

sections.title: A route survives navigation
sections.code:
User is viewing:
/lessons/42

User refreshes

The application can read the URL
and know which view should be shown.

sections.text: A state-only page switch can lose its meaning when the application reloads because the component state is recreated.
Think About Shareability
Ask whether another person can receive a URL and arrive at the same meaningful view. This is one of the clearest practical reasons to model major views as routes.
Think About Browser History
Users expect Back to take them through meaningful navigation. A route system gives the application a structured relationship with the browser's history.
Flashcard Review

sections.title: Recall
sections.code:
Q: What does client-side routing map?
A: URLs to application views.

Q: Why not use state to represent every page?
A: The URL/history/shareability semantics would be missing.

Q: What should local UI state represent?
A: Temporary or component-level UI conditions that do not need their own URL.

Q: What does a route provide?
A: A navigable URL-to-view mapping.

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson implements actual routes and navigation components/hooks. Dynamic route parameters and nested routes follow after that.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is conceptual. Do not memorize router APIs yet. First understand why routing exists and how it differs from ordinary component state.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why does a React application need routing?' A strong answer is: 'Routing connects meaningful URLs to views, so users can navigate between application views while preserving browser history, refresh behavior, and shareable URLs. Client-side routing can perform those internal transitions without requiring a full document reload each time.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why not just store the current page in useState?' Because that makes the visible page independent from the URL. Back/forward behavior, bookmarks, refreshes, and shareable links become difficult or incorrect.
Another follow-up is: 'Should every UI state become a route?' No. Modals, expanded cards, dropdowns, and similar local UI states generally do not need their own navigable URL.
Reflect
Take the Lesson Workspace from the previous module. Which views deserve their own URLs? Which interactions should remain component state? Explain what a user should be able to bookmark.
A useful route tells you what view the user is in. Use local state for temporary UI behavior that does not need to become a navigable location.

sections.label: Pass the recall check by correctly explaining client-side routing, distinguishing routes from local UI state, and explaining why URL/history/shareability matter.
sections.hint: Ask: should this state have a meaningful URL that a user can bookmark, refresh, revisit, or share?

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Routing gives important application views meaningful URLs and connects those URLs to views. Client-side routing can handle internal navigation without a full page reload, while preserving useful browser navigation semantics. Do not model every page as a local state toggle: major navigable views need routes, while temporary component UI such as expanded cards and modals usually remains ordinary state.

exercises.title: Route or Local State?
exercises.brief: Classify common UI transitions as routes or local UI state and justify each decision from URL, sharing, refresh, and history requirements.

quiz.question: What does client-side routing conceptually provide?
options: A mapping between URLs and application views.
A replacement for component state.
A way to remove browser history.
A CSS layout system.
quiz.explanation: Routing connects navigable URL locations to the appropriate application views.

quiz.question: Why is using local state as the only representation of multiple application pages problematic?
options: The page cannot contain JSX.
The URL, history, refresh behavior, and visible view can become disconnected.
React cannot render more than one component.
State automatically disables navigation.
quiz.explanation: Page-level navigation needs meaningful URL and browser-history semantics that a private component state value does not provide by itself.

quiz.question: Which is more likely to remain local UI state rather than become a route?
options: A lesson detail page.
Account Settings.
Whether a card's details are expanded.
A shareable search-results view.
quiz.explanation: An expanded/collapsed card is generally temporary component UI and does not need its own navigable URL.

summary: Routing connects meaningful URLs to application views. It lets a React application behave like a multi-view application while preserving browser navigation concepts such as history, back/forward behavior, refreshable locations, and shareable URLs. Local component state is still appropriate for temporary UI behavior such as modals and expanded cards. The key decision is whether a view deserves its own meaningful navigable URL.
