Why is toggling pages with local state not a replacement for routing?
Why do URLs matter in an application?
How does routing relate to browser back and forward?
What makes a UI state a good candidate for a route?
What kinds of UI should remain local state?
What is the difference between a route and a component?

title: Routes and Navigation
description: Implement client-side routes and navigation so users can move between views without unnecessary full page reloads, using router links and navigation APIs.
mastery: The learner can define basic application routes, navigate between them with router-aware links, trigger navigation programmatically when appropriate, and explain why internal application navigation should not rely on ordinary document links.
learningObjectives: Define basic client-side routes for React views.
Navigate between routes using router-aware Link components.
Use a navigation hook such as useNavigate for programmatic navigation.
Observe how the URL changes as the application view changes.
Distinguish internal router navigation from ordinary browser document navigation.
Choose Link for declarative navigation and programmatic navigation when navigation follows an action.
Handle a basic route that does not match a known path.

sections.text: Turn the Routing Idea Into Code
The previous lesson established why routing exists. Now implement the basic pieces: route definitions and navigation between them.
The exact router API depends on the routing library and version, but the architectural idea remains the same: map URL paths to views and provide navigation that works with that routing system.
Define Routes

sections.title: Basic route configuration

sections.text: Each Route connects a URL path to the element that should render when that path matches.
Navigate With Link

sections.title: Router-aware navigation

sections.text: Link communicates that this is application navigation handled by the router rather than an ordinary document navigation.
The Important Difference: Link vs a

sections.title: Router navigation
sections.code: <Link to="/lessons">Lessons</Link>

sections.title: Ordinary document link
sections.code: Lessons

sections.text: For internal routes in a router-based single-page application, use the router's navigation mechanism. An ordinary anchor can trigger a full document navigation instead of keeping the current client-side application running.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not use a plain <a href> for ordinary internal router navigation when the application expects client-side route transitions. Use the router-aware Link component.
Interactive Practice: Click Through the Routes

sections.title: Routes and Navigation Playground
sections.instructions: Wire the supplied navigation so Home, Lessons, and Settings render at their routes. Change the links and click between views. Observe the URL after each navigation and compare router Link behavior with a plain anchor.

sections.text: Programmatic Navigation

sections.title: Navigate after an action

sections.text: useNavigate is useful when navigation is a consequence of an event or application action rather than a simple visible destination link.
Link vs useNavigate

sections.title: Choose deliberately
sections.code:
Visible destination in the UI
→ Link

Navigation after an action
→ useNavigate

Example:
'Open Settings'
→ Link

'Save successful, now go to Lessons'
→ useNavigate

sections.text: Drill 1: Repair Internal Navigation

sections.title: Navigation Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The app uses plain anchors for internal pages. Replace them with router-aware navigation and make the Save button navigate programmatically to the lesson list after the action completes.

sections.text: Relative and Absolute Destinations

sections.title: Path-based destination
sections.code: <Link to="/lessons">Lessons</Link>

sections.text: The route destination identifies where the application should navigate. More advanced relative routing will appear with nested routes later.
Unknown Routes

sections.title: Basic fallback route
sections.code:
<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
  <Route path="/lessons" element={<Lessons />} />
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>

sections.text: A fallback route gives the application a deliberate response when the requested path does not match one of the known routes.
Observe the Browser URL

sections.title: Navigation should have visible location semantics
sections.code:
Click Lessons
→ URL becomes /lessons
→ Lessons view renders

Click Settings
→ URL becomes /settings
→ Settings view renders

sections.text: The address bar is now part of the application experience instead of merely reflecting whichever document happened to load.
Drill 2: Add the Missing Route

sections.title: Route Configuration Drill
sections.instructions: The navigation contains a link to /lessons/featured, but the application has no matching route. Add the correct route and a fallback route. Then verify each navigation target renders the expected view.

sections.text: Routing Does Not Replace Components
Each route still renders a component tree. The router determines which high-level view is active; the component architecture inside that view still follows the principles from Module 3-3.

sections.title: Two layers
sections.code:
Routing layer
→ Which view belongs at this URL?

Component layer
→ How is that view built?

sections.text: Navigation Is Part of User Flow

sections.title: Example flow
sections.code:
Lessons
  ↓ click
Lesson Details
  ↓ Save
Lessons
  ↓ click
Settings

sections.text: Some transitions are links the user can choose directly. Others happen after actions. Use the navigation mechanism that expresses the user flow clearly.
What's Being Deferred?
Dynamic route parameters are next. Nested routes and shared layouts follow after that. Query parameters and navigation state are intentionally deferred to a later lesson.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is about basic route definitions and navigation. Do not solve dynamic route data loading or complex nested layouts yet.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you navigate inside a React Router application?' A strong answer is: 'I define the routes, use Link for normal user-facing navigation, and use useNavigate when navigation needs to happen programmatically after an action.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why not use a normal anchor?' For internal router navigation, the router-aware Link preserves the client-side routing model instead of forcing unnecessary document navigation.
Another follow-up is: 'When would you use useNavigate?' When navigation is a consequence of application logic, such as redirecting after a successful save or login.
Reflect
Take the Lesson Workspace from Module 3-3. Which links should be declarative Link components? Which user actions might need programmatic navigation after the action succeeds?

sections.title: Let the navigation mechanism express intent

sections.text: A visible destination is naturally a Link. A navigation caused by an action is naturally programmatic. Both update the route; they simply express different user-flow intentions.

sections.label: Complete the live routing Playground and both navigation drills. The learner must define working routes, navigate through Link without full document navigation, and use programmatic navigation for an action-driven redirect.
sections.hint: Internal destination link → Link. Navigation caused by an application action → useNavigate.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Routes connect URL paths to React views. Router-aware Link components are used for ordinary internal navigation, while useNavigate is useful when navigation follows application logic such as a successful action. A fallback route handles unknown locations. The important architectural distinction is that routing chooses the active view from the URL, while component architecture determines how that view is built.

exercises.title: Routes and Navigation Playground
exercises.brief: Define basic routes and navigate between views while observing URL changes.

exercises.title: Navigation Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Replace internal anchors with router-aware Link navigation and add programmatic navigation after an action.

exercises.title: Route Configuration Drill
exercises.brief: Add a missing route and a not-found fallback, then verify each destination.

quiz.question: Which component is the normal choice for an internal user-facing navigation link?
options: Link from the router
A plain a element
useState
useEffect
quiz.explanation: Router-aware Link participates in client-side navigation.

quiz.question: When is useNavigate especially appropriate?
options: When navigation is a consequence of application logic or an event.
Only when rendering a heading.
Only when defining CSS.
When you want to replace every Link.
quiz.explanation: Programmatic navigation is useful after actions such as save, login, or other application events.

quiz.question: Why can a plain internal <a href> be the wrong choice in a router-based app?
options: It can trigger ordinary document navigation instead of the intended client-side route transition.
Anchors cannot contain text.
React cannot render anchors.
It prevents the URL from changing.
quiz.explanation: Router-aware navigation keeps internal navigation within the application's client-side routing model.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a fallback route such as path="*"?
options: To render a deliberate not-found view for unmatched paths.
To match only the home page.
To disable browser history.
To make every route dynamic.
quiz.explanation: A catch-all route gives the application a defined response when no other route matches.

summary: Basic routing connects URL paths to React views. Define routes, use Link for declarative internal navigation, and useNavigate when navigation follows application logic. Router-aware navigation keeps internal transitions within the client-side routing model, while a catch-all route provides a deliberate response for unknown paths. Routing selects the active view; component architecture determines how that view is built.
interviewQuestions: How do you define routes in a React application?
What is the difference between Link and useNavigate?
Why should internal navigation use router-aware links?
When is programmatic navigation appropriate?
Why might an application define a fallback route?
How does routing interact with component architecture?
What happens when a user navigates to a path that has no matching route?

title: Dynamic Routes
description: Implement routes with dynamic URL segments such as /lessons/:id, read the captured parameter inside the matched component, and handle cases where the parameter does not correspond to real data.
mastery: The learner can define a dynamic route, read its URL parameter, use that parameter to select or load the corresponding data, and render a deliberate not-found state when the parameter does not match a real item.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of a dynamic route parameter.
Define a route with a dynamic segment such as /lessons/:id.
Read a dynamic route parameter inside the rendered component.
Use a parameter to select or request the corresponding data.
Handle a parameter that does not match real data.
Distinguish a URL parameter from ordinary component props.
Navigate between dynamic URLs and observe the parameter changing live.

sections.text: One Route Pattern, Many Resources
The previous lesson used fixed routes such as /lessons and /settings. Real applications often have many resources of the same type: lesson 1, lesson 2, lesson 3, and so on.
A dynamic route lets one route pattern represent all of those individual resources.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A dynamic segment such as :id is a placeholder in the route pattern. When the URL matches, the router captures the actual value and makes it available to the route's component.
Define a Dynamic Route

sections.title: One pattern for many lesson pages
sections.code:
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';

<Routes>
  <Route path="/lessons/:id" element={<LessonDetail />} />
</Routes>

sections.text: The :id segment means that /lessons/1, /lessons/2, and /lessons/42 can all match the same route pattern.

sections.title: Pattern matching
sections.code:
Route pattern
/lessons/:id

URLs
/lessons/1     → id = 1
/lessons/2     → id = 2
/lessons/42    → id = 42

sections.text: Read the Route Parameter

sections.title: useParams

sections.text: The parameter comes from the URL, not from a normal parent-to-child prop. The router supplies it through its route context.
Use the Parameter to Find Data

sections.title: Find a lesson by id

sections.text: The URL parameter is a string, so converting or comparing IDs deliberately avoids accidental type mismatches.
The Most Important Branch: Not Found

sections.title: Valid and invalid parameters
sections.code:
/lessons/2
→ matching lesson found
→ render lesson detail

/lessons/999
→ no matching lesson
→ render not-found state

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not assume that every dynamic parameter represents valid data. A URL can be syntactically valid while pointing to a resource that does not exist.
Interactive Practice: Change the URL

sections.title: Dynamic Route Playground
sections.instructions: Navigate between /lessons/1, /lessons/2, /lessons/3, and an unknown lesson ID. Predict which lesson title should appear before each navigation and verify the not-found behavior for an unknown ID.

sections.text: Dynamic Routes Turn URLs Into Data

sections.title: URL parameter as input
sections.code:
URL
/lessons/42
     ↓
router
     ↓
id = "42"
     ↓
select/load lesson 42
     ↓
render detail

sections.text: This is what makes dynamic routes useful for data-driven pages: the URL identifies which resource the view should display.
Dynamic Route Parameters Can Drive Data Fetching

sections.title: Conceptual API pattern

sections.text: The next data-loading patterns can combine route parameters with effects so a route such as /lessons/42 loads lesson 42. The important concept here is that the route parameter identifies the requested resource.
Drill 1: Repair the Missing Not-Found Case

sections.title: Dynamic Route Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The route reads the id and searches the lesson collection, but crashes or renders an invalid value when no lesson exists. Add a deliberate not-found branch, then test a valid and invalid URL.

sections.text: Route Parameter vs Query Parameter

sections.title: Different URL roles
sections.code:
Path parameter
/lessons/42
→ identifies a specific lesson

Query parameter
/lessons?search=react
→ modifies or filters a collection view

sections.text: Do not use a path parameter when the value is really a filtering or optional query. The distinction becomes especially useful when building search and filtering features.
Nested Dynamic Segments

sections.title: Conceptual route
sections.code:
/courses/:courseId/lessons/:lessonId

courseId → identifies the course
lessonId → identifies the lesson

sections.text: More complex dynamic route structures become useful when the URL itself expresses resource relationships. Nested route configuration comes next.
Do Not Trust the Parameter Type
Route parameters arrive through the URL and should be treated as external input. If your application expects a numeric ID, validate or normalize it before using it as numeric data.

sections.title: Normalize a numeric id

sections.text: Drill 2: Validate the Parameter

sections.title: Dynamic Parameter Drill
sections.instructions: The application expects numeric lesson IDs. Add validation for the route parameter and distinguish an invalid ID format from a valid-looking ID that simply does not match a lesson.

sections.text: Dynamic Route Debugging

sections.title: When the detail page is wrong
sections.code:
1. What exact URL did the browser request?
2. Did the route pattern match?
3. What parameter value was captured?
4. Is the parameter the expected type/format?
5. Does the data source contain a matching item?
6. Is the not-found branch handled deliberately?

sections.text: This separates routing errors from data lookup errors. A route can match correctly even when its parameter points to data that does not exist.
What's Being Deferred?
Nested routes are next. They will show how a shared layout can remain mounted while a dynamic child view changes inside it.
Loading data directly from the route parameter will build on the fetching patterns from Module 3-2 rather than being introduced as a new architectural concept here.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on capturing and interpreting dynamic URL parameters. Shared layouts and nested route composition come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a dynamic route?' A strong answer is: 'It is a route pattern containing a dynamic segment, such as /lessons/:id, where the router captures the actual URL value so the application can identify which resource to display.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What happens if /lessons/999 does not exist?' The route can still match, but the application must handle the missing resource deliberately, for example with a not-found state.
Another follow-up is: 'Is the route parameter a number automatically?' No. URL parameters arrive from the URL and should be treated as strings until the application validates or converts them.
Reflect

Design a lesson-detail URL for your projects. What information should be encoded in the path, and what should remain a query parameter? What should happen when someone manually changes the URL to an ID that does not exist?

sections.title: The URL identifies the resource; the UI handles the outcome

sections.text: A dynamic route can successfully capture an ID, but that does not guarantee the requested resource exists. Routing and data validation are separate responsibilities.

sections.label: Complete the dynamic-route Playground and both drills. The learner must navigate between different dynamic URLs, correctly read the route parameter, render matching data, and distinguish invalid parameters from valid-but-missing resources.
sections.hint: Route pattern captures the parameter. Normalize/validate it, look up the data, and handle no match deliberately.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Dynamic routes use placeholders such as :id to represent many related URLs with one route definition. The router captures the actual value, which the matched component can use to select or load the appropriate resource. Parameters arrive from the URL and should be validated or normalized when necessary. A matching route does not guarantee matching data, so a deliberate not-found state is part of a robust dynamic route.

exercises.title: Dynamic Route Playground
exercises.brief: Navigate between different dynamic lesson URLs and observe the captured parameter and displayed lesson.

exercises.title: Dynamic Route Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Add a deliberate not-found branch for a dynamic parameter that does not correspond to real data.

exercises.title: Dynamic Parameter Drill
exercises.brief: Validate numeric route parameters and distinguish invalid formatting from valid-but-missing resources.

quiz.question: What does :id represent in /lessons/:id?
options: A fixed URL segment.
A dynamic route parameter captured from the URL.
A query parameter.
A React state variable.
quiz.explanation: The :id segment is a placeholder whose actual value comes from the matched URL.

quiz.question: What should the application do when /lessons/999 matches the dynamic route but lesson 999 does not exist?
options: Assume the data exists.
Render a deliberate not-found state.
Create the missing lesson automatically.
Treat the route as invalid syntax.
quiz.explanation: A valid route pattern can still identify a resource that does not exist.

quiz.question: What type should you assume a route parameter has when you first read it?
options: Always number.
String from the URL.
Boolean.
Object.
quiz.explanation: Route parameters come from URL text and should be explicitly converted when numeric data is required.

summary: Dynamic routes let one route pattern represent many resource-specific URLs, such as /lessons/:id. The router captures the actual URL parameter, and the matched component can use it to select or load the relevant data. Parameters should be treated as URL input and normalized when necessary. A dynamic route can match even when the requested resource does not exist, so a deliberate not-found outcome must be handled.

title: Nested Routes
description: Build nested routes so a shared layout such as navigation or a sidebar stays mounted while child route content changes inside it.
mastery: The learner can define a parent route with nested child routes, render shared layout UI once, use an outlet for child content, and explain why nested routing is preferable to duplicating the same layout in every route.
learningObjectives: Explain why nested routes are useful for shared application layouts.
Define child routes under a parent route.
Render shared layout UI once for a route group.
Use an outlet to render the currently matched child route.
Navigate between nested child routes.
Recognize when multiple routes should share a common layout.
Avoid duplicating navigation/sidebar layout markup across sibling route components.

sections.text: The Same Layout Should Not Be Copied Into Every Page
Imagine a course area with a sidebar and navigation that should remain visible while the main content changes between Overview, Lessons, and Progress.
You could copy the sidebar into all three route components. But then one shared layout exists in three places.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Nested routes let a parent route own shared layout UI while child routes provide the changing content inside that layout.
The Duplication Problem

sections.title: Duplicated layout

sections.text: The route-specific content changes, but the layout structure is repeated.
Create a Shared Layout Route

sections.title: Layout component

sections.text: The layout owns the sidebar and main content region. Outlet is the location where the active child route renders.
Nest the Routes

sections.title: Parent route with children
sections.code:
<Routes>
  <Route path="/course" element={<CourseLayout />}>
    <Route path="overview" element={<Overview />} />
    <Route path="lessons" element={<Lessons />} />
    <Route path="progress" element={<Progress />} />
  </Route>
</Routes>

sections.title: Nested route tree
sections.code:
/course
└── CourseLayout
    ├── overview
    ├── lessons
    └── progress

sections.text: When /course/lessons is active, CourseLayout renders once and the Lessons component appears inside its Outlet.
The Outlet Is the Child-Route Slot

sections.title: Think of Outlet as a slot

sections.text: The child route decides what appears inside that slot.
Interactive Practice: Swap the Child View

sections.title: Nested Routes Playground
sections.instructions: Complete the shared CourseLayout and nested routes. Navigate between Overview, Lessons, and Progress and observe that the layout stays shared while only the child content changes.

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not duplicate the shared layout
sections.text: If multiple route views use the same navigation, sidebar, or shell, do not copy that markup into every route component. Put the shared UI in a parent layout and render the changing child view through Outlet.
Nested Paths Express Structure

sections.title: URL hierarchy
sections.code:
/course
/course/overview
/course/lessons
/course/progress

sections.text: The URL structure and component structure can communicate the same relationship: these are views inside a common course area.
Drill 1: Refactor Duplicated Layout

sections.title: Nested Layout Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The three route components each duplicate the same sidebar. Refactor the routes so one CourseLayout owns the sidebar and Outlet renders the active child content. The visible behavior should remain equivalent.

sections.text: Nested Routes and Dynamic Segments

sections.title: A nested dynamic route
sections.code:
<Route path="/courses/:courseId" element={<CourseLayout />}>
  <Route path="lessons/:lessonId" element={<LessonDetail />} />
</Route>

sections.text: Nested routes can combine with dynamic route parameters. The layout can provide the course shell while the child identifies the specific lesson.

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
/courses/7/lessons/42

courseId = 7
lessonId = 42

CourseLayout
    ↓
LessonDetail

sections.text: Nested Layouts Can Be Multiple Levels Deep

sections.title: Conceptual hierarchy
sections.code:
ApplicationLayout
└── CourseLayout
    └── LessonLayout
        └── LessonDetail

sections.text: This lets different levels of the application provide different shared UI without repeating it in every leaf route.
Drill 2: Add a Nested Child

sections.title: Nested Dynamic Route Drill
sections.instructions: Extend the CourseLayout with a dynamic lesson child route. The course layout should remain visible while /course/lessons/:lessonId displays the selected lesson inside Outlet.

sections.text: Nested Routes Reduce Layout Duplication

sections.title: Before
sections.code:
Overview
└── Sidebar

Lessons
└── Sidebar

Progress
└── Sidebar

sections.title: After
sections.code:
CourseLayout
├── Sidebar
└── Outlet
    ├── Overview
    ├── Lessons
    └── Progress

sections.text: There is now one implementation of the shared layout.
The Parent Route Owns the Shell
A useful way to reason about nested routes is that the parent route owns the persistent shell while child routes own the changing view.

sections.title: Responsibility
sections.code:
CourseLayout
→ navigation
→ sidebar
→ shared controls
→ Outlet

Child route
→ page-specific content

sections.text: Do Not Put Everything Into One Layout
Nested routes are useful when UI actually persists across related views. Do not create nested layouts merely to make the route tree look sophisticated.
Navigation Paths Can Be Relative

sections.title: Inside /course
sections.code:
<Link to="lessons">Lessons</Link>
<Link to="progress">Progress</Link>

sections.text: Relative navigation can make child route definitions easier to read because they express destinations relative to the parent route.
Nested Route Debugging

sections.title: When child content does not appear
sections.code:
1. Does the parent route match?
2. Is the child route nested under that parent?
3. Does the parent render <Outlet />?
4. Does the Link target the correct nested path?
5. Does the child route match the URL?

sections.text: A missing Outlet is one of the most common conceptual mistakes: the child route may match correctly but have nowhere inside the parent layout to render.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson covers navigation state such as the current location and query parameters. More advanced routing concerns such as data routers and route-level loading are outside this lesson.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Nested routing solves shared layouts. The parent provides persistent UI; Outlet provides the insertion point for child route content.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why use nested routes?' A strong answer is: 'They let a parent route render shared UI such as navigation or a sidebar while child routes render the changing content inside an Outlet, avoiding duplicated layouts.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is Outlet?' It is the location in a parent route's element where the currently matched child route renders.
Another follow-up is: 'What happens if the parent has nested routes but no Outlet?' The parent layout can render, but the child route has no place inside it to render its element.
Reflect
Think about a course application with a persistent course sidebar and several child pages. Which elements should live in the course layout, and which should change inside Outlet?
When several related routes share the same shell, make the shell the parent route and let the child route occupy the Outlet.

sections.label: Complete the nested-routes Playground and both drills. The learner must keep shared layout UI in one parent, render child content through Outlet, and implement a nested dynamic lesson route.
sections.hint: Shared shell → parent route. Changing page content → child route. Child content appears through Outlet.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Nested routes let a parent route own persistent layout UI while child routes provide changing content through Outlet. This removes duplicated navigation/sidebar/layout markup and mirrors the information architecture of related views. Nested routes can also contain dynamic segments, allowing structures such as /courses/:courseId/lessons/:lessonId.

quiz.question: Why are nested routes useful?
options: They let shared layout UI persist while child route content changes.
They replace all React components.
They prevent URLs from changing.
They make every route global state.
quiz.explanation: Nested routes are designed for shared parent layouts with changing child views.

quiz.question: What does Outlet do?
options: It stores route parameters.
It provides the location where the matched child route renders inside the parent.
It navigates back in browser history.
It replaces Link.
quiz.explanation: Outlet is the insertion point for nested child-route content.

quiz.question: What is the architectural mistake this lesson is specifically trying to prevent?
options: Using dynamic route parameters.
Duplicating shared layout UI in every route instead of nesting routes under one layout.
Using Link components.
Rendering child components.
quiz.explanation: A shared parent layout removes duplicated navigation/sidebar/shell code.

summary: Nested routing models shared application shells cleanly. A parent route renders persistent navigation, sidebar, or other layout UI and places an Outlet where the active child route should appear. Child routes can be ordinary or dynamic. This avoids duplicating the same layout in every page and makes the route hierarchy reflect the application's information architecture.

title: Navigation State
description: Read navigation information directly from the router, including the current location and query parameters, and use that information to drive UI without creating unnecessary duplicate local state.
mastery: The learner can read the current location and query parameters from the router, use them to derive UI, distinguish URL-derived state from component-owned state, and avoid duplicating navigation information in local state.
learningObjectives: Explain what navigation state represents in a routed React application.
Read the current location from the router.
Read query parameters from the URL.
Use URL-derived values directly to drive rendering or filtering.
Explain the difference between route state and local component state.
Recognize when navigation information should remain in the URL instead of duplicated React state.
Update navigation state through router navigation rather than maintaining a second local source of truth.
Explain why query parameters are useful for shareable/filterable application views.

sections.text: The URL Can Already Store Important State
A routed application has more than just path segments. The browser location also includes query parameters and navigation history. These values can describe what the user is currently looking at.
The important architecture question is whether that information should be read directly from the router or copied into another piece of React state.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Navigation state describes the application's current location: pathname, search/query parameters, and history-related navigation context. When a value already lives in the URL, prefer reading it from the router rather than creating an unnecessary duplicate source of truth.
Read the Current Location

sections.title: useLocation

sections.text: The location object describes the current router location. The pathname is the path portion of the URL.
Query Parameters

sections.title: Example URL
sections.code:
/lessons?search=react&status=complete

pathname
→ /lessons

search/query string
→ ?search=react&status=complete

sections.text: Query parameters are useful for filters, searches, sorting, pagination, and other view configuration that should be represented in the URL.

sections.title: Read query parameters

sections.text: URL-Driven Filtering

sections.title: Derive the filter from the URL

sections.text: Now the URL itself identifies the current search. A user can refresh or share the URL and the application still knows which filter should be active.
The Common Anti-Pattern

sections.title: Duplicating URL state

sections.text: Unless the local state represents a deliberate editable draft, this creates two representations of the same conceptual navigation value.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not copy navigation-derived data into local state simply because the component needs to read it. The router is already the source of truth for the current URL.
Navigation State Can Be Updated Through Navigation

sections.title: Update query parameters

sections.text: The URL changes, the router updates, and components reading the query parameter receive the new navigation state.
Interactive Practice: Drive the UI From the URL

sections.title: Navigation State Playground
sections.instructions: Modify the query parameter and observe the rendered filter state. Then change the filter through the UI and watch the URL update. Refresh or navigate directly to another query URL and verify the UI follows the URL.

sections.text: Pathname Can Also Drive the UI

sections.title: Read the current path

sections.text: In most cases route matching should determine which route component renders, but a component may still need the current location for UI such as breadcrumbs, analytics context, or active navigation styling.
Navigation State vs Component State

sections.title: Ask where the information lives
sections.code:
URL path / query
→ navigation state
→ read from the router

Temporary local UI condition
→ component state
→ useState

sections.text: The two can work together, but they should not accidentally represent the same conceptual value.
A Useful URL Design

sections.title: Search view
sections.code:
/lessons?search=react&status=complete

Path
→ identifies the collection view

search
→ search filter

status
→ completion filter

sections.text: Keeping view configuration in the URL makes that state inspectable, bookmarkable, and shareable.
Drill 1: Remove Duplicate Navigation State

sections.title: Navigation State Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The component copies the search query from the URL into local state and can therefore drift out of sync. Repair it so the URL remains the source of truth and the list follows the URL directly.

sections.text: History Is Navigation State Too

Navigation changes create browser history entries. Users can move backward and forward through previous locations, so application navigation should respect that history rather than maintaining a disconnected local version of the current location.

sections.title: History sequence
sections.code:
/lessons
    ↓
/lessons?search=react
    ↓
/lessons?search=hooks

Back
→ /lessons?search=react

sections.text: When the URL is the source of truth for the filter, moving backward in history naturally restores the previous filter value.
Navigation State Can Make UI Shareable

sections.title: Share this
sections.code:
https://example.com/lessons?search=hooks

Recipient opens it
→ router reads the same URL
→ UI shows the same search configuration

sections.text: This is one of the biggest practical reasons to keep meaningful navigation state in the URL.
When Local State Is Still Appropriate

sections.title: Local draft vs committed URL state

sections.text: A local draft can be valid if it intentionally differs from the committed navigation state. The important distinction is that the two values have different meanings.
Drill 2: Decide What Belongs in the URL

sections.text: Navigation State Debugging

sections.title: When URL and UI disagree
sections.code:
1. What does the address bar currently contain?
2. Is the component reading the router location/query?
3. Is there a second local copy of that value?
4. Which value is the UI actually rendering?
5. Does navigation update the URL or only local state?
6. Does browser Back restore the expected UI?

sections.text: The first debugging question should be whether the router and the component agree about the current location.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson is the module capstone: a multi-page React application combining nested routes, dynamic parameters, and shared layout.
More advanced URL serialization, data routers, and sophisticated history manipulation are intentionally deferred.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Use navigation state for information that is meaningfully part of the current location. Keep temporary local UI state local, and derive values rather than duplicating them.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is navigation state?' A strong answer is: 'It is information associated with the current router location, such as the pathname, query parameters, and navigation history context. Components can read it directly from the router.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why shouldn't you copy query parameters into local state?' Because the URL already represents the navigation state. Copying it creates a second source of truth that can become stale or require synchronization effects.
Another follow-up is: 'When should a filter belong in the URL?' When the filter is meaningful to the location and users benefit from refreshable, bookmarkable, shareable state.
Reflect
Take the lesson search feature from earlier. Which parts of the search experience should be reflected in the URL? Which parts should remain temporary local state?

sections.title: Let the URL be the source of truth for navigation

sections.text: When a value defines where the user is or how that location is configured, read it from the router rather than creating another local copy.

sections.label: Complete the navigation-state Playground, repair drill, and decision drill. The learner must read and update query state through the router, keep the URL as the source of truth, and distinguish navigation state from local UI state.
sections.hint: URL-derived value → read it from the router. Temporary component behavior → local state. Derived value → calculate it.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Navigation state includes information such as the current pathname, query parameters, and browser navigation history. When that information already lives in the URL, the router should generally remain the source of truth. This makes filters and other meaningful view configuration refreshable, bookmarkable, shareable, and naturally compatible with browser Back/Forward behavior. Do not duplicate navigation-derived values in local state unless the local value intentionally represents a different concept, such as an editable draft.

quiz.question: What is a good source of truth for a search filter that should be shareable?
options: A URL query parameter.
A hidden DOM property.
A separate duplicate state value with no URL.
A random child component's local state.
quiz.explanation: Meaningful navigation configuration belongs in the URL when users benefit from sharing and restoring it.

quiz.question: Why can copying a query parameter into local state be problematic?
options: It creates a second representation that can drift from the URL.
Query parameters cannot contain strings.
React cannot read URLs.
Local state always disappears before rendering.
quiz.explanation: Duplicating navigation state can create synchronization problems.

quiz.question: Which value is most likely local component state?
options: The current pathname.
The search query in a shareable URL.
Whether a confirmation modal is currently open.
The current dynamic route id.
quiz.explanation: A modal's open state is temporary component UI rather than navigation state.

summary: Navigation state represents information tied to the current router location, including pathname and query parameters. When a value is already encoded in the URL, read it directly from the router and update it through navigation rather than maintaining a duplicate local source of truth. This makes meaningful view configuration shareable, refreshable, and compatible with browser history. Temporary UI behavior remains local state, while calculated values remain derived.

title: Build a Multi-Page React App
description: Build a complete multi-page React application that combines nested routes, dynamic parameters, shared layouts, and meaningful application information architecture.
mastery: The learner can design and implement a multi-page React application with nested routes, dynamic parameters, shared layouts, and navigation state, while keeping the route structure aligned with the application's information architecture.
learningObjectives: Design a route hierarchy for a multi-page React application.
Implement a shared layout with nested child routes.
Use dynamic route parameters for resource-specific views.
Use router-aware navigation between major application views.
Handle missing dynamic resources deliberately.
Use navigation state such as query parameters where appropriate.
Keep shared layout UI out of individual leaf routes.
Explain why the route hierarchy represents the application's information architecture.
Test route behavior including direct URL entry, navigation, back/forward, dynamic parameters, and not-found cases.

sections.text: The Routing Module Capstone

You have now learned why applications need routing, how to define routes and navigate between them, how dynamic parameters identify specific resources, how nested routes provide shared layouts, and how navigation state lives in the URL.
Now build a complete multi-page React application using those ideas together.

sections.title: This is a build brief
sections.text: There is no new routing theory to memorize. Use the previous lessons to design and implement the application's route hierarchy.
Project Brief: Forge Academy

Build a multi-page Forge Academy application where users can browse courses, enter a course workspace, inspect individual lessons, and navigate among related course views without duplicating the shared course layout.

sections.title: Required product views
sections.code:
Home

Courses

Course workspace
→ Overview
→ Lessons

Lesson detail

Not found

sections.text: Required Route Information Architecture

sections.title: Recommended route hierarchy
sections.code:
/                         → Home
/courses                  → CourseList
/courses/:courseId        → CourseLayout
/courses/:courseId/overview → Overview
/courses/:courseId/lessons  → LessonList
/courses/:courseId/progress → Progress
/courses/:courseId/lessons/:lessonId → LessonDetail
*                         → NotFound

sections.text: This hierarchy is a starting point derived from the feature requirements. Your implementation may use equivalent route structures, but the relationships must remain meaningful.
The Shared Course Layout

sections.title: Persistent course shell
sections.code:
/courses/:courseId
└── CourseLayout
    ├── Course navigation
    ├── Course heading/context
    └── Outlet
        ├── Overview
        ├── LessonList
        └── Progress

sections.text: The course layout should not be duplicated in each child route. It owns the shared structure and provides the Outlet for the current child view.
Dynamic Course and Lesson Identity

sections.title: Resource-specific URLs
sections.code:
/courses/react
→ courseId = react

/courses/react/lessons/props
→ courseId = react
→ lessonId = props

sections.text: Root-Cause Reflection
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How did you design the route structure?' A strong answer is: 'I started with the application's information architecture: courses are a collection, a course is a resource, and lessons belong within that course. I represented those relationships in the URL hierarchy and used a shared course layout for the child views.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why nested routes instead of putting everything at the top level?' Because the course context and layout are shared by Overview, Lessons, and Progress, so nesting models that relationship and avoids duplicated layout code.

Another follow-up is: 'What happens with an invalid course or lesson ID?' The route pattern can match, but the data lookup must produce a deliberate not-found outcome rather than crashing or rendering undefined data.
Reflect

Which route in your application carries the most information? Does its URL communicate the resource hierarchy clearly enough that another developer could understand the product structure without opening the code?

You have now moved from basic route concepts to a working multi-page architecture: route definitions, navigation, dynamic resources, nested layouts, navigation state, and a complete application hierarchy.

sections.label: Submit the Multi-Page React App for manual/rubric evaluation. The project must meet the functional requirements for top-level routes, nested routes, dynamic parameters, shared layout, navigation, and not-found handling, while the route hierarchy must reflect the application's information architecture.
sections.hint: Design the URL structure first. Then make the component tree and nested layouts follow that structure. Shared shell → parent route; resource identity → dynamic parameter; changing child view → Outlet.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A multi-page React application should have a route hierarchy that reflects the product's information architecture. Nested routes keep shared layouts in one parent, dynamic parameters identify specific resources, router-aware navigation handles internal transitions, and deliberate not-found states handle missing resources. The capstone is successful when the routes make sense to a user and developer, not merely when the individual views render.

title: Local State vs Global State
description: Learn to distinguish component-local state from application-wide shared state and make the simplest state-ownership decision before reaching for a global store.
mastery: The learner can explain the difference between local and global state, identify who needs a value, and choose local state when one component or a small local subtree owns the information.
learningObjectives: Explain what local component state is.
Explain what global state is.
Distinguish component-owned state from state shared across the application.
Decide whether a value actually needs global access.
Recognize when lifting state up is sufficient instead of introducing a global store.
Explain why local state is usually the default choice.
Identify the unnecessary-complexity risk of globalizing state.

sections.text: Level 4 Starts With a State Decision

You already know useState, props, lifting state up, and component architecture. Now the question becomes larger: what should remain local to a component, and what genuinely needs to be shared across distant parts of the application?
Before learning a global state library, learn to recognize when one is actually justified.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Local state belongs to one component or a nearby subtree. Global state is shared data that needs to be accessible across distant parts of the application.
Local State

sections.title: One component owns the value

sections.text: Only this card needs to know whether its own details are expanded. Globalizing that value would add coordination without providing a real benefit.
Global State

sections.title: A value shared across distant areas
sections.code:
Application
├── Header
│   └── AccountMenu
│
├── Dashboard
│   └── Notifications
│
└── Settings
    └── AccountPreferences

All three areas need the same current user/preferences.

sections.text: When distant components need to read and update the same information, repeatedly threading that value through unrelated ancestors and children can become cumbersome. That is where a global store can become useful.
Local Does Not Mean 'Only One Line of Code'
Local state can be shared by a small subtree through normal props and lifted state. The distinction is about scope and ownership, not how much code accesses the value.

sections.title: Scope spectrum
sections.code:
One component
    ↓
Local state

Small related subtree
    ↓
Lifted state / props

Many distant areas
    ↓
Potential global state

sections.text: The Default Should Be Local
Start with the smallest scope that satisfies the feature. Move state outward only when another component actually needs it.

sections.title: Decision sequence
sections.code:
Does one component need it?
→ local state

Do nearby siblings need it?
→ consider lifting state up

Do distant unrelated branches need it?
→ consider shared/global state

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not reach for global state just because a value might someday be useful elsewhere. Globalizing local state adds complexity, increases coupling, and can expand the number of components affected by updates.
Examples of Good Local State

sections.title: Usually local
sections.code:
Modal open/closed
Accordion expanded/collapsed
Input draft
Hovered state
Temporary UI selection
Animation state

sections.text: These values usually describe behavior or presentation close to the component that owns them.
Examples That May Need Wider Scope

sections.title: Potentially shared
sections.code:
Authenticated user
Shopping cart
Application-wide theme
Shared notification state
Cross-page preferences
Feature configuration used by distant branches

sections.text: These are candidates, not automatic global-state requirements. Their actual usage determines the right scope.
Global Does Not Mean Server-Owned

State scope and data origin are separate questions. A value can originate on the server and still be represented locally or globally in the client. Conversely, a client preference can be global without coming from a server.

sections.title: Two different questions
sections.code:
Who owns the data?
→ scope: local / shared / global

Where does the data originate?
→ client / server / derived

sections.text: Architecture Before Library
A global state library does not solve an unclear state model. First decide what information needs to be shared and why. Only then should a store implementation be introduced.
Mental Model Check

sections.title: Local or Global?
sections.instructions: For each value, decide whether it should remain local, be lifted to a nearby common parent, or potentially be global. Justify the scope from the components that actually need the value.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A LessonCard's expanded/collapsed state.
Decision: __________________
Reason: _______________________

Scenario B

Decision: __________________
Reason: _______________________

Scenario C

Decision: __________________
Reason: _______________________

Scenario D
A temporary tooltip is open over one button.
Decision: __________________
Reason: _______________________

Scenario E
The application's theme is changed in Settings and affects distant pages.
Decision: __________________
Reason: _______________________

sections.text: A Real-World Analogy

Think of state ownership like information in an organization. A note needed only by one team stays in that team's workspace. Information that several nearby teams coordinate around belongs with their shared manager. Company-wide information needs a company-wide source.
You would not put every team's scratch notes into the company database just in case someone might need them someday.
What Global State Costs

sections.title: Potential costs
sections.code:
More coupling
More places that can change the data
More components affected by updates
Harder ownership decisions
More architecture to understand
More testing surface

sections.text: Global state can be useful. The point is not to avoid it forever; the point is to use it when the scope of the information justifies it.
What Global State Gives You

sections.title: Potential benefits
sections.code:
Distant components can access shared data

Shared actions can update one source of truth

Less manual prop threading across unrelated branches

Cross-page or application-wide state can remain coordinated

sections.text: The benefit appears when the shared access is a real requirement, not a hypothetical future need.
Think in Terms of Consumers

sections.title: Who reads and writes this value?
sections.code:
Component A reads
Component B reads
Component C writes
Component D writes

If those components are far apart,
a shared store may be justified.

sections.text: Quiz Yourself

sections.title: Recall
sections.code:
Q: What is local state?
A: State scoped to one component or nearby subtree.

Q: What is global state?
A: Shared state accessible across distant areas of the application.

Q: What is the default decision?
A: Keep state local until sharing requires a wider scope.

Q: When might a global store help?
A: When multiple distant components need coordinated read/write access.

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson sharpens the decision: when global state is actually needed. Zustand's concrete API is intentionally deferred to lesson-4-1-3.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is a judgment framework. Do not learn a store API yet. First become good at deciding whether the application actually needs global state.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between local and global state?' A strong answer is: 'Local state belongs to a component or small subtree and is accessed through that component hierarchy. Global state is shared across distant parts of the application and is useful when those parts need coordinated access to the same data.'

A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use global state?' Say that you first ask who needs to read and write the value. If distant, unrelated branches genuinely need coordinated access, global state may be appropriate.
Another follow-up is: 'Why not make everything global?' Because globalizing unnecessary state increases complexity, coupling, and the scope of updates.
Reflect

Take the multi-page app from Module 3-4. Which state is clearly page-local? Which state might be shared across distant routes? Which state would become harder to manage if you put it into a global store?
Do not ask 'Could this be global?' Ask 'Who actually needs to read and change this, and how far apart are those consumers?'

sections.label: Pass the recall check by correctly distinguishing local from global state and explaining why the smallest sufficient scope should be preferred.
sections.hint: One component → local. Nearby shared subtree → lift state. Distant coordinated consumers → potentially global.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Local state is scoped to one component or nearby subtree. Global state is shared across distant parts of the application. The default is to keep state as local as possible, lifting it only when nearby components need synchronized access and considering global state only when genuinely distant consumers need the same coordinated data. State scope is an architectural decision that should come before choosing a global-state library.

exercises.title: Local or Global?
exercises.brief: Classify application values as local, lifted/shared, or potentially global and justify the scope from actual consumers.

quiz.question: What is local state?
options: State accessible to every component in the application.
State scoped to one component or nearby subtree.
Only state stored on a server.
State that can never change.
quiz.explanation: Local state belongs to a component or small related subtree.

quiz.question: When is global state potentially justified?
options: When one button needs a temporary hover value.
When multiple distant components need coordinated access to the same changing data.
Whenever a string appears in JSX.
Whenever a component has more than one state variable.
quiz.explanation: Global state is useful when genuinely distant application areas need shared read/write access.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid globalizing every piece of state?
options: Global state cannot hold objects.
It adds unnecessary coupling and complexity and can broaden the scope of updates.
Global state only works on servers.
Local state cannot use props.
quiz.explanation: Globalizing unnecessary state makes the architecture harder to reason about.

summary: Local state belongs to one component or nearby subtree. Global state is shared across distant areas of an application. The correct scope depends on the actual consumers and writers of the value. Start local, lift state for nearby shared needs, and consider global state when distant parts of the application genuinely need coordinated access. This lesson is about making that decision before choosing a global-state tool.
interviewQuestions: What is local state?
What is global state?
When should state remain local?
When does lifting state up solve the problem without global state?
When is a global store justified?
Why can globalizing too much state be harmful?
How do you decide the scope of a state value?
What should you decide before choosing a global state library?

title: When Global State Is Actually Needed
description: Learn to recognize the situations where application-wide shared state is genuinely justified, and avoid globalizing state simply because it might be useful later.
mastery: The learner can identify when multiple distant components genuinely need coordinated read/write access to the same data, distinguish that situation from ordinary local or lifted state, and explain the complexity introduced by unnecessary global state.
learningObjectives: Explain when global state is genuinely needed.
Identify distant components that need coordinated access to the same changing data.
Distinguish global-state requirements from problems solved by props or lifting state up.
Recognize premature globalization of state.
Explain the tradeoff between convenient shared access and increased application complexity.
Use actual state consumers and writers as evidence when deciding state scope.

sections.text: Global State Needs a Real Reason
The previous lesson established the default: keep state local and widen its scope only when the feature actually requires it.
This lesson sharpens the decision. Global state becomes useful when multiple distant areas of the application need coordinated read/write access to the same information.

sections.title: The decision rule
sections.text: Ask who needs to read the value, who needs to change it, and how far apart those consumers are. Distant consumers with shared read/write needs are the strongest signal that global state may be justified.
A Nearby Problem Does Not Need Global State

sections.title: Search page
sections.code:
LessonPage
├── SearchBox
└── LessonList

Both need:
searchQuery

sections.text: This is a shared-state problem, but it is local to one feature. The parent can own query and pass it down. A global store would solve a larger problem than the application actually has.
A Distant Consumer Problem

sections.title: Application-wide user state
sections.code:
App
├── Header
│   └── AccountMenu
│
├── Dashboard
│   └── WelcomePanel
│
├── Courses
│   └── EnrollmentActions
│
└── Settings
    └── ProfileEditor

All need coordinated access to:
currentUser

sections.text: These consumers can be far apart in the component tree. Passing currentUser through unrelated layers can create substantial prop plumbing. A shared application store may be justified.
Global State Is About Reach, Not Importance
A value can be very important without being global. A critical piece of lesson-editing state can still belong entirely inside the lesson editor.

sections.title: Do not confuse these ideas
sections.code:
Important
≠
Global

Global means:
shared across distant application areas

sections.text: The Prop-Drilling Signal

sections.title: Potential warning sign
sections.code:
App
 ↓ user
Layout
 ↓ user
Page
 ↓ user
Toolbar
 ↓ user
AccountMenu

sections.text: If several intermediate components exist mainly to pass data through and do not otherwise care about that data, the architecture may be carrying a shared value farther than the component hierarchy naturally supports.
That is a signal to investigate global state, not automatic proof that a global store is required.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not globalize state 'just in case'
sections.text: Making state global because another component might eventually need it creates unnecessary shared coupling. Global scope should respond to real application requirements, not hypothetical future consumers.
Global State Has a Cost

sections.title: What you gain
sections.code:
Easy access from distant components
Shared actions
One coordinated source of truth

sections.title: What you pay
sections.code:
More shared coupling
More places can update the value
Larger impact radius for changes
More state architecture to understand
More potential consumers of updates

sections.text: The right question is not 'Can a store make this easier?' It usually can. The question is whether the problem is large enough to justify introducing that shared architecture.
A Real-World Analogy

Imagine a company directory. Employee contact information is useful to many distant teams, so one shared source makes sense. A checklist used by one designer on one task does not belong in that directory just because someone else might eventually see it.
Four Questions Before Going Global

sections.title: Decision checklist
sections.code:
1. How many components need this value?
2. Are those components actually distant in the tree?
3. Do multiple components need to change it?
4. Would normal props/lifting state become awkward or misleading?

sections.text: If the answers are mostly no, a global store is probably solving the wrong problem.
Case A: Theme
A theme setting affects navigation, dashboards, dialogs, and settings across the application. Many distant components need to read it, and a settings screen needs to change it.

sections.title: Likely conclusion
sections.code:
Many distant readers
+
One or more distant writers
+
Application-wide behavior

→ Global state is a reasonable candidate.

sections.text: Case B: Modal Visibility
A confirmation modal belongs to one page and is opened by one local action.

sections.title: Likely conclusion
sections.code:
One small feature
+
Local consumer
+
No distant coordination

→ Keep it local.

sections.text: Case C: Shopping Cart
A cart is displayed in a header, modified on product pages, reviewed in a cart page, and used during checkout.

sections.title: Likely conclusion
sections.code:
Many distant readers
+
Many distant writers
+
One shared domain concept

→ Global state may be justified.

sections.text: Case D: Lesson Draft
A lesson editor maintains temporary unsaved text while the user edits one lesson.

sections.title: Likely conclusion
sections.code:
One editing workflow
+
Temporary draft
+
No distant consumers

→ Keep it local.

sections.title: Consumer Map Drill
sections.instructions: Map the readers and writers for each state value. Then decide whether its scope should be local, lifted, or global.

sections.text: Global State vs Server State
A piece of data being fetched from a server does not automatically mean it belongs in a global client-side store. Server ownership and client state scope are separate design questions.

sections.title: Separate the questions
sections.code:
Question 1
Where does the data come from?
→ server / client / derived

Question 2
Who needs access to it?
→ local / shared / global

sections.text: The next module will go deeper into application data flow, caching, synchronization, and server-owned data.
Global State vs URL State

Navigation data belongs in the URL when the user should be able to bookmark, share, refresh, and revisit that state. A global store should not replace meaningful URL state simply because it provides convenient access.

sections.title: Examples
sections.code:
Current lesson URL
→ route state

Search filter intended to be shareable
→ query parameter

Authenticated user
→ possible global client state

Local modal
→ component state

sections.text: Global State vs Derived Data
A value that can be calculated from existing state does not become more appropriate for global state merely because the calculation is used in several places.

sections.title: Derived example
sections.code:
completedCount
= lessons.filter(...).length

Do not create a separate global value
if it can be derived from the canonical lesson data.

sections.text: Decision Framework

sections.title: Choose the smallest scope that works
sections.code:
Local
→ one component

Lifted/shared
→ a related subtree

Global
→ distant coordinated consumers

URL
→ navigation/shareable state

Derived
→ calculated from canonical data

Server-owned
→ data whose source of truth lives remotely

sections.text: What This Means for Zustand

Zustand comes next. The point of learning the library is not to turn every state value into a store. It is to have a lightweight mechanism available when the architecture actually calls for global shared state.
This is why the curriculum teaches the decision framework before the concrete Zustand API.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson introduces Zustand's concrete API: stores, actions, and selectors. Persistence follows after that.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: You are deciding whether global state is justified, not yet deciding how to implement it. Zustand is the next step.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'When do you actually need global state?' A strong answer is: 'When multiple distant components genuinely need coordinated read and write access to the same data, and normal props or lifted state would create unnecessary plumbing or unclear ownership.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is a sign you are globalizing too early?' Say that if the value currently has only one local consumer or a small related subtree, a global store is likely unnecessary.
Another follow-up is: 'Is server data automatically global client state?' No. Where data comes from and how widely the UI needs access to it are different questions.
Reflect

Pick one value from the multi-page app you built in Module 3-4. List every component that reads it and every component that changes it. Based on those real consumers, does it actually deserve global scope?

sections.title: Global state should solve a visible problem

sections.text: Do not choose global state because the library is convenient. Choose it because the application's data flow makes shared distant ownership a real requirement.

sections.label: Pass the decision check by correctly identifying when global state is justified and explaining why premature globalization adds unnecessary complexity.
sections.hint: Look for multiple distant readers/writers of the same value. Nearby shared state is usually solved with lifting; local UI remains local.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Global state is genuinely useful when multiple distant parts of an application need coordinated access to the same changing information. Nearby shared state can usually be handled with lifting and props, while local UI state should remain local. The decision should be based on actual readers and writers, not hypothetical future requirements. Server ownership, URL state, derived data, and client global state are separate concepts that should not be conflated.

exercises.brief: Classify real application scenarios as local, lifted/shared, or global based on actual consumers and writers.

exercises.title: Consumer Map Drill
exercises.brief: Map readers and writers for representative state values and determine the smallest appropriate scope.

quiz.question: What is the strongest signal that global state may be justified?
options: A value is important.
A value might be useful someday.
Multiple distant components genuinely need coordinated read/write access to the same data.
The component has more than one state variable.
quiz.explanation: Global state exists to solve real distant shared-access requirements.

quiz.question: Why is putting a page-local search query into a global store usually unnecessary?
options: Search values cannot be strings.
The problem is local to one feature and can usually be solved by lifting state within that feature.
Global stores cannot contain query values.
Search must always be server-owned.
quiz.explanation: A local feature does not require application-wide state.

quiz.question: Which situation is the clearest candidate for global state?
options: One card's expanded state.
A temporary tooltip.
A cart updated by product pages and checkout and displayed in a distant header.
A local input draft.
quiz.explanation: The cart has multiple distant readers and writers around one shared domain concept.

quiz.question: Does data coming from a server automatically need to be placed in a global client store?
options: Yes, always.
No. Data origin and client-side state scope are separate decisions.
Only if the response is JSON.
Only if more than one component renders it.
quiz.explanation: Server ownership does not automatically determine whether client state should be local, shared, cached, or global.

summary: Global state is justified when multiple distant components genuinely need coordinated read/write access to the same changing data. Nearby shared state should generally stay within the relevant subtree, and local UI state should remain local. Globalizing state prematurely introduces unnecessary coupling and complexity. Decide scope from actual consumers and writers, and keep separate the questions of state scope, server ownership, URL state, and derived values.

How does URL state differ from global state?
What questions should you ask before introducing a global store?

title: Zustand Fundamentals
description: Build a minimal Zustand store with state and actions, subscribe to only the state slices a component needs, and use selectors to avoid unnecessary component updates.
mastery: The learner can create a Zustand store with state and actions, consume selected slices of that store from React components, update shared state through store actions, and explain why selecting the entire store can cause unnecessary re-renders.
learningObjectives: Explain what Zustand provides at a conceptual level.
Create a Zustand store containing shared state.
Define actions that update store state.
Read Zustand state from React components.
Use selectors to subscribe to only the state slice a component needs.
Update shared state through store actions.
Explain why reading the entire store can cause unnecessary re-renders.
Distinguish a store's state from the components that consume it.

sections.text: Now the Tool Has a Job

The previous two lessons answered whether global state is needed. This lesson introduces Zustand as the concrete mechanism for one justified use case: shared state that needs convenient access across distant parts of the component tree.
Zustand keeps the implementation relatively small: define a store, add state and actions, then select the pieces each component needs.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A Zustand store is a shared state container. Components subscribe to selected pieces of that store and use store actions to request updates.
A Minimal Store

sections.title: State + action

sections.text: The store contains the shared value count and an action increment that updates it.
Read State in a Component

sections.title: Select one value

sections.text: The component subscribes to count. When count changes, this component can re-render with the new value.
Call an Action

sections.title: Select the action

sections.text: The action is also selected from the store. The component does not need to know how the store updates count internally.
The Store Is Not the Component

sections.title: Separate responsibilities
sections.code:
Zustand store
→ shared state
→ actions

React component
→ rendering
→ user interaction
→ selecting required store values

sections.text: The store owns shared application information. Components consume the store and render UI around it.
Selectors Matter

sections.title: Good
Too broad
sections.code: const store = useCounterStore();

sections.text: Selecting a specific slice communicates exactly what the component cares about. Reading the entire store can make the component respond to changes it does not actually use.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not read the entire Zustand store in every component just because it is convenient. Select only the state and actions the component needs so subscriptions remain focused.
Interactive Practice: Shared Counter

sections.title: Zustand Fundamentals Playground
sections.instructions: Complete the store with count and actions, then create components that select only the pieces they need. Change the counter and observe the shared output across components.

sections.text: Actions Express Domain Changes

sections.title: Prefer meaningful actions

sections.text: Actions can express domain operations rather than forcing every component to manipulate the underlying state structure directly.
Multiple Components Can Share the Same Store

sections.title: Header and checkout consume the same state

sections.text: Neither component needs to receive the cart through multiple intermediate props. Both can access the same shared store directly.
Selectors Define Subscriptions

sections.title: Think in slices
sections.code:
Store
├── user
├── theme
├── cart
└── notifications

Header
→ selects user

CartIcon
→ selects cart item count

ThemeToggle
→ selects theme + action

sections.text: The component's selector describes its subscription. Narrow selectors keep each consumer focused on the state it actually needs.
Drill 1: Narrow the Store Selection

sections.title: Selector Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The components currently read the entire store. Change each component to select only the specific values/actions it uses. Then identify which store changes should be relevant to each component.

sections.text: Local State Still Has a Place

sections.title: Store + local UI state

sections.text: Using a global store does not mean every piece of UI state should move into it. The cart is shared; whether the panel is expanded is local UI state.
Drill 2: Build a Small Shared Store

sections.title: Global Cart Store Drill
sections.instructions: Create a small cart store with items, addItem, removeItem, and a derived item count selector. Build separate CartBadge and CartPanel components that subscribe only to what they need. Keep the panel's expanded state local.

sections.text: Do Not Rebuild the Store in Components
The store should remain the shared source of truth. Components should select and use it rather than creating parallel copies of the same global data.

sections.title: Avoid
sections.code:
Global store: cart
Component state: cart
Another component state: cart

Three copies of one concept.

sections.title: Prefer
sections.code:
Global store: cart
      ↓
Components select the slices they need

sections.text: Selectors Can Also Express Derived Information

sections.title: Select a computed slice

sections.text: The component does not need a separate itemCount state value if it can be calculated from the canonical cart items.
Keep Store Design Small

sections.title: A small domain store
sections.code:
cart
├── items
├── addItem
└── removeItem

sections.text: The purpose of the store is to make one shared domain easy to coordinate. Avoid creating one huge global object containing every state value in the application.
Debugging Zustand Updates

sections.title: When a component does not update correctly
sections.code:
1. Is the store action actually updating state?
2. Is the component selecting the right slice?
3. Is the UI reading the selected value?
4. Is another source of truth shadowing the store?
5. Is a derived value being duplicated in state?

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
Persistence comes next. That lesson will add storage so selected store data can survive a browser reload.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson introduces the core store model and selectors. Persistence, derived-state design, and broader store architecture are handled in subsequent lessons.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is Zustand?' A strong answer is: 'Zustand is a lightweight state-management library that lets you create a shared store with state and actions, then consume selected slices of that store from React components.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why use selectors?' Say that selectors let components subscribe to only the state they need rather than the entire store, helping avoid updates caused by unrelated state changes.

Another follow-up is: 'Should all component state move into Zustand?' No. Shared application state belongs in the store when the architecture calls for it; local presentation state should remain local.
Reflect

Take a global-state candidate from the previous lesson, such as a cart or authenticated user. What would the store contain? Which components would read which slices? Which actions would those components need?
A component should know exactly which part of shared state it depends on. Narrow selectors make that dependency visible and keep subscriptions focused.

sections.label: Complete the Zustand Playground and both drills. The learner must create a working store, update it through actions, consume selected state slices, and avoid broad whole-store subscriptions.
sections.hint: Store = shared state + actions. Component = select the slice it needs. Keep local UI state local.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Zustand provides a small mechanism for shared application state: create a store, define state and actions, and let components select the slices they need. Selectors are important because they keep subscriptions narrow and make component dependencies explicit. A Zustand store should not replace local component state or become a giant container for unrelated domains.
