quiz.question: What are the basic pieces of a Zustand store?
options: Shared state and actions that update it.
Only React components.
Only URL parameters.
Only server responses.
quiz.explanation: A Zustand store can contain shared state and actions for changing that state.

quiz.question: Why should a component generally select a specific store slice?
options: To make its dependency on shared state explicit and avoid reacting to unrelated changes.
Because Zustand cannot store objects.
Because selectors prevent all state updates.
Because every component must use a unique store.
quiz.explanation: Narrow selectors keep component subscriptions focused.

quiz.question: Which state should remain local even when an application uses Zustand?
options: A globally shared cart.
Authenticated user information shared across distant components.
Whether one local panel is currently expanded.
A shared theme preference.
quiz.explanation: A UI state used by one component does not need to become global just because a store exists.

quiz.question: What is a warning sign in a Zustand component?
options: It selects one small slice it needs.
It reads the entire store even though it only uses one value.
It calls a domain action.
It keeps a local modal state locally.
quiz.explanation: Broad whole-store reads can create unnecessary subscriptions and make dependencies less precise.

summary: Zustand is introduced only after the curriculum has established when global state is justified. A store contains shared state and actions; React components consume the store through selectors and trigger actions to update it. Components should select only the slices they need rather than reading the entire store. Local UI state remains local, and the store should remain focused on a coherent shared domain rather than becoming a giant application-wide container.

title: Persisted State
description: Learn how to persist selected Zustand store data to browser storage so it survives page reloads, while deciding carefully which state is appropriate to persist.
mastery: The learner can configure persisted Zustand state, verify that selected data survives a reload, distinguish durable user preferences from inappropriate sensitive or rapidly changing data, and explain the tradeoffs of client-side persistence.
learningObjectives: Explain what persisted client state means.
Explain how browser storage can preserve selected state across reloads.
Configure persistence for a Zustand store.
Verify restored state after a page reload.
Choose which store data should and should not be persisted.
Recognize the risk of persisting sensitive information.
Recognize when rapidly changing data should not be blindly cached in browser storage.
Explain the difference between in-memory state and persisted state.

sections.text: A Store Normally Starts Fresh
A Zustand store normally lives in the running JavaScript application. Refresh the browser and that in-memory state is recreated.
Sometimes that is exactly what you want. Other values, such as a user's preferred theme or dismissed onboarding choice, should survive a reload.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Persisted state copies selected application state into browser storage so the application can restore it after a reload.
What Persistence Changes

sections.title: Without persistence
sections.code:
Store state
    ↓
Browser refresh
    ↓
Store recreated
    ↓
Initial values

sections.title: With persistence
sections.code:
Store state
    ↓
Browser storage
    ↓
Browser refresh
    ↓
Store rehydrates
    ↓
Previously persisted values

sections.text: A Persistent Zustand Store

sections.title: Persist a theme preference

sections.text: The persist middleware connects the store to storage. After changing the theme, reloading the application can restore the persisted value.
Persistence Is Selective
Not every piece of state belongs in browser storage. The important architectural decision is what should survive a reload.

sections.title: Good persistence candidates
sections.code:
Theme preference
Dismissed onboarding state
User-selected display preferences
Non-sensitive local preferences

sections.title: Potentially inappropriate
sections.code:
Passwords
Access tokens or other secrets
Highly sensitive personal information
Ephemeral UI state
Rapidly changing data that should be freshly synchronized

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not persist sensitive or rapidly changing data simply because storage makes it easy. Persistence should be intentional and based on the meaning, sensitivity, freshness requirements, and lifetime of the data.
Interactive Practice: Persist a Preference

sections.text: The exercise deliberately includes state with different lifetimes. Theme and onboarding preference can reasonably survive a reload; modalOpen usually should not.
Persist Only the Appropriate Slice

sections.title: Select what gets stored

sections.text: The exact persistence configuration can vary, but the architectural principle is important: persist only the data whose lifetime and sensitivity justify storage.
Persistence Does Not Make Data Authoritative
Browser storage is a client-side copy. It does not automatically become the authoritative source for server-owned data.

sections.title: Do not confuse these
sections.code:
Server database
→ authoritative application data

Browser storage
→ local persisted client copy

sections.text: A persisted client value can be stale or invalid relative to the server, so persistence should not be used to bypass appropriate synchronization.

sections.text: Persistence and Hydration

sections.title: Conceptual lifecycle
sections.code:
Application starts
      ↓
Store created with defaults
      ↓
Persisted storage is read
      ↓
Stored values are restored
      ↓
Components render from restored state

sections.text: This restoration step is often called rehydration. The important idea is that persisted values can be loaded back into the store when the application starts.
Be Careful With Initial UI Assumptions

If a component assumes the store always starts with default values, persistence can expose a mismatch between the initial state and the restored state. Build UI behavior around the fact that rehydration can change the store's values.
Persistence Is Not a Cache for Everything

Storage can survive reloads, but persistence is not automatically a replacement for proper data-fetching and caching strategies. Server-owned information can need freshness, invalidation, and synchronization that browser storage alone does not provide.
Drill 2: Persist Preferences, Not Everything

sections.title: Persisted Store Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The store currently persists every field, including ephemeral and inappropriate values. Restrict persistence to durable non-sensitive preferences and explain why the excluded fields should remain in memory.

sections.text: State Lifetime Is an Architecture Property

sections.title: Different lifetimes
sections.code:
Milliseconds
→ transient UI interaction

Minutes
→ temporary editing session

Across route changes
→ application state

Across reloads
→ persisted state

Across devices/users
→ server-owned data

sections.text: Thinking about lifetime helps determine where a value should live and whether it should be persisted at all.
Privacy and Security Matter
Anything stored in browser storage should be treated as client-accessible data. Do not place secrets or sensitive information there simply because a persistence middleware makes it easy.
Debugging Persisted State

sections.title: When persisted state behaves strangely
sections.code:
1. What storage key is being used?
2. Which fields are actually persisted?
3. Is an old stored value overriding defaults?
4. Is the stored value still compatible with the current state shape?
5. Should this value survive a reload at all?
6. Is the browser copy stale relative to the server?

sections.text: When debugging, inspect the actual browser storage rather than assuming the store contains only its default values.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson covers derived state and selectors. It focuses on computing values from canonical state rather than persisting or storing duplicate computed fields.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Persistence determines whether selected state survives a reload. It does not solve server synchronization, caching freshness, or data ownership.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you persist Zustand state?' A strong answer is: 'I would use Zustand's persistence middleware to store selected state in browser storage, but I would explicitly choose which fields belong there based on their lifetime, sensitivity, and freshness requirements.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What would you not persist?' Avoid sensitive secrets, ephemeral UI state, and rapidly changing data that needs authoritative synchronization.
Another follow-up is: 'Does persisted browser state become the source of truth for server data?' No. It is only a client-side persisted copy and may be stale.
Reflect
Take the global-state candidates from the previous lesson. Which should survive a full browser reload? Which should reset? What does that tell you about the intended lifetime of each value?
The easiest value to persist is not necessarily the right value to persist. Decide first what the user should reasonably expect to survive a reload.

sections.label: Complete the persisted-state Playground and both drills. The learner must configure persisted Zustand state, verify restoration after reload, and correctly exclude inappropriate values.
sections.hint: Ask whether the value should survive reload, whether it is sensitive, and whether a client copy can safely become stale.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Persisted state allows selected client state to survive a browser reload. Zustand persistence can restore values from browser storage, but persistence should be selective. Durable non-sensitive preferences are common candidates; secrets, ephemeral UI state, and rapidly changing server-owned data generally require different treatment. Browser storage is a persisted client copy, not automatically the authoritative source of server data.

options: Selected client state can survive a browser reload.
All server data becomes permanently fresh.
Every component automatically becomes global.
All state becomes secure.
quiz.explanation: Persistence stores selected client state so it can be restored after reload.

quiz.question: Which is a reasonable persistence candidate?
options: A password typed into a login form.
A modal currently open on one page.
A user's non-sensitive theme preference.
A rapidly changing live server metric.
quiz.explanation: A durable non-sensitive preference is a typical browser-persistence candidate.

quiz.question: Why should rapidly changing server-owned data not automatically be persisted in browser storage?
options: It may become stale and require synchronization or freshness handling.
Browser storage cannot contain arrays.
Zustand cannot store server data.
Persisted values cannot be strings.
quiz.explanation: A persisted client copy can outlive the freshness of the server source.

quiz.question: What does rehydration mean in a persisted store?
options: Restoring persisted values into the store when the application starts.
Deleting the browser storage.
Resetting all state to defaults.
Converting server data to JSX.
quiz.explanation: Rehydration restores previously persisted client state into the running store.

summary: Persisted Zustand state survives browser reloads by storing selected values in browser storage and restoring them when the application starts. Persistence should be intentional: durable, non-sensitive preferences are common candidates, while secrets, ephemeral UI state, and rapidly changing server-owned data should generally not be persisted blindly. Browser storage is a client-side copy and does not automatically become the authoritative source of truth.

title: Derived State and Selectors
description: Learn to compute values from existing canonical state instead of storing duplicate computed values, and use selectors to expose exactly the information components need.
mastery: The learner can identify derived values, remove unnecessary duplicated state, write Zustand selectors that compute the required value from canonical state, and explain how deriving instead of storing prevents stale state.
learningObjectives: Explain what derived state is.
Distinguish canonical state from values that can be calculated from it.
Identify state that should not be stored separately.
Write derived values directly from existing React state.
Use Zustand selectors to compute values from store state.
Avoid duplicated state that can become stale.
Explain why selectors are useful for both derivation and focused subscriptions.

sections.text: Not Every Value Deserves a Storage Slot
A state model should contain the information the application actually needs to remember. Many other values can be calculated from that canonical state whenever they are needed.
Those calculated values are derived state.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Store the source data. Derive values that can be calculated from that source. Do not create another state value merely because a calculation is used in the UI.
A Simple Example

sections.title: Derived value in React

sections.text: percentage does not need its own state because completed and total already contain the information needed to calculate it.
The Duplicate-State Trap

sections.title: Unnecessary duplicate state
sections.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const [itemCount, setItemCount] = useState(0);

sections.text: Now two pieces of state describe one underlying concept. Every operation that changes items must remember to update itemCount too.

sections.title: Potentially stale
sections.code:
items = [A, B]
itemCount = 2

Remove B

items = [A]
itemCount = ???

sections.text: Prefer Derivation

sections.title: Calculate instead
sections.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);

const itemCount = items.length;

sections.text: There is now one source of truth. The count always follows the current items.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not store computed values as independent state
sections.text: If a value can be calculated from existing canonical state, storing another copy creates a synchronization problem. The duplicate can become stale.
Derived State Inside a Zustand Store

sections.title: Select a computed value

sections.text: The selector computes itemCount from the canonical items array. There is no separate itemCount field to keep synchronized.
More Useful Derived Selectors

sections.title: Completed count
Remaining count

sections.text: Both values come from the same canonical lessons collection.
Interactive Practice: Derive Instead of Store

sections.title: Derived State Playground
sections.instructions: The store contains duplicated values that can become stale. Remove the unnecessary derived fields and replace them with selectors that calculate the required results from canonical state.

sections.text: Canonical State vs Derived State

sections.title: Think in layers
sections.code:
Canonical
lessons
    ↓
Derived
completedCount
remainingCount
completionPercentage

Do not store all four if one can be computed from the first.

sections.text: The canonical data is the information the application actually needs to own. Derived values are views of that information.
Selectors Are Small Read Models
A selector can be thought of as a small read model: it converts the store's canonical state into exactly the value the component needs.

sections.title: Store to component
sections.code:
Store
├── lessons
├── filters
└── user

Component
→ selector(state)
→ derived slice
→ render

sections.instructions: For every value in the store, decide whether it is canonical state or derived state. Remove only the duplicated computed values and replace them with selectors.

sections.text: Derived State Can Depend on Multiple Values

sections.title: Filter + canonical collection

sections.text: The selector can combine canonical state values to create the exact view needed by the component.
Be Careful With Derived Selectors
A selector should express a meaningful read of the store. It should not become a huge hidden business layer that is difficult to understand or reuse.

sections.title: Good selector
sections.code: state.items.length

sections.title: Potentially overgrown selector
sections.code:
state
→ filter
→ sort
→ transform
→ network decision
→ mutate another system
→ return UI-specific object

sections.text: Keep selectors focused on deriving read values. Larger domain transformations may deserve separate functions.
Derivation Prevents Synchronization Effects

sections.title: Avoid this

sections.text: This creates another synchronization relationship for something that can be calculated directly.

sections.title: Prefer this
sections.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const count = items.length;

sections.text: Derived Values Can Be Computed at the Point of Use
You do not have to give every derived value a named selector. A local calculation can be perfectly appropriate when it is simple and specific to one component.

sections.title: Local derivation

sections.text: Use a reusable selector when the derived calculation is shared or benefits from a stable named abstraction. Otherwise, a small local calculation may be clearer.

sections.text: Selectors and Focused Subscriptions
Selectors serve two related purposes: they derive the read value a component needs and define the portion of the store that the component subscribes to.

sections.title: One selector, two benefits
sections.code:
Selector
├── describes what the component reads
└── keeps the subscription focused

sections.text: Don't Store the Selector Result

sections.title: Usually unnecessary

sections.text: The second state value merely duplicates the selector result. Let the selector remain the source of the current derived value.
Debugging Stale Derived Values

sections.title: When a computed value is wrong
sections.code:
1. What is the canonical source state?
2. Is the value actually derived from it?
3. Is there a second stored copy?
4. Is the selector reading the current source?
5. Is a stale local state value shadowing the selector?

sections.text: When derived data is stale, look for duplicate storage before adding another effect.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson steps back from individual selectors and asks how to design the complete application's state shape before implementing stores.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Derived state is about avoiding duplicate storage and keeping read models synchronized with canonical state. The next lesson applies that thinking to the full application's state architecture.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is derived state?' A strong answer is: 'It is a value that can be calculated from canonical state. I generally derive it instead of storing another copy because duplicate state can become stale.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why are Zustand selectors useful?' They let a component subscribe to a focused slice of the store and can compute the exact read value the component needs.

Another follow-up is: 'Should every derived value be a selector?' No. Small values specific to one component can be calculated locally. A reusable selector is useful when the derived read is shared or benefits from a named abstraction.
Reflect

Think about your previous Zustand store. Which fields were truly canonical? Which ones could have been calculated from them? What bug would appear if one of the stored computed fields were forgotten during an update?
Canonical state stores the facts the application needs to own. Selectors and calculations create the views of those facts that the UI needs.

sections.label: Complete the derived-state Playground and both drills. The learner must remove duplicate computed state, replace it with correct derivation/selectors, and choose appropriately between reusable selectors and local calculations.
sections.hint: Ask whether the value is a fact the application must own or a value that can always be calculated from existing facts.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Derived state is information that can be calculated from canonical state. Storing it separately creates synchronization work and can make the value stale. Zustand selectors provide a focused way to read and derive values from a store while keeping component subscriptions narrow. Use reusable selectors for shared read models and simple local calculations for values that are specific to one component.

summary: Derived state is calculated from canonical application state rather than stored as another independent fact. This prevents duplicate sources of truth and stale values. Zustand selectors can both focus a component's subscription and compute a useful read model from store state. Shared derived values can become reusable selectors; small one-off calculations can remain local to the component.

title: Designing Application State
description: Learn to design an application's state model before implementing stores by deciding what belongs in local, global, derived, or server-owned state.
mastery: The learner can take a feature's data requirements, classify its values as local, global, derived, or server-owned, identify canonical sources of truth, and sketch a coherent application state shape before writing a store.

Distinguish local, global, derived, and server-owned data.
Identify canonical sources of truth for an application's state.
Decide which values should survive across components or routes.
Recognize state that should not be stored because it is derived.
Separate client-owned state from server-owned data.
Design a state shape around domain data rather than individual UI screens.
Explain how poor state shape creates duplication and synchronization problems.

sections.text: Design the State Before the Store

You have now learned how to identify global state, create a Zustand store, persist selected values, and derive computed values with selectors. The next step is deciding what the application should actually store.
A store is an implementation detail. The state model should come first.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Start with the domain information the application needs to remember. Classify each value as local, global, derived, or server-owned. Only then decide how stores and components should implement that model.
Four State Categories

sections.title: State-design map
sections.code:
LOCAL
→ one component or small subtree

GLOBAL
→ distant components need coordinated access

DERIVED
→ calculated from canonical state

SERVER-OWNED
→ authoritative source exists remotely

sections.text: These categories solve different problems. Do not put everything that changes into one global store.
Start With Domain Facts

sections.title: Course application facts
sections.code:
Course
Lesson
User
Enrollment
Completion status
Theme preference
Current search filter
Selected lesson
Visible lesson count

sections.text: These values sound similar because they all affect the UI, but they have different ownership and lifetimes.
Classify the Facts

sections.title: One possible classification
sections.code:
Course / Lesson data
→ server-owned

Authenticated user
→ potentially global client state,
  with server-side authority

Theme preference
→ global + persisted client state

Search filter
→ URL/navigation state if shareable

Modal open state
→ local

Completed lesson count
→ derived

Selected lesson id
→ route/navigation state when represented in URL

sections.text: The exact classification depends on the product requirements. The important skill is explaining why a value belongs in a particular category.
The Common Mistake: Designing Around the Screen

sections.title: Screen-driven state
sections.code:
DashboardState
SettingsState
CoursePageState
LessonPageState

Each screen stores whatever it currently needs.

sections.text: This can create duplicated representations of the same domain data. A course may appear in the dashboard, course page, and progress screen, but there should not automatically be three independent copies of the course concept.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not design the state shape around individual screens or UI components. Design it around the underlying domain information and its ownership. Screens are views of the data, not necessarily separate sources of truth.
Canonical Data First

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Canonical
lessons

Derived
completedCount
remainingCount
progressPercentage

Do not store all four.

sections.text: Canonical state represents the facts the application actually owns or needs to remember. Derived values are computed views.
Design Around Ownership

sections.title: Ownership questions
sections.code:
Who creates this value?
Who can change it?
Who needs to read it?
How long should it live?
Should it survive a reload?
Does the server own the authoritative version?
Can it be derived from something else?

sections.text: These questions often reveal the correct category without needing to think about the implementation library yet.
Think About Lifetime

sections.title: Lifetime is a design clue
sections.code:
One interaction
→ local

One page/feature
→ lifted/shared

Across distant application areas
→ potentially global

Across reloads
→ potentially persisted

Authoritative across users/devices
→ server-owned

sections.text: Think About Authority

A crucial design question is which system is authoritative for a value. A browser preference can be client-owned. A user's enrollment status is usually authoritative on the server. A filter query may be authoritative in the URL for the current navigation.

Theme
→ browser/application preference

→ server

Current route
→ URL/router

Expanded card
→ component state

sections.text: Avoid the Giant Store

sections.title: Suspicious global store
sections.code:
useAppStore

sections.text: A giant store makes every state problem look like one problem. It hides ownership boundaries and encourages unrelated parts of the application to depend on one another.
Prefer Domain and Feature Boundaries

sections.title: Possible organization
sections.code:
auth
→ current user / authentication-related client state

preferences
→ theme / durable UI preferences

cart
→ shared cart state

course feature
→ UI-specific state around course interactions

server data
→ appropriate server-data mechanism

sections.text: The exact store boundaries depend on the application. The principle is to keep related data together and unrelated concerns separate.
Do Not Confuse Global State With a Store
Global state is the architectural concept. A Zustand store is one implementation mechanism. You can have global information represented through other mechanisms, including context or URL state.

sections.title: Architecture before tool
sections.code:
Need identified
    ↓

    ↓
Source of truth identified
    ↓
Scope determined
    ↓
Implementation mechanism selected

sections.text: The State Shape Should Survive UI Redesign
One way to test your model is to imagine a major visual redesign. If the UI changes but the underlying domain facts remain the same, the core state model should not need to be reinvented.
Scenario Test

sections.title: Imagine a redesign
sections.code:
Today:
Course list is a grid.

Tomorrow:
Course list becomes a table.

Question:
Did courses themselves change?

No.

Therefore:
The domain state should not be shaped around 'grid cards'.

sections.text: Scenario Test: New Consumer

Imagine a notification bell is added to the header and needs the current user's unread notifications. The state model should answer whether that information is server-owned, globally accessible, locally derived, or navigation state without being rebuilt around the new component.
Scenario Test: New Route

Imagine a new route `/courses/:courseId/progress` is added. The route should consume the existing course/enrollment information rather than creating a second progress data source simply because a new screen was introduced.
State Design Checklist

sections.title: Before implementing a store
sections.code:
□ What are the domain facts?
□ What is server-owned?
□ What is client-owned?
□ What needs to be global?
□ What can remain local?
□ What belongs in the URL?
□ What can be derived?
□ What should survive reloads?
□ Where is the canonical source of truth?
□ Are unrelated domains unnecessarily combined?

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you design application state?' A strong answer is: 'I start with the domain data and identify the source of truth for each value. Then I classify state as server-owned, global client state, local state, navigation state, or derived data. I choose the smallest scope that satisfies the actual consumers and avoid storing values that can be derived.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why design the state shape before choosing Zustand?' Because Zustand is an implementation tool. If the state model is wrong, putting it into a store only makes the wrong architecture easier to access.

Another follow-up is: 'How do you avoid a giant global store?' Separate state by domain/feature, keep local UI local, keep URL state in the URL, and avoid duplicating derived or server-owned information.
Reflect

Take the multi-page Forge Academy application. Whiteboard its full state model before opening the code. Which facts are canonical? Which values are derived views? Which values are navigation state? Which data should never be owned by the client store?

sections.title: Design the information model, not the screen

sections.text: Screens come and go. Domain facts and ownership relationships usually persist. Build the state model around those durable concepts.

sections.label: Pass the state-design checkpoint by producing a coherent whiteboard model that classifies the application's major values as local, global, derived, navigation, or server-owned and identifies a canonical source of truth.
sections.hint: Start from domain facts and authority. Then determine scope, lifetime, persistence, and derivation.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Designing application state means deciding what the application actually needs to own before implementing stores. Begin with domain facts, identify the authoritative source for each value, and classify information as local, global, derived, navigation, or server-owned. Keep state at the smallest scope that satisfies the real consumers, derive computed values instead of duplicating them, and avoid designing state around individual screens or a giant global store.

summary: Application state design begins with the domain rather than the UI. Identify canonical facts, determine authority and lifetime, and classify values as local, global, derived, navigation, or server-owned before choosing an implementation. This avoids giant stores, duplicated data, and screen-specific sources of truth. The goal is a state model that remains coherent even when the UI or route structure changes.

title: State Management Project
description: Design and implement a real application state model with clear local/global boundaries, persisted preferences, focused Zustand selectors, and derived values rather than duplicated state.
mastery: The learner can design and implement a coherent state architecture for a small application, selecting appropriate state scope, using Zustand for genuinely shared state, persisting appropriate values, deriving computed data, and keeping unrelated state out of one giant store.

This project combines every state-management concept from Module 4-1. There is no major new theory to learn.
Your job is to design the state model first and then implement only the state that the feature genuinely needs.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Walk me through your state architecture.' A strong answer is: 'I started from the domain facts and classified each value by ownership and lifetime. Preferences are persisted global client state, saved lesson IDs are shared global state, progress counts are derived, and per-card expansion is local UI state.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why not put all of this into one Zustand store?' Because the state has different responsibilities and lifetimes. Separate domains make ownership clearer and reduce unrelated coupling.
Another follow-up is: 'Why not store progressPercentage?' Because it can always be derived from the canonical lesson data, so storing it creates unnecessary synchronization work.
Reflect
What would happen if the visual design changed completely but the underlying lesson domain stayed the same? Which pieces of your state architecture should remain unchanged?
You have now moved from deciding whether global state is needed to designing, implementing, persisting, and deriving shared application state with clear boundaries.

sections.label: Submit the State Management Project for manual/rubric grading. The project must meet the functional and architecture requirements for persistence, focused Zustand selectors, derived values, and clear local/global boundaries.
sections.hint: Design first, then implement. Keep one canonical source for each domain fact, derive computed values, persist only appropriate preferences, and split unrelated global concerns into focused stores.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The State Management Project applies the entire module as one architecture exercise. A strong solution starts from domain data, gives each concept a clear source of truth, uses Zustand only for genuinely shared state, persists only durable appropriate values, derives computed summaries from canonical data, and keeps local UI state local. The quality of the architecture matters as much as the working behavior.

title: Client-Side Data Flow
description: Learn to trace how server data moves through a client application—from request and response into application state or cache and finally into rendered UI—and identify the source of truth at each stage.
mastery: The learner can trace a piece of server data from request through client state/cache to rendered UI, identify which layer is authoritative, and explain how user updates move back through the system.
learningObjectives: Explain client-side data flow from server request to rendered UI.
Distinguish server-owned data from client-side representations of that data.
Identify the source of truth for a given data value.
Trace how fetched data enters application state or a cache.
Trace how state/cache changes produce UI updates.
Explain how user actions can send changes back to the server.
Recognize duplicate sources of truth as a data-flow risk.
Describe the role of loading and error state in the client-side data flow.

sections.text: The Application Is a Data Pipeline
The previous module focused on deciding where client state should live. This module turns to application data itself: how information moves between the server, the client, and the UI.
A production interface is rarely just 'fetch and render.' Data can be cached, transformed, updated, invalidated, and synchronized over time.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Request → server response → client representation/cache → component reads data → UI renders. User actions can send mutations back to the server, after which the client must reconcile its representation.
Trace One Piece of Data

sections.title: Course title flow
sections.code:
Server database
      ↓
API response
      ↓
Client data layer/cache
      ↓
Component reads course.title
      ↓
React renders <h1>
      ↓
User sees title

sections.text: Every step is a possible place for stale data, transformation, or ownership confusion. Tracing the path helps you find where a bug actually lives.
Server-Owned vs Client-Owned

sections.title: Different authorities
sections.code:
Course title
→ server-owned

Theme preference
→ client-owned

Current route
→ URL/router-owned

Progress percentage
→ derived from canonical data

sections.text: The client can hold a copy of server-owned data, but that copy does not automatically become authoritative.
The Source of Truth Question

sections.title: Ask first
sections.code:
Where is the authoritative value?

Server?
Client store?
URL?
Component state?
Derived calculation?

sections.text: Many frontend bugs are really source-of-truth bugs: two places believe they own the same value, and eventually they disagree.
Example: Loading a Course

sections.title: Initial request
sections.code:
User opens /courses/react
        ↓
Client requests course data
        ↓
loading = true
        ↓
Server responds
        ↓
client stores/caches course
        ↓
loading = false
        ↓
UI renders course

sections.text: Loading is part of the data flow too. The UI needs to communicate that the data has not arrived yet rather than pretending a missing value is the same thing as an empty result.
Example: Updating a Course

sections.title: Mutation flow
sections.code:
User edits title
        ↓
Client sends update request
        ↓
Server accepts/rejects update
        ↓
Client updates or invalidates cached data
        ↓
Components receive current data
        ↓
UI re-renders

sections.text: A mutation introduces an additional synchronization problem: the client representation must eventually agree with the server's authoritative result.
Do Not Create a Second Server Data Source

sections.title: Potentially problematic
sections.code:
const serverCourse = useCourse();
const [localCourse, setLocalCourse] = useState(serverCourse);

sections.text: Now the application may have two representations of the same course. Unless localCourse is an intentional draft with a different meaning, synchronization becomes harder.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not lose track of which layer is the source of truth. A fetched server entity, a cache entry, a local draft, and a derived value can look similar in code while having completely different ownership.

sections.text: The Cache Is a Client Representation

A cache stores data so the client can reuse it without requesting it again immediately. That makes it useful for performance, but it also means the client representation can become older than the server data.

sections.title: Cache relationship
sections.code:
Server
  ↑ authoritative
  │
  │ response
  ↓
Client cache
  ↑ reusable representation
  │
  ↓
Components / UI

sections.text: The next lesson focuses specifically on how caching and synchronization manage this relationship over time.
User Actions Travel the Other Direction

sections.title: Read and write paths
sections.code:
READ
Server → client data layer → UI

WRITE
UI → client action → server mutation
                     ↓
             updated client data

sections.text: Keeping the read path and write path visible makes it easier to reason about synchronization.
Loading, Error, and Empty Are Different

sections.title: Request lifecycle
sections.code:
idle
 ↓
loading
 ├── success + data
 ├── success + empty
 └── error

sections.text: These states belong to the client-side representation of the request. They tell the UI what the current data flow means at that moment.
A Real-World Analogy

Think of the server as the official ledger and the client cache as a working copy on your desk. The copy makes work faster, but you still need to know when it is outdated and when an update has been accepted by the official ledger.
Data-Flow Debugging

sections.title: When the UI shows stale data
sections.code:
1. What did the server return?
2. What did the client cache/store receive?
3. Did the mutation succeed?
4. Was the cached value updated or invalidated?
5. Which component consumed the value?
6. Is another local copy overriding it?

sections.text: Do not start by changing the component rendering code. First trace the data from its source to the UI.
Flashcard Review

sections.title: Recall
sections.code:
Q: What is the source of truth?
A: The authoritative place where a value is owned.

Q: Is a client cache automatically authoritative?
A: No. It is a client representation of data.

Q: What is the read path?
A: Server → client data layer → UI.

Q: What is the write path?
A: UI → client action → server mutation → updated client representation.

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses on caching and synchronization strategies: avoiding redundant network requests while preventing indefinitely stale client data.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson establishes the data-flow mental model. Caching policies, invalidation, retries, and normalization come later in the module.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How does server data get to the UI?' A strong answer is: 'The client requests the data, receives a server response, stores or caches the client representation, and components read that representation to render the UI. If the user mutates data, the client sends the change to the server and reconciles its representation with the resulting authoritative state.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is the source of truth?' Explain that it depends on the value: server data may be server-owned, navigation values may live in the URL, local UI values belong to components, and computed values should be derived.
Another follow-up is: 'Why can a client cache be dangerous?' Because it can become stale relative to the authoritative server data if synchronization and invalidation are not handled.
Reflect

Take the State Management Project from Module 4-1. Which values in that project were actually server-owned even though the UI displayed them through client state? Where would a stale client copy create a visible bug?
When a production UI is wrong, trace the value from source of truth to client representation to component before changing rendering code.

sections.label: Pass the recall check by correctly tracing server → client data layer/cache → component → UI and identifying the authoritative source of truth for representative values.
sections.hint: For every value ask: who owns it, where is the client copy, who consumes it, and what happens when it changes?

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Client-side data flow is the path from server request to client representation and finally to rendered UI, with mutations traveling back toward the server and requiring reconciliation. The key skill is source-of-truth tracing: know which layer is authoritative, which layers merely represent or derive the value, and where stale or duplicated copies can appear. Caching improves reuse and performance, but it creates a synchronization responsibility that the next lessons address.

summary: Client-side data flow traces server data from request and response through a client representation or cache into components and the rendered UI. User mutations travel back to the server and require the client representation to be reconciled. The central discipline is source-of-truth tracing: distinguish authoritative server data from cached client copies, local drafts, URL state, and derived values. This mental model sets up the next lessons on caching and synchronization.

title: Caching and Synchronization
description: Learn how client-side caching reduces redundant network requests and why cached data must be synchronized with the authoritative server source over time.
mastery: The learner can explain why client caches exist, implement a simple cache/reuse check, identify when cached data is stale, and describe an invalidation or refresh strategy that keeps the client representation aligned with the server.

sections.text: Why Cache Data?
The previous lesson traced server data through the client to the UI. A cache adds another concern: if the application has already fetched data, should it request the same data again?
A cache keeps a reusable client copy so repeated reads can avoid redundant network requests.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Request once → store a reusable client copy → reuse it when appropriate → refresh or invalidate it when it may no longer represent current server data.
Without a Cache

sections.title: Repeated requests
sections.code:
Open Dashboard
→ request /api/courses/react
→ receive course

Open Course page
→ request /api/courses/react again
→ receive same course

Return to Dashboard
→ request again

sections.text: Some repeated requests may be necessary, but many applications can avoid redundant work by reusing a recent client copy.
With a Cache

sections.title: Reuse an existing response
sections.code:
Open Dashboard
→ request course
→ cache course

Open Course page
→ cache hit
→ render cached course

Return to Dashboard
→ cache hit

sections.text: The application can respond faster and reduce unnecessary network traffic.
A Cache Is Not the Server

sections.title: Authority
sections.code:
Server
↑
authoritative data

Client cache
↓
reusable representation

sections.text: The cache is useful precisely because it is a copy. That also means the copy can become stale.
The Staleness Problem

sections.title: Stale cache
sections.code:
10:00
Server title = "React Basics"
Cache title = "React Basics"

10:05
Another client changes title to "React Foundations"

10:06
Our cache still says:
"React Basics"

→ stale data

sections.text: Caching introduces a tradeoff: fewer requests versus freshness. A production application needs a rule for deciding when cached data is good enough and when it should be refreshed.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not cache forever
sections.text: A cache without an invalidation or refresh strategy can display stale information indefinitely. Reusing data is valuable only when the application has a clear idea of how long that data remains acceptable.
Simple Cache With a Timestamp

sections.title: Cache freshness check

sections.text: This is a simple freshness policy: use a cached value for a limited period, then request a newer version.
Interactive Practice: Cache or Fetch?

sections.title: Caching and Synchronization Playground
sections.instructions: Change the freshness window and request sequence. Observe when the application uses cached data and when it performs a new request. Predict whether each request should hit the cache or the network before running it.

sections.text: Cache Invalidation

A cache can become stale before its normal freshness window expires. When the application knows that a mutation changed a cached resource, it may need to invalidate or update the affected cache entry.

sections.title: Mutation-aware invalidation
sections.code:
Cached course
      ↓
User edits course
      ↓
Server accepts update
      ↓
Invalidate old cache
      ↓
Next read fetches fresh course

sections.text: The exact strategy depends on the application and data layer. The core concept is that a known mutation can make an old client copy unsafe to reuse.
Update the Cache Instead

sections.title: Alternative strategy
sections.code:
User updates course
      ↓
Server returns updated course
      ↓
Replace cached course with returned data
      ↓
Other consumers read the updated value

sections.text: Instead of invalidating and waiting for another request, an application can update its cached representation when the server returns the authoritative updated object.
Three Basic Synchronization Strategies

sections.title: Strategy A — Time-based freshness
sections.code:
Use cache for a defined period
→ refresh after it becomes old

sections.title: Strategy B — Invalidate after mutation
sections.code:
Known update occurs
→ mark cached data stale
→ refetch when needed

sections.title: Strategy C — Update cache from mutation result
sections.code:
Server returns updated resource
→ replace cached copy

sections.text: These strategies can be combined. The appropriate choice depends on the freshness requirements of the data.
Freshness Depends on the Data

sections.title: Different freshness needs
sections.code:
Static course description
→ can tolerate longer cache lifetime

User profile
→ should refresh after profile mutation

Live inventory
→ may require frequent synchronization

Security-sensitive authorization state
→ should not rely blindly on stale client cache

sections.text: There is no universal cache lifetime. The product's data requirements determine the appropriate strategy.
Cache Keys Must Identify the Data

sections.title: Good cache keys
sections.code:
course:react
course:vue
lesson:react:props
lessons?search=hooks

sections.text: The cache key needs to distinguish different requests. If two different queries share the same key accidentally, one response can incorrectly replace or satisfy another.
Drill: Find the Cache Bug

sections.title: Cache Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The cache incorrectly stores every course under the same key and never invalidates after an update. Fix the key and add an invalidation step after a successful update.
sections.initialCode: Bug: every course is cached under the same key 'course'. Fetch 'react', then 'vue' -- notice 'vue' still shows the react data. Fix the key in the code panel.

sections.text: Avoid Global 'Clear Everything' Invalidation
Clearing the entire cache after every small update is simple, but it can destroy useful cached data and cause unnecessary requests.

sections.title: Prefer targeted invalidation
sections.code:
Update course:react
→ invalidate course:react

Do not automatically invalidate:
course:vue
course:angular
unrelated user preferences

sections.text: Synchronization Is More Than Refetching

Synchronization means keeping the client representation consistent enough with the authoritative source for the product's requirements. Refetching is one method, but updating or invalidating known affected data are other methods.
Drill: Choose the Synchronization Strategy

sections.title: Cache Strategy Drill
sections.instructions: Choose the most appropriate basic synchronization strategy for each scenario and explain why. Consider freshness requirements and whether mutations provide updated server data.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A mostly static course description.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario B
A profile editor receives the updated profile from the server after save.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario C
A course title is edited successfully and other pages use a cached copy.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario D
A rapidly changing value must remain close to current.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario E
Two searches use different query parameters.
What must differ?
_______________________________

sections.text: Caching Is Not Persistence

sections.title: Different purposes
sections.code:
Cache
→ reuse data to reduce network work
→ freshness/invalidation matters

Persisted state
→ survive browser reloads
→ lifetime and sensitivity matter

sections.text: A cache may be in memory and disappear on reload. Persisted state may survive reloads even when the value does not represent server data. Do not treat the two concepts as interchangeable.
Debugging Stale Data

sections.title: When the UI shows an old value
sections.code:
1. What cache key was used?
2. Was there a cache hit?
3. How old was the cached value?
4. Did another action mutate the server data?
5. Was the relevant cache entry invalidated?
6. Did the mutation response contain a newer representation?
7. Is another local copy overriding the cache?

sections.text: Use the request timeline and cache state as evidence. The visible stale UI is the symptom; the synchronization policy is often the root cause.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses on loading states and skeletons, especially how to provide stable layout while asynchronous data is arriving.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson teaches basic caching and synchronization strategies. More sophisticated query libraries, cache invalidation frameworks, optimistic updates, and background revalidation are outside the current scope.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why cache client data?' A strong answer is: 'Caching avoids redundant network requests and can make repeated reads faster. But the cached copy can become stale, so the application needs a freshness or invalidation strategy.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you keep cached data synchronized?' Explain that the application can use a freshness window, invalidate affected entries after mutations, or replace cached data with the server's updated response.
Another follow-up is: 'Is clearing the entire cache after every update a good strategy?' It is simple but often too broad. Prefer targeted invalidation when you know which resource changed.
Reflect

Think about a course application. Which data could tolerate a longer cache lifetime? Which data needs immediate synchronization after a mutation? What evidence would tell you that your cache policy is too aggressive or too stale?

sections.title: A cache needs a freshness story

sections.text: Caching is not simply 'keep the last response.' Decide when the cached representation is acceptable, when it becomes stale, and how the application restores consistency.

sections.label: Complete the caching Playground and both repair/strategy drills. The learner must correctly predict cache hits, identify stale data, use meaningful cache keys, and choose a reasonable invalidation or refresh strategy.
sections.hint: Cache for reuse, not forever. Identify the resource precisely, define freshness, and synchronize after known mutations.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Caching reduces redundant network requests by keeping reusable client copies of data. The tradeoff is freshness: a cache can become stale relative to the server. Good caching therefore includes meaningful cache keys plus a freshness or synchronization strategy, such as time-based refresh, targeted invalidation after mutations, or replacing the cache with an updated server response. Caching and persistence solve different problems.

exercises.brief: Predict and verify cache hits and network requests using a simple freshness-window cache.

exercises.title: Cache Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Fix an incorrect cache key and add targeted synchronization after a successful mutation.

exercises.title: Cache Strategy Drill
exercises.brief: Choose an appropriate freshness/invalidation strategy for different data requirements.

quiz.question: Why use a client-side cache?
options: To avoid redundant network requests and reuse recent data.
To make server data permanently authoritative on the client.
To eliminate all need for synchronization.
To ensure data never changes.
quiz.explanation: Caching reuses data and can reduce unnecessary network work.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of caching data indefinitely?
options: The UI may show stale information.
React can no longer render lists.
URLs stop working.
The server automatically deletes the cache.
quiz.explanation: Cached data can become older than the authoritative server data.

quiz.question: What should happen to a cached course after the application successfully updates that course?
options: Always ignore the update.
Invalidate or replace the affected cache entry.
Clear every piece of application state.
Keep the old course forever.
quiz.explanation: A known mutation can make the old cached representation stale.

quiz.question: Why do cache keys need to identify the requested resource?
options: To prevent different resources or queries from incorrectly sharing one cached response.
To make the cache persistent across devices.
To remove the need for HTTP.
To ensure every request is a cache miss.
quiz.explanation: Distinct data needs distinct cache identities.

summary: Client-side caching reduces redundant network requests by reusing recent data, but the cache is only a client representation and can become stale. A robust cache needs meaningful keys and a freshness/synchronization strategy. Basic strategies include time-based freshness, targeted invalidation after mutations, and replacing cached data with the server's updated response. Caching should not be confused with persistence.

title: Loading States and Skeletons
description: Build loading and skeleton interfaces that communicate asynchronous progress clearly while keeping layout stable and reducing perceived wait.
mastery: The learner can implement distinct loading UI, use skeleton placeholders that approximate the eventual layout, preserve layout stability while data loads, and explain why a blank screen or poorly sized loader creates a weak user experience.
learningObjectives: Explain why loading state is part of the application's data flow.
Implement a clear loading state while asynchronous data is unavailable.
Distinguish a loading state from an empty state and an error state.
Build a skeleton UI that approximates the final content layout.
Preserve approximate dimensions during loading to reduce layout shift.
Choose when a skeleton is more appropriate than a simple loading indicator.
Test loading UI against slow responses rather than only fast local requests.

sections.text: Loading Is a Real UI State

The previous lessons traced and cached application data. But a request does not produce data instantly. The interface has a period where it knows what it is trying to load but does not yet have the final content.
That period needs a deliberate visual representation.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Loading UI answers the user's question: 'Is the application working, and what should I expect to appear here?' A skeleton goes further by showing the approximate shape of the incoming content.
The Weakest Loading State

sections.title: Blank while waiting

sections.text: The user receives no feedback. A blank area does not communicate whether the request is in progress, failed, or simply returned no results.
A Basic Loading Indicator

sections.title: Explicit loading state

sections.text: This is already better because the user knows the application is doing work.
Loading Is Not Empty

sections.title: Different meanings
sections.code:
loading
→ data has not arrived yet

empty
→ request completed successfully, but there is no content

error
→ request did not complete successfully

sections.text: These states should not collapse into one generic 'nothing here' interface.
Why Skeletons?

A skeleton approximates the shape of the eventual content. Instead of showing one small spinner while the page structure is unknown, the user sees placeholders where cards, titles, text, and controls are expected.
Layout Stability
A good skeleton approximately reserves the space that the real content will occupy. When the content arrives, the page does not suddenly rearrange itself as dramatically.

sections.title: Without stable space
sections.code:
Loading
→ tiny spinner
→ content appears
→ page jumps

With skeleton
→ placeholder occupies expected area
→ content replaces placeholder
→ smaller visual shift

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not use one tiny spinner for every loading experience
sections.text: A generic spinner can hide the structure of the page and make the layout jump when content arrives. When the final content has a predictable shape, a skeleton can communicate progress while preserving that structure.
Interactive Practice: Toggle Loading

sections.title: Loading States Playground
sections.instructions: Toggle loading, success, empty, and error states. Compare a blank loading state, a spinner/message, and a skeleton. Observe which version best communicates what the user should expect and which keeps the layout stable.

sections.text: Skeletons Should Match the Content

sections.title: Good correspondence
sections.code:
Final card
→ title line
→ metadata line
→ status line
→ action area

Skeleton card
→ title placeholder
→ metadata placeholder
→ status placeholder
→ action placeholder

sections.text: The closer the skeleton matches the structure and approximate dimensions of the real content, the more useful it is for maintaining visual stability.
Do Not Over-Design the Skeleton
A skeleton is a temporary representation. It does not need to reproduce every visual detail of the final component. Its main jobs are to communicate progress and reserve predictable space.
Loading State at Different Granularities

sections.title: Page-level
sections.code:
Entire page waits for initial data
→ page skeleton

sections.title: Section-level
sections.code:
Header is ready
Course content is loading
→ skeleton only the course section

sections.title: Item-level
sections.code:
One expandable card loads independently
→ skeleton only that card

sections.text: Prefer the smallest loading boundary that accurately represents what is actually waiting.
Do Not Blank Out Ready Content
Suppose the page header has already loaded, but a related lesson list is fetching. Replacing the entire page with a spinner throws away information that is already available.

sections.title: Prefer partial loading
sections.code:
Header
✓ ready

Course summary
✓ ready

Lesson list
⏳ loading skeleton

sections.text: Drill: Improve a Loading Experience

sections.title: Skeleton Repair Drill
sections.instructions: Replace the blank/spinner-only loading experience with a section-level skeleton that reserves the same approximate space as the loaded cards. Keep the ready header visible while only the data-dependent section is loading.

sections.text: Skeletons and Accessibility
A loading interface should still communicate its state appropriately to assistive technologies. The visual skeleton should not be the only signal that content is loading.

sections.title: Conceptual loading region
sections.code:
<section
  aria-busy="true"
  aria-label="Loading lessons"
>
  <LessonSkeleton />
  <LessonSkeleton />
</section>

sections.text: The exact accessibility implementation depends on the component, but the principle is consistent: loading status should be meaningful beyond visual decoration.
Slow Network Testing
Loading UI often looks perfect during local development because the request completes almost immediately. Test under delayed network conditions so you can actually observe the loading state.

sections.title: Test deliberately
sections.code:
Fast response
→ verify normal result

Slow response
→ verify loading/skeleton

Very slow response
→ verify the page remains understandable

Failure
→ error state handled separately

sections.text: Avoid Skeleton Flash

If a response is nearly instantaneous, a large skeleton can appear and disappear so quickly that it creates visual noise. Real applications may use thresholds or other strategies to avoid showing a loading state for trivial delays.
The right behavior depends on the interaction and performance characteristics. The lesson's key point is to design loading deliberately rather than blindly rendering a spinner for every request.
Loading Is Part of the Component Contract

sections.title: Data-dependent component
sections.code:
idle
↓
loading
↓
success / empty / error

sections.text: A component that consumes asynchronous data should have an intentional visual response for the period when the data is unavailable.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses on retry behavior and user-facing error recovery. Skeleton design here is about communicating loading; retry logic is a separate concern.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson covers loading representation and layout stability. Error recovery, retry timing, and backoff are handled next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why use skeletons instead of a spinner?' A strong answer is: 'A skeleton communicates the expected structure of the incoming content and can preserve approximate layout dimensions, which reduces perceived waiting and visual layout shifts.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Should every request show a skeleton?' No. The loading treatment should match the granularity and importance of the content. A section-level skeleton may be better than blanking the entire page.
Another follow-up is: 'How is loading different from empty?' Loading means the request has not produced final data yet; empty means the request succeeded but there is no matching content.
Reflect

Look at the multi-page application you built earlier. Which areas could load independently? Where would a page-level skeleton be appropriate, and where would a section-level skeleton provide a better experience?

sections.title: Show the shape of what is coming

sections.text: A useful skeleton does not merely say 'wait.' It gives the user a stable visual model of where the incoming content will appear.

sections.label: Complete the loading Playground and skeleton repair drill. The learner must correctly distinguish loading from empty/error, produce a layout-stable skeleton, and keep unrelated ready content visible.
sections.hint: Loading = data not ready. Empty = successful request with no content. Skeleton = approximate the final layout so the interface remains stable.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Loading is a real application state that deserves deliberate UI. Skeletons are especially useful when the final content has a predictable shape because they communicate progress while reserving approximate space and reducing layout shifts. Prefer the smallest loading boundary that matches the actual pending data, keep already-ready content visible, and distinguish loading clearly from empty and error states.

exercises.title: Loading States Playground
exercises.brief: Toggle loading, success, empty, and error states and compare blank, spinner, and skeleton-based loading experiences.

exercises.title: Skeleton Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Replace a spinner-only section with a layout-stable skeleton while keeping unrelated ready UI visible.

quiz.question: What does a loading state communicate?
options: The application is waiting for data or work to complete.
The request successfully returned zero results.
The server permanently deleted the data.
The component has no UI.
quiz.explanation: Loading means the final result is not available yet.

quiz.question: Why can a skeleton be better than a generic spinner?
options: It communicates the expected content structure and can reduce layout shifts.
It guarantees faster network requests.
It replaces error handling.
It makes all data local.
quiz.explanation: Skeletons provide structural context and reserve approximate content space.

quiz.question: Which state means a request completed successfully but no content matched?
options: Loading.
Empty.
Error.
Pending.
quiz.explanation: Empty is a successful result with zero matching content.

quiz.question: What is generally better when only one section of a page is waiting for data?
options: Blank the entire page.
Show a loading/skeleton state only for the affected section.
Hide the browser.
Persist the old loading state forever.
quiz.explanation: Partial loading preserves useful content that is already ready.

summary: Loading states communicate that asynchronous work is in progress. Skeletons can improve the experience when the final content has a predictable structure because they reserve approximate space and reduce layout shifts. Loading must remain distinct from empty and error states. Prefer appropriately scoped loading boundaries and keep already-ready content visible instead of blanking the entire interface.

Why use a skeleton instead of only a spinner?
How does a skeleton reduce layout shift?
What is the difference between loading, empty, and error?
Should an entire page be replaced by a loading state when only one section is waiting?
How would you test loading UI realistically?
What makes a good skeleton?
How can loading states be communicated accessibly?

title: Retries and Error States
description: Build resilient data-fetching flows that distinguish transient failures from permanent errors, provide clear user-facing recovery, and retry deliberately rather than indefinitely.
mastery: The learner can represent an error state explicitly, implement bounded retry behavior, provide a clear manual recovery action, and explain why retrying indefinitely can hide failures and waste resources.
learningObjectives: Explain why production interfaces need explicit error states.
Distinguish transient failures from errors that should be shown immediately.
Implement bounded retry behavior for a failed request.
Provide a user-visible retry action.
Explain why retrying indefinitely is dangerous.
Use retry limits or stopping conditions.
Preserve useful UI context while a data section is unavailable.
Explain the difference between a loading state, empty state, and error state.

sections.text: A Failed Request Is Part of the Product

Network requests fail. Connections drop, servers temporarily become unavailable, requests time out, and services return errors. A production interface should treat these outcomes as part of normal application behavior rather than as impossible exceptions.
The goal is not to make failures invisible. The goal is to make them understandable and recoverable.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A robust data request has at least three user-facing outcomes: loading, success/empty, and error. Some errors are transient and may justify a bounded retry; others need a clear error message or corrective action.
Error Is Not Empty

sections.title: Different meanings
sections.code:
Loading
→ still waiting

Empty
→ request succeeded, no matching data

Error
→ request failed or could not produce usable data

sections.text: A failed request should not silently become an empty list because that can mislead the user into thinking the data simply does not exist.
A Basic Error State

sections.title: Explicit failure UI

sections.text: This keeps the meaning of the request outcome explicit.
Not Every Error Should Retry

sections.title: Potentially transient
sections.code:
Temporary network interruption
Temporary service outage
Request timeout
Rate-limited request

sections.title: Likely not fixed by immediate retry
sections.code:
Invalid request parameters
Permission denied
Authentication failure
Resource does not exist

sections.text: Retrying a request makes sense only when another attempt has a reasonable chance of succeeding without first requiring a different user or application action.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not retry forever
sections.text: Indefinite retries can create request storms, waste bandwidth, hide a real failure, and prevent the user from understanding that intervention is required.
A Bounded Retry

sections.title: Simple retry loop

sections.text: The stopping condition is the important part: after the retry budget is exhausted, the application surfaces the failure instead of continuing indefinitely.
Backoff Spaces Out Attempts

sections.title: Simple exponential backoff
sections.code:
Attempt 1
→ wait 250ms

Attempt 2
→ wait 500ms

Attempt 3
→ wait 1000ms

Then stop

sections.text: A delay between retries can reduce pressure on a temporarily unavailable service. The exact timing policy depends on the application and infrastructure.
Interactive Practice: Retry a Failing Request

sections.title: Retry and Error-State Playground
sections.instructions: Use the mock request to simulate failures before success. Add bounded retry behavior and expose the final failure with a Try again action. Observe how the number of attempts changes with different retry limits.

sections.text: Manual Retry Is Part of Recovery

After automatic retry attempts are exhausted, the user should usually have a clear way to try again. A retry button also tells the user that the application recognizes the problem rather than silently waiting forever.

sections.title: Simple recovery UI

sections.text: Error Messages Should Be Useful

sections.title: Weak
sections.code: Something went wrong.

sections.title: Better
sections.code:
We couldn't load your lessons.
Check your connection and try again.

sections.text: The user needs enough information to understand the current situation and decide what to do next.
Do Not Hide Useful Context
If the header and course summary are already loaded, an error in the lesson list does not necessarily mean the entire page should disappear.

sections.title: Partial failure
sections.code:
Header
✓ available

Course summary
✓ available

Lesson list
⚠ failed
→ Try again

sections.text: Error boundaries and data-specific error states can be scoped to the part of the application that actually failed. React's Error Boundary mechanism is appropriate for render-time errors; data request failures can also be represented directly in the data-loading state. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Error Boundaries Are a Different Mechanism

A network request failing and a component throwing during rendering are not necessarily the same kind of failure. React Error Boundaries handle errors thrown during rendering, while request logic should generally expose request failures through its data/error state. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

sections.title: Conceptual separation
sections.code:
Data request fails
→ request error state
→ show retry/error UI

Component render throws
→ Error Boundary
→ show component-level fallback

sections.text: Retry State Needs a Clear Lifecycle

sections.title: Typical lifecycle
sections.code:
idle
 ↓
loading
 ↓
retrying
 ├── success
 └── exhausted
      ↓
    error
      ↓
 manual retry

sections.text: The exact state machine can be simpler, but the UI should make the current phase understandable.
Drill 1: Repair Infinite Retry

sections.title: Retry Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The request below retries forever after failure. Add a bounded retry budget, expose the final error, and provide a manual Try again control.
sections.initialCode:
(not run yet)

The always-failing button is capped at 20 attempts here so it can't actually hang your browser -- but notice it still burns through all 20 before this simulator gives up. Add a real retry budget in the code panel.

sections.text: Retry Budgets and User Intent
Automatic retries should be small and deliberate. Manual retry represents a new user decision and can restart the request process after the automatic budget has been exhausted.
Not Every HTTP Error Should Be Retried

sections.title: Illustrative decision
sections.code:
Temporary network problem
→ retry may help

Server unavailable
→ retry may help

Invalid request
→ fix request; retrying unchanged request won't help

Not found
→ show missing-resource state

Permission denied
→ user/application action may be required

sections.text: The exact retry policy depends on the API and application. The important principle is that retrying should have a reason.
Error UI Should Preserve Recovery

sections.title: Recovery loop
sections.code:
Request fails
    ↓
Explain failure
    ↓
Offer recovery
    ↓
Retry
    ↓
Success OR another explicit failure

sections.text: Drill 2: Choose the Correct Response

sections.title: Error Strategy Drill
sections.instructions: For each failure, decide whether to automatically retry, show an immediate error, or require a different user/action path. Explain the reason.

Scenario A
A request times out once, then the network is available again.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario B
The API returns 404 for /lessons/999.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario C
The API rejects a malformed request with validation errors.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario D
A server temporarily returns a 503.
Strategy: ______________________
Why: ___________________________

Scenario E

Next action: ____________________

sections.text: Loading, Retry, Error, and Empty Together

sections.title: Complete request model
sections.code:
idle
 ↓
loading
 ↓
 ├── success + data
 ├── success + empty
 └── transient failure
       ↓
    bounded retry
       ├── success
       └── exhausted → error + recovery

sections.text: Thinking about these states together produces a much more robust data-loading experience than treating the request as simply 'data or no data.'
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson moves from request behavior to data structure: normalized state. It addresses duplicated nested entities and how a flat ID-keyed representation makes updates more consistent.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson covers retry policy and user-facing recovery. More advanced resilience techniques such as optimistic updates, circuit breakers, and sophisticated retry libraries are outside the current scope.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you handle a failed network request?' A strong answer is: 'I would represent the failure explicitly, distinguish transient failures from permanent ones, use a small bounded retry policy when retrying is reasonable, and then expose a clear manual recovery action if automatic attempts fail.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why not retry forever?' Because it can waste resources, create request storms, hide the actual failure, and keep the user from understanding that intervention is needed.

Another follow-up is: 'Are render errors and request errors the same?' No. React Error Boundaries are designed to catch render-time errors, while request failures are normally represented as part of the data/request state. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Reflect
Look at the data-loading flows in your earlier projects. Which failures are likely transient? Which failures require the user to change something before another attempt can succeed?
A good error state does more than announce that something broke. It tells the user what happened, preserves useful context, and provides the next reasonable recovery action.

sections.label: Complete the retry Playground and both drills. The learner must implement bounded retries, expose an explicit final error state, provide manual recovery, and distinguish transient failures from failures that should not be retried automatically.
sections.hint: Retry only when another attempt has a reasonable chance of success. Bound the attempts, then explain the failure and offer recovery.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Network failures are normal application states and should be represented explicitly. Retry transient failures cautiously with a finite budget, then expose the error and a manual recovery path. Do not retry indefinitely or retry unchanged requests when the underlying problem is permanent. Keep request errors distinct from render-time errors handled by Error Boundaries, and preserve already-working UI when only one data section has failed.

exercises.brief: Replace an infinite retry loop with a bounded retry strategy and explicit final failure.
