exercises.brief: Choose appropriate retry or recovery behavior for transient, validation, missing-resource, and service-unavailable failures.

quiz.question: Why should automatic retries be bounded?
options: To prevent endless requests and make failure eventually visible.
Because APIs can never succeed twice.
To hide network problems.
Because retry logic only works once.
quiz.explanation: A finite retry budget prevents request storms and allows the UI to surface a real failure.

quiz.question: Which failure is the strongest candidate for automatic retry?
options: A malformed request.
A 404 missing resource.
A temporary timeout or service-unavailable response.
A permission error that requires user action.
quiz.explanation: Transient network/service failures may succeed when retried later.

quiz.question: What should happen after the automatic retry budget is exhausted?
options: Keep retrying silently.
Show an explicit error and provide a reasonable recovery action.
Pretend the request returned empty data.
Clear the entire application state.
quiz.explanation: The user should understand that the automatic attempts failed and be given a way to retry deliberately.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of a React Error Boundary?
options: Catch errors thrown during React rendering and show fallback UI.
Retry every failed network request.
Cache API responses.
Validate every URL parameter.
quiz.explanation: React Error Boundaries handle render-time errors; request failures are generally represented separately in request/data state. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}

summary: Retries and error states make asynchronous interfaces resilient to failure. Explicitly distinguish loading, success/empty, and error outcomes. Retry only failures that are plausibly transient, keep the automatic retry budget finite, and then provide clear error messaging and a manual recovery path. Do not confuse request failures with render-time errors handled by React Error Boundaries.

Which failures are appropriate for automatic retry?
Why should retries be bounded?
What is exponential backoff?
What should the user see after retries are exhausted?
How do request errors differ from render-time errors?
What is the role of an Error Boundary?
How would you preserve useful page content when one data section fails?

title: Data Normalization
description: Learn to represent related application entities in flat, ID-keyed structures so each entity has one canonical copy and updates remain consistent across the interface.
mastery: The learner can identify duplicated nested entities, normalize them into ID-keyed collections with relationship references, read normalized data back into useful UI shapes, and explain why normalization reduces inconsistent updates.
learningObjectives: Explain what data normalization means in client application state.
Identify duplicated nested entities in application data.
Convert nested entity data into flat ID-keyed collections.
Represent relationships with IDs instead of duplicated objects.
Read normalized data back into a view model for rendering.
Update one canonical entity without manually synchronizing duplicated copies.
Recognize when normalization is beneficial and when a simpler structure is sufficient.
Explain how normalized data supports consistent updates.

sections.text: Why Data Shape Matters
The previous lessons focused on how data moves and how interfaces recover from network problems. This lesson focuses on what the data looks like once it reaches the client.
When related entities are nested repeatedly, the same entity can appear in several places. Updating one copy can then leave the others stale.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Normalize shared entities into flat ID-keyed collections. Store each entity once, then represent relationships with IDs. Build the nested shape needed by a component when you read the data.
The Duplication Problem

sections.title: Nested duplicated data

sections.text: The instructor object appears once for every lesson. If Ada's name or other information changes, the application may have multiple copies to update.
Normalized Representation

sections.title: Flat entities

sections.text: Each entity has one canonical copy. Relationships are represented by IDs.
Why the Update Gets Easier

sections.title: Nested duplication
sections.code:
Update Ada
→ find every lesson containing Ada
→ update every nested copy
→ hope none were missed

sections.title: Normalized
sections.code:
Update instructorsById.ada
→ every consumer reading instructor id 'ada'
  sees the same canonical entity

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not duplicate shared entities because nesting looks convenient
sections.text: If the same entity appears in several places in application state, copying the full object into every location creates multiple sources of truth. Normalize shared entities when that duplication makes updates difficult or inconsistent.
Normalization Is Not 'Flatten Everything'
The goal is not to remove all nesting from every object. Normalize entities that are shared, independently updated, or referenced in multiple places. A simple local object may not need normalization.

sections.title: Good candidate
sections.code:
User appears in:
Header
Course cards
Comments
Settings

sections.title: Probably unnecessary
sections.code: One local form's temporary validation message

sections.title: Common normalized shape

sections.text: An object keyed by ID provides direct access to a canonical entity and makes updates straightforward.
Relationships Become References

Reading Normalized Data

sections.title: Resolve a lesson view

sections.text: The UI can reconstruct the nested relationship when it needs it. Normalized state optimizes the source-of-truth model; the rendered view does not have to look normalized.
View Models Can Be Nested

Normalized state
      ↓
selector / lookup
      ↓
view model

component

sections.text: This separation lets the application store canonical entities efficiently while still giving components the convenient shape they need to render.

sections.text: Normalized Updates Are More Predictable

sections.title: One canonical update

sections.text: Every comment referencing u1 can now resolve the updated user. There is no second user object that needs manual synchronization.
Normalize Collections When Relationships Matter
Normalization becomes particularly useful when entities participate in many relationships or appear in multiple collections.

sections.title: Example relationship graph
sections.code:
User
 ├── comments
 ├── enrollments
 └── saved lessons

Lesson
 ├── course
 ├── instructor
 └── comments

sections.text: Duplicating entire objects through each relationship can cause a graph of overlapping copies. IDs let the application represent the graph without duplicating the entities themselves.
Do Not Normalize Purely Local Data

sections.title: Probably not worth normalizing
sections.code:
Form state
Temporary animation state
One component's local configuration
One-off UI messages

sections.text: Normalization adds indirection. Use it when that indirection solves real duplication or update-consistency problems.

sections.text: Normalization and Selectors
Normalized state often works naturally with selectors. A selector can resolve IDs into the view model that a component needs.

sections.title: Resolve course lessons

sections.text: The store remains normalized while the component receives a convenient array.
Normalization and Caching
A client cache can also benefit from normalized data because multiple cached responses may refer to the same entity. A canonical entity representation makes targeted updates easier to reason about.

sections.title: Shared entity
sections.code:
Course list cache
      ↘
       coursesById.react
      ↗
Course detail cache

sections.text: The same course can be referenced by multiple views without requiring independent copies of the entire entity.
Normalization Is an Implementation Strategy

You do not need to normalize every API response at the network boundary. The useful question is whether the application's state representation benefits from canonical entities and explicit relationships.
Debugging Normalized Data

sections.title: When a relationship renders incorrectly
sections.code:
1. Does the parent collection contain the expected ID?
2. Does the referenced entity exist in its byId collection?
3. Is the relationship ID correct?
4. Is the selector resolving the right entity?
5. Is the UI accidentally using stale duplicated data?

sections.text: Normalization changes the debugging path: inspect IDs and entity maps instead of searching through many nested object copies.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson is synthesis practice. It combines normalization with the module's other resilience techniques: caching, loading, and error handling.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Normalization is about data shape and canonical entity representation. It does not by itself solve fetching, caching freshness, retries, or UI resilience.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is data normalization?' A strong answer is: 'It means storing shared entities once in flat ID-keyed collections and representing relationships with IDs, rather than duplicating full nested objects in multiple places.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why is that useful?' Because one canonical entity can be updated once, and every consumer that references it can resolve the same current version.
Another follow-up is: 'Should every object be normalized?' No. Normalization adds indirection, so it is most useful for shared, independently updated, or repeatedly nested entities.
Reflect
Take a data shape from one of your previous projects. Find one entity that appears in multiple nested locations. What inconsistency could happen if one copy changed but another did not?
When the same domain entity appears in many places, store it once and reference it by ID. Let selectors build the nested view that the UI needs.

sections.label: Complete the normalization Playground and both drills. The learner must convert duplicated nested entities into flat ID-keyed collections, reconstruct a useful view through lookups, and correctly identify cases where normalization is or is not justified.
sections.hint: Shared entity → one canonical byId record. Relationships → IDs. UI shape → reconstruct through selectors/lookups.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Data normalization keeps shared entities in flat ID-keyed collections and represents relationships through IDs. This creates one canonical copy of each entity, making updates more consistent and reducing synchronization bugs caused by duplicated nested objects. Components can reconstruct convenient nested view models through selectors. Normalize when shared relationships and repeated entities justify the added indirection, not every piece of data by default.

quiz.question: What is the main goal of normalizing application data?
options: Store shared entities once and reference them by ID.
Remove all objects from the application.
Make every API response smaller.
Prevent all network requests.
quiz.explanation: Normalization reduces duplicated entity copies and creates a canonical representation.

quiz.question: What should a relationship usually contain in normalized data?
options: A complete duplicated object.
An entity ID/reference.
A random array index.
A rendered JSX element.
quiz.explanation: IDs connect entities while each entity remains canonical in its own collection.

quiz.question: When is normalization especially useful?
options: For a temporary local message.
When the same independently updated entity appears in many places.
For every boolean in a form.
Only when using CSS modules.
quiz.explanation: Shared and repeatedly referenced entities are strong candidates for normalization.

quiz.question: How can a component get a convenient nested view from normalized state?
options: By duplicating the entire entity tree back into state.
By resolving IDs through selectors or lookup functions.
By storing every relationship twice.
By ignoring the relationships.
quiz.explanation: Selectors/lookups can assemble the view model needed for rendering from canonical normalized entities.

summary: Data normalization represents shared application entities once in flat ID-keyed collections and uses IDs to express relationships. This avoids duplicated nested objects and makes updates consistent because consumers resolve the same canonical entity. Selectors can reconstruct convenient nested view models for the UI. Normalization is most valuable when entities are shared, independently updated, or referenced repeatedly; simple local data does not need to be normalized automatically.
interviewQuestions: What is data normalization?
Why is duplicated nested entity data dangerous?
How do ID-keyed collections improve updates?
How do you reconstruct a nested view from normalized state?
When is normalization worth the added indirection?
Should all application data be normalized?
How can normalization work with selectors?
How can normalized data make cache updates easier to reason about?

title: Building Resilient Interfaces
description: Apply caching, loading states, retries, error handling, and normalized data together so individual failures remain contained and the interface continues to provide useful functionality.
mastery: The learner can build a data-driven interface that handles slow and failed requests gracefully, uses cached data appropriately, keeps normalized entities consistent, and isolates partial failures so one unavailable data source does not blank the entire application.
learningObjectives: Apply caching, loading, retry, error, and normalization patterns together.
Design interfaces that continue working when one data source fails.
Keep loading and error boundaries scoped to the affected data section.
Reuse cached data while managing freshness.
Retry transient failures with a finite budget.
Represent related entities without duplicated nested copies.
Provide useful fallback UI while preserving available content.
Debug a resilient interface by tracing each data source independently.

sections.text: Now Combine the Techniques

The previous lessons taught each technique separately: caching, loading states, retries, error handling, and normalization. This lesson is practice-focused. The goal is to use those techniques together in an interface where not everything succeeds at the same time.

sections.title: The rule
sections.text: A resilient interface expects partial failure. Keep useful sections available, isolate failing data sources, make loading and recovery explicit, and keep the underlying data representation consistent.
The Fragile Interface

sections.title: Everything depends on one request
sections.code:
Dashboard request fails
        ↓
Entire page crashes / blanks
        ↓
User loses every piece of information

sections.text: This design assumes the entire page has one success state. Production interfaces often have several independent data sources that can succeed or fail separately.
A More Resilient Model

sections.title: Independent data sections
sections.code:
Header
✓ available

Course summary
✓ available

Progress
⚠ temporarily unavailable
→ Retry

Recommended lessons
✓ cached data available

sections.text: The user still has useful information and can understand what is unavailable.
Practice Rule 1: Boundaries Match Data Dependencies

sections.title: Separate request state
sections.code:
courseState
→ loading / success / error

progressState
→ loading / success / error

recommendationsState
→ loading / cached / error

sections.text: Do not create one global loading/error flag when separate parts of the interface depend on different requests.
Practice Rule 2: Cached Data Can Be Better Than Blank Data

sections.title: Stale-while-revalidate style experience
sections.code:
Cached content exists
        ↓
Render cached content
        ↓
Request fresh data
        ↓
Fresh data succeeds
→ replace cached content

Fresh request fails
→ keep useful cached content
→ show refresh/error indication

sections.text: A cached response can allow the interface to remain useful while a fresh request runs or temporarily fails.
Practice Rule 3: Retry Only the Failing Operation

sections.title: Partial recovery
sections.code:
Progress request fails
        ↓
Retry Progress only

Do not refetch:
Header
Course summary
Lesson list
unless they actually need refreshing

sections.text: Targeted retries preserve successful work and reduce unnecessary network traffic.
Practice Rule 4: Keep Data Canonical

sections.title: Normalized entity data
sections.code:
coursesById
lessonsById
usersById

Components resolve relationships
→ no duplicated nested entities

sections.text: Resilience becomes harder when every feature keeps its own nested copy of the same entity. A canonical normalized representation makes updates and recovery easier to reason about.

sections.text: The Resilient Interface Checklist

sections.title: Review before calling it production-ready
sections.code:
DATA FLOW
□ Know the source of truth for each data value.
□ Cache only when reuse is useful.
□ Have a freshness/synchronization strategy.

LOADING
□ Loading state is explicit.
□ Skeleton/placeholder matches the affected content.
□ Ready UI is not unnecessarily blanked.

ERRORS
□ Error state is explicit.
□ Transient failures have bounded retry.
□ User has a recovery action after exhaustion.
□ One failed section does not automatically destroy unrelated sections.

DATA SHAPE
□ Shared entities have a canonical representation.
□ Relationships use IDs when normalization is justified.
□ UI reconstructs the view it needs.

TESTING
□ Slow response tested.
□ Failed request tested.
□ Retry exhaustion tested.
□ Cache-hit behavior tested.
□ Partial failure tested.

sections.text: The Main Failure Mode

sections.title: Do not treat the page as one giant success/failure switch
sections.text: A resilient interface assumes that different parts of the page can be in different states at the same time: one can be ready, another loading, another showing cached data, and another recovering from an error.
Production Thinking

sections.title: What users actually experience
sections.code:
Fast network
→ content appears quickly

Slow network
→ stable loading UI

Transient failure
→ limited retry

Persistent failure
→ clear error + recovery

Partial outage
→ unaffected sections remain usable

Stale cache
→ useful existing content + refresh path

sections.text: This is what resilience means in practice: the interface remains useful under imperfect conditions instead of assuming that every request succeeds immediately.
Debugging a Resilient Interface

sections.title: Trace the failing boundary
sections.code:
1. Which data source failed?
2. Was there usable cached data?
3. What loading state did the section enter?
4. Was a retry appropriate?
5. Was the retry bounded?
6. What did the user see after failure?
7. Did unrelated data remain usable?
8. Is duplicated data causing inconsistent rendering?

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson is the module capstone: a production data project combining caching, loading/error handling, and normalized data into one feature.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is synthesis practice. It intentionally introduces no new major data-flow theory; the capstone next applies the same techniques end-to-end.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What makes a data-driven interface resilient?' A strong answer is: 'It assumes slow and failed requests are normal. It isolates data dependencies, shows scoped loading and error states, retries transient failures within a limit, reuses cached data appropriately, and preserves unaffected parts of the UI.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What happens if one request fails?' Say that the failure should usually be isolated to the affected section when the rest of the page remains useful.
Another follow-up is: 'Why normalize in a resilient application?' Because canonical entities reduce duplicate representations, making updates and recovery more predictable across multiple consumers.
Reflect
Imagine the progress API for your dashboard is down while the lesson list and course summary work normally. What should the user still be able to do? Sketch the UI state for each section.
A failure should affect no more of the interface than the failed dependency requires. Preserve successful work and make recovery local to the failed operation.

sections.label: Complete all three resilience Playground drills without hints. The learner must isolate partial failures, preserve useful cached content during refresh failures, and correctly normalize related entities.
sections.hint: Separate data boundaries, preserve usable content, bound retries, and keep one canonical copy of shared entities.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Resilient interfaces combine the module's individual data-flow techniques. Independent data sections should have independent loading and error boundaries. Cached content can keep the UI useful during revalidation, retries should target transient failures and remain bounded, and shared entities should have one canonical representation when normalization is justified. The central principle is graceful partial failure: preserve everything that still works and isolate what does not.

quiz.question: What should happen when one independent dashboard request fails?
options: Blank the entire application.
Isolate the failure to the affected section when possible.
Hide all cached data.
Retry every request in the application forever.
quiz.explanation: Resilient interfaces preserve unaffected content and scope failure to its dependency.

quiz.question: What can a client do when fresh data fails but usable cached data exists?
options: Erase the cached content immediately.
Keep the cached content visible and expose the refresh/error state.
Pretend the request succeeded with fresh data.
Retry every unrelated request.
quiz.explanation: Useful cached content can preserve continuity while the client communicates that fresh data is unavailable.

quiz.question: Why should retries target the failing operation?
options: To preserve successful data and avoid unnecessary network work.
To make all requests fail together.
Because other requests cannot be cached.
Because retrying unrelated requests improves normalization.
quiz.explanation: Targeted recovery preserves successful work and limits unnecessary network traffic.

quiz.question: What is the value of normalized entities in a resilient interface?
options: Every component gets a private copy.
Shared entities have one canonical representation, reducing inconsistent updates across consumers.
Normalization eliminates loading states.
Normalization automatically retries requests.
quiz.explanation: Canonical entities make updates more predictable when multiple views reference the same data.

summary: Building resilient interfaces is synthesis practice across the module. Keep data dependencies independent, provide scoped loading and error states, use bounded targeted retries, preserve usable cached data during refresh failures, and normalize shared entities where duplication would create inconsistency. A resilient UI does not require every request to succeed; it preserves useful functionality and isolates failures to the smallest reasonable boundary.

What should the UI do when cached data exists but refresh fails?
Why should retries target individual failed operations?
How do loading and error boundaries follow data dependencies?
Why does normalized data help resilient applications?
How would you test an interface under partial network failure?
What does graceful degradation mean in a frontend application?

title: Production Data Project
description: Build a production-style data-driven feature that applies the module's caching, loading/error handling, and normalized-data techniques together.
mastery: The learner can deliver a working production-style feature that applies caching, loading and error handling, and normalized data, while demonstrating that the interface behaves correctly under slow and failed network conditions.

Implement caching where repeated data access benefits from reuse.
Provide deliberate loading and error states.
Handle transient failures without retrying indefinitely.
Use normalized data where duplicated entities would create inconsistent updates.
Test the feature under slow network conditions.
Test the feature under failed network conditions.
Explain the architecture and tradeoffs behind the implementation.

sections.text: Module Capstone
This is the capstone for Data Flow and Application Data. The preceding lessons have already taught the individual techniques. Your task is to combine them into one production-style feature.
The project is intentionally a requirements brief rather than another theory lesson.

sections.title: Project goal
sections.text: Build a production-style data-driven feature that demonstrates caching, loading/error handling, and normalized data. Your implementation should remain useful when the network is slow or when one or more requests fail.
Core Requirements

sections.title: Required capabilities
sections.code:
CACHING
□ Reuse previously fetched data where appropriate.
□ Use meaningful cache identities/keys.
□ Have an explicit freshness or synchronization strategy.
□ Do not allow stale cached data to remain indefinitely without a policy.

LOADING
□ Show intentional loading UI.
□ Loading UI should preserve useful layout where practical.
□ Distinguish loading from empty and error states.

ERROR HANDLING
□ Show a clear error state when data cannot be loaded.
□ Retry transient failures deliberately.
□ Automatic retries must be bounded.
□ Provide a useful recovery path after failure.
□ One failed section must not unnecessarily destroy unrelated working UI.

DATA SHAPE
□ Normalize shared entities where duplication would create inconsistent copies.
□ Represent relationships with IDs where normalization is justified.
□ Keep one canonical representation of shared entities.

TESTING
□ Test slow responses.
□ Test request failures.
□ Test retry exhaustion.
□ Test cache reuse.
□ Test partial failure.
□ Test successful recovery.

sections.text: Choose a Production-Style Feature

The source plan specifies a production-style feature rather than a single mandated application domain. Choose a feature substantial enough to exercise all three required techniques: caching, resilient loading/error handling, and normalized data.

+
At least one relationship between entities
+
At least one asynchronous request
+
At least one operation that can fail

Enough UI surface to demonstrate partial loading/failure

sections.text: Required Test Matrix

sections.title: Do not submit without these tests
sections.code:
CACHE
□ First request goes to the network/source.
□ Repeated eligible request can reuse cached data.
□ Cache identity distinguishes different resources/queries.
□ Refresh/invalidation policy is observable or explainable.

LOADING
□ Slow response displays intentional loading UI.
□ Loaded layout does not unexpectedly jump.
□ Loading state is scoped to the affected data.

ERROR
□ Failed request produces an explicit error state.
□ User receives a recovery action.

RETRY
□ Transient failure can recover within the retry budget.
□ Retry budget is finite.
□ Exhausted retries become an explicit failure.

NORMALIZATION
□ Shared entities are not duplicated unnecessarily.
□ Relationship lookups resolve the correct canonical entity.

PARTIAL FAILURE
□ One failed source does not blank unrelated successful content.

RECOVERY
□ A successful retry restores the appropriate UI state.
□ Client/cache state is synchronized appropriately after recovery.

sections.text: Network Simulation
The source explicitly warns against optimizing for the happy path. Your test harness should make imperfect conditions easy to trigger.

sections.title: Useful development controls
sections.code:
Normal
Slow
Fail once
Fail repeatedly
Return stale cached data
Return updated data
Fail only one section

sections.text: These controls make the resilience characteristics of the implementation observable during review.
Quality Review

sections.title: Before submission
sections.code:
DATA FLOW
□ Source of truth is documented.
□ Client cache is not treated as permanently authoritative.

CACHE
□ Cache keys are meaningful.
□ Freshness/invalidation behavior is deliberate.

LOADING
□ Loading UI is scoped and stable.

ERRORS
□ Failure is visible.
□ Recovery is available.
□ Retries are bounded.

DATA SHAPE
□ Shared entities have one canonical representation when normalized.
□ UI reads are derived from canonical data.

RESILIENCE
□ Partial failure is handled.
□ Slow responses are handled.
□ Happy path is not the only tested path.

sections.text: Architecture Review

sections.title: Defend the design
sections.code:
Why did you cache this data?
_______________________________

What makes a cache entry stale?
_______________________________

How do you synchronize after mutation?
_______________________________

Why is this entity normalized?
_______________________________

Which failures are retryable?
_______________________________

Why is the retry budget finite?
_______________________________

Why does this loading/error state belong to this section?
_______________________________

What remains usable when one request fails?
_______________________________

sections.text: Anti-Patterns to Check

sections.title: Reject these designs
sections.code:
□ Cache forever with no freshness policy.
□ Retry forever.
□ Turn a failed request into an empty success state.
□ Blank the entire page because one section failed.
□ Duplicate the same entity in several nested structures.
□ Use one global loading/error flag for unrelated requests.
□ Optimize only for fast successful requests.
□ Add complexity without being able to explain the data-flow reason.

sections.text: Manual/Rubric Review
This capstone is manually/rubric graded. Functionality and code quality both matter.

sections.title: Evaluation dimensions
sections.code:
FUNCTIONALITY
→ cache behavior
→ loading behavior
→ error/retry behavior
→ normalized data behavior
→ partial-failure behavior

CODE QUALITY
→ clear ownership
→ understandable data flow
→ appropriate boundaries
→ deliberate synchronization
→ maintainable data shape

sections.text: Reflection

Identify the most important resilience decision in your project. Was it the cache policy, error boundary, retry strategy, normalized data shape, or partial-failure design? Explain what would have gone wrong with the simpler but less resilient alternative.

Production-quality data interfaces are not defined only by what happens when every request succeeds. They are defined by how useful and understandable the interface remains when the network is slow, stale, or failing.

sections.label: Submit the Production Data Project for manual/rubric grading. The output must demonstrate caching, loading/error handling, normalized data, and deliberate behavior under slow and failed network conditions. Evaluation covers functionality and code quality.
sections.hint: Do not optimize only for the happy path. Make cache behavior, slow loading, retry exhaustion, partial failure, and recovery observable and testable.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The Production Data Project is the synthesis point for Module 4-2. A strong feature uses caching to avoid needless requests while managing freshness, gives asynchronous data deliberate loading and error states, retries transient failures within a finite budget, and normalizes shared entities when duplication would create inconsistent state. The project must be evaluated under slow and failed network conditions, not only the happy path.

exercises.title: Production Data Architecture Planner
exercises.brief: Plan the feature's data flow, caching policy, normalization, loading/error boundaries, retry policy, and synchronization strategy before implementation.

exercises.title: Production Data Project
exercises.brief: Implement the complete production-style feature and exercise its cache, loading, retry, error, normalization, and partial-failure behavior.

exercises.title: Resilience Test Matrix
exercises.brief: Verify slow responses, failed requests, retry exhaustion, cache reuse, partial failure, and successful recovery.

quiz.question: What is the central requirement of the Production Data Project?
options: Optimize only the fast successful path.
Build a production-style feature combining caching, loading/error handling, and normalized data.
Put every response in global state.
Avoid all client-side caching.
quiz.explanation: The capstone synthesizes the module's data-flow and resilience techniques.

quiz.question: What condition must the capstone explicitly be tested against?
options: Only an ideal fast network.
Slow and failed network conditions.
Only an empty database.
Only a large screen.
quiz.explanation: The project is specifically intended to demonstrate production behavior under imperfect network conditions.

quiz.question: What should happen when one independent data source fails while another has already succeeded?
options: Blank the whole page automatically.
Keep successful content usable and isolate the failed section where possible.
Retry every request forever.
Treat the failed request as an empty success.
quiz.explanation: Resilience means preserving useful functionality and containing failures.

quiz.question: What is a key reason to test slow and failed network conditions?
options: To prove the happy path works twice.
To verify that the interface remains useful and understandable when requests do not behave ideally.
To eliminate the need for error states.
To make caching unnecessary.
quiz.explanation: Production-style resilience is measured under imperfect conditions, not only successful fast responses.

summary: The Production Data Project is the Module 4-2 capstone. It requires a production-style feature that combines caching, loading/error handling, retries, and normalized data. The project must be tested under slow and failed network conditions and should preserve useful functionality during partial failure. The source explicitly emphasizes both functionality and code quality in the manual/rubric evaluation.

Why did you choose the cache policy you used?
How do you decide when cached data is stale?
