How did you isolate partial failures?
Why did you normalize some entities?
How did you keep cached and server data synchronized?
How did you test the feature under slow and failed network conditions?
What tradeoffs did you make between freshness, performance, and complexity?

title: Why We Test
description: Understand why automated tests matter in frontend development: they catch regressions early and document expected behavior as executable specifications.
mastery: The learner can explain what automated tests provide, distinguish regression prevention from debugging after the fact, and describe tests as executable documentation of expected behavior.
learningObjectives: Explain why frontend applications need automated tests.
Explain how tests catch regressions early.
Describe tests as executable specifications of expected behavior.
Distinguish proactive regression detection from discovering bugs only after release.
Explain how a test can document intended application behavior.
Recognize that testing is part of development rather than only a response to production bugs.

prerequisites.note: The source also conceptually assumes Level 3 React fluency rather than treating completion of Level 3 as a strict checkbox.

sections.text: Why Test Software at All?
As applications grow, changes become harder to reason about. A developer can fix one behavior while accidentally breaking another behavior that was working previously.
Automated tests provide a repeatable way to check expected behavior so regressions can be detected early.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A test is an executable statement of expected behavior. When the application changes, the test can tell you whether that expectation still holds.
A Regression

sections.title: What a regression looks like
sections.code:
Before change
→ Save button works
→ lesson appears in list

Developer changes lesson state

After change
→ Save button still renders
→ lesson no longer appears

Existing behavior was broken
→ regression

sections.text: The bug may not be related to the developer's visible goal, which is why regressions can be easy to miss when testing manually.
Tests Catch the Regression Early

sections.title: Without automated tests
sections.code:
Change code
 ↓
Ship
 ↓
User discovers bug
 ↓
Investigate

sections.title: With automated tests
sections.code:
Change code
 ↓
Run tests
 ↓
Regression detected
 ↓
Fix before release

sections.text: The value is not simply that tests find bugs. They move feedback closer to the change that introduced the problem.
Tests as Executable Specifications

sections.title: Human documentation
sections.code: A saved lesson should appear in the learner's saved list.

sections.title: Executable documentation
sections.code:
Test:
When a lesson is saved,
the saved list contains that lesson.

sections.text: The test turns the expected behavior into something the computer can repeatedly verify.
Tests Communicate Intent

A good test tells another developer what behavior matters. It can answer questions such as: What should happen after this click? What should this function return? What should happen when the request fails?

sections.title: Test as communication
sections.code:
Feature requirement
      ↓
Expected behavior
      ↓
Automated test
      ↓
Executable specification

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not treat tests as an afterthought
sections.text: Writing tests only after a production bug has already happened misses much of their value. Tests can encode important expectations while the feature is being developed so later changes can be checked automatically.
Why Manual Testing Is Not Enough

Manual testing is still useful, especially for exploratory work and visual behavior. But a human repeatedly checking the same regression-prone behavior is slower and less reliable than an automated check that can run consistently.

sections.title: Manual repetition
sections.code:
Make change
→ click through feature
→ inspect result
→ repeat for every future change

sections.title: Automated repetition
sections.code:
Make change
→ run test suite
→ verify expected behavior automatically

sections.text: A Real-World Analogy

Think of automated tests like a checklist that can perform itself. A checklist written on paper tells you what should be checked; an automated test both records the expectation and performs the check.
What Makes a Useful Test?

sections.title: Useful test
sections.code:
Given a saved lesson
When the user opens Saved Lessons
Then that lesson appears

sections.text: A useful test connects an input or action to an observable expected result.
The Test Should Describe Behavior

sections.title: Behavior-focused
sections.code:
click Save
→ expect lesson to appear in Saved Lessons

sections.title: Implementation-focused
sections.code: expect setState to have been called once

sections.text: Implementation details can be useful in some lower-level tests, but this course's testing progression will increasingly focus on behavior that matters to the application and its users.
Tests Become More Valuable as Risk Increases

sections.title: Higher regression risk
sections.code:
Shared utility
↓
Data transformation
↓
Reusable component
↓
Critical user workflow

sections.text: Not every line of code needs the same level of testing. Testing effort should reflect the behavior and risk that matter.
Interactive Thinking Exercise

sections.title: Why Test?
sections.instructions: For each scenario, identify the expected behavior that would be worth protecting with an automated test and explain what regression the test would catch.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A user saves a lesson and it should appear in Saved Lessons.

Expected behavior:
____________________________

Regression protected against:
____________________________

Scenario B
A search for "routing" should display matching lessons.

Expected behavior:
____________________________

Regression protected against:
____________________________

Scenario C
A failed request should show a retry option.

Expected behavior:
____________________________

Regression protected against:
____________________________

sections.text: Tests and Refactoring
Tests can make refactoring safer because they provide evidence that important behavior still works after internal changes.

sections.title: Refactor confidence
sections.code:
Working behavior
      ↓
Write test for important behavior
      ↓
Refactor implementation
      ↓
Run test
      ↓
Behavior preserved?

sections.text: The implementation can change while the expected behavior remains stable.
Tests Are Not a Guarantee of Correctness
A passing test suite only tells you that the tested expectations currently hold. If the tests do not cover an important behavior, a regression can still escape.

sections.title: Important distinction
sections.code:
Tests passing
≠
Everything is correct

Tests passing
=
Tested expectations currently hold

sections.text: Good testing therefore includes choosing meaningful behaviors to protect, not simply maximizing the number of assertions.
What Will Come Next?
The next lessons turn this mental model into concrete tests: first small unit tests, then component tests, then integration tests, followed by applied behavior-focused testing practice.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is conceptual. You do not need to learn test-runner syntax yet. First understand why tests exist and what they are supposed to protect.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why do we write automated tests?' A strong answer is: 'They catch regressions early and document expected behavior as executable specifications. That gives the team fast feedback when changes break important behavior.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Are tests only for bugs that already happened?' No. One of their biggest benefits is encoding important expectations before future changes break them.
Another follow-up is: 'Do passing tests prove the application is correct?' No. They demonstrate that the behaviors covered by those tests currently meet their expectations.
Reflect

Think about the Production Data Project from Module 4-2. Which behaviors would be most valuable to protect with automated tests? Which failures would be especially costly if a future refactor silently broke them?

sections.title: Test the behavior you cannot afford to lose

sections.text: A useful test protects an important expectation. Start with behavior that matters, then choose the test level that best expresses that behavior.

sections.label: Pass the recall check by explaining how automated tests catch regressions early and act as executable specifications of expected behavior.
sections.hint: Tests are not only bug detectors after release. They preserve important expectations and provide fast feedback when later changes break them.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Automated tests provide two closely related benefits: they catch regressions early and they document expected behavior in executable form. Testing is therefore a development practice, not merely an after-the-fact response to production bugs. Good tests protect meaningful behavior and give developers faster, repeatable feedback when implementation changes.

exercises.title: Why Test?
exercises.brief: Identify behavior worth protecting with tests and explain what future regression each test would catch.

quiz.question: What are two core benefits of automated tests?
options: They catch regressions early and document expected behavior as executable specifications.
They eliminate all bugs and replace code review.
They make every application faster.
They replace manual exploratory testing completely.
quiz.explanation: The lesson frames automated tests as early regression detection plus executable documentation of expected behavior.

quiz.question: Why is treating tests as something written only after a production bug a weak approach?
options: It misses the opportunity to encode important expectations before future changes break them.
Tests cannot be written after bugs.
Production bugs never need tests.
It makes tests execute more slowly.
quiz.explanation: Tests provide preventative value when they protect important behavior before regressions happen.

quiz.question: What does a passing test suite actually establish?
options: The entire application is correct.
The behaviors covered by the tests currently satisfy their expectations.
There can be no future regressions.
Manual testing is no longer necessary.
quiz.explanation: Tests provide evidence about the behavior they cover; they do not prove every aspect of the application is correct.

summary: Automated tests catch regressions early and act as executable specifications of expected behavior. They make important expectations repeatable and give developers fast feedback when refactoring or extending an application. Tests are not a guarantee that an application is entirely correct, and their value depends on protecting meaningful behavior rather than merely accumulating assertions.
interviewQuestions: Why do we write automated tests?
How do tests catch regressions early?
What does it mean to call a test an executable specification?
Why should testing not be an afterthought?
Do passing tests prove an application is correct?
How do tests support refactoring?
What makes a behavior worth protecting with a test?
How is automated testing different from manual exploratory testing?

title: Unit Tests
description: Write focused unit tests for pure functions and logic using Vitest, and learn what makes a test worth keeping.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what a unit test verifies versus what it deliberately ignores.
Write unit tests for pure functions using Vitest's describe/it/expect API.
Use arrange-act-assert structure to keep tests readable.
Identify when a function is hard to unit test and why that's a design signal.
Distinguish a brittle test (breaks on refactor) from a resilient one (breaks on behavior change).

sections.text: A Unit Test Verifies One Small Thing in Isolation

A unit test calls a single function or module with known inputs and checks the output, without involving the DOM, network, or other modules. If a test needs a database, a browser, or three other files to pass, it's not really a unit test anymore.

sections.title: The function under test
A first Vitest test

sections.text: Arrange, Act, Assert

Most good unit tests follow the same three-part shape: set up the inputs (arrange), call the function (act), check the result (assert). Naming this structure, even just in your head, keeps tests from turning into a tangle of unrelated checks.

sections.title: Arrange / act / assert made explicit

sections.text: Testing Edge Cases, Not Just the Happy Path

The most valuable tests usually aren't the ones that confirm normal input works — they're the ones that pin down behavior at the edges: zero, negative numbers, empty strings, empty arrays, and invalid input.

sections.title: Edge cases and error behavior

sections.text: Common Mistake: Testing Implementation Instead of Behavior

A brittle test asserts on internal details, like the exact order of internal helper calls. A resilient test asserts on the public contract: given this input, that output. If you refactor the internals without changing behavior, a resilient test still passes; a brittle one breaks for no real reason.

sections.title: Brittle vs. resilient

sections.text: When a Function Resists Unit Testing

If a function is hard to unit test — it reads global state, triggers side effects, or does five unrelated things — that's usually a signal the function itself needs to be split up, not that testing is the wrong tool. Pure functions (same input always produces same output, no side effects) are the easiest and most valuable to unit test.

sections.title: Debug Lab — Fix the Failing Test
sections.instructions: The test expects calculateTax to round to two decimals but the implementation doesn't round at all. Fix the implementation (not the test) so it passes.
hints: Compare the raw multiplication result to the expected value — how many decimal places does the test expect?
Math.round only rounds to whole numbers by default; multiply, round, then divide back to get two-decimal precision.
The fix belongs in calculateTax's return statement, not in the test assertion.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can write a Vitest unit test for a pure function using arrange-act-assert, cover at least one edge case and one error case, and explain in their own words why a test that checks Math.round was called is more brittle than one that checks the final numeric output.

exercises.title: Test a Validation Function
exercises.brief: Write a `isValidEmail(email)` function plus a Vitest suite covering: a normal valid email, a missing @ symbol, an empty string, and a trailing whitespace case. Aim for at least 4 test cases.

quiz.question: What makes a function easy to unit test?
options: It's a pure function with no side effects and no external dependencies.
It logs its internal steps to the console.
It calls the network to fetch fresh data on each run.
It depends on the current date and time.
quiz.explanation: Pure functions are the easiest to unit test because the same input always produces the same output, with nothing external to mock or control.

quiz.question: Why is asserting on 'Math.round was called' considered a brittle test?
options: It runs slower than other assertions.
It couples the test to implementation details that could change without changing behavior.
Math.round cannot be spied on in Vitest.
It only works in Node, not the browser.
quiz.explanation: Testing that a specific internal function was called ties the test to how the result is computed, not what the result is — a refactor that keeps the same output would break this test for no real reason.

quiz.question: Which of these is the best edge case to add to a discount-calculation test suite?
options: Testing the same 20% discount twice.
Testing that the function's name is spelled correctly.
Testing with percentOff at exactly 0 and exactly 100.
Testing with a price that is a round number.
quiz.explanation: The genuinely useful edge cases are the boundaries: 0% and 100% discount, since those are where off-by-one or division errors tend to surface. Testing the function's spelling isn't a meaningful test at all.

quiz.question: What does 'arrange-act-assert' describe?
options: A linting rule enforced by ESLint.
A naming convention for test file paths.
The order Vitest runs test files in.
A three-step structure for organizing a single test: set up inputs, call the code, check the result.
quiz.explanation: Arrange-act-assert is a structuring convention that keeps individual tests readable and focused on one behavior at a time.

summary: Unit tests check one small, isolated piece of logic — usually a pure function — against known inputs and outputs. Structuring tests as arrange-act-assert keeps them readable, and covering edge cases (boundaries, invalid input) is where unit tests earn their value. The key discipline is testing observable behavior, not internal implementation, so tests survive refactors instead of breaking on every internal change.
interviewQuestions: What's the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
Why are pure functions easier to unit test than functions with side effects?
Give an example of a brittle test and explain how you'd make it more resilient.
What edge cases would you test for a function that parses a date string?

title: Component Tests
description: Test React components with React Testing Library by rendering them and asserting on what a user would see, not on internal state.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Render a component in a test using React Testing Library and query it the way a user would.
Explain why RTL favors queries by role/text over querying by CSS class or test id.
Simulate user interaction with fireEvent/userEvent and assert on the resulting UI.
Test conditional rendering paths (loading, error, empty, success) for a component.
Recognize when a component test is really testing implementation instead of user-visible behavior.

sections.text: Testing What the User Sees, Not What React Does Internally

React Testing Library (RTL) is built around one guiding rule: the more your tests resemble how users interact with your app, the more confidence they give you. That means querying rendered output by visible text, labels, and roles — not by digging into component internals or state.

sections.title: The component under test
A first RTL test

sections.text: Querying by Role Is the Preferred Approach

getByRole matches how assistive technology sees the page, which means a passing test is also a small accessibility check. Prefer getByRole, getByLabelText, and getByText over getByTestId or querying CSS classes.

sections.title: Querying by role

sections.text: Simulating User Interaction
userEvent simulates real user actions — typing, clicking — more realistically than firing raw DOM events, including things like focus changes that fireEvent skips.

sections.title: Typing and clicking

sections.text: Testing Every Rendering Path

A component that fetches data typically has at least four states worth testing: loading, error, empty, and success. Skipping the loading/error/empty states is one of the most common gaps in real test suites.

sections.title: Testing conditional states

sections.text: Common Mistake: Reaching into Component Internals

If a test imports a component's internal state hook, or asserts on a class name that has nothing to do with what the user sees, it will break the moment you refactor markup — even if the user-facing behavior is identical. That's testing implementation, not behavior.

sections.title: Debug Lab — Wrong Query
sections.instructions: This test fails because it queries by a CSS class that doesn't reliably identify the button for a screen reader user. Rewrite the query to use getByRole instead, matching on the button's accessible name.
hints: screen.getByRole('button', { name: '...' }) matches on the button's visible text as its accessible name.
Replace document.querySelector('.btn-danger') with a role-based query from screen.
The button's accessible name here is simply its text content: 'Delete'.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can render a component with RTL, query it by role or label text rather than CSS class, simulate a user interaction with userEvent, and write at least one test for a non-happy-path rendering state (loading, error, or empty).

exercises.title: Test a Toggle Component
exercises.brief: Build a `Toggle` component with a button that switches between 'On' and 'Off' text on click. Write RTL tests covering: initial render state, the state after one click, and the state after two clicks (back to the original).

quiz.question: Why does React Testing Library favor getByRole over getByTestId?
options: getByRole matches how the page is perceived by assistive technology, so it also functions as a lightweight accessibility check.
getByTestId is slower to execute.
getByTestId is deprecated in the current version.
getByRole is the only query that works with async components.
quiz.explanation: Role-based queries mirror how a screen reader user finds elements, so tests written this way double as a basic accessibility signal.

quiz.question: What does userEvent.type more accurately simulate compared to fireEvent.change?
options: It skips validation logic entirely.
It simulates the sequence of real keystrokes and focus behavior a user would produce.
It renders the component twice for speed.
It only works with textarea elements.
quiz.explanation: userEvent simulates a fuller, more realistic interaction sequence — including focus — rather than firing a single synthetic change event.

quiz.question: Which rendering states are most commonly missed in a real component test suite?
options: The component's props types.
The default happy-path render.
Loading, error, and empty states.
The component's file name.
quiz.explanation: Teams often test only the success path and skip loading, error, and empty states — exactly the states most likely to have real bugs.

quiz.question: A test queries `document.querySelector('.btn-danger')` instead of `screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })`. What's the risk?
options: None — both queries are equally robust.
getByRole is only available in Vitest, not Jest.
querySelector cannot be used inside a test file.
The class-based query breaks if the class name changes during a refactor, even if the button's behavior is unchanged.
quiz.explanation: The risk is the class-based query being coupled to styling details that can change independently of behavior — it's testing implementation, not the user-facing contract.

summary: Component tests with React Testing Library render a component and interact with it the way a user would — querying by role, label, or visible text rather than internal state or CSS classes. userEvent simulates realistic interactions, and a thorough suite covers loading, error, empty, and success states, not just the happy path. The discipline is the same as unit testing: assert on observable behavior, not implementation.
interviewQuestions: Why does React Testing Library discourage querying by CSS class or component internals?
How would you test a component that shows different UI for loading, error, and success states?
What's the difference between fireEvent and userEvent, and when would you choose one over the other?
How do role-based queries relate to accessibility?

title: Integration Tests
description: Test how several units work together — a form talking to validation logic, a component talking to a mocked API — instead of testing each piece alone.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what an integration test covers that a unit test and a component test each miss on their own.
Mock a network request with MSW so a component's real data-fetching logic runs against fake data.
Write a test that exercises a full user flow across multiple components.
Decide where to draw the boundary of an integration test so it stays fast and reliable.

sections.text: Between Unit and End-to-End

A unit test checks one function in isolation. An end-to-end test drives a real browser against a real (or staging) backend. Integration tests sit in between: several real units — components, hooks, validation logic — working together, with only the true edges (network, time) faked.

sections.title: A form that depends on validation and a submit handler
Testing the real interaction between input, validation, and submit

sections.text: Mocking the Network Boundary with MSW

Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts real fetch/XHR calls at the network level, so your component's actual data-fetching code runs unmodified — only the server response is faked. This is more realistic than mocking fetch itself.

sections.title: Setting up a mock server

sections.text: Where to Draw the Boundary

Integration tests are more expensive and slower than unit tests, so the goal isn't to integration-test everything — it's to cover the flows where components genuinely depend on each other's behavior, and let unit tests cover the pure logic pieces separately.
Common Mistake: Mocking Too Much

If you mock every child component and every hook, you're left testing wiring that doesn't reflect real behavior. Mock only the true external boundary (network, timers, browser APIs) and let your real code run through everything else.

sections.title: Debug Lab — Over-Mocked Test
sections.instructions: This test mocks the SignupForm's internal validation function directly, which means it never actually verifies the real validation logic runs. Rewrite it to test through the real component instead of mocking its internals.
sections.initialCode:
Email typed by test'not-an-email'

The current test mocks validateEmail to always return true, so it can never catch a real validation bug. Compare both runs, then fix the test in the code panel to use the real validation logic.
hints: Remove the vi.mock call for validateEmail so the real validation logic actually runs during the test.
The test should assert that an invalid email produces a visible error message, not that submission was blocked silently.
Mocking the exact thing you're trying to test defeats the purpose of an integration test.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can explain the distinction between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests, use MSW to mock a network boundary while leaving real component/fetch logic untouched, and identify when a test is over-mocking to the point of no longer verifying real behavior.

exercises.title: Test a Search-and-Fetch Flow
exercises.brief: Build a SearchBox component that fetches /api/search?q=... on submit and renders results. Use MSW to mock the endpoint and write an integration test covering: typing a query, submitting, and seeing the mocked results render.

quiz.question: What does an integration test cover that a pure unit test does not?
options: How several real units behave together, rather than one function in isolation.
Whether the code compiles without errors.
The exact CSS applied to an element.
The performance of the production build.
quiz.explanation: Integration tests exercise multiple real pieces working together — the value they add over unit tests is verifying that the pieces actually cooperate correctly.

quiz.question: Why does MSW intercept requests at the network level instead of mocking the fetch function directly?
options: It's required by React.
It lets your real fetching code run unmodified, only faking the actual server response.
It makes tests run in a real browser.
It removes the need for a test runner.
quiz.explanation: Intercepting at the network boundary means your component's real request logic executes exactly as it would in production — only the response contents are faked.

quiz.question: What's the risk of mocking a component's own internal validation function in an integration test?
options: It makes the test run faster with no downside.
It's required for the test to compile.
The test stops verifying the actual validation logic, so real bugs in that logic go undetected.
It's more readable than testing through the real component.
quiz.explanation: Mocking the exact logic under test means the test can pass even when the real validation is broken — the opposite of what an integration test is for.

quiz.question: Which boundary is most appropriate to mock in an integration test?
options: The component's own render output.
Every child component in the tree.
The component's props.
The true external boundary — network requests, timers, or browser APIs.
quiz.explanation: Mocking only genuine external boundaries keeps the test realistic while still avoiding real network calls or timing flakiness.

summary: Integration tests verify that multiple real units — components, hooks, validation logic — work correctly together, sitting between narrow unit tests and full end-to-end tests. Tools like MSW let you mock only the true network boundary so the rest of your real code runs as it would in production. The main failure mode to avoid is over-mocking: if you mock the logic you're trying to verify, the test stops proving anything.
interviewQuestions: How would you decide whether a given test should be a unit test or an integration test?
Why might mocking too many dependencies in a test actually reduce your confidence in the code?
How does MSW differ from mocking the fetch function directly?
Describe a real flow in an app you've built that would be a good candidate for an integration test.

title: Testing User Behaviour
description: Practice writing tests around real user flows end-to-end within a component tree, combining what you've learned about unit, component, and integration tests.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Write a test suite around a multi-step user flow (fill form, submit, see confirmation).
Choose the right test type (unit, component, integration) for each part of a feature.
Use userEvent to simulate a realistic multi-step interaction.
Assert on user-visible outcomes at each step of the flow.

sections.text: Testing a Flow, Not Just a Component

Real user behavior rarely stops at one interaction — it's a sequence: type an answer, click next, see a new question, submit, see a result. Testing user behavior means writing a test that walks through that sequence the way a person would, checking the visible outcome at each step.

sections.title: A two-step quiz flow
Walking through the flow in a test

sections.text: Picking the Right Layer for Each Assertion

A well-rounded suite doesn't only test the full flow — it also unit-tests any pure logic extracted from the component (like scoring or validation), and component-tests individual pieces in isolation where that's cheaper and more precise. The full-flow test is there to catch things the layered tests can't: whether the pieces actually connect.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can write a test that walks through a multi-step user flow using userEvent, asserting on the visible outcome after each meaningful step, and can explain which parts of the same feature would be better covered by a narrower unit or component test instead.

exercises.title: Test a Multi-Step Checkout
exercises.brief: Build a two-step checkout flow (enter shipping info, then confirm order) and write a test that walks through both steps with userEvent, asserting the confirmation screen shows the entered shipping details.

quiz.question: What does a full user-flow test verify that isolated unit and component tests can't?
options: That the pieces of the feature actually connect and work together as a sequence.
That each function has correct TypeScript types.
That the CSS bundle size is under a target.
That the component re-renders the minimum number of times.
quiz.explanation: A flow test's unique value is catching integration problems between steps — bugs that only show up when the pieces are wired together.

quiz.question: In a multi-step form, where should the scoring/validation logic ideally be tested?
options: Only within the full end-to-end flow test.
As a separate unit test if it's extracted into a pure function, in addition to being exercised by the flow test.
Only manually before each release.
Never — visual review is enough.
quiz.explanation: Extracting logic into a pure function lets you unit-test it directly and precisely, while the flow test still confirms it's wired in correctly.

quiz.question: Which assertion best matches 'testing user behaviour' rather than internal state?
options: Checking that a specific reducer action was dispatched.
Checking a component's internal step variable equals 2.
Checking that the confirmation text the user would read is visible on screen.
Checking that a useState call happened exactly once.
quiz.explanation: User-behaviour tests assert on what's visible and actionable to the user, not on internal implementation details like state variables or dispatched actions.

summary: Testing user behaviour means walking through a realistic multi-step interaction with userEvent and asserting on what the user would actually see at each step, rather than internal state. It complements — not replaces — narrower unit and component tests: extract pure logic where you can and unit-test it directly, then use a flow test to confirm the pieces are correctly wired together.

resources.label: Kent C. Dodds — Testing Implementation Details

interviewQuestions: How would you structure tests for a multi-step checkout flow across unit, component, and integration levels?
What's the tradeoff between a few broad flow tests and many narrow unit tests?
How do you decide how much of a flow to cover in a single test versus splitting it up?

title: Capstone: Test Suite
description: Write a complete test suite for a small feature, combining unit, component, and integration tests at the level a real code review would expect.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Plan a test suite by identifying which parts of a feature need unit, component, or integration coverage.
Write and run a complete suite for a small multi-component feature with a mocked API.
Review a test suite for brittleness, over-mocking, and missing edge cases.
Explain test coverage decisions the way you would in a pull request description.

sections.text: The Capstone Brief

You're given a small 'Task List' feature: a form to add a task, a list that fetches existing tasks from /api/tasks, and a delete button per task. Your job is to write a complete test suite covering the pure logic, the components in isolation, and the feature as an integrated whole — the same scope a reviewer would expect before merging this to production.

sections.title: The feature to test

sections.text: Planning the Coverage Before Writing Code

A strong plan for this feature: unit-test any extracted validation logic (empty/whitespace-only task text); component-test TaskForm and TaskList in isolation (empty state, rendering a list, calling onAdd/onDelete with the right arguments); integration-test the full page against a mocked /api/tasks endpoint with MSW, covering add, delete, and the empty state after all tasks are removed.
What a Reviewer Checks For

Before you consider the suite done, check it against the same brittleness and over-mocking issues covered earlier in this module: are queries role/label-based, not class-based? Is only the network boundary mocked? Are edge cases (empty input, empty list, delete-the-last-item) covered, not just the happy path?

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can produce a complete, layered test suite for a small multi-component feature — unit tests for extracted logic, component tests for each piece in isolation, and an integration test against a mocked API — and can justify each coverage decision in reviewer-facing language.

exercises.title: Write the Full Task List Suite
exercises.brief: Implement TaskForm, TaskList, and a parent TaskPage that fetches from /api/tasks. Write: a unit test for a validateTaskText helper, component tests for TaskForm and TaskList (including their empty states), and an MSW-backed integration test that adds a task and deletes it, ending on the empty state.

quiz.question: For the Task List feature, which layer should test 'submitting an empty task does nothing'?
options: Only an end-to-end browser test.
It can't be tested at all.
Only the full integration test.
A component test on TaskForm, or a unit test if the check is extracted into a pure function.
quiz.explanation: This is a narrow, isolated behavior of TaskForm — testing it at the component (or unit, if extracted) level is faster and more precise than requiring the full integrated flow.

quiz.question: What should the integration test for this feature mock?
options: Only the /api/tasks network endpoint, via MSW.
The TaskForm and TaskList components themselves.
React's useState hook.
Nothing — it should hit the real backend.
quiz.explanation: The true external boundary here is the network call; mocking it with MSW while running the real components and logic gives the most realistic integration test.

quiz.question: Deleting the only remaining task should result in what, and how would you verify it?
options: The list container disappearing entirely, verified by checking it's removed from the DOM tree.
The empty-state message becoming visible, verified with a role/text-based query after the delete interaction.
A console warning, verified by spying on console.warn.
Nothing observable — it doesn't need a test.
quiz.explanation: The user-visible outcome is the empty-state message appearing — that's what the test should assert on, following the same user-behaviour-first approach from earlier lessons.

summary: A production-grade test suite layers unit tests (pure logic), component tests (individual pieces in isolation, including empty/error states), and integration tests (the feature wired together, with only the network boundary mocked). Planning the coverage before writing tests — deciding what belongs at each layer — is what separates a thorough suite from a pile of redundant or brittle tests.
interviewQuestions: Walk through how you'd plan test coverage for a small CRUD feature before writing any test code.
How would you explain your test coverage decisions in a pull request description?
What's a sign that a test suite has too much overlapping coverage, and how would you trim it?

title: Why Accessibility Matters
description: Understand who accessibility is for, why it's a core engineering concern rather than an optional polish step, and what 'inaccessible' actually looks like in real code.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Name at least three categories of disability that frontend accessibility work addresses (visual, motor, auditory, cognitive).
Explain why accessibility is a correctness issue, not a visual-design preference.
Identify a concrete example of inaccessible markup and why it fails.
Connect accessibility to legal, ethical, and product-quality reasons a team would prioritize it.

sections.text: Accessibility Is Not a Visual Feature

It's easy to assume accessibility mainly means color contrast and text size. In practice it covers far more: whether a screen reader user can navigate your interface at all, whether someone who can't use a mouse can complete a purchase, whether captions exist for a video, whether a form's error messages are announced to someone who can't see them turn red.
Who This Actually Affects

Disability isn't one category. Visual (blindness, low vision, color blindness), motor (limited or no use of a mouse, tremor), auditory (deafness, hard of hearing), and cognitive (attention, memory, processing differences) each require different things from your interface — and many people fall into more than one category, temporarily or permanently.

sections.title: Looks fine, fails silently
sections.code: Submit

sections.text: This 'button' is invisible to keyboard users (a div isn't focusable by default) and invisible to screen readers as an actionable control (it has no button role). It looks identical to a real button visually, which is exactly why this class of bug slips through code review so often — it fails for users who aren't in the room.
Accessibility Is a Correctness Issue

A feature that's unusable for a meaningful group of real users isn't a finished feature with a missing nice-to-have — it's an incomplete implementation of the actual requirement. Framing it this way (rather than as 'polish') is what keeps it from being deprioritized under deadline pressure.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can explain, in their own words, why a div with an onclick handler is inaccessible even though it looks and functions identically to a real button for a mouse user, and can name at least three distinct categories of disability accessibility work addresses.

exercises.title: Audit a Familiar Interface
exercises.brief: Pick a website you use often. Try navigating one core flow (like a search or checkout) using only your keyboard — no mouse. Write down every point where you got stuck or where focus went somewhere unexpected.

quiz.question: Why is a `<div onclick=...>` used as a button considered inaccessible?
options: It renders slower than a real button element.
It can't be styled with CSS.
It isn't keyboard-focusable and has no button semantics for assistive technology, even though it looks like a button.
Browsers block onclick handlers on div elements.
quiz.explanation: A div has no built-in keyboard focusability or accessible role, so keyboard and screen reader users can't perceive or activate it as a button, even though it's visually identical to one.

quiz.question: Which of these is a motor accessibility concern?
options: Color contrast between text and background.
Whether error text is only conveyed through color.
Whether captions exist on a video.
Whether an interface can be fully operated without a mouse.
quiz.explanation: Motor accessibility is about whether someone with limited or no ability to use a mouse can still operate every part of the interface, typically via keyboard.

quiz.question: Why does the lesson frame accessibility as a 'correctness issue' rather than 'polish'?
options: Because a feature unusable by a real group of users is an incomplete implementation of the requirement, not a missing extra.
Because accessibility bugs are always easier to fix than visual bugs.
Because accessibility only matters for government websites.
Because polish items don't need to be fixed before release.
quiz.explanation: Treating accessibility as core correctness — not a nice-to-have — is what prevents it from being cut under deadline pressure.

summary: Accessibility covers far more than color contrast — it spans visual, motor, auditory, and cognitive needs, and determines whether real users can actually use your product at all. Markup that looks correct to a sighted mouse user can be completely broken for a keyboard or screen reader user, which is why accessibility has to be treated as a correctness requirement, not a cosmetic afterthought.

resources.label: W3C WAI — Introduction to Web Accessibility

interviewQuestions: Why might a UI that looks fine visually still be completely broken for a screen reader user?
What are the main categories of disability frontend accessibility work needs to account for?
How would you make the case to a team that accessibility work shouldn't be deprioritized under a deadline?

title: Semantic Interfaces
description: Use native HTML elements for their intended purpose so assistive technology gets accurate structure and behavior for free, and learn when ARIA is genuinely needed.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain why native elements (button, nav, main, a) come with built-in accessibility behavior that a div does not.
Rewrite a div-based fake interactive element as its correct native equivalent.
State the 'first rule of ARIA': don't use ARIA if a native element already does the job.
Identify when ARIA attributes are actually necessary versus when they're compensating for avoidable markup choices.

sections.text: Native Elements Come With Behavior Built In

A real <button> is focusable, activatable with Enter and Space, and announced as 'button' by screen readers automatically. A <a href> is keyboard-navigable and announced as a link, with distinct browser history behavior. None of that has to be reimplemented — using the right element gets it for free.

sections.title: Wrong vs. right
sections.code: Menu

sections.text: The First Rule of ARIA

The official first rule of ARIA use is: if a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of re-purposing an element and adding ARIA to fix it. ARIA can describe a role, but it can't grant keyboard behavior — you'd still have to hand-implement focus and key handling yourself.

sections.title: ARIA patching a div vs. just using the native element
sections.code: Submit

sections.text: Landmarks Give Structure to the Page

Elements like <main>, <nav>, <header>, <footer>, and <aside> act as landmarks — screen reader users can jump directly between them instead of reading the whole page linearly. A page built entirely out of <div>s has no landmarks at all.

sections.title: A page with real landmarks
sections.code:
...
...

Dashboard

...
...

sections.text: Common Mistake: Reaching for ARIA First

It's tempting to add role and aria-* attributes to fix an accessibility issue quickly. But if the underlying element is wrong (a div instead of a button, a span instead of a heading), ARIA is patching a symptom — and it's easy to get ARIA attributes subtly wrong in ways that make things worse, not better.

sections.title: Refactor Lab — Replace the Fake Button
sections.instructions: This dropdown trigger uses a div with an onclick handler and no keyboard support. Rewrite it as a real button element so it's keyboard-accessible without adding any ARIA.
sections.initialCode: Options
hints: Replace the outer div with a button element, keeping the same onclick handler.
A native button element is focusable and activatable with Enter/Space without any extra attributes.
You can still apply the dropdown-trigger class to the button for styling — the fix is only about the element type.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can rewrite a div-based fake interactive control as its correct native HTML equivalent, state the first rule of ARIA in their own words, and explain what native keyboard behavior a button or link element provides for free.

exercises.title: Audit and Fix a Page's Semantics
exercises.brief: Given a page built entirely from <div> and <span> elements (a header, a nav list, a main content area, and a 'load more' clickable div), rewrite it using the correct semantic and landmark elements throughout.

quiz.question: What does a native <button> element provide that a <div onclick=...> does not, by default?
options: Faster rendering.
Keyboard focusability and activation with Enter/Space, announced correctly to assistive tech.
Automatic form validation.
A larger click target.
quiz.explanation: Native interactive elements come with built-in keyboard behavior and accessible roles that a div has to have manually reimplemented to match.

quiz.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA'?
options: Always add role attributes to every interactive element.
ARIA attributes should only be used in forms.
Use a native HTML element with the needed semantics instead of re-purposing an element and patching it with ARIA.
aria-label is required on every element.
quiz.explanation: The first rule of ARIA use is to prefer a native element that already has the right semantics, since ARIA alone doesn't grant behaviors like keyboard interaction.

quiz.question: Why do landmark elements like <main> and <nav> matter for accessibility?
options: They improve SEO rankings only.
They reduce the page's bundle size.
They are required for CSS Grid to work.
They let screen reader users jump directly between page regions instead of reading linearly.
quiz.explanation: Landmarks give screen reader users direct navigation between page regions — jumping straight to 'main' or 'nav' instead of tabbing through everything sequentially.

quiz.question: Adding `role="button"` and `tabindex="0"` to a div makes it fully equivalent to a real button. True or false?
options: False — you'd still need to manually implement Enter/Space key handling; ARIA describes a role but doesn't add behavior.
True, this is the standard recommended pattern.
True, but only in Chrome.
False, because ARIA attributes are ignored by all screen readers.
quiz.explanation: ARIA can announce a role, but it doesn't grant keyboard behavior — you'd still have to add your own keydown handling to fully match native button behavior, which is why using an actual button is simpler and safer.

summary: Native HTML elements come with accessibility behavior built in — keyboard focus, activation, and correct semantic roles — that a generic div or span doesn't have on its own. The first rule of ARIA is to reach for the right native element before patching a wrong one with ARIA attributes, and landmark elements like main and nav give screen reader users real navigational structure across the page.

resources.label: W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices — No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA

interviewQuestions: Why is a native button generally preferred over a div with role="button"?
What is the first rule of ARIA, and why does it exist?
How do landmark elements help screen reader users navigate a page?

title: Keyboard Navigation
description: Make sure every interactive element in your UI can be reached and operated using only a keyboard, in a logical order.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Test an interface using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space, without a mouse.
Explain what tabindex values 0, -1, and positive numbers each do, and why positive values are usually a mistake.
Identify and fix a custom component (like a modal or dropdown) that traps or loses keyboard focus.
Recognize a visible focus indicator as a requirement, not a style choice to remove.

sections.text: Tab Order Should Match Visual and Logical Order

By default, the browser tabs through elements in DOM order. If your DOM order doesn't match the visual layout (common with CSS Grid/Flexbox reordering), keyboard users experience a confusing, non-linear tab order even though the page looks fine visually.

sections.title: A visual-only reorder that breaks tab order

sections.text: tabindex: 0, -1, and Positive Numbers

tabindex="0" adds an element to the natural tab order at its DOM position — useful for making a genuinely custom interactive element focusable. tabindex="-1" removes it from the tab sequence but allows programmatic focus (via .focus() in JS) — useful for things like moving focus into a newly opened modal. Positive tabindex values override the natural order entirely and are almost always a mistake — they create a second, hard-to-maintain tab order that fights the DOM.
Never Remove the Focus Outline Without Replacing It

`outline: none` is one of the most common accessibility regressions — it removes the only visual cue a keyboard user has for where they are on the page. If you don't like the default outline, replace it with your own visible focus style; never delete it outright.

sections.title: Wrong vs. right

sections.text: Focus Traps in Custom Components

A custom dropdown or modal that doesn't manage focus can leave a keyboard user stuck — tabbing past it into background content, or unable to tab out of it at all. Every custom interactive component needs deliberate keyboard behavior, not just visual behavior.

sections.title: Debug Lab — Restore the Focus Outline
sections.instructions: This button removes its focus outline entirely, making it invisible to keyboard users where their focus is. Replace the removed outline with a visible custom focus style instead of deleting it.
hints: Never set outline: none without providing a replacement focus style in the same rule.
A visible border or outline in a contrasting color satisfies the requirement — outline-offset helps it stand out from the button's own border.
focus-visible can be used instead of focus if you only want the style to show for keyboard focus, not mouse clicks.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can navigate a full interface using only the keyboard, correctly explain the difference between tabindex 0, -1, and positive values, and identify why removing outline: none without a replacement is a regression rather than a style improvement.

exercises.title: Keyboard-Only Audit
exercises.brief: Take a small multi-section page you've built earlier in this course. Unplug your mouse (or just don't use it) and complete a full task using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space. Document every place focus got lost, skipped an element, or had no visible indicator.

quiz.question: What does tabindex="-1" do?
options: Makes the element the first stop in tab order.
Removes the element from the natural tab sequence, but still allows it to receive focus programmatically via JavaScript.
Disables the element entirely.
Adds the element to the tab order twice.
quiz.explanation: tabindex="-1" is commonly used for things like moving focus into a modal on open, via .focus() in code, without adding the element to the regular Tab-key sequence.

quiz.question: Why is a positive tabindex value (e.g. tabindex="3") usually discouraged?
options: Positive values are removed automatically by modern browsers.
It only works in Firefox.
It creates a separate, hand-maintained tab order that conflicts with the natural DOM order and becomes hard to keep correct as the page changes.
It's identical in effect to tabindex="0".
quiz.explanation: Positive tabindex values override natural DOM order, creating a fragile secondary ordering system that's easy to break as the page evolves.

quiz.question: What is wrong with `button:focus { outline: none; }` on its own?
options: Nothing — it's a recommended reset.
It makes buttons unclickable with a mouse.
It's a CSS syntax error.
It removes the only visual indicator of keyboard focus without providing any replacement.
quiz.explanation: Removing outline without a replacement focus style leaves keyboard users with no way to see where they currently are on the page.

summary: Every interactive element needs to be reachable and operable with a keyboard alone, in an order that matches the page's visual and logical structure. tabindex="0" and "-1" have specific, narrow uses; positive tabindex values should be avoided. Never remove the focus outline without replacing it with an equally visible custom style, and test custom components like modals and dropdowns for focus traps.
interviewQuestions: Walk through how you'd test a page for keyboard accessibility without any special tools.
What's the difference between tabindex 0 and -1, and when would you use each?
Why is removing the default focus outline considered a common accessibility regression?

title: Focus Management
description: Deliberately move keyboard focus for dynamic UI — modals, route changes, toasts — so keyboard and screen reader users aren't left stranded.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Move focus into a modal when it opens and back to the trigger element when it closes.
Trap focus within an open modal so Tab doesn't escape to background content.
Announce dynamic content changes (like a toast notification) using aria-live.
Manage focus correctly after a client-side route change in a single-page app.

sections.text: When a Modal Opens, Focus Has to Go Somewhere Deliberately

If focus isn't moved when a modal opens, a keyboard user is still 'focused' on whatever was behind it — they can't perceive that a modal even appeared. Move focus onto the modal (or its first focusable element) when it opens, and back to the button that triggered it when it closes.

sections.title: Moving focus on open/close

sections.text: Trapping Focus Inside an Open Modal

While a modal is open, Tab shouldn't be able to move focus to elements behind it — that's called a focus trap, and it's expected modal behavior (not to be confused with the negative kind of 'trap' where a user gets stuck with no way out at all, which is what happens when Escape and the close button don't also work).
Announcing Dynamic Changes with aria-live

A toast notification that appears and disappears is invisible to a screen reader user unless it's inside an aria-live region — that tells assistive tech to announce content changes inside it without requiring focus to move there.

sections.title: An announced toast

sections.text: Focus After Route Changes in an SPA

In a traditional multi-page site, the browser resets focus to the top of the document on navigation. A single-page app has to do this manually — otherwise a keyboard/screen-reader user navigating between pages keeps their focus (and screen reader position) stuck on whatever was previously on screen, with no indication a new page loaded.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can implement open/close focus movement for a modal, explain why aria-live is needed for dynamic content like toasts, and explain what breaks for a keyboard/screen-reader user if focus isn't reset after a client-side route change.

exercises.title: Fix a Focus-Losing Modal
exercises.brief: Given a Modal component that opens/closes but never moves focus, add: focus onto the modal when it opens, focus back to the trigger button when it closes, and Escape-key support to close it.

quiz.question: Why does a modal need to move focus onto itself when it opens?
options: Because without it, a keyboard/screen-reader user has no way to perceive that a modal appeared at all.
To improve the animation performance.
It's only needed for mobile devices.
To satisfy a CSS requirement.
quiz.explanation: If focus stays on the underlying page, a keyboard or screen reader user gets no signal that new content (the modal) has appeared.

quiz.question: What does aria-live="polite" on a toast notification container do?
options: It makes the toast fade in more slowly.
It causes the toast to be announced by assistive technology when its content changes, without requiring focus to move there.
It prevents the toast from being read at all.
It moves keyboard focus onto the toast.
quiz.explanation: aria-live regions are announced automatically by screen readers when their content changes, which is exactly what a toast needs since it isn't focused.

quiz.question: In a single-page app, why does focus need to be manually managed after a client-side route change?
options: It doesn't — browsers handle this automatically for SPAs too.
Because React automatically breaks focus on every re-render.
Because the browser's automatic focus-reset behavior on navigation only happens on a full page load, which SPA route changes don't trigger.
Only Safari requires this.
quiz.explanation: A full page navigation resets focus to the document automatically; a client-side route change in an SPA doesn't, so the app has to move focus deliberately (often to the new page's heading) to signal the change.

summary: Dynamic UI — modals, toasts, and client-side route changes — needs deliberate focus management, because none of these have the automatic focus behavior a full page load provides. Move focus into a modal on open and back to the trigger on close, use aria-live for content that appears without moving focus, and move focus (typically to the new page's heading) after SPA route changes.
interviewQuestions: How would you implement accessible focus management for a modal dialog?
What's the purpose of an aria-live region, and when would you use one?
Why do single-page apps need extra work to handle focus correctly on route changes?

title: Labels, Roles, and Accessible Names
description: Give every interactive element and image an accurate accessible name, so assistive technology announces what a control actually does.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what an 'accessible name' is and how it's computed for common elements.
Correctly associate a <label> with its form input using htmlFor/for.
Use aria-label and aria-labelledby for controls that have no visible text label.
Write meaningful alt text for images, and know when alt="" is the correct choice.

sections.text: What an Accessible Name Actually Is

The accessible name is the short string a screen reader announces to identify a control — 'Submit button', 'Email, edit text'. For many elements it's computed automatically from visible text; for icon-only buttons and unlabeled inputs, it has to be supplied explicitly, or the control gets announced as nothing useful at all.

sections.title: An icon button with no accessible name
sections.code:
<!-- Announced to a screen reader as just 'button' -->
<button><svg>...</svg></button>

<!-- Fixed: gives the button a real accessible name -->
<button aria-label="Close menu"><svg>...</svg></button>

sections.text: Associating Labels with Form Inputs

A visible <label> only counts as the input's accessible name if it's programmatically associated via htmlFor matching the input's id (or by wrapping the input inside the label). Text that merely sits near an input visually is not connected to it for assistive technology.

sections.title: Correct vs. incorrect label association

sections.text: aria-label and aria-labelledby

aria-label supplies an accessible name directly as a string, useful when there's no visible label text at all. aria-labelledby instead points to the id of another element whose text should be used as the name — useful when a heading elsewhere already visually serves that purpose.

Billing Address

...

sections.text: Alt Text: Meaningful, or Deliberately Empty

Every content-carrying image needs alt text describing what it conveys, not just what it depicts literally. A purely decorative image (with no informational value) should use alt="" — an empty but present alt attribute — so screen readers skip it entirely instead of reading a meaningless filename.

sections.title: Meaningful vs. decorative
Fix Lab — Unlabeled Search Input
sections.instructions: This search input has a placeholder but no accessible name — placeholders disappear on focus and aren't a reliable substitute for a label. Add a proper label, using aria-label since there's no room for a visible label in this design.
sections.initialCode: <input type="search" placeholder="Search products...">
hints: Placeholders are not an accessible name — they don't reliably substitute for a label.
Add an aria-label attribute describing what the input is for, e.g. 'Search products'.
The placeholder can stay for sighted users; aria-label is what fixes the accessibility gap.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can correctly associate a label with an input via htmlFor/id, add an accessible name to an icon-only button using aria-label, and correctly choose between meaningful alt text and alt="" for a given image.
