quiz.question: Why doesn't a placeholder work as a substitute for a <label>?
options: Placeholders require JavaScript to render.
Placeholders are not supported in any modern browser.
Placeholders can only be used on textarea elements.
Placeholders disappear once the field has a value or is focused, and aren't reliably exposed as an accessible name.
quiz.explanation: Placeholder text vanishes once a value is entered and isn't consistently treated as the input's accessible name, which is why a real label (or aria-label) is required.

quiz.question: What connects a <label> to its input as its accessible name?
options: htmlFor on the label matching the input's id (or wrapping the input inside the label).
Simply placing the label text visually near the input in the layout.
Giving both elements the same className.
Putting them in the same <div>.
quiz.explanation: Only a programmatic association — via htmlFor/id or wrapping — makes the label text count as the input's accessible name; visual proximity alone does not.

quiz.question: When is alt="" the correct choice for an image?
options: Never — every image needs descriptive alt text.
When the image is purely decorative and conveys no information beyond what surrounding text already provides.
Only for background-image CSS properties.
When the image is very large in file size.
quiz.explanation: An empty alt attribute tells screen readers to skip the image entirely — correct for purely decorative images, since announcing them would just add noise.

summary: The accessible name is what assistive technology announces to identify a control, and for icon-only buttons, placeholder-only inputs, and unlabeled sections it has to be supplied deliberately — via a properly associated <label>, aria-label, or aria-labelledby. Images need alt text that conveys their actual informational content, or an empty alt="" if they're purely decorative.

resources.label: W3C WAI — An Alt Decision Tree

interviewQuestions: How do you give an icon-only button an accessible name?
What's the difference between aria-label and aria-labelledby?
How would you decide whether an image needs descriptive alt text or an empty alt attribute?

title: Capstone: Accessibility Audit
description: Run a full accessibility audit of a real interface, combining automated tooling with a required manual keyboard and screen reader pass, and produce fixes.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Run an automated accessibility scan (axe or Lighthouse) and correctly interpret its results.
Explain why automated tools catch roughly a third of real accessibility issues at most, and can't be the only check.
Perform a manual keyboard-only pass and a manual screen reader pass on a real interface.
Produce and prioritize a fix list from combined automated and manual findings.

sections.text: Automated Tools Are a Starting Point, Not the Finish Line

Tools like axe DevTools and Lighthouse's accessibility audit can reliably catch things like missing alt text, insufficient color contrast, and missing form labels — but industry research on tools like axe consistently finds they catch well under half of real WCAG issues. Anything requiring judgment — is this tab order logical? Does this aria-live actually get announced usefully? — needs a human.

sections.title: Running an automated scan
sections.code:
npm install --save-dev @axe-core/cli
npx axe http://localhost:3000

sections.text: The Manual Pass Is Required, Not Optional

This audit isn't complete with automated results alone. You must also: (1) complete a full core task using only the keyboard — no mouse — and note every place focus is lost, skipped, or unclear; and (2) complete the same task with a screen reader running (VoiceOver on macOS, NVDA on Windows, or a mobile screen reader), noting anything announced incorrectly, not announced at all, or confusingly labeled. Automated-tool results alone do not satisfy this capstone.

sections.title: Manual verification checklist
sections.code:
Keyboard pass:
[ ] Every interactive element is reachable via Tab
[ ] Tab order matches visual/logical order
[ ] Every custom control (modal, dropdown, tabs) works with keyboard only
[ ] Focus is always visibly indicated
[ ] No keyboard trap exists anywhere

Screen reader pass:
[ ] Every control announces an accurate name and role
[ ] Form errors are announced when they appear
[ ] Dynamic content changes (toasts, loading states) are announced
[ ] Images are announced with meaningful text, or skipped if decorative
[ ] Page landmarks (main, nav) are present and correctly announced

sections.text: Prioritizing the Fix List

Not every finding is equal. A missing accessible name on the primary 'Buy Now' button blocks a core task and should be fixed first; a slightly suboptimal heading hierarchy on a secondary page is real but lower priority. Rank findings by how completely they block a user from completing a core task, not by how many findings a tool reports in one category.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner has run an automated accessibility scan AND completed a full manual keyboard-only pass AND a full manual screen reader pass on the same real interface, has documented specific findings from each (not just the automated results), and has produced a fix list prioritized by real user impact rather than raw finding count. An audit that skips the manual keyboard/screen-reader verification does not meet this capstone's requirement.

exercises.title: Full Audit of a Real Feature
exercises.brief: Pick a real feature you've built earlier in this course (or a small provided app). Run an automated scan with axe or Lighthouse. Then complete a full keyboard-only pass and a full screen-reader pass of the same feature, documenting specific findings from each. Produce a prioritized fix list and implement fixes for the top three issues.

quiz.question: Why can't an automated accessibility scan alone satisfy a real audit?
options: Automated tools are always wrong.
Automated tools don't run in CI.
Automated tools reliably catch only a portion of real issues and can't judge things requiring human judgment, like whether tab order is logical.
Automated tools only check color contrast.
quiz.explanation: Automated tools are strong on mechanically checkable rules (missing alt text, contrast ratios) but can't evaluate judgment calls like whether an interaction actually makes sense to a keyboard or screen reader user.

quiz.question: What must a complete accessibility audit under this capstone include?
options: An automated scan only.
A design review meeting.
A survey of users about color preferences.
An automated scan, a manual keyboard-only pass, and a manual screen reader pass, all on the same real interface.
quiz.explanation: The capstone explicitly requires manual keyboard and screen reader verification in addition to automated tooling — automated results alone don't satisfy it.

quiz.question: How should findings be prioritized in the fix list?
options: By how completely each issue blocks a user from completing a core task, not by raw count within a tool's category.
Alphabetically by issue name.
By which are cheapest to fix.
By which tool reported them.
quiz.explanation: Impact-based prioritization ensures the fixes that actually unblock real users get done first, rather than chasing whichever category has the most automated findings.

summary: A real accessibility audit combines automated scanning (fast, but only catches a fraction of real issues) with a required manual keyboard-only pass and a manual screen reader pass on the same interface, since those are the only ways to catch issues that require human judgment. Findings should be prioritized by how much they block a real user from completing a core task, and the audit isn't complete without both the automated and manual verification steps.

resources.label: WebAIM — Screen Reader User Survey (methodology and testing notes)

interviewQuestions: Why isn't an automated accessibility scan sufficient on its own?
Walk through how you'd manually test a feature for keyboard accessibility.
How would you prioritize a list of accessibility findings for a team with limited time before a release?

title: What Makes a Web App Slow?
description: Build a diagnostic mental model for frontend performance by identifying whether slowness comes from network work, JavaScript execution, rendering, asset delivery, or unnecessary application work before choosing an optimization.
mastery: The learner can diagnose common frontend performance symptoms by identifying the likely bottleneck category and explain why measurement should precede optimization.
learningObjectives: Explain why perceived web performance depends on more than raw JavaScript execution time.
Distinguish network, JavaScript, rendering, asset, and unnecessary-work bottlenecks.
Connect visible performance symptoms to likely underlying causes.
Explain why performance work should begin with measurement and diagnosis.
Recognize that an optimization is only useful when it addresses an actual bottleneck.
Describe why premature optimization can add complexity without improving user experience.

sections.text: Performance Starts With Diagnosis

A page that feels slow is not necessarily slow for one single reason. The browser may be waiting for the network, downloading a large asset, executing expensive JavaScript, recalculating layout, painting too much UI, or doing unnecessary work.
Before choosing a performance technique, identify which kind of work is actually taking time.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Measure first → identify the bottleneck → optimize that bottleneck → measure again.
A Page Can Be Slow in Different Ways

sections.title: Common bottleneck categories
sections.code:
NETWORK
→ waiting for HTML, JavaScript, data, images, fonts

JAVASCRIPT
→ parsing, compilation, execution, expensive calculations

RENDERING
→ layout, paint, compositing, excessive UI work

ASSETS
→ large images, bundles, fonts, media

UNNECESSARY WORK
→ repeated requests, repeated calculations, avoidable re-renders

sections.text: These categories can overlap. For example, a large JavaScript bundle is both an asset-delivery problem and a source of JavaScript parsing and execution work.
Symptom vs Cause

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Symptom:
Dashboard takes a long time to become interactive.

Possible causes:
→ large JavaScript bundle
→ expensive startup calculation
→ too many components rendering
→ slow API request
→ large third-party dependency

sections.text: The visible symptom does not identify the cause automatically.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not optimize by instinct
sections.text: Adding memoization, splitting components, or rewriting code without first finding the bottleneck can increase complexity while leaving the real performance problem untouched.
Network Slowness

sections.title: A network-heavy page
sections.code:
Browser
 ↓ request
Server
 ↓ response
Browser
 ↓ parse/process
Render

sections.text: If the browser is waiting on a slow API or downloading large resources, changing React rendering behavior may not solve the main problem.
JavaScript Slowness

sections.title: Heavy client work
sections.code:
Download JS
 ↓
Parse/compile
 ↓
Execute expensive code
 ↓
UI becomes responsive

sections.text: A large or computationally expensive client application can spend substantial time working before the user can interact smoothly.
Rendering Slowness

sections.title: Rendering pipeline
sections.code:
State changes
 ↓
React work
 ↓
DOM updates
 ↓
Style/layout/paint work
 ↓
Pixels on screen

sections.text: Rendering problems occur when the browser or application repeatedly performs more UI work than necessary.
Asset Slowness

sections.title: Typical expensive assets
sections.code:
Large hero image
Large JavaScript bundle
Multiple font files
Video/media
Uncompressed static resources

sections.text: Sometimes the highest-value performance improvement is simply reducing what the browser has to download.
Perceived vs Actual Performance

Users judge performance by what they can see and do. A page can technically complete a lot of work quickly yet still feel slow if useful content appears late, the interface blocks interaction, or the layout shifts repeatedly.

sections.title: User experience
sections.code:
Can I see useful content?
Can I interact yet?
Does the interface respond to me?
Does content keep moving around?

sections.text: A Simple Diagnostic Loop

sections.title: Performance diagnosis
sections.code:
1. What feels slow?
2. When does it become slow?
3. Which work happens during that period?
4. What evidence identifies the bottleneck?
5. What is the smallest useful optimization?
6. Did the measurement improve afterward?

sections.text: Interactive Thinking Exercise

sections.title: Performance Diagnosis Playground
sections.instructions: For each symptom, identify the most likely bottleneck category and name one measurement or observation you would use before choosing an optimization.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
The initial page waits 3 seconds before any API data arrives.

Likely bottleneck:
____________________________

Evidence to inspect:
____________________________

Scenario B
The first load downloads a very large JavaScript file.

Likely bottleneck:
____________________________

Evidence to inspect:
____________________________

Scenario C
Typing in a large editor causes visible lag.

Likely bottleneck:
____________________________

Evidence to inspect:
____________________________

Scenario D
A dashboard repeatedly performs expensive calculations after small state changes.

Likely bottleneck:
____________________________

Evidence to inspect:
____________________________

sections.text: Measure Before Memoizing

Memoization can reduce repeated computation or rendering work, but only when repeated work is actually a meaningful cost. If a component spends nearly no time rendering, memoizing it may add complexity without a meaningful improvement.
Measure Before Code Splitting

Code splitting can reduce the amount of JavaScript loaded up front. But if the page is primarily blocked by a slow API or oversized image, splitting a tiny JavaScript module may not materially change the experience.
Measure Before Rewriting Components
A component that looks complicated is not automatically a performance bottleneck. Complexity in source code and measured runtime cost are different things.
Performance Budgets Are About Tradeoffs

A faster experience usually means asking the browser to do less work, do it later, or do it more efficiently. Every optimization also carries engineering cost, so the improvement should justify that cost.

sections.title: The tradeoff
sections.code:
Optimization
→ less runtime/network work

but possibly
→ more code
→ more complexity
→ harder maintenance
→ new failure modes

sections.text: A Real-World Analogy

Imagine a restaurant where customers complain that meals take too long. Adding more cooks might help, but only if the kitchen is the bottleneck. If the real problem is that ingredients arrive late, adding cooks increases complexity without solving the wait.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson focuses specifically on React rendering and re-renders. Once you understand how rendering work is triggered, memoization becomes a tool you can apply based on evidence rather than instinct.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is a diagnostic opener. It establishes performance bottleneck categories and a measure-first mindset; concrete React optimization techniques come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What makes a React application slow?' A strong answer is: 'It can be slow for several reasons: network or asset delivery, JavaScript parsing and execution, rendering work, or unnecessary repeated work. I would measure the actual bottleneck before choosing an optimization.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is the first thing you do when someone says the app is slow?' Ask what feels slow, reproduce the issue, measure the relevant work, and identify the bottleneck before changing code.

Another follow-up is: 'Should you always memoize expensive-looking components?' No. Memoization is useful when measured repeated work matters; otherwise it can add complexity without meaningful benefit.
Reflect

Think about a performance complaint you have encountered before. What was the symptom? What evidence did you actually have about the cause? What optimization would you have chosen differently if you had measured first?

sections.title: Find the bottleneck, then fix it

sections.text: Performance engineering is diagnosis first and optimization second. The best optimization is the one that measurably reduces the work responsible for the user's problem.

sections.label: Pass the recall check by correctly classifying common performance symptoms and explaining why measurement should precede optimization.
sections.hint: Ask what work the browser is waiting on or repeatedly performing: network, assets, JavaScript, rendering, or unnecessary work.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A slow web app can be blocked by network requests, asset size, JavaScript execution, rendering work, or unnecessary repeated work. The visible symptom does not automatically reveal the cause, so performance work should begin with measurement and diagnosis. Optimize the actual bottleneck, then measure again to verify that the change improved the user experience.

exercises.title: Performance Diagnosis Playground
exercises.brief: Classify common frontend performance symptoms and identify what evidence should be gathered before optimizing.

quiz.question: What should you generally do before choosing a performance optimization?
options: Measure and identify the actual bottleneck.
Memoize every component.
Rewrite the entire component tree.
Add more state.
quiz.explanation: Performance work should target measured bottlenecks rather than assumptions.

quiz.question: Which problem is most likely network/asset-related?
options: A 10 MB JavaScript bundle delays first interaction.
A pure function takes 10 microseconds.
A button uses a native HTML element.
A component has a descriptive name.
quiz.explanation: Large downloaded assets can delay loading and increase subsequent parsing and execution work.

quiz.question: Why can premature optimization be harmful?
options: It can add complexity without addressing the actual bottleneck.
Optimizations always make applications slower.
Measurements are unnecessary.
Performance bugs only occur on servers.
quiz.explanation: An optimization is valuable when it reduces the work responsible for the observed problem.

summary: Frontend performance problems come from different categories of work: network and asset delivery, JavaScript parsing/execution, rendering, or unnecessary repeated work. A visible symptom does not identify the bottleneck by itself. The correct workflow is measure, diagnose, optimize the actual bottleneck, and measure again. The next lessons narrow this diagnostic model to React rendering and concrete optimization techniques.
interviewQuestions: What can make a web application feel slow?
How do you diagnose a performance problem?
Why should measurement come before optimization?
How can a large JavaScript bundle affect performance?
How can rendering work cause UI lag?
Why is perceived performance different from raw execution time?
When can memoization fail to improve performance?
What evidence would you gather before changing a slow React component?

title: Rendering and Re-Renders
description: Build a mental model for when React components re-render, what work is repeated, and why unnecessary re-renders can become a performance cost without assuming that every re-render is a problem.
mastery: The learner can explain what causes React components to re-render, distinguish a re-render from a DOM update, identify common sources of repeated rendering work, and explain why performance decisions should be based on measured cost rather than the number of renders alone.
learningObjectives: Explain what a React re-render means.
Identify common causes of component re-renders such as state and prop changes.
Distinguish React rendering work from browser DOM updates.
Explain how parent rendering can affect child rendering.
Recognize that a re-render is not automatically a performance bug.
Identify unnecessary repeated work as a potential performance cost.
Explain why profiling and measurement should precede memoization.
Describe the relationship between state changes, rendering, reconciliation, and commits.

sections.text: What Is a Re-Render?
A React re-render means React calls a component again to calculate what its UI should look like for the current state and props.
That does not mean the browser necessarily replaces every DOM node. React compares the resulting element tree and commits the changes that are actually needed.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: State or props change → React renders to determine the next UI → React reconciles the result → only necessary changes are committed to the DOM.
Rendering Is Not the Same as DOM Replacement

sections.title: Conceptual flow
sections.code:
State change
    ↓
Component function runs
    ↓
React calculates next element tree
    ↓
Reconciliation
    ↓
Necessary DOM changes
    ↓
Browser presents the result

sections.text: Developers sometimes say 'the whole page re-rendered' when they really mean that React performed rendering work. The browser does not necessarily reconstruct the entire visible page.
What Causes a Component to Render?

sections.title: Common triggers
sections.code:
Local state changes

Parent renders and produces the child again

Props change

Context value changes

External store subscription reports an update

sections.text: The exact propagation behavior depends on the component tree and optimization mechanisms, but these are common causes of React rendering work.
Local State Change

sections.title: A local state update

sections.text: Clicking the button changes local state, so React needs to render the component again using the new count.
Parent Rendering Can Cause More Work

sections.title: Parent and child

sections.text: When Parent renders, React also evaluates the child position in the resulting tree. Whether that becomes expensive depends on what the child does and how the application is structured.
The Important Distinction

sections.title: Do not jump from render count to bug
sections.code:
Many renders
≠
Automatically slow

Instead ask:
How expensive is each render?
How often does it happen?
Does the work affect interaction or frame time?
Is the work actually unnecessary?

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Not every re-render is expensive or undesirable. React is designed to re-render as state and props change. Performance work matters when repeated rendering creates measurable user-facing cost.
A Cheap Re-Render

sections.title: Small computation

sections.text: Rendering a simple component such as this is unlikely to be a meaningful performance bottleneck on its own.
An Expensive Re-Render

sections.title: Repeated expensive work

sections.text: If SearchResults runs expensive filtering and sorting on every render while the source inputs have not meaningfully changed, repeated computation can become a real performance concern.
Rendering Work vs Effects

Rendering calculates UI. Effects perform synchronization with systems outside React. Keeping those concepts distinct helps explain why adding effects purely to derive values can create unnecessary work.

sections.title: Prefer derivation
sections.code:
State
 ↓
render
 ↓
computed UI value

sections.title: Potentially unnecessary synchronization
sections.code:
State
 ↓
render
 ↓
effect
 ↓
set derived state
 ↓
another render

sections.text: This lesson is about rendering mechanics, but the broader performance lesson is to avoid unnecessary extra work when a value can be calculated directly.
Interactive Thinking Exercise

sections.title: Render Diagnosis
sections.instructions: For each scenario, identify what causes rendering work and decide whether the render is automatically a problem or needs measurement first.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A button updates its local count state.

Render trigger:
____________________________

Is it automatically a performance bug?
____________________________

Scenario B
A parent updates state and contains a complex child tree.

Render trigger:
____________________________

What should you investigate?
____________________________

Scenario C
A search component filters 100,000 records on every keystroke.

Render trigger:
____________________________

Why might this be expensive?
____________________________

Scenario D
A simple label component renders again after a parent update.

Is the render automatically a problem?
____________________________

sections.text: Render Scope Matters

When a state value changes, the location of that state in the component tree matters. State placed high in the tree can cause more of the tree to participate in rendering work than state kept closer to the component that uses it.

sections.title: State scope
sections.code:
State near the root
→ potentially wider rendering work

State near the feature using it
→ potentially narrower rendering work

sections.text: This does not mean state should always be moved downward. Shared state belongs at an appropriate common boundary. The performance consideration is to avoid unnecessarily broad update scope.
Props and Identity

Props are inputs to a component. In some cases, parent rendering also creates new object, array, or function values. Those new identities can matter to child rendering and become particularly relevant when memoization is introduced.

sections.title: New object on every render

sections.text: The config object is newly created on each Parent render. Whether that matters depends on what Child does and how its props are compared. Do not optimize this merely because the object is recreated; measure the actual cost first.
Why Memoization Comes Later

Memoization can sometimes prevent work caused by unchanged inputs, but using it correctly requires understanding what renders and why. This lesson deliberately stops before introducing memo, useMemo, and useCallback.

sections.title: Concept before tool
sections.code:
Understand renders
      ↓
Identify unnecessary work
      ↓
Measure the cost
      ↓
Choose memoization only if it addresses the problem

sections.text: Re-Render vs Re-Mount

sections.title: Re-render
sections.code:
Component remains in the tree
→ renders again with current inputs

sections.title: Re-mount
sections.code:
Previous component instance is removed
→ a new instance is created

sections.text: These are different lifecycle events. A re-mount can reset local state and recreate the component instance, while an ordinary re-render does not mean the component has been newly mounted.
Why the Distinction Matters

sections.title: Potential symptom
sections.code:
Input unexpectedly loses its text

Possible cause:
component was remounted
rather than merely re-rendered

sections.text: Performance debugging and correctness debugging sometimes overlap. Understanding rendering and mounting helps distinguish the two.
Profiling the Question

sections.title: Ask the profiler
sections.code:
Which component rendered?
How long did the work take?
How often does it happen?
What caused the update?
Which interaction triggered the work?

sections.text: The goal is to turn 'this component renders too much' into a measurable statement about actual work and user impact.
A Simple Diagnostic Example

sections.title: Observed
sections.code:
Typing in search input
→ results component renders 10 times

Question:
Is 10 renders actually slow?

Measure:
Each render = 0.2ms

Conclusion:
Probably not the bottleneck.

sections.text: The correct optimization decision depends on cost, not the render count alone.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson introduces memoization—React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback—and explains when these tools can reduce repeated work and when they simply add complexity.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson builds the rendering mental model. It intentionally does not teach the memoization APIs yet.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What causes a React component to re-render?' A strong answer is: 'State or props changes can trigger rendering, and parent/context/external-store updates can also cause related components to participate in rendering. I would then measure whether the resulting work is actually expensive.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Does a re-render mean the entire DOM is recreated?' No. React calculates the next UI, reconciles it with the previous result, and commits the changes that are needed.
Another follow-up is: 'Are unnecessary re-renders always bad?' No. A re-render can be cheap. The important question is whether repeated rendering creates measurable performance cost.
Reflect

Think about a component tree from your previous applications. Which state changes cause large parts of the tree to render? Which of those renders are actually expensive, and which are probably cheap enough to ignore?
A render count is a clue, not a verdict. Performance work should ask how much work the render performs and whether that work affects the user's experience.

sections.label: Pass the recall check by explaining React's render/reconciliation flow, identifying common render triggers, and distinguishing re-rendering from an actual performance problem.
sections.hint: State/props/context/store updates can trigger rendering. Rendering is not the same as replacing the DOM, and render frequency alone does not establish a performance problem.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

React re-renders components when relevant inputs change, then reconciles the resulting UI with the previous result and commits necessary changes. Re-renders are normal and are not automatically performance bugs. The important question is how much work a render performs, how often that work occurs, and whether it affects the user's experience. This mental model prepares you to evaluate memoization as a targeted tool rather than a default optimization.

exercises.title: Render Diagnosis
exercises.brief: Identify rendering triggers and distinguish normal re-rendering from potentially expensive repeated work.

quiz.question: What does a React re-render mean?
options: React runs the component to calculate the next UI.
The browser deletes and recreates the entire document.
The component is always remounted.
The server sends new HTML.
quiz.explanation: Rendering calculates the next UI; React then reconciles it with the previous result.

quiz.question: Is every re-render a performance problem?
options: Yes.
No. The cost of the work and its user impact matter more than render count alone.
Only in development mode.
Only when props exist.
quiz.explanation: Many renders can be cheap, while a smaller number of expensive renders can matter much more.

quiz.question: How is a re-render different from a re-mount?
options: A re-render recalculates UI for an existing component; a re-mount creates a new component instance.
They are exactly the same.
A re-render always resets state.
A re-mount only changes CSS.
quiz.explanation: A re-mount creates a new instance, while an ordinary re-render does not imply that the component instance was replaced.

quiz.question: What should you ask before deciding that a component re-renders too much?
options: How expensive is the render and does it affect the user experience?
Does the component have more than five lines?
Does it use JSX?
Can the component be given a new name?
quiz.explanation: Performance diagnosis needs evidence about actual work and user impact.

summary: React re-renders when relevant inputs such as state or props change, then reconciles the next UI and commits necessary DOM changes. Rendering is not the same as recreating the entire DOM, and a re-render is not automatically a performance bug. Measure the amount and cost of repeated work before deciding that memoization or another optimization is necessary.
interviewQuestions: What causes a React component to re-render?
What happens during a React render?
Does a React re-render recreate the entire DOM?
What is the difference between a re-render and a re-mount?
Are unnecessary re-renders always a performance problem?
How would you determine whether a re-render is expensive?
How can state placement affect rendering scope?
Why should you understand re-render mechanics before using memoization?

title: Memoization
description: Learn how React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback can prevent unnecessary repeated work when measured performance costs justify them, and recognize when memoization adds complexity without meaningful benefit.
mastery: The learner can explain what React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback do, choose the appropriate memoization technique for a measured bottleneck, and justify when memoization should not be added.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of React.memo.
Explain the purpose of useMemo.
Explain the purpose of useCallback.
Distinguish component memoization from value memoization and function-identity memoization.
Identify situations where stable references matter for child rendering or dependency comparisons.
Recognize when memoization has little or no useful performance benefit.
Avoid memoizing everything by default.
Explain why memoization should follow measurement and profiling.

sections.text: Memoization Is a Performance Tool, Not a Default

The previous lesson established that re-renders are normal and that render count alone does not prove a performance problem. Memoization gives React ways to reuse previous work when the relevant inputs have not changed.
The important question is not 'Can I memoize this?' Almost anything can be wrapped in a memoization technique. The useful question is 'Does memoization remove meaningful repeated work?'

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Measure repeated work → identify a real cost → choose the smallest memoization technique that addresses that cost → measure again.
Three Different Memoization Tools

sections.title: The roles
sections.code:
React.memo
→ memoize a component's rendered result based on props

useMemo
→ memoize a calculated value

useCallback
→ memoize a function reference

sections.text: These tools solve related but different problems. Using the wrong one can add complexity without addressing the actual bottleneck.
React.memo

sections.title: Memoized child component

sections.text: React.memo can allow React to skip rendering the child when its props are considered unchanged. This is most useful when the child is relatively expensive to render and receives stable props.
Memoization Only Helps If Props Are Stable

sections.title: New object every render

sections.text: The options object is newly created each time Parent renders. A memoized child receiving that object may still see a changed prop identity on every render.
useMemo

sections.title: Memoize expensive derived work

sections.text: useMemo caches the result of a calculation until one of its dependencies changes. It can be useful when the calculation is meaningfully expensive and often repeated with the same inputs.
Do Not useMemo Every Calculation

sections.title: Usually unnecessary

sections.text: A tiny string concatenation is already extremely cheap. Wrapping it in useMemo can make the code harder to read without producing a meaningful performance benefit.
useCallback

sections.title: Stable function reference

sections.text: useCallback memoizes the function reference until its dependencies change. This can matter when the function is passed to a memoized child or participates in another identity-sensitive dependency relationship.
useCallback Does Not Make the Function Faster
The main value of useCallback is stable function identity. It does not automatically make the callback's body execute faster.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not memoize everything by default
sections.text: Memoization has a cost in code complexity and dependency management. Apply it when measurement shows repeated rendering or calculation is a meaningful problem and the memoization actually prevents that work.
Interactive Practice: Choose the Tool

sections.title: Memoization Playground
sections.instructions: For each scenario, choose React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, or no memoization. Focus on what kind of repeated work or reference instability actually matters.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A large list item is expensive to render and receives the same props across many parent renders.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario B
Filtering and sorting 100,000 records repeatedly makes typing visibly lag.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario C
A tiny string is built from two names.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario D

Choice:

Scenario E

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

sections.text: React.memo and Parent State

sections.title: Potentially useful pairing

sections.text: If Child is expensive and value remains equivalent, memoization may prevent unnecessary child work when Parent updates for unrelated reasons.
But Memoization Adds a Comparison

React.memo does not make rendering free. React has to compare props to determine whether it can reuse the previous result. For a cheap component, the comparison may provide little or no useful benefit.

sections.title: The tradeoff
sections.code:
Without memo
→ render child

With memo
→ compare props
→ maybe skip child render

Useful when:
render cost > memoization overhead

sections.text: Reference Identity Matters
JavaScript objects and functions are reference values. Creating a new object or function creates a new identity, even if its contents or behavior look the same.
Why useMemo and useCallback Can Work Together With memo

sections.title: Stable object + stable callback

sections.text: Stable values can allow a memoized child to observe unchanged props. But adding all three techniques is not automatically correct; there should be a measured reason for the complexity.
Drill 1: Repair Unnecessary Memoization

sections.title: Memoization Repair Drill
sections.instructions: Review the component and decide which memoization is justified. Remove unnecessary memoization and retain only the optimization that addresses the measured expensive calculation.

sections.text: Memoizing a Function Is Not the Same as Memoizing Its Result

sections.title: Compare
sections.code:
useMemo
→ remembers a calculated value

useCallback
→ remembers a function reference

sections.text: They are conceptually related, but the thing being stabilized is different.
Dependencies Must Be Correct

sections.title: Correct dependency relationship

sections.text: If dependencies are wrong, memoization can return stale values or recreate work more often than intended. Memoization is therefore not just a performance feature; it creates dependency-management responsibilities.
Memoization and Correctness
A memoized value must still represent the current inputs. Never remove a real dependency just to make a memoized calculation run less often.

sections.title: Bad optimization

sections.text: Drill 2: Find the Dependency Bug

sections.title: Memoization Dependency Drill
sections.instructions: Fix the memoized calculation so it remains correct when the underlying inputs change. Explain why each dependency belongs in the dependency list.

sections.text: When No Memoization Is the Better Choice

sections.title: Skip memoization when
sections.code:
The work is already cheap.

The component rarely renders.

Profiling shows no meaningful cost.

The optimization makes dependencies harder to reason about.

The added complexity is greater than the performance benefit.

sections.text: Readable code is itself an engineering benefit. Do not trade it for a theoretical optimization with no measured impact.
A Practical Decision Tree

sections.title: Memoization decision
sections.code:
Is there a measured performance problem?
        ↓ no
   Don't optimize yet.

        ↓ yes

Is repeated calculation expensive?
        ↓ yes
   Consider useMemo.

Is an expensive child rendering with equivalent props?
        ↓ yes
   Consider React.memo.

Does a memoized child receive a changing function reference?
        ↓ yes
   Consider useCallback.

Measure again.

sections.text: Memoization Is Not a Substitute for Good State Design

If a component renders too much because state is unnecessarily global, adding memoization around many children can hide rather than solve the architectural problem. Sometimes moving state closer to where it is used is the better optimization.

sections.title: Architecture before optimization
sections.code:
Unnecessary global update
→ large render scope

Better state placement
→ narrower update scope

Then consider memoization
→ only if expensive work remains

sections.text: Testing Memoized Components

Behavior tests should generally continue to verify the same user-visible behavior before and after memoization. Memoization is an implementation optimization and should not change the feature contract.
Debugging Memoization

sections.title: When memoization doesn't help
sections.code:
1. Did the component actually render frequently?
2. Was its render cost significant?
3. Are props changing identity every render?
4. Is the memo comparison itself worthwhile?
5. Are dependencies recreating the memoized value?
6. Did state architecture create broader work than necessary?

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson moves beyond memoization to code splitting and lazy loading. It targets a different performance category: reducing the JavaScript the browser has to load before the user needs it.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson covers React's primary memoization tools and their tradeoffs. Bundle size and route-level code splitting are handled next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is React.memo?' A strong answer is: 'It can skip rendering a component when its props have not meaningfully changed. I use it when profiling shows an expensive child is rendering unnecessarily, not by default everywhere.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is useMemo?' It memoizes the result of a calculation until its dependencies change. It is useful when repeated computation is meaningfully expensive.
Another follow-up is: 'What is useCallback?' It memoizes a function reference. It matters mainly when referential identity affects something such as a memoized child or a dependency relationship.
Reflect

Look at a component from an earlier project that uses memoization. Can you explain what measured problem each memoization call solves? If you cannot, that is evidence the optimization may deserve review.
Memoization is valuable when it removes expensive repeated work. If you cannot identify the repeated cost it is preventing, prefer simpler code until measurement gives you a reason to optimize.

sections.label: Complete the memoization Playground and both drills. The learner must choose between React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, or no memoization based on the type of repeated work, repair unnecessary memoization, and fix dependency errors.
sections.hint: memo → component result. useMemo → calculated value. useCallback → function identity. All three require a measured reason and correct dependencies.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

React.memo can skip unnecessary child rendering when props are stable, useMemo can reuse an expensive calculated value, and useCallback can stabilize a function reference. These tools are valuable when they address measured repeated work or identity-related rendering costs. They also add comparison and dependency complexity, so the default should be to keep code simple until profiling demonstrates a reason to memoize.

exercises.brief: Choose the appropriate memoization technique for different performance scenarios.

exercises.title: Memoization Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Remove unnecessary memoization and retain only the optimization justified by an expensive repeated calculation.

exercises.title: Memoization Dependency Drill
exercises.brief: Repair an incorrect useMemo dependency list so memoized results remain correct when inputs change.

quiz.question: What does React.memo primarily memoize?
options: A component's rendered result based on its props.
A network response.
A DOM node permanently.
A CSS stylesheet.
quiz.explanation: React.memo can allow React to skip rendering a component when its props are considered unchanged.

quiz.question: What does useMemo memoize?
options: A calculated value.
A component's CSS.
A server response.
A DOM element.
quiz.explanation: useMemo caches a calculation result until one of its dependencies changes.

quiz.question: What is the primary reason to use useCallback?
options: To make the callback execute faster.
To preserve a function reference across renders when identity matters.
To replace every event handler with state.
To persist the function after reload.
quiz.explanation: useCallback stabilizes function identity; it does not inherently make the function body faster.

quiz.question: When should you generally add memoization?
options: Every time a component renders.
When profiling or reasoning identifies meaningful repeated work that memoization can reduce.
Whenever a component has props.
Only for components with more than 50 lines.
quiz.explanation: Memoization should be driven by measured or clearly justified performance needs.

summary: Memoization provides three related tools with different jobs: React.memo can reuse a component result when props remain equivalent, useMemo can reuse an expensive calculated value, and useCallback can stabilize a function reference. None should be applied automatically. Correct dependencies and stable inputs are essential, and every optimization should have a measurable reason. Simpler code is preferable when memoization does not remove meaningful work.

title: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
description: Learn how to reduce initial JavaScript work by splitting application code into smaller chunks and loading routes or components only when they are needed.
mastery: The learner can explain the difference between a single large JavaScript bundle and split chunks, implement route- or component-level lazy loading, and identify situations where deferred loading can improve initial user experience without unnecessarily delaying critical content.
learningObjectives: Explain what code splitting means.
Explain why a large JavaScript bundle can hurt initial load performance.
Distinguish eager loading from lazy loading.
Implement React lazy loading for a non-critical component or route.
Use Suspense to provide a loading boundary for lazy content.
Identify appropriate candidates for route-level or component-level splitting.
Avoid splitting code so aggressively that normal navigation becomes unnecessarily fragmented.
Explain the tradeoff between initial bundle size and deferred loading.

sections.text: Do Not Ship Everything Up Front
Memoization reduces repeated work after code is already running. Code splitting targets a different problem: how much JavaScript the browser has to download and process before the user needs it.
A large application may contain code for routes and features the user never visits during the current session.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Critical code loads first. Non-critical code can be separated into chunks and downloaded when the user reaches the feature that needs it.
One Large Bundle

sections.title: Eager application
sections.code:
Initial page
 ↓
Download all JavaScript
 ↓
Parse/compile/process all of it
 ↓
Application becomes usable

sections.text: If the application contains many large routes or infrequently used features, the user may pay the cost of downloading code they never use.
Split Into Chunks

sections.title: Split application
sections.code:
Initial page
 ↓
Download critical chunk
 ↓
Become interactive

Later:
User opens Reports
 ↓
Download Reports chunk
 ↓
Render Reports

sections.text: The user still eventually downloads the feature code when needed, but the initial page does not have to pay the entire application's JavaScript cost.
Code Splitting and Lazy Loading Are Related

sections.title: Concepts
sections.code:
Code splitting
→ separate code into chunks

Lazy loading
→ defer loading a chunk until it is needed

sections.text: In practice, these ideas often appear together: a bundler creates separate chunks and the application requests one of those chunks only when the feature is rendered.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not make every component lazy
sections.text: Splitting everything can create excessive loading boundaries and extra network work. Defer code when it is meaningfully non-critical or large enough that moving it out of the initial bundle has a useful payoff.
React.lazy

sections.title: Lazy component

sections.text: The import is deferred until React needs to render the lazy component. Suspense provides the UI shown while that code is being loaded.
Route-Level Splitting

sections.title: A route is a strong candidate

sections.text: Routes are often natural code-splitting boundaries because users typically need only the route they are currently visiting.
Component-Level Splitting

sections.title: Defer a heavy feature

sections.text: A large feature that is not immediately needed can sometimes be split without delaying the rest of the dashboard.
Interactive Practice: Lazy Load a Route

sections.title: Code Splitting Playground
sections.instructions: Convert the non-critical Settings route into a lazy-loaded route and provide a useful Suspense fallback. Keep the main Courses route available immediately.

sections.text: Suspense Is the Loading Boundary

sections.title: A useful fallback
sections.code:
Loading settings…

} >

sections.text: The fallback should communicate that the deferred feature is loading. For larger sections, a skeleton or layout-preserving placeholder may be better than a generic message.
Do Not Hide the Critical Page Behind a Non-Critical Chunk

sections.title: Poor split
sections.code:
Initial dashboard
 ↓
Wait for dashboard + analytics + settings + help
 ↓
Show dashboard

sections.title: Better split
sections.code:
Initial dashboard
 ↓
Show essential dashboard

Later:
Analytics chunk
Settings chunk
Help chunk

sections.text: Code splitting should reduce critical work, not simply move the same critical dependency into a delayed request.
Loading Tradeoffs

sections.title: Eager loading
sections.code:
Pros
→ no deferred chunk request
→ feature ready immediately

Cons
→ larger initial payload

sections.title: Lazy loading
sections.code:
Pros
→ smaller initial payload
→ defer unused code

Cons
→ feature has a loading boundary
→ may introduce a later network request

sections.text: The decision depends on how large the feature is, how likely the user is to need it, and whether delaying it creates a meaningful interaction cost.
Drill 1: Choose the Split Boundary

sections.title: Lazy Loading Decision Drill
sections.instructions: Decide which features should stay in the initial bundle and which are good candidates for lazy loading. Consider importance, size, frequency of use, and whether the feature is needed for the first interaction.

Choice: _______________________
Why: __________________________

Scenario B

Choice: _______________________
Why: __________________________

Scenario C
A tiny button component used on every page.
Choice: _______________________
Why: __________________________

Scenario D
A large rich-text editor opened only when editing content.
Choice: _______________________
Why: __________________________

Scenario E
A settings route rarely visited.
Choice: _______________________
Why: __________________________

sections.text: Code Splitting Is Not Free

A split chunk still has to be fetched, parsed, and executed when the user needs it. Excessive splitting can produce many network requests and loading states, especially when the application is divided into tiny pieces without a meaningful performance reason.
Measure the Bundle

sections.title: Before optimization
sections.code:
Initial JavaScript
→ 1.8 MB

sections.title: After meaningful splitting
sections.code:
Initial JavaScript
→ 900 KB

Settings chunk
→ 300 KB

Analytics chunk
→ 600 KB

sections.text: The useful question is not whether there are more chunks. It is whether critical startup work was reduced and the resulting user experience improved.
Drill 2: Repair the Split

sections.title: Code-Splitting Repair
sections.instructions: The application lazily loads a tiny shared button while eagerly loading a large analytics page. Reverse the priorities: keep the tiny ubiquitous control eager and defer the large rarely used analytics feature.

sections.text: Prefetching Can Change the Tradeoff

An application may sometimes request non-critical code before the user actually needs it, based on a strong expectation that the feature will be used soon. This can reduce the delay at navigation time while preserving a smaller critical payload.

sections.title: Conceptual strategy
sections.code:
Initial page
 ↓
Critical code

User shows intent
 ↓
Prefetch likely next chunk
 ↓
Navigate
 ↓
Chunk already available or closer to ready

sections.text: Prefetching is an optimization technique in its own right and should also be driven by evidence and product behavior rather than applied everywhere.
Route-Level Splitting Is Often the First Choice
Large applications frequently have natural route boundaries. A user visiting the course dashboard may not need the settings, admin, or reports code until they navigate there.

sections.title: Natural boundaries
sections.code:
Courses
Settings
Reports
Admin
Help

sections.text: Don't Split Critical Dependencies Blindly
If the initial page cannot render or become useful without a module, moving that module into a lazy chunk may simply replace one delay with another.
Lazy Loading and Error Handling

Deferred code is another network dependency. The application should be prepared for the chunk request to fail and should provide an appropriate recovery experience rather than assuming lazy loading always succeeds.

sections.title: Deferred code lifecycle
sections.code:
Need component
 ↓
Request chunk
 ├── success
 │    ↓
 │  Render feature
 │
 └── failure
      ↓
    Error recovery

sections.text: Debugging Code Splitting

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
Is the initial bundle actually too large?

Which chunk contains the cost?

Is the feature genuinely non-critical?

Does the lazy boundary add noticeable waiting?

Does the loading fallback preserve the layout?

What happens if the chunk fails?

sections.text: Testing Lazy-Loaded UI

Behavior tests can verify the user-visible loading state and eventual feature appearance. The test should focus on the experience rather than asserting the exact number of JavaScript chunks produced by the bundler.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses on image and asset optimization, another way to reduce the amount of work and data the browser must process.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on JavaScript code splitting and deferred component/route loading. Image formats, compression, responsive assets, and media optimization come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is code splitting?' A strong answer is: 'It separates application code into multiple chunks so the browser does not have to download and process all of the application's JavaScript up front. Lazy loading then requests a chunk when the feature that needs it is used.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Where would you split a React application?' Route boundaries are often strong candidates, as are large features that are not needed for the initial experience.
Another follow-up is: 'What is the downside of lazy loading?' The deferred feature needs another request and a loading state, and excessive splitting can add complexity and unnecessary network work.
Reflect
Look at your current application's routes. Which routes contain substantial code that a typical user may never visit during their first session? Which code must remain in the critical initial path?

sections.title: Ship what the user needs now

sections.text: A useful split reduces critical startup work without turning ordinary interactions into a maze of tiny loading boundaries.

sections.label: Complete the Code Splitting Playground and both drills. The learner must lazy-load an appropriate route/feature, provide a useful fallback, and choose sensible eager vs deferred boundaries based on criticality and size.
sections.hint: Keep critical, ubiquitous code eager. Defer large or rarely needed features. A split is only valuable when it reduces meaningful initial work.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Code splitting separates an application's JavaScript into chunks, while lazy loading defers a chunk until the feature that needs it is used. Route-level and large-feature boundaries are often strong candidates. Use Suspense to provide a useful loading boundary, measure bundle impact, and avoid excessive splitting. The goal is not more chunks; it is less critical startup work and a better user experience.

exercises.brief: Convert a non-critical route into a lazy-loaded route with an appropriate Suspense fallback.

exercises.title: Lazy Loading Decision Drill
exercises.brief: Choose sensible eager/deferred boundaries based on criticality, size, and expected usage.

quiz.question: What is the main goal of code splitting?
options: Reduce the amount of JavaScript the browser must download and process up front.
Make every component load in a separate request.
Remove all JavaScript from the application.
Guarantee that every route renders instantly.
quiz.explanation: Code splitting reduces critical initial JavaScript work by separating code into chunks.

quiz.question: What does lazy loading add on top of code splitting?
options: It defers requesting a split chunk until the feature needs it.
It permanently removes the feature.
It makes the chunk smaller automatically.
It disables Suspense.
quiz.explanation: Lazy loading delays retrieval of a split chunk until it is needed.

quiz.question: Which is generally a strong candidate for route-level lazy loading?
options: A tiny button used on every screen.
A large rarely visited admin route.
The primary component required for the first paint.
A shared icon.
quiz.explanation: Large, infrequently used routes are natural candidates for deferred loading.

quiz.question: What is a downside of excessive lazy loading?
options: It can add extra requests, loading states, and complexity.
It always increases the initial bundle.
It removes the need for performance measurement.
It makes native HTML inaccessible.
quiz.explanation: Splitting is a tradeoff; too many tiny boundaries can create unnecessary loading overhead.

summary: Code splitting reduces critical JavaScript by separating application code into chunks, while lazy loading defers fetching a chunk until a feature needs it. Route-level and large non-critical feature boundaries are often effective. Suspense provides the loading boundary for lazy content. The goal is not to maximize the number of chunks but to reduce meaningful initial work without making normal interactions unnecessarily delayed or fragmented.

title: Error Boundaries
description: Contain rendering errors to a small part of the UI with error boundaries, instead of letting one broken component take down the whole app.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what an error boundary catches and what it deliberately does not catch.
Implement an error boundary component and wrap a risky UI section in it instead of the whole app.
Explain why error boundaries must currently be class components in React.
Design fallback UI that lets the rest of the page keep working when one section fails.

sections.text: One Broken Component Shouldn't Take Down the Whole App

By default, an uncaught error thrown during render unmounts the entire React tree — a bug in a single widget can blank the whole page. Error boundaries let you contain that failure to just the part of the UI that broke, showing a fallback there while everything else keeps working.

sections.title: A minimal error boundary

sections.text: Why It Has to Be a Class Component

getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch are lifecycle methods with no hook equivalent yet — there is currently no useErrorBoundary hook. Error boundaries are one of the few remaining places a class component is still the standard, correct tool, even in an otherwise fully hooks-based codebase.
Wrap the Risky Section, Not the Whole App

A single error boundary around the entire app means any failure anywhere blanks the whole page — barely better than the default. Instead, wrap individual risky or independent sections (a third-party widget, a chart, a comments section) so a failure there degrades gracefully while the rest of the page, like navigation and the main content, keeps working.

sections.title: Scoped, not global

sections.text: What Error Boundaries Do Not Catch

Error boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the tree below them. They do not catch errors in event handlers, in async code (like a fetch callback), in server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the boundary itself. Event handler errors need their own try/catch.

sections.title: Event handler errors need try/catch, not an error boundary

sections.text: Common Mistake: Assuming One Boundary Covers Everything

Teams sometimes add a single top-level error boundary and consider error handling done. It catches render-time crashes, but a click handler that throws will still go completely uncaught unless it has its own try/catch.

sections.title: Fix Lab — Scope the Boundary Correctly
sections.instructions: This app wraps the entire tree in one ErrorBoundary, so a crash in the optional 'RelatedItems' widget blanks the whole page including navigation. Move the boundary so it only wraps RelatedItems, letting the rest of the page survive.
hints: Move Nav and MainContent outside the ErrorBoundary entirely.
Wrap only the component that's actually risky (RelatedItems) inside the boundary.
The goal is that a crash in RelatedItems shows its own fallback while Nav and MainContent keep rendering normally.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can implement an error boundary as a class component, wrap a single risky UI section in it rather than the whole app, and correctly explain that event handler and async errors require their own try/catch since error boundaries don't catch those.

exercises.title: Contain a Flaky Widget
exercises.brief: Given a Dashboard with a Header, a MainContent area, and a third-party StockTicker widget that occasionally throws during render, wrap only the StockTicker in an error boundary with a fallback message, and verify the rest of the dashboard keeps rendering when it throws.

quiz.question: What does a React error boundary catch?
options: Errors thrown inside event handlers.
Errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the component tree below it.
Errors thrown inside async fetch callbacks.
Errors thrown during server-side rendering.
quiz.explanation: Error boundaries specifically catch render-phase errors in their child tree — not event handler errors, async errors, or SSR errors, which need their own handling.

quiz.question: Why should an error boundary usually wrap a specific risky section rather than the entire app?
options: Wrapping smaller sections is required for the boundary to compile.
React requires at least three error boundaries per app.
A single top-level boundary means any failure anywhere blanks the whole page, barely improving on the default behavior.
It has no effect either way.
quiz.explanation: Scoping boundaries to independent, risky sections lets unrelated parts of the page keep working when one section fails, which is the whole point of using them.

quiz.question: Why must an error boundary currently be written as a class component?
options: This is a Vite-specific restriction, not a React one.
Class components render faster than function components.
Hooks cannot be used inside any component that renders children.
getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch have no hook equivalent yet.
quiz.explanation: There's currently no hook equivalent for these two lifecycle methods, making error boundaries one of the few remaining necessary uses of a class component.

summary: Error boundaries contain render-time crashes to a specific part of the UI instead of letting them unmount the entire app, and are still one of the few places a class component is the correct, standard tool since there's no hook equivalent for componentDidCatch. Scope boundaries around individual risky sections rather than the whole app, and remember they don't catch event handler or async errors — those still need their own try/catch.
