title: Graceful Failure
description: Design interfaces that degrade usefully when something goes wrong — a failed request, a slow connection, a broken third-party script — instead of leaving the user with a blank screen or silent failure.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Distinguish a graceful failure from a silent failure and from a hard crash.
Design a fallback experience for a feature that depends on an unreliable resource (network, third-party script).
Combine error boundaries, retry logic, and clear user-facing messaging into one coherent failure strategy.
Evaluate whether a given error state actually tells the user what happened and what they can do next.

sections.text: Three Ways an Interface Can Fail

A hard crash blanks the screen or throws a visible error, and everyone notices. A silent failure is worse — the UI looks fine but data is wrong, missing, or stale, and no one notices until it's a support ticket or a bad decision. A graceful failure sits between: something did break, the user is told clearly what, and the rest of the app keeps working.
Combining What You've Already Built

Graceful failure isn't a new technique — it's combining pieces from earlier in this module and course: error boundaries (lesson-4-5-5) contain render crashes to one section; retries and error states (lesson-4-2-4) handle failed requests; loading/error/empty states (lesson-2-4-6) give every async UI a defined failure state instead of an undefined one.

sections.title: A feature with a real failure strategy

sections.text: A Good Error Message Answers Two Questions

What happened, and what can the user do about it. 'Something went wrong' answers neither. 'Recommendations couldn't load right now — try again' answers both, briefly, without blaming the user or exposing internal error details they can't act on.

sections.title: Weak vs. useful error messaging
sections.code:
Weak:  "An error occurred."
Weak:  "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined"
Useful: "We couldn't save your changes. Check your connection and try again."

sections.text: Non-Critical Features Should Fail Quietly Into Nothing

Not every failure deserves an alert. If 'recommended products' fails to load, hiding that section entirely is often better UX than showing an error message for a feature the user didn't specifically ask for — reserve visible error messaging for things the user is actively trying to do, like submitting a form or completing checkout.
Common Mistake: One Generic Error State for Everything

Reusing the same 'Something went wrong' fallback for every possible failure treats a failed payment the same as a failed avatar image — both look identically alarming to the user, even though only one of them actually needs their attention.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can design a failure strategy for a given feature that specifies exactly what happens on failure (visible message with a retry, silent hide, or something else) based on how critical that feature is to the user's current task, and can rewrite a generic 'something went wrong' message into one that states what happened and what the user can do.

exercises.title: Design Failure States for Three Features
exercises.brief: For each of: (1) a checkout payment step, (2) a 'related articles' widget, (3) a user's profile avatar image — decide and implement what should happen if the underlying request/resource fails: visible error with retry, silent fallback, or something else. Justify each choice in one sentence.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a silent failure from a graceful one?
options: In a silent failure the UI looks fine while data is actually wrong or missing, unnoticed; a graceful failure is visible and clearly communicated.
A silent failure happens faster.
There is no meaningful difference.
A graceful failure always crashes the app.
quiz.explanation: A silent failure is dangerous precisely because nothing looks wrong even though something is — a graceful failure is the opposite: visible, clear, and non-crashing.

quiz.question: Why might a failed 'recommended products' widget be better handled by hiding it entirely rather than showing an error message?
options: Error messages are never appropriate anywhere in an app.
It's a non-critical feature the user didn't specifically request, so a visible alert would be disproportionate to its importance.
Hiding failures is always the best choice for every feature.
It reduces the JavaScript bundle size.
quiz.explanation: Reserving visible error messaging for things the user is actively trying to do (like checkout) and letting non-critical features fail quietly avoids over-alarming users about things that don't affect their actual task.

quiz.question: What two things should a good user-facing error message communicate?
options: The exact stack trace and error code.
Only an apology.
What happened and what the user can do about it.
The internal service name that failed.
quiz.explanation: A useful error message briefly states what happened and gives the user an actionable next step, like retrying — raw technical details aren't actionable for most users.

summary: Graceful failure means designing deliberately for what happens when something breaks — combining error boundaries, retry logic, and clear messaging so the user is neither left staring at a blank crash nor silently given wrong data. Not every failure deserves a visible alert: reserve that for things the user is actively trying to do, and let non-critical features fail quietly. A good error message states what happened and what the user can do next.

resources.label: web.dev — Error handling for a resilient front end
Nielsen Norman Group — Error Message Guidelines

interviewQuestions: How would you decide whether a failed feature should show a visible error or fail silently?
What makes an error message actually useful to a user, versus just technically accurate?
How do error boundaries, retry logic, and defined loading/error states fit together into one failure strategy?

title: Performance Investigation Challenge
description: Diagnose and fix a genuinely slow, semi-realistic application using profiling and the performance techniques learned throughout the module, while explaining the actual root cause rather than optimizing the first suspicious-looking code.
mastery: The learner can reproduce a performance problem, profile the application to isolate the actual bottleneck, apply an appropriate fix, verify that the problem improved, and explain the root cause independently.
learningObjectives: Reproduce a real performance symptom before changing code.
Use profiling and browser performance tools to identify the actual bottleneck.
Distinguish symptoms from root causes.
Apply an evidence-based optimization rather than guessing.
Verify the performance improvement after the fix.
Explain why the chosen optimization addresses the diagnosed bottleneck.
Avoid optimizing the first slow-looking code without evidence.
Use the performance techniques from the module in combination where appropriate.

sections.text: The Performance Investigation Challenge
This is the module capstone. You are given a slow, semi-realistic application and a symptom, but not the cause.
Your job is to investigate the problem using the profiling and performance techniques from this module, identify the actual bottleneck, fix it, and explain why your fix works.

sections.title: The capstone rule
sections.text: Do not start by editing the code that looks suspicious. Reproduce the problem, profile it, isolate the bottleneck, then choose the smallest appropriate fix.
The Seeded App

The application should contain enough realistic work to make profiling meaningful: a dashboard with a large data set, an expensive derived calculation, multiple UI sections, and at least one piece of code that is inefficient but not necessarily the primary bottleneck.

sections.title: Example symptom
sections.code:
User types into the dashboard search field
        ↓
UI visibly lags
        ↓
Characters appear late
        ↓
Developer is tempted to blame the input component

sections.text: The input itself may not be the root cause. The investigation should determine what work happens after each keystroke.
Phase 1: Reproduce

sections.title: Reproduction checklist
sections.code:
□ Start from a known application state.
□ Perform the exact interaction that feels slow.
□ Confirm the symptom is repeatable.
□ Record what the user experiences.
□ Do not optimize yet.

sections.text: A problem that cannot be reproduced consistently is harder to investigate. First create a repeatable scenario.
Phase 2: Form a Hypothesis

sections.title: Possible hypotheses
sections.code:
A. Search calculation is expensive.
B. Too many components are rendering.
C. A large asset is blocking the interaction.
D. A state update is causing unnecessarily broad work.
E. A third-party dependency is doing expensive work.

sections.text: A hypothesis is useful because it gives you something to investigate. It is not proof.
Phase 3: Profile

sections.title: Evidence to collect
sections.code:
React rendering profile
→ which components render and how long they take

Browser Performance profile
→ long tasks, scripting, rendering, main-thread work

Network information
→ request size/timing when relevant

Bundle/resource information
→ code and asset weight when relevant

sections.text: Use the tool that matches your hypothesis. If the interaction is CPU-bound, a network panel alone will not identify the expensive JavaScript work.
Phase 4: Isolate

sections.title: From symptom to cause
sections.code:
Slow search
 ↓
Search input updates state
 ↓
Dashboard renders
 ↓
Results calculation runs
 ↓
100,000 records filtered + sorted
 ↓
Main thread blocked

Root cause:
Repeated expensive calculation

sections.text: The root cause is the expensive repeated work, not simply the fact that the input changes state.
Phase 5: Choose the Fix

sections.title: Possible fixes
sections.code:
Memoization
→ when expensive derived work repeats with unchanged inputs

React.memo
→ when expensive child rendering repeats unnecessarily

State restructuring
→ when update scope is unnecessarily broad

Code splitting
→ when critical JavaScript delivery is the bottleneck

Asset optimization
→ when large resources dominate loading cost

Error boundary / graceful failure
→ when a failure causes an unnecessarily broad UI outage

sections.text: The correct fix depends on the evidence. The challenge is not to demonstrate that every technique can be used; it is to select the technique that addresses the actual bottleneck.
Phase 6: Verify

sections.title: After the fix
sections.code:
Repeat the exact reproduction
 ↓
Profile again
 ↓
Compare before vs after
 ↓
Confirm the user-visible symptom improved
 ↓
Confirm no important behavior regressed

sections.text: Phase 7: Explain the Root Cause
Fixing the bug is only part of the capstone. You must explain what caused the performance problem.

sections.title: Strong explanation
sections.code:
Symptom:
Search typing lagged.

Root cause:
Every keystroke triggered an expensive filter/sort over 100,000 records.

Evidence:
Profiler showed the calculation dominated the interaction's main-thread time.

Fix:
Memoized the derived result using its real inputs.

Verification:
The same search interaction completed substantially faster.

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not fix the first slow-looking code you find
sections.text: The first suspicious component is not necessarily the bottleneck. The capstone is testing whether you can use profiling evidence to distinguish correlation from the actual cause.
Challenge Workspace

sections.title: Performance Investigation Challenge
sections.instructions: Investigate the seeded slow application. Do not inspect the intended fix first. Reproduce the symptom, record a hypothesis, use profiling to identify the bottleneck, implement the smallest justified fix, rerun the same scenario, and document the root cause.

sections.text: Investigation Log

sections.title: Root-Cause Investigation Log
sections.instructions: Fill this out while completing the challenge. The answer should reflect evidence you actually gathered rather than the optimization you guessed first.
sections.initialCode:
SYMPTOM
What feels slow?
_______________________________

REPRODUCTION
What exact interaction reproduces it?
_______________________________

HYPOTHESIS
What do you initially suspect?
_______________________________

EVIDENCE
What did the profiler/tools show?
_______________________________

BOTTLENECK
What work is actually expensive?
_______________________________

FIX
What did you change?
_______________________________

WHY THIS FIX
Why does it address the measured cause?
_______________________________

VERIFICATION
What changed in the after measurement?
_______________________________

ROOT CAUSE
Explain the actual cause in one paragraph.
_______________________________

sections.text: Do Not Confuse Symptom and Root Cause

sections.title: Weak diagnosis
sections.code:
The search input is slow.
→ memoized the input component.

sections.title: Stronger diagnosis
sections.code:
Typing changes search state.
→ that triggers a large derived calculation.
→ calculation dominates interaction time.
→ reduce/reuse that repeated work.

sections.text: Challenge Variant: A Different Bottleneck

sections.title: Possible alternate seed
sections.code:
Symptom:
Initial dashboard feels slow.

Evidence:
Large analytics route is included in the initial JavaScript.

Potential fix:
Route-level code splitting.

Important:
Do not add memoization just because React renders.

sections.text: A strong challenge environment can randomize or swap the bottleneck so learners cannot solve the capstone from memory.
Challenge Variant: Rendering Bottleneck

sections.title: Another possible seed
sections.code:
Symptom:
Typing causes expensive list rendering.

Evidence:
A large set of expensive children renders repeatedly.

Potential fix:
Architectural narrowing or React.memo with stable props.

Verification:
Profile the interaction before and after.

sections.text: Challenge Variant: Asset Bottleneck

sections.title: Another possible seed
sections.code:
Symptom:
Initial page loads slowly.

Evidence:
Several oversized images dominate transfer.

Potential fix:
Appropriate source dimensions + compression + deferred non-critical images.

sections.text: Challenge Variant: Failure Bottleneck

sections.title: Another possible seed
sections.code:
Symptom:
One rendering failure blanks the dashboard.

Evidence:
A risky widget throws and there is one global failure boundary.

Potential fix:
Isolate the risky section with a narrower error boundary and useful fallback.

sections.text: Required Evidence

sections.title: Submission evidence
sections.code:
□ Reproducible performance symptom.
□ Initial hypothesis.
□ Profiling/tool evidence.
□ Identified bottleneck.
□ Applied fix.
□ Before/after comparison.
□ Root-cause explanation.
□ Confirmation that normal functionality still works.

sections.text: Quality Bar

sections.title: Strong submission
sections.code:
Evidence before optimization

Smallest justified change

No unnecessary collection of optimizations

Before/after verification

Clear root-cause explanation

No major functional regression

sections.text: Failure Modes

sections.title: What will not pass
sections.code:
□ 'I added memo and it felt faster.'
□ No profiling evidence.
□ Fix targets unrelated code.
□ Root cause is described only as the symptom.
□ No before/after comparison.
□ Multiple random optimizations make the cause unclear.

sections.text: Final Defense
Be prepared to defend the diagnosis as though you were reviewing a production performance incident with another engineer.

sections.title: Five questions
sections.code:
1. What exactly was slow?
2. How did you reproduce it?
3. What evidence proved the bottleneck?
4. Why does your fix address that bottleneck?
5. How did you verify the fix did not merely move the cost elsewhere?

sections.text: Module Completion
After this challenge, Module 4-5 is complete. The learner should now be able to investigate performance problems instead of treating optimization as a collection of memorized tricks.

sections.label: Pass the Debug Lab by reproducing the seeded slow-app problem, profiling to identify the actual bottleneck, resolving the bug, and explaining the root cause in the learner's own words.
sections.hint: The first slow-looking code is only a hypothesis. Profile it, isolate the expensive work, fix that work, and verify the improvement.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Performance engineering is an investigation discipline. Reproduce the symptom, form a hypothesis, collect profiling evidence, isolate the actual bottleneck, apply the smallest justified fix, and measure again. A passing capstone requires both a working fix and an accurate root-cause explanation—not merely a change that happens to make the app feel faster.

exercises.title: Root-Cause Investigation Log
exercises.brief: Document the symptom, hypothesis, evidence, bottleneck, fix, verification, and root cause during the performance investigation.

exercises.title: Performance Investigation Challenge
exercises.brief: Reproduce, profile, isolate, fix, and verify a seeded performance problem in a semi-realistic application.

quiz.question: What should you do before changing the suspicious-looking code in a performance challenge?
options: Profile and collect evidence about the actual bottleneck.
Memoize every component.
Rewrite the input component.
Split every route.
quiz.explanation: The challenge specifically tests evidence-based diagnosis instead of guessing.

quiz.question: What makes a strong root-cause explanation?
options: It repeats the user-visible symptom.
It identifies the underlying work responsible for the symptom and cites the evidence used to identify it.
It lists every optimization attempted.
It names the first component you noticed.
quiz.explanation: Root-cause analysis connects the symptom to the underlying expensive work using evidence.

quiz.question: What must happen after the fix?
options: Stop once the code looks cleaner.
Reproduce and measure the same scenario again to verify improvement.
Remove all profiling tools.
Add another optimization immediately.
quiz.explanation: Before/after verification establishes whether the fix actually improved the diagnosed problem.

summary: The Performance Investigation Challenge is the capstone for Performance and Resilience. It presents a symptom without revealing its cause and requires the learner to reproduce the issue, profile the application, isolate the real bottleneck, apply an evidence-based fix, verify the improvement, and explain the root cause. The critical skill is investigation rather than memorizing a particular optimization.
interviewQuestions: How would you investigate a slow React application?
Why should you profile before optimizing?
How do you distinguish a performance symptom from its root cause?
What evidence would prove that memoization is useful?
How would you verify that a performance fix worked?
How would you investigate a large initial bundle?
How would you investigate a rendering bottleneck?
What makes a good performance incident explanation?

title: Image and Asset Optimization
description: Learn to reduce the amount of image and static-asset work a browser must download and process by choosing appropriate dimensions, formats, loading strategies, and delivery approaches.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain why images and static assets can become major performance costs.
Identify oversized images and assets that deliver more data than the interface needs.
Choose image dimensions appropriate to the rendered size.
Explain the value of modern image formats and compression.
Use responsive image techniques where appropriate.
Distinguish critical visual assets from below-the-fold assets.
Apply lazy loading to appropriate non-critical images.
Explain why asset optimization should be measured against actual network and rendering costs.
Avoid shipping unnecessarily large assets or loading all media eagerly.

sections.text: Images Can Be the Performance Bottleneck
The previous lesson reduced JavaScript work through code splitting. Images and other static assets create a different cost: the browser must download, decode, and display them.
A visually simple page can still be expensive if it ships large images that are displayed at much smaller dimensions.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Send the smallest asset that still provides the required visual quality, load it at the right time, and avoid downloading content the user does not currently need.
The Oversized Image Problem

sections.title: Unnecessary work
sections.code:
Original image
→ 3000 × 2000
→ 2.5 MB

Rendered card
→ 300 × 200

Browser downloads:
→ much more data than the UI needs

sections.text: Large source dimensions can increase network transfer and decoding work even when the browser ultimately displays the image at a small size.
Use Appropriate Dimensions

sections.title: Better asset sizing
sections.code:
Card display
→ approximately 300px wide

Useful source candidates
→ 320px
→ 640px for higher-density displays

Avoid
→ 3000px source for every card

sections.text: The right dimensions depend on the rendered size and the display density you need to support.
Compression Matters
Images contain information that can often be compressed significantly without an unacceptable visual difference. The correct compression level depends on the image type and product requirements.

sections.title: Think in terms of tradeoffs
sections.code:
Higher quality
→ larger asset
→ potentially slower transfer

More compression
→ smaller asset
→ potentially lower visual quality

sections.text: Use Appropriate Formats

sections.title: General selection idea
sections.code:
Photographic imagery
→ use an efficient photographic format

Illustrations / graphics
→ use a format appropriate to the visual characteristics

Transparency/vector graphics
→ choose a format that preserves the needed properties

sections.text: The correct choice depends on the content and browser support requirements. The performance goal is to avoid paying for unnecessary bytes or quality.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not optimize only by shrinking CSS dimensions
sections.text: Setting width and height in CSS does not reduce the bytes the browser downloads. The source asset itself should be appropriately sized and encoded.
Responsive Images

sections.title: Different sources for different widths

sections.text: Responsive image hints allow the browser to choose an appropriate source for the display context instead of receiving one oversized image for every device.
Lazy Load Non-Critical Images

sections.title: Below-the-fold image

sections.text: Images that are not needed immediately can often be deferred so the initial page does not compete with them for network and processing resources.
Do Not Lazy Load Everything
An important above-the-fold image may be part of the initial visual experience. Deferring every image can make critical content appear later than necessary.

sections.title: Think about priority
sections.code:
Critical hero image
→ likely needs early delivery

Image far below the fold
→ candidate for lazy loading

Tiny icon used immediately
→ probably not a lazy-loading candidate

sections.text: Interactive Practice: Optimize the Image

sections.title: Image Optimization Playground
sections.instructions: Review the image configuration and identify which changes reduce unnecessary bytes or defer non-critical work. Keep the critical hero image available quickly while optimizing lower-page media.

sections.text: Width and Height Attributes

sections.title: Reserve the image's space

sections.text: Providing intrinsic dimensions helps the browser understand the image's expected geometry and can reduce layout movement while the resource loads.
Asset Optimization Is More Than Images

sections.title: Other assets
sections.code:
Fonts
Icons
Video
Audio
SVGs
JavaScript
CSS
Static JSON/data files

sections.text: The same performance questions apply: how large is the resource, when is it needed, and can it be delivered more efficiently?
Fonts Can Affect Loading

sections.title: Font cost
sections.code:
Download font
 ↓
Parse font
 ↓
Apply font
 ↓
Potential visual changes

sections.text: Large families with many unused weights or styles can increase asset cost. Load only the font variations that the product actually needs.
SVGs and Icons
Icons should also be appropriate to their role. A huge raster image is usually a poor fit for a simple interface icon when a lightweight vector representation would communicate the same visual.
Drill 1: Choose the Asset Strategy

sections.title: Asset Strategy Drill
sections.instructions: Choose an appropriate delivery strategy for each resource. Consider whether the asset is critical, how large it is, and how the user encounters it.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
A large hero image visible immediately above the fold.
Strategy:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario B
A gallery of 40 images far below the fold.
Strategy:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario C
A 20KB logo used in the header.
Strategy:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario D
A 2MB image displayed in a 280px-wide card.
Strategy:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario E
A page loads six font weights but uses only two.
Strategy:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

sections.text: Avoid Loading Media That the User Cannot See Yet
A page containing many below-the-fold images can compete with more important resources even though the user does not need those images during the first interaction.

sections.title: Priority-based loading
sections.code:
Initial viewport
→ critical content/assets

Near viewport
→ prepare as appropriate

Far below viewport
→ defer when appropriate

sections.text: Do Not Create a Low-Quality Experience to Save Bytes
Asset optimization is a tradeoff. Excessive compression, visibly degraded imagery, or delayed critical content can make the product feel worse even if transfer size decreases.
Measure Asset Cost

sections.title: Useful evidence
sections.code:
Resource size
Transfer size
Request timing
Decode/processing cost
Number of requests
When the asset becomes visible
Impact on the initial experience

sections.text: Use browser development tools and performance measurements to identify which assets actually contribute meaningful cost.
Drill 2: Repair the Asset Loading

sections.title: Asset Loading Repair
sections.instructions: Optimize the gallery so the first visible image remains available quickly while lower-page images use smaller appropriate sources and deferred loading. Avoid changing the user-visible dimensions of the cards.

sections.text: Critical Assets vs Decorative Assets

sections.title: Ask what the asset does
sections.code:
Communicates important information
→ optimize carefully + preserve accessibility

Decorative visual
→ can often be deferred or simplified

Brand-critical above-the-fold visual
→ prioritize appropriately

sections.text: Performance choices should not accidentally remove meaningful information. Asset optimization and accessibility remain connected.
Asset Optimization and Accessibility

A smaller image is not automatically an accessible image. Meaningful images still need appropriate alternative text, while purely decorative images should not add unnecessary information to the accessibility tree.
Debugging Asset Problems

sections.title: When an image-heavy page is slow
sections.code:
1. Which images are largest?
2. What dimensions are actually displayed?
3. Are there responsive source options?
4. Are below-the-fold images loading immediately?
5. Are critical images competing with non-critical resources?
6. Are formats/compression appropriate?
7. Does optimization preserve visual quality and accessibility?

sections.text: The Broader Asset Rule

sections.title: For every asset
sections.code:
Do I need it?

Do I need it now?

Can I make it smaller?

Can I choose a better format?

Can I load only the version appropriate to the user's device/context?

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson moves from individual optimizations to production measurement: using performance tools and budgets to determine whether the application's real user experience is improving.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on asset size, format, dimensions, and loading priority. Detailed performance measurement and budgets come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you optimize a page with large images?' A strong answer is: 'I would measure the asset sizes and loading timeline first, make the sources appropriate to their rendered dimensions, use efficient encoding, provide responsive variants where useful, and defer non-critical images while prioritizing important above-the-fold content.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Does CSS width reduce image download cost?' No. CSS changes display size; the source asset still has to be downloaded and decoded unless the browser can choose a more appropriate resource.

Another follow-up is: 'Should every image use lazy loading?' No. Critical images may need earlier delivery, while below-the-fold or otherwise non-critical images are stronger candidates for lazy loading.
Reflect
Inspect the image assets in one of your projects. Find the largest files, compare them with their rendered sizes, and identify which resources are loaded before the user needs them.

sections.title: Send only what the user needs

sections.text: Asset performance is a simple question applied repeatedly: do we need this resource, do we need it now, and can we deliver a smaller appropriate version?

sections.label: Complete the Image Optimization Playground and both asset-strategy drills. The learner must identify oversized resources, choose appropriate loading priority, and preserve critical content while reducing unnecessary asset work.
sections.hint: Match source dimensions to rendered size, use appropriate encoding, defer non-critical media, and prioritize what the user needs first.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Images and static assets can dominate a page's performance cost. Optimize them by choosing appropriate dimensions and encoding, using responsive sources when helpful, and deferring non-critical resources. CSS display dimensions alone do not make an oversized source cheaper to download. The goal is to reduce unnecessary bytes and processing while preserving visual quality, accessibility, and critical content availability.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: The learner can identify oversized or unnecessarily expensive assets, choose appropriate image dimensions and loading strategies, and explain how asset choices affect network transfer, rendering, and perceived performance.

exercises.title: Image Optimization Playground
exercises.brief: Identify oversized image sources, choose appropriate dimensions and loading priority, and optimize critical versus non-critical media.

exercises.title: Asset Strategy Drill
exercises.brief: Choose appropriate delivery strategies for hero images, below-the-fold galleries, logos, oversized card images, and fonts.

exercises.title: Asset Loading Repair
exercises.brief: Improve gallery loading by reducing unnecessary source size, adding appropriate deferred loading, and preserving layout dimensions.

quiz.question: Does changing an image's CSS width automatically reduce the number of bytes downloaded?
options: Yes, always.
Only for SVGs.
Only in development.
No. The source resource still needs to be downloaded unless the browser can select a more appropriate resource.
quiz.explanation: Display dimensions do not change the size of the source resource itself.

quiz.question: Which image is generally the strongest candidate for lazy loading?
options: A large gallery image far below the fold.
A small logo in the header.
A critical hero image immediately visible above the fold.
An icon required for the first interaction.
quiz.explanation: Non-critical below-the-fold imagery can often be deferred.

quiz.question: Why use responsive image sources?
options: To guarantee every device downloads the largest image.
To let the browser choose an appropriate resource for the display context.
To replace all alt text.
To eliminate CSS.
quiz.explanation: Responsive image hints can reduce unnecessary transfer by serving a source appropriate to the display context.

quiz.question: What should guide asset optimization?
options: Reduce bytes at any cost.
Use lazy loading for everything.
Measured cost, user needs, visual quality, accessibility, and loading priority.
Always choose the smallest possible image.
quiz.explanation: Asset optimization is a tradeoff between performance and product requirements.

summary: Image and asset optimization reduces the network and processing work required to display a page. Match image sources to rendered dimensions, use appropriate encoding and responsive sources, and defer non-critical media. Do not confuse CSS display size with source-resource size. Prioritize critical assets, preserve accessibility and visual quality, and use measurement to verify that asset changes actually improve the experience.

title: Performance Measurement and Budgets
description: Measure real performance with Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse, and set performance budgets so regressions are caught before they ship rather than discovered by users.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what LCP, INP, and CLS each measure and why they were chosen as Core Web Vitals.
Run a Lighthouse audit and interpret its performance score and diagnostics.
Set a performance budget for a metric (e.g. bundle size, LCP) and explain why an unenforced budget tends to erode over time.
Distinguish lab data (Lighthouse, synthetic tests) from field data (real user metrics) and know when each is appropriate.

sections.text: You Can't Improve What You Don't Measure

Everything covered earlier in this module — rendering, memoization, code splitting, error boundaries, image optimization — is guesswork without a way to measure whether it actually made the experience faster for real users. Measurement turns performance work from intuition into something you can verify and defend.
Core Web Vitals: What They Actually Measure

LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures how long the biggest visible element takes to render — a proxy for 'does this feel loaded.' INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures how responsive the page is to real user interactions like clicks and taps. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much visible content unexpectedly moves around during load — the classic 'I went to tap a button and the page jumped' problem.

sections.title: Good thresholds (as of current Core Web Vitals guidance)
sections.code:
LCP: good <= 2.5s
INP: good <= 200ms
CLS: good <= 0.1

sections.text: Lighthouse: Lab Data, Not Field Data

Lighthouse runs a synthetic, single-run audit under simulated network/CPU conditions — useful for catching regressions locally or in CI, but it's not what real users actually experienced. Field data (from real user sessions, e.g. via the Chrome UX Report or your own analytics) reflects actual device and network diversity, and is the data that ultimately matters.

sections.title: Running Lighthouse from the CLI
sections.code: npx lighthouse https://example.com --view

sections.text: Setting a Performance Budget

A performance budget is a hard limit — bundle size, LCP, number of network requests — that's checked automatically, not just aspired to. Without enforcement, performance quietly regresses one 'small' dependency or one unoptimized image at a time, and nobody notices until the app feels slow.

sections.title: A simple bundle-size budget in a CI config

sections.text: Common Mistake: Optimizing Without a Baseline

Making a change and assuming it helped, without measuring before and after, means you can't tell a real improvement from noise — or from a change that actually made things worse in a way that wasn't obvious by eye.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can explain what LCP, INP, and CLS each measure, run a Lighthouse audit and identify at least one actionable diagnostic from it, and set up a simple enforced performance budget (e.g. a bundle-size limit) rather than an unenforced target.

exercises.title: Baseline, Change, Remeasure
exercises.brief: Run Lighthouse against a page you've built earlier in this course to record a baseline. Make one real performance improvement (image optimization, code splitting, or memoization from earlier lessons). Re-run Lighthouse and report the measured before/after difference in at least one Core Web Vital.

quiz.question: What does CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measure?
options: How long the largest visible element takes to render.
The total JavaScript bundle size.
How responsive the page is to clicks and taps.
How much visible content unexpectedly shifts position during load.
quiz.explanation: CLS captures unexpected visual movement during load — the frustrating experience of content jumping just as a user is about to interact with it.

quiz.question: Why is Lighthouse data called 'lab data' rather than 'field data'?
options: Because it's a synthetic, single-run audit under simulated conditions, not a record of what real users actually experienced.
Because it only works in a testing lab environment, not on the internet.
Because it can only be run by Google employees.
There's no meaningful distinction between lab and field data.
quiz.explanation: Lab data is useful for catching regressions in a controlled environment, but real user (field) data reflects the actual diversity of devices and networks your users have.

quiz.question: Why does a performance budget need to be enforced automatically rather than just aspired to?
options: Automatic enforcement is required by Lighthouse.
Unenforced targets tend to erode gradually as small regressions accumulate unnoticed.
Manual review is always more accurate than automated checks.
It has no real effect on outcomes either way.
quiz.explanation: Without an automatic check, performance regresses in small increments that individually seem harmless, until the cumulative effect is a genuinely slow app.

summary: Performance work only becomes verifiable through measurement — Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) give concrete, user-centered metrics, Lighthouse provides fast lab-data feedback for local and CI use, and real field data from actual users is what ultimately matters. Enforced performance budgets prevent the gradual, unnoticed regressions that happen when performance is only ever aspired to rather than automatically checked.
interviewQuestions: What are the Core Web Vitals, and what does each one actually measure?
What's the difference between lab data and field data, and when would you rely on each?
How would you set up a performance budget for a team, and why does it need to be enforced automatically?

title: Why Frontend Security Matters
description: Understand the frontend's real attack surface and why 'the backend handles security' is a dangerous myth.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Name at least three attack categories that specifically target the frontend.
Explain why client-side validation and security checks can never be trusted as the only line of defense.
Identify concrete ways frontend code choices (rendering untrusted HTML, storing tokens) directly create vulnerabilities.

sections.text: The Frontend Has a Real Attack Surface

It's tempting to think of security as a backend concern — auth, database access, server config. But the frontend runs in an environment the attacker fully controls: the user's browser, with full access to the DOM, network requests, and anything the frontend stores or renders. XSS, CSRF, and insecure token storage are all frontend-originated vulnerabilities.
'The Backend Handles Security' Is a Dangerous Myth

A backend that validates input correctly still can't protect a user from an XSS payload that runs entirely in their own browser via frontend code rendering untrusted content. Client-side validation is a UX convenience, not a security boundary — every check that matters for security has to be enforced again on the server, because a determined attacker bypasses the frontend entirely and talks to your API directly.

sections.title: A frontend-only vulnerability

sections.text: This Module's Scope

The rest of this module covers the specific, recurring frontend security issues that come up in real code review: XSS and sanitization, CSRF and same-origin policy, CORS, and safe token storage — ending with a capstone audit applying a real checklist to a real app.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can name at least three frontend-originated attack categories, explain concretely why client-side validation alone is not a security boundary, and identify dangerouslySetInnerHTML-style rendering of untrusted content as a direct frontend vulnerability.

exercises.title: Find the Frontend-Only Vulnerabilities
exercises.brief: Review three small code snippets (rendering unsanitized HTML, storing a token in localStorage, trusting a client-side role check to hide an admin action). For each, explain what an attacker could actually do, without involving the backend at all.

quiz.question: Why is 'the backend handles security' considered a dangerous assumption?
options: Because backends are always poorly secured.
Because frontends can't make network requests.
Because some vulnerabilities, like XSS from unsanitized rendering, execute entirely within the user's browser and don't require any backend involvement.
Because it's technically correct and frontend security doesn't matter.
quiz.explanation: Certain classes of attack are entirely client-side in nature — a backend, however well-secured, has no ability to prevent an XSS payload from executing once the frontend renders it.

quiz.question: Why can't client-side validation be relied on as a security boundary?
options: It's too slow to be useful.
It's only a performance optimization, not related to security at all.
Client-side validation doesn't exist in modern frameworks.
Because an attacker can bypass the frontend entirely and send requests directly to the API, skipping any client-side checks.
quiz.explanation: Any check enforced only in frontend code can be trivially bypassed by talking to the backend API directly, which is why security-relevant checks must also be enforced server-side.

quiz.question: What makes `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with unsanitized user content dangerous?
options: It executes any embedded script content from that user input directly in other users' browsers.
It slows down rendering.
It's deprecated in current React versions.
It only works with numbers.
quiz.explanation: Rendering untrusted content as raw HTML allows an attacker to inject and execute arbitrary script in the context of anyone who views that content — a classic stored XSS vector.

summary: The frontend has a real, distinct attack surface — it runs entirely in an environment the attacker controls (the browser), and vulnerabilities like XSS can execute with no backend involvement at all. Client-side validation is a UX convenience, not a security boundary, since any check enforced only in the browser can be bypassed by talking to the API directly. This module covers the recurring frontend security issues that come up in real code review.

Give an example of a vulnerability that's entirely frontend-originated.
How would you explain to a junior engineer why 'the backend handles that' isn't a sufficient answer to a security question about a frontend feature?

title: XSS and Input Sanitization
description: Understand reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS, and why APIs like dangerouslySetInnerHTML are dangerous by default.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Distinguish reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS by where the malicious payload comes from and executes.
Explain why React's default JSX rendering is safe from XSS, and exactly what bypasses that safety.
Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering it, using a library rather than hand-written escaping.
Identify other DOM APIs beyond dangerouslySetInnerHTML that can introduce XSS.

sections.text: Three Flavors of XSS

Reflected XSS: a malicious payload comes in through a URL parameter or form input and is immediately reflected back into the page's HTML. Stored XSS: the payload is saved (e.g. in a comment) and executes for every user who later views it — generally more dangerous since it doesn't require tricking one specific user into clicking a crafted link. DOM-based XSS: the vulnerability is entirely client-side — JavaScript takes untrusted data (like location.hash) and inserts it into the DOM unsafely, without the payload ever touching the server.
Why JSX Is Safe by Default

sections.title: This is safe -- React escapes it automatically

sections.text: JSX escapes values interpolated with {} by default — this is why React is meaningfully safer than manually building HTML strings. The safety only breaks when you explicitly opt out of it.

sections.title: This is the opt-out, and it's dangerous with untrusted content

sections.text: Sanitizing When You Genuinely Need Raw HTML

Sometimes rendering real HTML is a legitimate requirement (a rich-text editor's output, for example). In that case, run it through a sanitization library like DOMPurify first — never hand-roll your own escaping logic, since XSS payload variations are numerous and easy to miss.

sections.title: Sanitizing before rendering

sections.text: Other Ways XSS Sneaks In

dangerouslySetInnerHTML isn't the only risk. Directly setting element.innerHTML outside React, constructing URLs from user input and using them as href/src without validation (a javascript: URL scheme is a classic vector), and rendering unescaped SVG content can all introduce the same class of vulnerability.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can distinguish reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS by their source, explain why plain JSX interpolation is safe while dangerouslySetInnerHTML is not, and correctly sanitize untrusted HTML with a real library before rendering it.

exercises.title: Fix an XSS Vulnerability
exercises.brief: Given a CommentSection component that renders user comments with dangerouslySetInnerHTML and no sanitization, integrate DOMPurify to sanitize the content before rendering, and explain in one sentence which XSS category this vulnerability belonged to.

quiz.question: What distinguishes stored XSS from reflected XSS?
options: Stored XSS only affects mobile browsers.
Stored XSS's payload is saved and executes for every subsequent viewer, rather than requiring a specific crafted link to be clicked.
Reflected XSS is more dangerous than stored XSS.
There is no real difference between the two.
quiz.explanation: Because a stored payload persists and affects every viewer automatically, it generally has a much larger blast radius than reflected XSS, which needs a victim to follow a specifically crafted link.

quiz.question:
Why is plain JSX interpolation like `

{text}

` safe from XSS by default?
options: React blocks all script tags in the entire application.
JSX doesn't allow user-generated content at all.
JSX automatically escapes interpolated values instead of rendering them as executable HTML.
It isn't safe — this is a common misconception.
quiz.explanation: React's JSX interpolation escapes values by default, which is exactly why the vulnerability only appears once you explicitly opt out via dangerouslySetInnerHTML or similar.

quiz.question: Why should you use a library like DOMPurify instead of writing your own HTML sanitization logic?
options: Custom sanitization is always faster.
There's no meaningful difference in safety.
DOMPurify is required by the HTML specification.
XSS payload variations are numerous and subtle, and a maintained library is far more likely to catch edge cases than hand-rolled logic.
quiz.explanation: Sanitization is a security-critical, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong problem — a maintained, widely-used library has had far more scrutiny than logic written for a single feature.

summary: XSS comes in three flavors — reflected, stored, and DOM-based — differing in where the malicious payload originates and how it reaches execution. JSX interpolation is safe by default because React escapes values automatically; that safety only breaks when you explicitly opt out with dangerouslySetInnerHTML or similar APIs. When raw HTML rendering is genuinely required, sanitize with a maintained library like DOMPurify rather than hand-rolled escaping.
interviewQuestions: What's the difference between reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS?
Why is dangerouslySetInnerHTML dangerous, and when (if ever) would you use it?
How would you safely render user-generated rich text content in a React app?

title: CSRF and the Same-Origin Policy
description: Understand what CSRF actually exploits, and how the browser's same-origin policy protects against it -- and where it doesn't.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain the mechanism CSRF actually exploits: a browser automatically attaching credentials (cookies) to any request to a site, regardless of which page initiated it.
Explain what the same-origin policy does and does not protect against.
Describe how CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies each mitigate CSRF, and why they work differently.

sections.text: What CSRF Actually Exploits

Cross-Site Request Forgery exploits one specific browser behavior: if you're logged into bank.com, and bank.com uses cookies for auth, then a request to bank.com from any other site — a malicious page you're tricked into visiting — will still automatically include your bank.com cookies. The browser doesn't check who initiated the request, only which domain it's addressed to.

sections.title: A CSRF attack in its simplest form
sections.code:
<!-- Hosted on evil.com, loaded while you're logged into bank.com -->
<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="1000">
  <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker-account">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>
<!-- Your browser automatically attaches your bank.com session cookie -->

sections.text: What the Same-Origin Policy Does and Doesn't Do

The same-origin policy prevents a script on evil.com from reading the response of a request to bank.com — so the attacker can't see your account balance this way. But it does not prevent the request from being sent with your cookies attached in the first place; a form submission or an image tag doesn't need to read the response to cause damage (like transferring money).
Mitigation 1: CSRF Tokens

A CSRF token is a random value the server embeds in a legitimate page and requires back on state-changing requests. Since evil.com can't read bank.com's page content (same-origin policy blocks that), it can't obtain a valid token to include in its forged request.
Mitigation 2: SameSite Cookies

sections.title: A cookie with SameSite protection
sections.code: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; SameSite=Strict; Secure; HttpOnly

sections.text: SameSite=Strict (or Lax) tells the browser not to send this cookie on requests initiated from a different site at all — directly closing the loophole CSRF depends on, rather than relying on the server to validate a token. Modern browsers default new cookies to SameSite=Lax if unspecified, which is part of why CSRF is somewhat less prevalent than it used to be, but it shouldn't be relied on as the only defense for sensitive actions.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can explain, using the bank.com/evil.com example structure, exactly what CSRF exploits and why the same-origin policy alone doesn't prevent it, and can explain how CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies each close the gap differently.

exercises.title: Diagnose a CSRF Gap
exercises.brief: Given a /api/change-password endpoint that only checks a valid session cookie and nothing else, explain exactly how an attacker could exploit it via CSRF, then describe the two mitigations from this lesson that would close the gap.

quiz.question: What browser behavior does CSRF fundamentally exploit?
options: The browser automatically attaches a site's cookies to any request addressed to that site, regardless of which page initiated the request.
Browsers execute JavaScript from any domain on any page.
Cookies are always readable by any website.
The same-origin policy doesn't exist in modern browsers.
quiz.explanation: CSRF relies on the browser's automatic cookie attachment — the request looks legitimate to the server because it carries valid credentials, even though a malicious site initiated it.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the same-origin policy alone prevent CSRF?
options: The same-origin policy has been deprecated.
It prevents evil.com from reading bank.com's response, but doesn't stop the forged request from being sent with cookies attached in the first place.
It only applies to GET requests.
It fully prevents CSRF on its own.
quiz.explanation: A CSRF attack often doesn't need to read the response — submitting a form that transfers money, for example, causes damage without the attacker ever seeing a response.

quiz.question: How does SameSite=Strict on a cookie mitigate CSRF?
options: It makes the cookie readable only by JavaScript.
It encrypts the cookie value.
It prevents the browser from sending that cookie on requests initiated from a different site, closing the exact loophole CSRF depends on.
It has no effect on cross-site requests.
quiz.explanation: SameSite restricts when a cookie is sent based on the request's origin, directly preventing the automatic-cookie-attachment behavior CSRF relies on.

summary: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic attachment of cookies to any request addressed to a given site, regardless of which page actually initiated that request. The same-origin policy blocks an attacker from reading the response, but doesn't stop the forged request itself from being sent with valid credentials. CSRF tokens (which an attacker can't read due to the same-origin policy) and SameSite cookies (which restrict when a cookie is sent at all) are the two standard mitigations, and they work through different mechanisms.
interviewQuestions: Explain what CSRF exploits, using a concrete example.
Why doesn't the same-origin policy alone prevent CSRF?
How do CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies each mitigate CSRF, and how do the mechanisms differ?

title: CORS in Practice
description: Debug a real CORS error by understanding preflight requests, allowed origins, and allowed headers.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Explain what CORS is actually for: letting a server explicitly opt certain cross-origin requests into being allowed.
Read a real CORS error message and identify which specific header or condition is missing.
Explain what triggers a preflight OPTIONS request versus a simple request.
Distinguish a CORS error (a browser-enforced restriction) from a server-side authorization failure.

sections.text: CORS Exists to Loosen a Default Restriction, Not Add One

By default, the same-origin policy blocks a page on app.com from reading responses from api.example.com via JavaScript. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism that lets api.example.com explicitly say 'requests from app.com are allowed to read my responses' via response headers. The restriction is the default; CORS headers are an opt-in exception to it.

sections.title: A real CORS error in the console
sections.code:
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.com'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is
present on the requested resource.

sections.text: This exact message means: the request actually reached the server and got a response, but the browser is refusing to let your JavaScript read that response because the server didn't include the header saying app.com is allowed to.
Simple Requests vs. Preflighted Requests

A 'simple' request (GET/POST with only a few standard headers, common content types) goes straight through. A request with a custom header (like Authorization), a JSON content type on certain methods, or methods like PUT/DELETE triggers a preflight: the browser first sends an OPTIONS request asking the server what's allowed, before sending the real request.

sections.title: Server response allowing the real request through
sections.code:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type

sections.text: A CORS Error Is Not an Authorization Failure

A common confusion: a CORS error means the browser blocked your JavaScript from reading an otherwise-successful response — it's not the same as a 401/403 from your own authorization logic. If you see a CORS error, the fix is almost always on the server (adding the right headers), not in your frontend request code.
Common Mistake: Wildcarding Access-Control-Allow-Origin With Credentials

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * combined with credentials: 'include' on the frontend is explicitly disallowed by browsers — you can't send credentialed requests to a wildcard-origin endpoint. If you need cookies/auth headers included, the server must specify your exact origin, not a wildcard.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can read a real CORS console error and correctly identify what's missing, explain what distinguishes a simple request from a preflighted one, and explain why a CORS error means the fix belongs on the server, not the frontend request code.

exercises.title: Diagnose Three CORS Errors
exercises.brief: Given three different real CORS console error messages (missing Allow-Origin, missing Allow-Headers for a custom header, and a wildcard-plus-credentials conflict), identify the specific cause and the correct server-side fix for each.

quiz.question: What does a 'No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header' error actually mean?
options: The request never reached the server.
The server returned a 500 error.
Your internet connection failed.
The request succeeded and the server responded, but the browser is blocking your JavaScript from reading that response because the server didn't authorize your origin.
quiz.explanation: CORS errors happen after a successful server response — the browser is the one blocking access to that response on the client side, not the server rejecting the request.

quiz.question: What triggers a preflight OPTIONS request?
options: A request using a custom header, certain content types, or methods like PUT/DELETE that fall outside the 'simple request' definition.
Every single request, with no exceptions.
Only requests to HTTPS endpoints.
Preflight requests were removed in modern browsers.
quiz.explanation: Requests outside the narrow 'simple request' definition trigger a preflight so the browser can confirm the server allows them before sending the actual request.

quiz.question: Why can't Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * be combined with credentialed requests?
options: It's a performance optimization only.
Browsers explicitly disallow sending credentials to a wildcard-origin endpoint, since that would let any site read authenticated responses.
There's no restriction — this combination works fine.
Wildcards are deprecated entirely.
quiz.explanation: Allowing credentials with a wildcard origin would defeat the purpose of CORS entirely, letting any site make authenticated requests on a user's behalf — browsers block this combination specifically.

summary: CORS is an opt-in exception to the same-origin policy's default restriction, letting a server explicitly allow specific origins to read its responses via headers. Requests with custom headers or certain methods trigger a preflight OPTIONS check first. A CORS error means the server responded but the browser blocked JavaScript from reading it — the fix belongs on the server, and a wildcard origin can never be combined with credentialed requests.
interviewQuestions: Walk through what happens, step by step, when a CORS error appears in the console.
What's the difference between a simple request and a preflighted request?
Why can't you combine a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin with credentialed requests?

title: Auth Patterns and Token Storage
description: Compare cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage for storing auth tokens, and understand why localStorage-stored JWTs are a common real-world mistake.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Compare cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage as places to store an auth token, by what each is and isn't protected against.
Explain what httpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie flags each protect against.
Explain concretely why storing a JWT in localStorage is vulnerable to XSS in a way an httpOnly cookie is not.
Describe the tradeoff CSRF protection introduces when moving from localStorage to cookie-based token storage.

sections.text: Where Can a Token Live?

localStorage and sessionStorage are both readable by any JavaScript running on the page — including an attacker's injected script if the page has an XSS vulnerability. A cookie marked httpOnly is invisible to JavaScript entirely; it's only ever sent automatically by the browser with requests, never readable via document.cookie.

sections.title: The XSS-plus-localStorage combination

sections.text: Why localStorage-Stored JWTs Are a Common Real-World Mistake

It's a very common pattern in tutorials and even production apps to store a JWT in localStorage because it's simple to read and attach manually to requests. The problem: it means a single XSS vulnerability anywhere on your site — even in a third-party script you loaded — gives an attacker full account takeover, since the token is trivially readable.
The Cookie Flags That Matter

sections.title: A properly configured auth cookie
sections.code: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict

sections.text: HttpOnly: invisible to JavaScript, closing the XSS-theft vector entirely. Secure: only sent over HTTPS, never plaintext HTTP. SameSite=Strict (or Lax): restricts cross-site sending, mitigating CSRF (covered in lesson-4-6-3) — the exact tradeoff moving to cookies introduces, since cookies are the mechanism CSRF exploits in the first place.
The Real Tradeoff

Moving auth to an httpOnly cookie closes the XSS-token-theft vector, but reopens a CSRF consideration that localStorage-based tokens didn't have (since manually-attached tokens aren't automatically sent by the browser). This is why cookie-based auth needs to be paired with CSRF protection (SameSite and/or CSRF tokens), not treated as a strictly safer drop-in replacement on its own.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner can explain concretely why an XSS vulnerability lets an attacker steal a localStorage-stored token but not an httpOnly cookie, name what each of HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite protects against, and explain the CSRF tradeoff that comes with moving auth to cookies.

exercises.title: Audit and Fix a Token Storage Pattern
exercises.brief: Given a login flow that stores a JWT in localStorage and manually attaches it as an Authorization header on every request, rewrite the flow to use an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie instead, and explain what additional protection (if any) is still needed.

quiz.question: Why can an XSS vulnerability steal a token stored in localStorage but not one stored in an httpOnly cookie?
options: httpOnly cookies can't be used for authentication.
localStorage tokens expire faster.
localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, including injected attacker scripts; httpOnly cookies are invisible to JavaScript entirely.
There's no real difference in exposure between the two.
quiz.explanation: The HttpOnly flag specifically prevents JavaScript access to the cookie, which is exactly the access an XSS payload would need to steal it — localStorage has no equivalent protection.

quiz.question: What does the Secure flag on a cookie do?
options: Encrypts the cookie's value.
Prevents the cookie from expiring.
Makes the cookie readable only by the current tab.
Ensures the cookie is only ever sent over HTTPS, never plaintext HTTP.
quiz.explanation: Secure restricts transmission to HTTPS connections, protecting the cookie from being intercepted over an unencrypted connection.

quiz.question: What tradeoff does moving auth from localStorage to an httpOnly cookie introduce?
options: It reopens a CSRF consideration, since cookies are automatically attached to requests by the browser in a way manually-attached tokens are not.
It makes XSS attacks easier.
It removes the need for HTTPS.
There is no tradeoff — cookies are strictly better in every respect.
quiz.explanation: The automatic-attachment behavior that protects against XSS-based theft is the same behavior CSRF exploits, so cookie-based auth needs to be paired with CSRF mitigations like SameSite or CSRF tokens.

summary: localStorage and sessionStorage are both readable by any JavaScript on the page, making tokens stored there vulnerable to theft via any XSS vulnerability — a very common real-world mistake. An httpOnly cookie is invisible to JavaScript entirely, closing that vector, but its automatic-attachment behavior reopens a CSRF consideration that needs its own mitigation (SameSite and/or CSRF tokens). Secure and SameSite flags round out a properly configured auth cookie.
interviewQuestions: Why is storing a JWT in localStorage considered risky?
What does the httpOnly flag protect against, specifically?
What tradeoff do you take on when moving auth tokens from localStorage to cookies?

title: Capstone: Security Audit of a Frontend App
description: Apply a real security checklist to a provided app, finding and remediating at least one real issue, mirroring lesson-4-4-6's audit structure.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Apply a structured security checklist covering XSS, CSRF, CORS, and token storage to a real codebase.
Identify and remediate at least one genuine security issue, not a theoretical one.
Prioritize findings by real exploitability and impact, not by category count.
Document findings the way a real security review would, with a specific fix, not just a flagged concern.

sections.text: The Audit Checklist

sections.title: Security audit checklist
sections.code:
XSS:
[ ] Any dangerouslySetInnerHTML (or innerHTML) usage sanitizes untrusted content
[ ] User-controlled values used in href/src are validated (no javascript: URLs)

CSRF:
[ ] State-changing requests (POST/PUT/DELETE) require more than just a valid session cookie
[ ] Auth cookies use SameSite

CORS:
[ ] Access-Control-Allow-Origin is not a wildcard on any endpoint that accepts credentials

Token storage:
[ ] Auth tokens are not stored in localStorage/sessionStorage
[ ] Auth cookies use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite

General:
[ ] No secrets or API keys are hardcoded in frontend source
[ ] Third-party scripts are loaded from trusted, pinned sources

sections.text: Applying the Checklist Is Only Half the Work

Running through this checklist against a real app will surface findings — but a finding without a specific fix isn't an audit, it's a list of worries. For each issue found, the audit must specify exactly what code changes, not just that something is 'a risk.'
Prioritizing Like a Real Review

A localStorage-stored auth token on an app with any XSS surface (e.g. any unsanitized rendering anywhere) is a critical, chained finding — fix the XSS and the token storage both, since either alone leaves the other exploitable. A missing SameSite flag on a low-privilege, read-only cookie is real but far lower priority. Rank by what an attacker could actually do, end to end.

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner has applied the full security checklist to a real app, identified and implemented a fix for at least one genuine issue (not a hypothetical one), and produced a prioritized findings writeup that specifies exact remediation, not just flagged concerns.

exercises.title: Full Security Audit
exercises.brief: Given a small provided app (or one you built earlier in this course) with at least two real, planted security issues among unsanitized rendering, localStorage-stored tokens, and a wildcard CORS config, run the full checklist, document each finding with a specific fix, prioritize them, and implement fixes for the highest-priority issue.

quiz.question: Why is a finding without a specific fix considered incomplete for this audit?
options: Findings never need fixes documented.
Because 'this is a risk' alone gives the team nothing actionable — a real audit specifies exactly what code needs to change.
Because audits are purely theoretical exercises.
Because only automated tools can propose fixes.
quiz.explanation: A useful audit gives the team a concrete path to remediation, not just a list of concerns — the same principle as the prioritized, actionable fix lists covered in the accessibility capstone.

quiz.question: Why would a localStorage-stored token combined with any XSS surface be ranked as a critical, chained finding?
options: Because it only affects mobile users.
Because localStorage is always slower than cookies.
Because either vulnerability alone leaves the other exploitable — the XSS is what makes the token theft possible in the first place.
It wouldn't be ranked as critical — these are unrelated, low-severity issues.
quiz.explanation: The two issues compound: the XSS vulnerability is the delivery mechanism, and the localStorage token is what makes that delivery mechanism valuable to an attacker — fixing only one still leaves real risk.

quiz.question: How should findings from this audit be prioritized?
options: Alphabetically by checklist category.
All findings are equally urgent by definition.
By which are easiest to fix first, regardless of severity.
By what an attacker could actually accomplish end-to-end, not by how many items fall in one checklist category.
quiz.explanation: Impact-based prioritization — same principle as the accessibility audit capstone — ensures the fixes that actually reduce real exploitable risk happen first.

summary: The security capstone applies a concrete checklist covering XSS, CSRF, CORS, and token storage to a real app, requiring genuine findings with specific fixes rather than theoretical concerns. Chained vulnerabilities (like localStorage tokens combined with an XSS surface) should be prioritized highest, since they compound into much greater real-world risk than either issue alone — the same impact-first prioritization principle used in the accessibility audit capstone.

resources.label: OWASP — Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — XSS Prevention

interviewQuestions: Walk through how you'd run a security audit on a frontend codebase you didn't write.
How would you prioritize a list of security findings for a team with limited time?
Describe a real or hypothetical vulnerability chain where two individually moderate issues combine into a critical one.

title: Why Architecture Matters
description: Understand why frontend architecture affects how easily a codebase can grow, change, and be understood by new engineers.
mastery: The learner can explain how architecture decisions affect the ability of a codebase to grow, change, and remain understandable, and can explain why architecture must be revisited as the application evolves.
learningObjectives: Explain why architecture matters in a frontend codebase.
Explain how architecture affects the ability of a codebase to grow.
Explain how architecture affects the cost of making changes.
Explain how architecture affects how quickly new engineers can understand a codebase.
Recognize architecture as an ongoing decision rather than a one-time setup exercise.
Identify signals that an existing architecture may need to be revisited.

prerequisites.source: module boundary inferred from sequence, not asserted in YAML

sections.text: Why Architecture Matters

A frontend application can work correctly and still have poor architecture. Architecture becomes visible when the codebase grows: adding a feature takes longer, a small change affects unrelated areas, or a new engineer cannot tell where a piece of logic belongs.
Architecture decisions determine how easily a codebase can grow, change, and be understood by new engineers.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Architecture is the set of decisions that shape how a codebase is organized and how its parts interact. Good architecture lowers the cost of understanding and changing the system as it grows.
A Small Application Can Hide Architecture Problems

sections.title: Early stage
sections.code:
5 components
3 routes
1 API

Almost any structure feels manageable.

sections.title: Later stage
sections.code:
80 components
20 routes
multiple data sources
shared state
team of engineers

The old structure now affects every change.

sections.text: Architecture decisions that were harmless in a small project can become expensive constraints as the number of features and contributors increases.
Architecture Affects Change

sections.title: Cheap change
sections.code:
Feature requirement
→ locate feature code
→ change feature
→ run focused checks
→ done

sections.title: Expensive change
sections.code:
Feature requirement
→ search many unrelated folders
→ trace hidden dependencies
→ change one place
→ discover unexpected coupling
→ fix unrelated breakage

sections.text: One practical measure of architecture quality is how predictable and contained normal changes are.
Architecture Affects Understanding
A codebase is read far more often than it is initially written. Engineers need to locate behavior, understand dependencies, and predict where a change belongs.

sections.title: New engineer question
sections.code:
Where does this feature live?

Where is its state?

Where does its data come from?

Which module owns this rule?

What can I safely change?

sections.text: An understandable architecture answers these questions with relatively little searching and guesswork.
Architecture Affects Growth
As new features are added, the architecture determines whether the codebase gains structure or simply accumulates more files and dependencies.

sections.title: Healthy growth
sections.code:
New feature
→ clear place
→ clear dependencies
→ limited surface area
→ existing features remain understandable

sections.title: Uncontrolled growth
sections.code:
New feature
→ add files wherever convenient
→ import existing internals
→ duplicate logic
→ shared folder grows without ownership
→ boundaries disappear

sections.text: Architecture Is Not a One-Time Decision
The source's key warning is that architecture should not be treated as a one-time setup decision. As the application, team, and constraints change, some earlier decisions may stop fitting the system.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not assume the architecture you choose at the beginning must remain unchanged forever. Architecture should be revisited as the application grows and new constraints appear.
Architecture Has Tradeoffs

There is rarely one universally correct frontend architecture. A structure that is useful for a small product may not be appropriate for a large multi-team application, and a structure optimized for one kind of team can be unnecessarily complicated for another.

sections.title: Possible constraints
sections.code:
Application size
Team size
Team ownership
Feature boundaries
Release frequency
Shared code
Technical dependencies
Expected growth

sections.text: Real-World Analogy

Think about a kitchen. A small kitchen can keep frequently used items almost anywhere because there are only a few people and tools. A professional kitchen needs explicit stations and responsibilities because many people work at the same time. The goal is not the most elaborate organization; it is an organization that reduces friction for the actual environment.
Architecture Problems Show Up as Friction

sections.title: Signals
sections.code:
A small feature requires edits across many unrelated areas.

Engineers repeatedly ask where new code should live.

Shared code is changed for one feature and unexpectedly breaks another.

Developers copy logic because the original ownership is unclear.

A new engineer needs unusually long explanations to make a small change.

sections.text: None of these signals proves that one specific architecture is wrong, but together they are reasons to examine the current boundaries.
Architecture Is About Boundaries

Later lessons in this module will go deeper into folder structures, feature-based organization, shared versus page-specific logic, and explicit module boundaries. For now, the core idea is that architecture creates boundaries around responsibilities and dependencies.

sections.title: Simple model
sections.code:
Feature A
  ↓
clear public boundary
  ↓
Feature B

sections.text: Clear boundaries make it easier to reason about what a change can affect.
Interactive Thinking Exercise

sections.instructions: For each scenario, identify what architectural problem might be emerging and explain why it makes future changes harder.

Likely architectural concern:
____________________________

Why:

Scenario D

Likely architectural concern:
