sections.text: Do Not Confuse Architecture With Folder Names

Folders are one visible expression of architecture, but architecture is broader. It includes ownership, dependencies, module boundaries, shared logic, data flow, and the rules that determine how parts of the system interact.

sections.title: Folder structure is only one layer
sections.code:
Architecture
├── folder/module organization
├── ownership
├── dependencies
├── public APIs
├── shared logic
└── boundaries

sections.text: The Goal Is Not Maximum Organization
More folders, more abstractions, and more layers do not automatically mean better architecture. Excess structure can make a small application harder to understand.

sections.title: Useful architecture
sections.code:
Enough structure to make changes predictable.

Not:

Structure for its own sake.

sections.text: Architecture and Team Growth
As more engineers contribute, implicit knowledge becomes less reliable. Architecture helps turn assumptions about ownership and boundaries into visible structure that multiple people can understand.
Architecture and Change Cost

sections.title: A useful question
sections.code:
How many unrelated things must I understand
before I can safely change this feature?

sections.text: A good architecture tends to reduce the number of unrelated concepts a developer needs to understand for a local change.
What Will Come Next?
The next lesson compares scalable folder structures. It looks at competing ways to organize a codebase and asks which structure remains navigable as the number of files grows.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson establishes why architecture matters. Detailed folder structures, feature organization, shared logic, module boundaries, and architecture tradeoffs are deliberately left for the following lessons.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why does frontend architecture matter?' A strong answer is: 'Architecture determines how easily a codebase can grow, change, and be understood. Good architecture makes ownership and dependencies clearer and keeps the cost of ordinary changes predictable as the application and team become larger.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Is good architecture permanent?' No. Architecture should be revisited as the application grows and its constraints change.

Another follow-up is: 'How do you know architecture is becoming a problem?' Look for friction: unclear ownership, changes spanning unrelated areas, duplicated logic, unexpected coupling, and difficulty onboarding engineers.
Reflect
Think about an application you have built. As it grew, which part became harder to change than it was at the beginning? What architectural decision contributed to that friction?
When evaluating architecture, do not ask only 'Does this work today?' Ask 'What will happen when this application becomes larger, changes more often, and has more people working on it?'

sections.label: Pass the recall check by explaining how architecture affects growth, change, and codebase understanding, and by identifying why architecture may need to be revisited as an application evolves.
sections.hint: Architecture is not primarily about folder aesthetics. It shapes ownership, dependencies, boundaries, and the cost of making changes.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Architecture matters because architecture decisions determine how easily a codebase can grow, change, and be understood by new engineers. A useful architecture reduces friction around ownership and dependencies without adding structure for its own sake. Most importantly, architecture is not a one-time decision: as the application and team grow, the architecture should be reconsidered when the existing structure begins creating unnecessary change or understanding costs.

Good architecture reduces change friction without adding structure for its own sake, and it should be revisited as the application and team evolve.

title: Scalable Folder Structures
description: Compare common frontend folder-organization strategies and learn how to structure a growing codebase so developers can locate related behavior without excessive searching or dependence on one global file-type hierarchy.
mastery: The learner can compare competing folder structures, explain their tradeoffs, identify when a structure stops scaling, and justify a more navigable organization based on the application's features and growth.
learningObjectives: Explain why folder structure matters as the number of files grows.
Compare file-type-based and feature-oriented organization.
Identify the strengths and weaknesses of organizing an application only by file type.
Recognize when a folder structure becomes difficult to navigate.
Choose an organization strategy based on the application's size and domain.
Explain how folder structure can communicate ownership and feature boundaries.
Critique an existing folder structure and propose a concrete improvement with a reason.

sections.text: Folders Are a Navigation System
As an application grows, developers spend increasing amounts of time locating code. Folder structure is one of the first signals they use to understand where a feature belongs.
A scalable structure should make related code discoverable without requiring developers to memorize the entire repository.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A folder structure is a map of the codebase. A good map helps engineers find the code that belongs together and understand how the application is divided.
A Common Starting Point: Organize by File Type

sections.title: Type-based structure
sections.code:
src/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── utils/
├── pages/
├── state/
└── styles/

sections.text: This approach is simple to understand at first. Components go with components, hooks with hooks, services with services, and so on.
The Problem Appears as Features Multiply

sections.title: Finding one feature
sections.code:
Need to change the 'Saved Lessons' feature

Look in:
components/
pages/
hooks/
services/
state/
utils/

Feature logic is distributed across the tree.

sections.text: The structure makes file type easy to find, but feature ownership harder to find.
Another Approach: Organize by Feature

sections.title: Feature-oriented structure
sections.code:
src/
├── features/
│   ├── saved-lessons/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   ├── state/
│   │   └── services/
│   ├── courses/
│   └── search/
├── shared/
└── app/

sections.text: Here, code related to a feature is grouped around that feature rather than separated solely by technical type.
The Core Tradeoff

sections.title: Type-based
sections.code:
Easy to answer:
'Where are the hooks?'

Harder to answer:
'Where does this feature live?'

sections.title: Feature-based
sections.code:
Easy to answer:
'Where does this feature live?'

May require more thought about:
'Which code is genuinely shared?'

sections.text: Neither organization is universally correct. The architecture should fit the application's size, domain, team, and expected growth.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not organize everything purely by file type
sections.text: A type-based structure can work well for a small codebase, but as features multiply it can scatter the implementation of one feature across many top-level directories and make ownership harder to see.
Small Applications Have Different Needs

sections.title: Small app
sections.code:
src/
├── components/
├── pages/
└── utils/

sections.text: For a small application, simplicity may be more valuable than elaborate boundaries. A structure can become less maintainable if the organizational system is more complicated than the codebase itself.
Growing Applications Need Stronger Grouping

sections.title: Growing app
sections.code:
src/
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── courses/
│   ├── progress/
│   └── saved-lessons/
├── shared/
└── app/

sections.text: As the domain becomes richer, grouping code around domain concepts can make ownership and navigation clearer.
Whiteboard: Compare Two Structures

sections.title: Folder Structure Whiteboard
sections.instructions: Compare the two proposed structures for the same application. Identify what each makes easy to find, what each makes difficult to find, and which you would choose as the application grows.
sections.initialCode:
APPLICATION
Features:
Auth, Courses, Search, Saved Lessons, Progress

OPTION A — FILE TYPE
src/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── state/
├── pages/
└── utils/

OPTION B — FEATURE
src/
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── courses/
│   ├── search/
│   ├── saved-lessons/
│   └── progress/
├── shared/
└── app/

What is easy to find in A?
_______________________________

What is difficult to find in A?
_______________________________

What is easy to find in B?
_______________________________

What becomes harder in B?
_______________________________

Which would you choose as the app grows?
_______________________________

Why?
_______________________________

sections.text: Folders Can Communicate Ownership
When feature code lives together, developers can more easily infer which team or domain owns that code. This can become increasingly useful as the organization grows.

sections.title: Ownership signal
sections.code:
features/courses/
→ course-specific UI
→ course-specific state
→ course-specific helpers
→ course-specific data logic

sections.text: The folder structure does not automatically enforce ownership. It gives the team a visible place from which ownership can be designed and communicated.
Shared Is a Real Decision
Feature-oriented structures still need places for genuinely shared code. The important question is whether code is actually shared and stable enough to deserve a common boundary.

sections.title: Possible shared code
sections.code:
shared/
├── ui/
├── formatting/
├── api/
└── config/

sections.text: This lesson does not yet go deeply into shared-vs-page logic; that distinction is handled later in the module.
Avoid a Giant Shared Folder

Once a repository contains a large 'shared' folder with dozens of unrelated utilities, components, hooks, and feature-specific helpers, the shared folder can become a new version of the same discoverability problem.

sections.title: Warning sign
sections.code:
shared/
├── useCourseSearch.js
├── SaveButton.jsx
├── formatProgress.js
├── enrollmentValidation.js
├── dashboardState.js
├── lessonCardHelpers.js
└── ...

sections.text: A common folder should represent genuinely common concepts, not simply code that someone did not know where else to put.
Folders Should Follow the Domain

A useful structure should reflect how the product itself is understood. If the product has clear domains such as courses, enrollment, progress, and billing, those concepts may be stronger organizing boundaries than generic technical categories.
Not Every File Needs a New Folder
Feature-oriented organization does not mean creating a deeply nested hierarchy for every tiny file. The goal is discoverability, not maximum nesting.

sections.title: Too much structure
sections.code:
features/
└── courses/
    └── ui/
        └── cards/
            └── lesson/
                └── metadata/
                    └── components/
                        └── Title.jsx

sections.text: An organization system can become difficult to navigate when the structure itself requires too much effort to traverse.
The Right Amount of Structure

sections.title: Useful test
sections.code:
Can a developer quickly answer:

'Where does this feature belong?'

'Where is the code I need to change?'

'What else might this change affect?'

sections.text: When Structure Should Change

sections.title: Refactoring signals
sections.code:
Folders become enormous.

Features are scattered across many top-level directories.

Developers frequently duplicate code because ownership is unclear.

Shared folders accumulate unrelated logic.

New contributors struggle to find relevant code.

sections.text: These signals can justify restructuring, but the goal should be incremental improvement rather than a rewrite simply for the sake of adopting a fashionable pattern.
Architecture Should Reduce Search Cost
A practical way to judge folder structure is to consider the amount of repository searching required for a normal task.

sections.title: Search cost
sections.code:
Task:
Change Saved Lessons behavior.

Low search cost:
features/saved-lessons/

High search cost:
components/
hooks/
state/
services/
utils/
pages/

sections.text: Feature Organization Is Not the Final Answer

Feature-based architecture introduces its own design decisions: what belongs inside a feature, what can be shared, and what one feature is allowed to import from another. Those boundaries are the subject of later lessons.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson goes deeper into feature-based architecture. It will move from folder organization into actual co-location of a feature's components, state, and logic, including how to avoid deep imports between feature internals.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson compares organizational strategies. It does not yet teach the full feature-based architecture pattern or its module boundaries.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you organize a growing React application?' A strong answer is: 'I would choose a structure that keeps related domain behavior discoverable and limits the amount of repository searching required for changes. For a small app, a simple type-based structure may be sufficient; as the product grows, feature-oriented organization can make ownership and related code easier to locate.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Is feature-based organization always better?' No. It is a tradeoff. The appropriate structure depends on application size, domain, team, and expected growth.
Another follow-up is: 'Why is a huge shared folder a problem?' Because it becomes a catch-all and recreates the discoverability and ownership problems that the architecture was supposed to solve.
Reflect
Open the source tree of one of your previous applications. Pick a feature and trace every file you need to understand before changing it. How many directories do you have to visit?
A folder structure is successful when developers can quickly find the code that belongs to a task and understand the likely impact of changing it.

sections.hint: Compare discoverability by file type versus discoverability by feature/domain. Neither is universally right; justify the choice against application size and growth.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Folder structure is a navigation system for the codebase. Type-based organization is simple and can work well for small applications, while feature-oriented organization can make larger applications easier to navigate by keeping domain-related code together. The important decision is not to maximize folders or follow a trend, but to reduce search cost, make ownership clearer, and keep the structure navigable as the application grows.

quiz.explanation: The lesson treats folder organization as a context-dependent architecture tradeoff.

Feature-oriented organization can reduce that search cost by grouping domain-related code, but it introduces its own boundary decisions. The correct structure is the one that fits the application's size and constraints while making ownership and changes easier to understand.

title: Feature-Based Architecture
description: Learn to organize frontend code around product features so components, state, and feature-specific logic stay together, while exposing clear boundaries that prevent features from becoming tightly coupled.
mastery: The learner can reorganize a small application around features, co-locate feature-specific components/state/logic, and explain why a feature should expose a small public surface rather than allowing other features to import its internals.
learningObjectives: Explain feature-based architecture.
Explain why co-locating a feature's components, state, and logic can improve navigability.
Reorganize type-based code into feature-oriented boundaries.
Identify which code belongs to a feature versus genuinely shared infrastructure.
Create a feature boundary that communicates ownership.
Avoid deep imports into another feature's internal files.
Expose a small, intentional public API from a feature.
Explain how feature boundaries reduce coupling.

prerequisites.description: Module 2-2 / ES Modules, especially lesson-2-2-6, because feature-based organization assumes import/export fluency.
prerequisites.source: Explicitly identified as a conceptual cross-module prerequisite in the source.

sections.text: From Folder Structure to Feature Ownership

The previous lesson compared folder organization strategies. Feature-based architecture takes that idea further by organizing code around product features rather than primarily around technical file types.
A feature can own its UI, state, data logic, and helpers when those pieces exist specifically to support that feature.

sections.title: The rule
sections.text: Co-locate a feature's components, state, and logic instead of scattering them across global type-based folders.
A Type-Based Codebase

sections.title: Before
sections.code:
src/
├── components/
│   ├── LessonCard.jsx
│   ├── SavedLessonList.jsx
│   └── SaveButton.jsx
├── hooks/
│   └── useSavedLessons.js
├── state/
│   └── savedLessonsStore.js
├── services/
│   └── savedLessonsApi.js
└── utils/
    └── savedLessonHelpers.js

sections.text: All the technical types are easy to locate, but finding everything that belongs to Saved Lessons requires searching multiple folders.
Move the Feature Together

sections.title: After
sections.code:
src/
├── features/
│   └── saved-lessons/
│       ├── components/
│       │   ├── LessonCard.jsx
│       │   ├── SavedLessonList.jsx
│       │   └── SaveButton.jsx
│       ├── hooks/
│       │   └── useSavedLessons.js
│       ├── state/
│       │   └── savedLessonsStore.js
│       ├── services/
│       │   └── savedLessonsApi.js
│       └── helpers/
│           └── savedLessonHelpers.js
├── shared/
└── app/

sections.text: Now the feature has a visible home. A developer working on Saved Lessons can begin inside one feature boundary instead of searching the entire repository.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not recreate coupling through deep imports
sections.text: Moving files into feature folders does not automatically create good architecture. If one feature imports deeply into another feature's internal files, the folders become cosmetic and the dependency boundary still erodes.
Feature Ownership

sections.title: A feature owns its internals
sections.code:
features/saved-lessons/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── state/
├── services/
└── helpers/

sections.text: Other parts of the application should not need to know how those internals are arranged unless that detail is intentionally part of the feature's public API.
Public API vs Internal Detail

sections.title: Feature boundary
sections.code:
features/saved-lessons/

public:
→ SavedLessonsPage
→ SavedLessonSummary

internal:
→ savedLessonsStore
→ helper functions
→ internal components
→ implementation-specific hooks

sections.text: The feature can choose to expose only the pieces other parts of the application genuinely need.
An Index Can Define the Entry Point

sections.title: Feature entry point
sections.code:
export { SavedLessonsPage } from './pages/SavedLessonsPage';
export { SavedLessonSummary } from './components/SavedLessonSummary';

sections.text: The exact convention can vary, but an intentional entry point makes it easier to change internal file locations without forcing every consumer to change.
Deep Import: Warning Sign

sections.title: Coupled import

sections.text: This import exposes a feature's internal state implementation to another part of the system.

sections.title: Boundary-respecting import

sections.text: The second form communicates that the consumer depends on a public feature contract rather than a specific internal file.
Interactive Practice: Reorganize a Feature

sections.title: Feature Architecture Playground
sections.instructions: Reorganize the provided type-based code into a feature-based structure. Keep the application behavior unchanged. Then identify which exports should remain public and which implementation details should stay inside the feature.
sections.initialCode:
TYPE-BASED SOURCE

src/
├── components/
│   ├── CourseCard.jsx
│   ├── EnrollmentButton.jsx
│   ├── SavedLessonList.jsx
│   └── SaveButton.jsx
├── hooks/
│   ├── useEnrollment.js
│   └── useSavedLessons.js
├── services/
│   ├── enrollmentApi.js
│   └── savedLessonsApi.js
├── state/
│   ├── enrollmentStore.js
│   └── savedLessonsStore.js
└── utils/
    ├── enrollmentValidation.js
    └── savedLessonHelpers.js

Task:
1. Create feature boundaries.
2. Move feature-specific code under the appropriate feature.
3. Identify genuinely shared code, if any.
4. Choose the public exports for each feature.
5. Explain one import that should NOT be allowed.

sections.text: Feature Boundaries Should Follow the Product
A feature boundary should correspond to something meaningful in the product or domain, such as authentication, courses, saved lessons, enrollment, or search.

sections.title: Product-oriented boundaries
sections.code:
features/
├── auth/
├── courses/
├── enrollment/
├── saved-lessons/
└── search/

sections.text: The exact boundaries depend on the application. The important point is that the organization follows meaningful behavior rather than an arbitrary collection of technical file types.
What Belongs Inside a Feature?

sections.title: Usually feature-owned
sections.code:
Feature UI
Feature-specific hooks
Feature state
Feature-specific API calls
Feature-specific validation
Feature-specific transformations
Feature-specific helpers

sections.text: If a piece of logic exists only because one feature needs it, keeping it with that feature usually makes ownership clearer.
What Might Be Shared?

sections.title: Potentially shared
sections.code:
Generic Button
Generic Modal
Date formatting utility
HTTP client configuration
Application-wide environment/configuration

sections.text: Whether something belongs in shared infrastructure depends on whether it is genuinely reusable and sufficiently stable. The next lesson explores shared versus page-specific logic in more detail.
Do Not Move Everything Into a Feature

Feature-based architecture does not mean every dependency must be duplicated. Generic UI or truly cross-cutting infrastructure can remain shared. The architectural skill is deciding what has a clear owner.
Feature Boundaries and Change Isolation

sections.title: Desired change path
sections.code:
Requirement
 ↓
One feature boundary
 ↓
Feature internals
 ↓
Focused change
 ↓
Limited unrelated impact

sections.text: The value of the architecture is not the directory name. It is the reduced uncertainty around ownership and change impact.
Avoid Importing Another Feature's Internals

sections.title: Bad dependency
sections.code:
features/search/
   ↓
features/saved-lessons/state/savedLessonsStore

sections.title: Better dependency
sections.code:
features/search/
   ↓
public API of saved-lessons

sections.text: The second approach allows Saved Lessons to change its internal organization without requiring unrelated features to know about those changes.
A Feature Can Still Have Layers
Feature-based organization does not mean everything lives in one flat folder. A feature can contain components, state, services, and helpers. The architectural boundary is the feature itself.
Drill: Find the Boundary Violation

sections.title: Feature Boundary Review
sections.instructions: Identify which imports violate feature boundaries and rewrite them so consumers use an intentional public surface.
sections.initialCode: Click each import to mark it as a fine public import or a boundary violation. Then check your answers.

sections.text: Public APIs Reduce Dependency Knowledge
A small public surface means consumers need to know less about another feature. This is one practical way module boundaries reduce coupling.

sections.title: More internal knowledge
sections.code:
Consumer knows:
→ folder layout
→ state file
→ hook file
→ helper file
→ implementation details

sections.title: Less internal knowledge
sections.code:
Consumer knows:
→ feature public API
→ supported inputs/outputs

sections.text: Refactoring Becomes Safer
When consumers depend on a public API instead of internal file locations, internal refactoring can happen without changing every consumer.

sections.title: Boundary benefit
sections.code:
Before
→ saved-lessons/state/store.js

Refactor
→ saved-lessons/state/store.ts

With a public API
→ consumers unchanged

sections.text: Architecture Is About Dependencies, Not Just Organization

A beautifully organized folder tree can still have poor architecture if features depend directly on one another's internals. The real test is whether the dependency relationships remain understandable and intentional.
What Will Come Next?

The next lesson addresses shared logic versus page logic. It builds on feature boundaries by asking which code should be reusable across multiple parts of the application and which code should remain local to a specific page or feature.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson introduces feature-based organization and feature public APIs. The next lesson handles the judgment call between shared logic and local/page-specific logic.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is feature-based architecture?' A strong answer is: 'It organizes code around product features so a feature's components, state, and specific logic are co-located. The feature then exposes an intentional public surface instead of allowing consumers to depend on its internal files.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why are deep imports into another feature's internals a problem?' They create tight coupling to implementation details, so internal changes require unrelated consumers to change.

Another follow-up is: 'Does everything need to live inside a feature?' No. Truly shared infrastructure can remain shared. The architectural task is deciding clear ownership rather than forcing every file into a feature.
Reflect

Pick one feature from a previous project and draw its boundary. Which components, state, and helpers would you place inside it? Which pieces would you intentionally expose to the rest of the application?

sections.title: Own the internals; expose the contract

sections.text: A feature should make its internal organization someone else's problem. Consumers should depend on the feature's supported interface, not its file tree.

sections.label: Complete the Feature Architecture Playground and boundary review. The learner must reorganize a small application around features and prevent consumers from importing feature internals directly.
sections.hint: Co-locate feature-specific code, identify genuinely shared infrastructure, and expose a small public API rather than deep internal imports.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Feature-based architecture co-locates a feature's components, state, and feature-specific logic so ownership and navigation are clearer. The pattern only works when dependency boundaries are real: consumers should use a feature's public API rather than importing its internal files. The result is less coupling and safer internal refactoring.

exercises.title: Feature Architecture Playground
exercises.brief: Reorganize a type-based codebase into feature-oriented boundaries and identify public versus internal code.

exercises.title: Feature Boundary Review
exercises.brief: Identify deep imports that expose feature internals and replace them with intentional public feature imports.

quiz.question: What does feature-based architecture primarily do?
options: Group all components into one folder.
Co-locate a feature's components, state, and logic around a product/domain feature.
Put every file in a separate directory.
Eliminate all shared code.
quiz.explanation: The lesson defines feature-based architecture around co-located feature-specific behavior.

quiz.question: Why are deep imports into another feature's internals undesirable?
options: They make imports shorter.
They couple consumers to implementation details and make internal refactoring harder.
They make React components impossible to render.
They prevent bundlers from working.
quiz.explanation: Deep imports erode the intended feature boundary.

quiz.question: What should a feature's public API generally expose?
options: Every internal helper and state variable.
Only the supported pieces other parts of the application genuinely need.
Its entire folder structure.
Every implementation-specific hook.
quiz.explanation: A smaller intentional public surface reduces dependency knowledge and coupling.

summary: Feature-based architecture organizes code around product features, co-locating their components, state, data logic, and helpers when those pieces are feature-specific. The architecture becomes meaningful when features expose intentional public APIs and consumers avoid importing internal files. This reduces coupling, clarifies ownership, and makes internal refactoring safer.
interviewQuestions: What is feature-based architecture?
Why can co-locating feature code improve maintainability?
What is a feature public API?
Why are deep imports into another feature's internals problematic?
What belongs inside a feature?
What kinds of code might remain shared?
How do feature boundaries reduce coupling?
How does feature-based architecture make refactoring safer?

title: Shared Logic vs Page Logic
description: Learn to distinguish genuinely reusable application logic from logic that belongs to one page or feature, so shared code remains intentional and page-specific behavior does not become unnecessarily coupled.
mastery: The learner can classify logic as shared or page/feature-specific, explain the tradeoff behind the classification, and avoid prematurely moving one-off logic into shared infrastructure.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between shared logic and page-specific logic.
Identify logic that is genuinely reused across multiple features.
Identify logic that should remain local to a page or feature.
Explain how premature sharing creates coupling.
Explain how duplication can sometimes be preferable to premature abstraction.
Use reuse evidence to decide when logic deserves a shared boundary.
Draw a clear shared-vs-page logic boundary for a sample application.

sections.text: Not Everything Should Be Shared
Feature-based architecture gives code a clear owner. The next question is what should remain inside that owner and what genuinely deserves a shared boundary.
The answer is not 'share everything that looks reusable.' The answer depends on actual reuse, ownership, stability, and coupling.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Keep logic local until there is a real reason to share it. Shared logic should represent a concept that multiple parts of the application genuinely depend on.
Page-Specific Logic

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
CourseDetailsPage
→ formats the course header
→ chooses which course sections to show
→ combines course-specific UI state
→ handles this page's local interaction flow

sections.text: If this logic exists only to support the Course Details page, putting it in a global shared folder makes ownership less clear.
Shared Logic

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Multiple features
→ formatCurrency()
→ useCurrentUser()
→ shared API client
→ common date formatting

sections.text: These are stronger candidates for shared infrastructure because multiple parts of the application genuinely use the same concept.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not put one-off page logic in 'shared' just in case it is reused someday
sections.text: Premature sharing can create coupling before the reusable abstraction is understood. A small amount of duplication can be cheaper than forcing unrelated pages to depend on a speculative abstraction.
Duplication Is Sometimes Healthier

sections.title: Two similar implementations
sections.code:
CoursePage
→ course-specific validation

EnrollmentPage
→ enrollment-specific validation

sections.text: The code may look similar, but similarity does not automatically mean the two pieces have the same responsibility. Combining them too early can make a future change unexpectedly affect both.
Shared Logic Has a Cost

sections.title: When you share
sections.code:
Page A ─┐
        ├→ shared helper
Page B ─┘

Change helper
→ potentially affects A and B

sections.text: A shared abstraction creates a dependency relationship. That relationship can be valuable when intentional, but expensive when the sharing was based only on superficial similarity.
The Reuse Test

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
Is this used by multiple features?

Do those consumers truly share the same behavior?

Is the behavior likely to evolve together?

Does sharing make the architecture clearer?

Would a change reasonably need to affect all consumers?

sections.text: These questions are more useful than simply asking whether two pieces of code look alike.
Whiteboard: Shared or Local?

sections.title: Shared vs Page Logic Whiteboard
sections.instructions: Classify each piece of logic as page/feature-specific or genuinely shared. Explain one concrete reason for each choice.
sections.initialCode:
APPLICATION

CourseDetailsPage
→ builds a course-specific progress summary

SavedLessonsPage
→ filters saved lessons by their title

CheckoutPage
→ validates the checkout address

Multiple pages
→ formatCurrency(amount)

Multiple features
→ authenticated API client

AdminReportsPage
→ converts report rows into its chart-specific structure

Your classification:

1. Course progress summary:
_______________________________

2. Saved lessons filtering:
_______________________________

3. Checkout address validation:
_______________________________

4. Currency formatting:
_______________________________

5. Authenticated API client:
_______________________________

6. Report chart transformation:
_______________________________

sections.text: Share Concepts, Not Just Code

Two functions can have similar code while representing different business concepts. Shared logic should generally capture a concept that is meaningfully common, not merely a convenient way to reduce line count.

sections.title: Weak reason to share
sections.code: The functions look similar.

sections.title: Stronger reason
sections.code:
They represent the same business rule
and should always change together.

sections.text: Shared Infrastructure vs Shared Feature Logic

sections.title: Infrastructure
sections.code:
HTTP client
routing utilities
configuration
logging
formatting primitives

sections.title: Feature logic
sections.code:
Course enrollment rules
saved-lesson rules
search ranking
progress calculations

sections.text: Feature logic can be shared inside a bounded feature without becoming application-wide infrastructure. Keep the ownership boundary visible.
Shared Logic Can Be Shared at Different Scopes

sections.title: Possible scopes
sections.code:
Local component
↓
Page
↓
Feature
↓
Shared application infrastructure

sections.text: Sharing does not have to mean moving code all the way to a global shared directory. Sometimes the correct scope is simply the feature that owns the behavior.
Page Logic Should Stay Close to Page Behavior
Keeping page-specific logic near the page makes it easier to understand the complete behavior of that page without navigating through a generic shared layer.

sections.title: Local ownership
sections.code:
features/courses/
└── pages/
    └── CourseDetailsPage/
        ├── CourseDetailsPage.jsx
        └── courseDetailsViewModel.js

sections.text: Premature Abstraction Creates Coupling

sections.title: Before
sections.code:
CoursePage
→ local helper

EnrollmentPage
→ local helper

sections.title: Premature abstraction
sections.code:
CoursePage ─┐
            ├→ sharedValidation
Enrollment ─┘

Course rule changes
→ shared validation changes
→ enrollment behavior may change

sections.text: If the two rules are actually different, the shared abstraction has created a dependency that did not exist before.
Drill: Repair an Over-Shared Codebase

sections.title: Shared Folder Cleanup
sections.instructions: Identify which modules should remain feature/page-specific and which deserve the shared boundary. Move only the logic that has a clear multi-feature reason to be shared.
sections.initialCode:
shared/
├── courseProgressFormatter.js
├── checkoutValidation.js
├── enrollmentValidation.js
├── formatCurrency.js
├── savedLessonFilter.js
├── useCurrentUser.js
└── apiClient.js

Features:
├── courses/
├── checkout/
├── enrollment/
└── saved-lessons/

Tasks:
1. Keep genuinely shared logic in shared/.
2. Move one-off feature logic back to its owner.
3. Explain why each moved module is not a shared concept.
4. Identify one module where sharing is clearly justified.

sections.text: How Do You Know When to Extract?

sections.title: Useful signals
sections.code:
Actual second consumer appears.

Both consumers require the same behavior.

The rule has one clear owner.

Changes should intentionally affect all consumers.

The abstraction reduces duplication without hiding important differences.

sections.text: A second real use case is often stronger evidence than a prediction about future reuse.
One Feature Can Share Internally

Shared logic does not necessarily belong at the application root. A feature can have several components that share one piece of feature-specific state or logic while still keeping that logic inside the feature boundary.

sections.title: Feature-local reuse
sections.code:
features/saved-lessons/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── state/
└── helpers/

Multiple feature components
→ share saved-lesson logic

Other features
→ do not depend on its internals

sections.text: Shared Logic Should Have a Stable Contract
Once logic becomes shared, changes become more consequential. A shared module benefits from a clear contract so consumers know what it promises.
Architecture Judgment, Not a Formula

There is no universal rule that says 'duplicate twice, extract on the third use.' The exact decision depends on domain meaning, change patterns, and whether the abstraction makes the architecture clearer.
What Will Come Next?
The next lesson focuses on designing explicit module boundaries: deciding what a module exposes publicly and what remains an internal implementation detail.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is about deciding the correct ownership scope for logic. Module public APIs and export boundaries are handled next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'When should logic be shared?' A strong answer is: 'When multiple parts of the application genuinely depend on the same concept or business rule and should evolve together. I avoid extracting one-off logic merely because it looks reusable.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Is duplication always bad?' No. A small amount of duplication can be safer than premature abstraction when two pieces of logic may evolve differently.

Another follow-up is: 'Does shared mean globally shared?' No. Logic may be shared within a feature, across a set of related pages, or across the whole application depending on its true ownership scope.
Reflect
Look through your own shared utilities. Pick one and ask: 'Who actually uses this? Do they depend on the same concept, or did I put it here because I did not know where else to put it?'

sections.title: Share because the concept is shared

sections.text: The strongest reason to share code is not that it looks similar. It is that the same concept, rule, or responsibility genuinely belongs to multiple consumers.

sections.label: Complete the Shared vs Page Logic Whiteboard and Shared Folder Cleanup exercises. The learner must correctly distinguish genuine shared logic from page/feature-specific logic and justify at least one boundary decision.
sections.hint: Ask who owns the behavior, who actually uses it, and whether those consumers should intentionally change together.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Shared logic should represent a genuinely shared concept or rule. Page- and feature-specific logic should stay close to its owner until there is evidence that a broader boundary is warranted. Premature abstraction can create coupling, while a small amount of duplication can sometimes preserve clearer ownership. Sharing also has scopes: local, page, feature, and application-wide.

exercises.title: Shared vs Page Logic Whiteboard
exercises.brief: Classify representative application logic as shared or page/feature-specific and explain the ownership decision.

exercises.title: Shared Folder Cleanup
exercises.brief: Remove one-off logic from an overgrown shared directory while preserving genuinely shared infrastructure.

quiz.question: When is logic a strong candidate for a shared boundary?
options: When two functions look vaguely similar.
When multiple consumers genuinely depend on the same concept or business rule.
When a developer does not know where else to put it.
Whenever a function exceeds 20 lines.
quiz.explanation: Shared logic should represent a genuinely shared concept or responsibility.

quiz.question: Why can premature abstraction be harmful?
options: It can create coupling between consumers that may actually need to evolve differently.
It always makes code longer.
It prevents functions from being reused.
It makes pages impossible to render.
quiz.explanation: Premature sharing creates dependencies before the common abstraction is well understood.

quiz.question: Does shared logic always belong in a global shared folder?
options: Yes.
No. Logic can be shared at a local, page, feature, or application scope depending on ownership.
Only if it uses TypeScript.
Only if three pages use it.
quiz.explanation: The correct sharing scope depends on where the concept is actually owned.

summary: The important architecture judgment is not whether code can be reused but whether it should be shared. Genuinely shared concepts and rules belong at an appropriate shared scope, while page- and feature-specific behavior should remain local until real reuse and common ownership justify extraction. Premature abstraction can create coupling, and modest duplication can sometimes be the clearer architectural choice.
interviewQuestions: When should logic be shared?
Why can premature abstraction be harmful?
Is duplication always a code smell?
What is the difference between feature-local and application-wide shared logic?
How do you decide whether two similar functions represent the same concept?
What signals tell you that a shared module has become a dumping ground?
How does shared logic affect coupling?
When should page-specific logic stay local?

title: Designing Boundaries
description: Learn to design explicit module boundaries by deciding what a module exposes publicly and what remains an internal implementation detail, so dependencies stay intentional and refactoring remains safer.
mastery: The learner can identify a module's intended consumers, choose a small public API, keep implementation details internal, and explain how explicit boundaries reduce coupling and protect future refactoring.
learningObjectives: Explain what a module boundary is.
Distinguish public API from internal implementation detail.
Decide which values or functions should be exported from a module.
Keep implementation-specific helpers private.
Explain how exports influence coupling between modules.
Recognize when exporting everything weakens a boundary.
Design a small public surface for a realistic feature module.
Explain how explicit boundaries make refactoring safer.

sections.text: A Module Boundary Is a Contract
A module boundary answers a simple question: what does this module promise to the rest of the application?
Anything exposed through the module's public API can become a dependency for other code. Anything kept internal remains free to change without requiring consumers to understand its implementation.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Public exports are the contract. Internal code is the implementation. The smaller and clearer the contract, the less implementation detail other modules need to know.
A Module With No Real Boundary

sections.title: Everything exported

sections.text: Technically all of these values are available to consumers. Architecturally, that means consumers can become dependent on details that were never meant to be part of the feature's contract.
A Smaller Public Surface

sections.title: Intentional exports

sections.text: Now the module communicates that consumers are expected to use the two saved-lesson operations, while the helper functions remain implementation details.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not export everything for convenience
sections.text: Every export creates a potential dependency. Exporting internal helpers, state structures, and temporary implementation details weakens the module boundary and makes future refactoring harder.
Public API Should Match Consumer Needs

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
What does another module actually need?
        ↓
Expose that concept.
        ↓
Keep supporting implementation private.

sections.text: The public API should be shaped around the supported use of the module, not around everything the implementation happens to contain.
Example: Search Feature

sections.title: Internal implementation

sections.text: Consumers need the search operation. They do not need to know how the query is normalized or how ranking is calculated.
Why Internal Details Should Stay Internal

sections.title: With a narrow boundary
sections.code:
Consumer
   ↓
searchLessons()
   ↓
internal helpers

Internal implementation can change
without changing the consumer.

sections.title: With a wide boundary
sections.code:
Consumer
→ normalizeSearchTerm()
→ scoreResult()
→ searchLessons()

Internal refactor
→ many consumers may break

sections.text: Whiteboard: Draw the Boundary

sections.title: Module Boundary Whiteboard

createStorageKey()
validateSavedLesson()

SAVED_LESSONS_STORAGE_VERSION
savedLessonsDebugState
SavedLessonsPage

PUBLIC API
_______________________________
_______________________________
_______________________________

INTERNAL
_______________________________
_______________________________
_______________________________

Why should the public surface stay small?
_______________________________

sections.text: A Feature Entry Point

sections.title: Barrel-style public API

sections.text: A feature entry point can make the intended public surface obvious. The exact project convention can differ, but the architectural idea is the same: consumers depend on a contract rather than internal file locations.
Internal Imports Can Stay Internal

sections.title: Inside the feature
sections.code:
SavedLessonsPage
 ↓
SavedLessonSummary
 ↓
savedLessonsStore
 ↓
internal helpers

sections.text: Internal modules can depend on one another without exposing every internal relationship to the rest of the application.
Public API and Change Safety

sections.title: Refactoring
sections.code:
Before:
searchLessons()
→ normalizeSearchTerm()

After:
searchLessons()
→ tokenizeQuery()
→ ranking engine

Consumer API unchanged.

sections.text: A boundary gives the implementation room to evolve while preserving the contract consumers depend on.
Do Not Hide Real Product Contracts

A boundary should not make a legitimate external dependency artificially difficult to access. If another part of the application genuinely needs a supported capability, expose it intentionally rather than forcing consumers into internal files.
Exporting Types and Values
The same boundary principle applies whether a module exposes functions, components, constants, types, or other values. What matters is whether consumers should be allowed to depend on the thing.
Drill: Shrink the Public Surface

sections.title: Export Review
sections.instructions: Review the module's exports. Keep the supported consumer-facing API and make the remaining implementation details private.

sections.text: The Cost of Wide APIs

sections.title: Wide public API
sections.code:
Module
├── public feature API
├── helper A
├── helper B
├── implementation state
├── cache details
└── temporary constant

Many consumers
→ can depend on all of them

sections.title: Narrow public API
sections.code:
Module
├── public feature API
└── internal implementation

Consumers
→ depend on supported concepts only

sections.text: Boundaries Are Social Contracts Too

A technically private implementation can still become a de facto public API if engineers routinely import it through internal paths. Teams need conventions that reinforce the intended boundary, such as feature entry points and avoiding deep imports.
Architecture Depends on Discipline
Folder structure and module exports are tools. They do not automatically create good architecture. Engineers have to respect the boundaries and review dependencies when new features are added.
Boundary Test

sections.title: Ask before exporting
sections.code:
Would I be comfortable supporting this as a dependency?

Would I be surprised if another module used this?

Could I change this implementation without wanting to update consumers?

Does this export represent a stable concept?

sections.text: If the answer suggests that consumers should not depend on the value, keep it internal.
Designing Boundaries Before Coding
Boundary decisions can be made while planning a feature. Before implementation, sketch what the feature needs to expose and what it should own internally.

sections.title: Planning sketch
sections.code:
Feature
│
├── Public
│   ├── Page
│   └── Supported component
│
└── Internal
    ├── State
    ├── Helpers
    ├── Data mapping
    └── Implementation details

sections.text: This prevents the public API from becoming an accidental by-product of file creation.
What Will Come Next?
The next lesson is Architecture Tradeoffs. It moves from designing one boundary to comparing broader architecture decisions across simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on module contracts and public versus internal detail. It does not yet ask you to choose between competing full-application architectures.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a module boundary?' A strong answer is: 'It is the contract between a module and its consumers: the intentionally exposed public API versus implementation details that remain internal.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why not export everything?' Because every export can become a dependency. A smaller public surface reduces coupling and gives the implementation more freedom to change.

Another follow-up is: 'How does this improve refactoring?' Consumers depend on stable concepts rather than internal file structure, so internal implementations can change without forcing unrelated consumers to change.
Reflect
Pick one feature module in your codebase. List every current export. Which exports are actual supported concepts, and which are implementation details that accidentally became public?

sections.title: Export the contract, not the implementation

sections.text: Before exporting something, ask whether you are prepared for another part of the application to depend on it. An export is an invitation to become coupled.

sections.label: Complete the Module Boundary Whiteboard and Export Review. The learner must identify a small public API, keep implementation-specific details internal, and explain how the boundary protects future refactoring.
sections.hint: Public = supported consumer-facing concept. Internal = implementation detail that consumers should not need to know.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A module boundary is a contract: the public API is what consumers are intentionally allowed to depend on, while internal implementation details remain free to change. Exporting everything weakens that boundary because every export can become a dependency. A narrow, intentional public surface reduces coupling, clarifies ownership, and makes internal refactoring safer.

exercises.title: Export Review
exercises.brief: Shrink an overly broad module API so consumers depend only on supported concepts.

quiz.question: What is a module boundary?
options: The contract defining what a module exposes publicly versus keeps internal.
A CSS border around a component.
A rule that every file must have one export.
A folder containing only React components.
quiz.explanation: The lesson defines boundaries as public API versus internal implementation detail.

quiz.question: Why should a module avoid exporting every internal helper?
options: Every export can become a dependency and make refactoring harder.
Helpers cannot be exported in JavaScript.
Exports always make the bundle smaller.
Internal helpers are automatically inaccessible.
quiz.explanation: A narrow public surface limits unnecessary coupling.

quiz.question: What is the best reason to expose a function from a module?
options: It is convenient for debugging.
It represents a supported concept that consumers genuinely need.
It might be useful someday.
It is currently the longest function.
quiz.explanation: Public APIs should expose intentional consumer-facing capabilities.

summary: Designing boundaries means deciding what a module promises to consumers and what remains an internal implementation detail. Public exports form a contract and should therefore be intentional and small. Keeping helpers, state structures, and temporary implementation details internal reduces coupling and gives engineers more freedom to refactor without changing unrelated consumers.

title: Architecture Tradeoffs
description: Learn to compare architecture decisions by explicitly weighing simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity instead of treating a popular pattern as universally correct.
mastery: The learner can evaluate competing architecture options against concrete application constraints, identify at least two meaningful tradeoffs for a decision, and justify a choice without claiming there is one universally correct architecture.
learningObjectives: Explain why architecture decisions always involve tradeoffs.
Compare simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity as architecture concerns.
Evaluate an architecture decision against real application constraints.
Identify at least two tradeoffs in a proposed architecture.
Distinguish a justified architecture decision from a popularity-driven choice.
Explain why the best architecture depends on context.
Communicate an architecture decision and its tradeoffs clearly.

sections.text: There Is No Free Architecture Choice
The previous lessons established folder organization, feature ownership, shared logic, and module boundaries. This lesson steps back and asks how to choose among competing architectural approaches.
Every architecture decision gives you something and costs you something. Good engineering makes those tradeoffs explicit.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Architecture is a tradeoff between competing goals. Choose deliberately based on the application's actual constraints rather than choosing a pattern because it is popular.
Four Useful Dimensions

sections.title: Tradeoff matrix
sections.code:
SIMPLICITY
→ How easy is the system to understand?

FLEXIBILITY
→ How easily can requirements change?

PERFORMANCE
→ What runtime/build/runtime-delivery costs does the choice introduce?

TEAM VELOCITY
→ How quickly can the team safely build and change features?

sections.text: These are not the only dimensions that matter, but they provide a practical starting framework for architecture discussions.
Example: One Large Shared Module

sections.title: Option A
sections.code:
One shared application module

Pros
→ simple to locate initially
→ fewer boundaries
→ low setup cost

Cons
→ ownership can become unclear
→ unrelated features can become coupled
→ large changes become harder to reason about

sections.text: Example: Feature Boundaries

sections.title: Option B
sections.code:
Separate feature modules

Pros
→ clearer ownership
→ better change isolation
→ easier feature-level navigation

Cons
→ more structure
→ more boundaries to understand
→ shared concepts require deliberate API design

sections.text: Neither option wins automatically. The right choice depends on the application's size, team, expected growth, and domain.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not choose an architecture because it is popular
sections.text: A pattern can be successful in many codebases and still be the wrong fit for yours. The justification should connect the architecture to the application's actual constraints.
Context Changes the Answer

sections.title: Small internal tool
sections.code:
Few developers
Few features
Low expected growth

→ simplicity may dominate

sections.title: Large product
sections.code:
Many developers
Many domains
Frequent feature work
Independent ownership

→ stronger boundaries may justify additional structure

sections.text: The architecture should fit the environment in which the codebase actually operates.
Whiteboard: Architecture Tradeoff Matrix

A: ______
B: ______

Tradeoff #1:
_______________________________

Tradeoff #2:
_______________________________

Choice:
_______________________________

Why does the choice fit these constraints?
_______________________________

sections.text: Tradeoffs Need Specific Constraints

A weak architecture argument says, 'Feature-based is cleaner.' A stronger argument says, 'We have multiple feature owners and frequent parallel changes, so stronger feature boundaries reduce the chance that unrelated teams depend on each other's internals.'

sections.title: Weak
sections.code: This architecture is better.

sections.title: Strong
sections.code:
Given our team size and independent feature ownership,
this boundary reduces cross-feature coupling,
at the cost of more explicit APIs and structure.

sections.text: Performance Is Not Always the Primary Constraint

Developers sometimes justify architecture entirely through performance even when the measured performance cost is negligible. A more complex design can hurt team velocity or readability without solving an actual performance problem.
Simplicity Has Real Value

Simple architectures are easier to explain, onboard, debug, and modify. Complexity should be introduced when it buys something important enough to justify the additional cognitive and maintenance cost.
Flexibility Also Has a Cost
A highly flexible architecture can require more abstractions, configuration, and indirection. If the product requirements are stable, that flexibility may never pay for its complexity.
Team Velocity Is an Architecture Concern
Architecture affects how quickly engineers can locate code, understand dependencies, make changes, review pull requests, and work in parallel.

sections.title: Team-level effects
sections.code:
Clear ownership
→ fewer accidental conflicts

Clear boundaries
→ smaller change surfaces

Complicated boundaries
→ more cognitive overhead

Weak boundaries
→ more coordination and coupling

sections.text: Architecture Decisions Should Be Reversible When Possible

Prefer decisions that can be changed incrementally when the uncertainty is high. Avoid introducing a highly expensive architecture commitment before the product provides evidence that the added structure is necessary.

sections.title: Incremental path
sections.code:
Simple structure
 ↓
Growth creates friction
 ↓
Introduce feature boundary
 ↓
Extract shared API where justified
 ↓
Expand architecture only as needed

sections.text: Architecture Is a Constraint Management Problem

A useful architecture discussion begins with constraints: who is building the product, how large it is, how quickly it changes, what performance requirements exist, and what kinds of ownership boundaries matter.
Drill: Challenge the Popular Choice

sections.title: Architecture Decision Review
sections.instructions: A team proposes an architecture because 'everyone uses it.' Challenge that reasoning. Identify the missing constraints and write a better decision statement.
sections.initialCode:
TEAM STATEMENT

'We should use this architecture because it is
popular and large companies use it.'

What constraints are missing?
_______________________________
_______________________________

What tradeoffs should be discussed?
_______________________________
_______________________________

Rewrite the decision:
_______________________________
_______________________________

sections.text: Two Tradeoffs Minimum
A good architecture review should not merely list one benefit. State what you gain and what you give up.

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Gain:
Better feature ownership.

Cost:
More module APIs to design and maintain.

Gain:
Safer independent changes.

Cost:
More explicit coordination at shared boundaries.

sections.text: Avoid Architecture Absolutes

sections.title: Weak claims
sections.code:
Always use feature folders.

Never share logic.

Always use micro-frontends.

Always prefer the most flexible architecture.

sections.text: Architecture decisions should be conditional on context. The word 'always' is often a warning sign in architecture discussions.
Tradeoffs and Technical Debt

Choosing a simpler architecture today can be entirely reasonable when growth is uncertain. The important part is recognizing the resulting tradeoff and knowing what signals would justify revisiting the decision.

sections.title: Explicit debt
sections.code:
Decision:
Keep simple structure for now.

Known tradeoff:
Feature boundaries may become harder later.

Revisit when:
Team ownership and feature count increase.

sections.text: Drill: Write the Architecture Decision

sections.title: Architecture Decision Record
sections.instructions: Write a concise architecture decision that states the context, chosen approach, two tradeoffs, and the condition that would cause you to revisit it.

sections.text: Architecture Communication

A technically good decision can still fail if the team cannot understand why it was made. Good architecture communication makes the context and tradeoffs visible so future engineers can tell whether the original decision still fits.
What Will Come Next?

The next lesson is the Architecture Review Challenge. It asks you to inspect an existing codebase and propose concrete, justified structural improvements rather than designing a new architecture from scratch.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson teaches how to reason about architecture choices. The next lesson applies that reasoning to an existing codebase in the module capstone.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you choose an architecture?' A strong answer is: 'I start with constraints—team size, application size, feature ownership, expected growth, performance requirements, and release patterns. Then I compare options and explicitly state the tradeoffs rather than assuming one pattern is universally best.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What tradeoffs matter most?' Common dimensions include simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity, but the priority depends on the product.
Another follow-up is: 'What if you're uncertain?' Prefer incremental and reversible decisions where practical, and define the signals that would cause the team to revisit the architecture.
Reflect
Choose one architecture decision in your current project. Write down what it improves, what it makes harder, and what future change would make you reconsider it.
When someone proposes an architecture, ask: 'What problem does this solve, what does it cost, and which constraints make that tradeoff worthwhile?'

sections.label: Complete the Tradeoff Matrix, Popular-Choice Review, and Architecture Decision Record. The learner must compare alternatives, identify at least two tradeoffs, and justify one choice against concrete constraints.
sections.hint: Name the constraints first. Then compare simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity. State both benefits and costs.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Every architecture choice trades off something. Simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity can pull in different directions, so architecture should be chosen against the application's actual constraints rather than popularity. Strong architecture decisions name alternatives, explain at least two tradeoffs, and identify what future evidence would justify revisiting the decision.

exercises.brief: Compare two architecture options across simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity, then justify a choice.

exercises.title: Architecture Decision Review
exercises.brief: Challenge a popularity-driven architecture proposal and rewrite it as a constraint-based decision.

exercises.title: Architecture Decision Record
exercises.brief: Write a concise decision record containing context, alternatives, tradeoffs, chosen approach, and revisit criteria.

quiz.question: What should primarily drive an architecture decision?
options: Popularity of the pattern.
The application's actual constraints and tradeoffs.
The number of folders the pattern creates.
What another company uses.
quiz.explanation: Architecture should fit the product, team, and technical constraints.

quiz.question: Which set contains useful architecture tradeoff dimensions from this lesson?
options: Simplicity, flexibility, performance, team velocity.
Colors, typography, animation, branding.
URL length, CSS class count, file extension, commit size.
Only runtime performance.
quiz.explanation: The lesson explicitly frames architecture decisions around simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity.

quiz.question: What should a strong architecture decision communicate?
options: Only the selected pattern.
The context, alternatives, benefits, costs, and reasons for choosing the approach.
That one pattern is universally correct.
Only expected performance.
quiz.explanation: Architecture decisions should make tradeoffs explicit.

quiz.question: What is a useful response when architecture uncertainty is high?
options: Commit immediately to the most complex design.
Prefer incremental or reversible decisions where practical and define when to revisit them.
Copy the architecture of the largest company available.
Avoid documenting the decision.

summary: Architecture choices are tradeoffs rather than universally correct answers. Evaluate options against concrete constraints and consider at least simplicity, flexibility, performance, and team velocity. A strong decision explains the alternatives, states both gains and costs, and identifies what future evidence would justify revisiting the choice. Popularity is not a substitute for architectural reasoning.

title: Architecture Review Challenge
description: Review an existing frontend codebase, identify architectural friction, and propose concrete, justified, incremental improvements based on feature ownership, shared logic, module boundaries, and explicit tradeoffs.
mastery: The learner can review an existing codebase, identify architectural problems, propose incremental structural improvements, justify those recommendations against real constraints, and explain the tradeoffs without defaulting to a full rewrite.
learningObjectives: Critique an existing frontend folder and module structure.
Identify unclear feature ownership and excessive coupling.
Identify inappropriate shared logic or misplaced page-specific logic.
Identify module boundaries that are too broad or too weak.
Propose concrete structural improvements.
Justify recommendations against the application's actual constraints.
Explain at least two tradeoffs for an architectural recommendation.
Prefer incremental improvements over unnecessary rewrites.
Communicate an architecture review clearly enough for another engineer to act on it.

sections.text: The Architecture Review Challenge
This is the Module 5-1 capstone. Instead of designing a new architecture from scratch, you will review an existing codebase and determine where its current structure creates unnecessary friction.
Your recommendations must be concrete, justified, and incremental. The goal is to improve the existing architecture without pretending that a complete rewrite is automatically the best answer.

sections.title: The capstone rule
sections.text: Improve the existing system where it creates real friction. Do not propose a full rewrite simply because you would organize the code differently from the beginning.
What You Are Reviewing

sections.title: Review dimensions
sections.code:
Folder structure

Feature ownership

Shared vs page-specific logic

Module public APIs

Deep imports and coupling

Change surface

Team/navigation friction

Architecture tradeoffs

sections.text: Start With the Current State
Do not redesign immediately. First map the existing architecture.

sections.title: Initial questions
sections.code:
Where does each major feature live?

Which modules own important behavior?

What is shared?

Which modules import other modules' internals?

Where does a normal feature change require edits?

Which parts of the structure are working well?

sections.text: Audit the Folder Structure

sections.title: Look for
sections.code:
Giant technical-type folders

Features scattered across unrelated directories

A shared folder containing feature-specific code

Deeply nested structures that are hard to navigate

Duplicated feature boundaries

Ambiguous ownership

sections.text: Audit Feature Ownership
Pick two or three representative features and trace their components, state, data access, and helpers. Ask whether each feature has a clear home.

sections.title: Feature trace
sections.code:
Feature
 ↓
UI
 ↓
state
 ↓
data/API logic
 ↓
helpers

Do these pieces have one understandable owner?

sections.text: Audit Shared Logic
Open the shared utilities, hooks, and components. Determine whether they are genuinely shared concepts or simply places where developers put logic they did not know where else to put.

sections.title: Warning signs
sections.code:
shared/useCourseSearch.js
shared/enrollmentValidation.js
shared/dashboardState.js
shared/savedLessonHelpers.js

sections.text: A large collection of feature-specific modules inside shared infrastructure is evidence that ownership may be unclear.
Audit Module Boundaries

sections.title: Look for boundary erosion
sections.code:
Feature A
→ Feature B internal store

Feature C
→ Feature B helper

Page D
→ another feature's implementation file

sections.text: These dependencies mean the folder structure may claim to have boundaries that the import graph does not actually respect.
Identify Change Friction

sections.title: Choose a real task
sections.code:
Example task:
'Add the ability to archive a saved lesson.'

Trace every file that would need to change.

Count unrelated modules involved.

Ask why each dependency exists.

sections.text: The change path is often a better architectural diagnostic than simply looking at the folder tree.
Whiteboard: Architecture Review Map

sections.title: Architecture Review Map
sections.instructions: Map the existing architecture before proposing changes. Identify feature ownership, shared logic, public APIs, and at least two concrete sources of architectural friction.
sections.initialCode:
EXISTING APPLICATION

Features:
Courses
Saved Lessons
Enrollment
Search
Progress

CURRENT STRUCTURE
src/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── pages/
├── services/
├── state/
├── shared/
└── utils/

Review:

1. Where does each feature's main logic live?
_______________________________

2. Which code is genuinely shared?
_______________________________

3. Which code appears misplaced?
_______________________________

4. Where do you see deep cross-feature dependencies?
_______________________________

5. Name two concrete friction points.
_______________________________
_______________________________

sections.text: Prioritize the Problems

sections.title: Prioritization criteria
sections.code:
How often does the problem slow engineers down?

How many features does it affect?

How much coupling does it create?

Does it block independent ownership?

Does fixing it unlock safer future changes?

Can it be improved incrementally?

sections.text: Do not turn every architectural imperfection into a migration project. Focus on changes that reduce meaningful friction.
Write Concrete Recommendations

sections.title: Weak recommendation
sections.code: Rewrite the architecture using feature folders.

sections.title: Strong recommendation
sections.code:
Move the Saved Lessons components, state, and
feature-specific helpers under a saved-lessons
boundary first. Keep its existing public page API.
Then update consumers to import through that boundary.

sections.text: A useful recommendation names what should change, where it should move, what dependency should change, and why the change reduces a specific architectural problem.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not prescribe a full rewrite by default
sections.text: A mature codebase contains working behavior, knowledge, and dependencies. A strong architecture review identifies the highest-value incremental changes instead of assuming the existing system must be discarded.
Show the Migration Path

sections.title: Incremental architecture change
sections.code:
Current shared structure
        ↓
Introduce one feature boundary
        ↓
Move one feature's internals
        ↓
Create public entry point
        ↓
Update consumers
        ↓
Repeat where evidence justifies it

sections.text: Architecture can evolve gradually. This reduces the risk of introducing many simultaneous changes that are difficult to review or roll back.
Tradeoffs Must Be Explicit

sections.title: Example recommendation
sections.code:
Recommendation:
Feature-based organization for major domains.

Gain:
Clear ownership and lower change surface.

Cost:
More module boundaries and explicit APIs.

Why it fits:
Multiple engineers work on independent domains.

sections.text: Every recommendation should state what it improves and what additional cost it introduces.
Capstone Review Template

sections.title: Architecture Review Challenge
sections.instructions: Complete the full architecture review. The final document should describe the existing structure, identify concrete problems, recommend incremental improvements, justify the tradeoffs, and define how you would migrate safely.

sections.text: Good Success Criteria

sections.title: Measure architectural improvement
sections.code:
A feature can be located faster.

Feature changes touch fewer unrelated modules.

Shared modules contain only genuinely shared concepts.

Cross-feature imports use public APIs.

Ownership is clearer.

A new engineer can explain the structure without tribal knowledge.

sections.text: Avoid Cosmetic Architecture
Moving files into new folders is not enough. The architecture is improved only if ownership, dependencies, and change surfaces become clearer.

sections.title: Cosmetic change
sections.code:
Move files
→ keep all deep imports
→ keep shared feature internals
→ no meaningful boundary

sections.title: Architectural change
sections.code:
Move feature
→ define public API
→ update consumers
→ remove deep imports
→ clarify ownership

sections.text: Review the Review

sections.title: Recommendation Quality Check
sections.instructions: Review your own proposed changes. Reject any recommendation that is driven only by preference or aesthetics. Each retained recommendation must identify a real problem, evidence, an improvement, and a tradeoff.

sections.text: Final Rubric

sections.title: Submission should demonstrate
sections.code:
□ Correct understanding of current architecture.
□ At least two concrete architectural findings.
□ Evidence for each finding.
□ Specific recommended improvements.
□ Explicit tradeoffs.
□ Incremental migration path.
□ Clear public/internal boundary thinking.
□ Correct shared-vs-feature ownership reasoning.
□ No unnecessary full rewrite.

sections.text: What Counts as Strong Work?

sections.title: Strong review
sections.code:
Specific
Evidence-based
Constraint-aware
Incremental
Tradeoff-aware
Actionable
Easy for another engineer to follow

sections.text: What Does Not Count?

sections.title: Weak review
sections.code:
Uses trendy architecture vocabulary

Proposes rewriting everything

Lists folder changes without explaining why

Treats all shared code as bad

Claims one architecture is universally correct

Provides no migration path

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you review an existing frontend architecture?' A strong answer is: 'I would first map the current structure and trace a few real feature changes. Then I would look for unclear ownership, inappropriate sharing, deep imports, and oversized change surfaces. I would prioritize the highest-friction areas and propose incremental fixes with explicit tradeoffs rather than starting with a rewrite.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you know whether your architecture recommendation worked?' Look for lower search cost, clearer ownership, fewer unrelated dependencies, and smaller change surfaces in real feature work.

Another follow-up is: 'What if your team disagrees with the architecture?' Make the constraints and tradeoffs explicit, compare the alternatives, and identify what evidence would distinguish the options.
Reflect
What is the single highest-value architectural change you would make in the application you just reviewed? What concrete developer friction does it remove, and what new cost does it introduce?

Senior architecture work is rarely about inventing the perfect system from scratch. It is about identifying the constraints, reducing the highest-value sources of friction, and evolving the architecture safely.

sections.label: Submit the Architecture Review Challenge for manual/rubric grading. The review must contain concrete findings, evidence, incremental recommendations, explicit tradeoffs, and a justified migration path.
sections.hint: Review first. Recommend second. Tie every recommendation to a real problem and constraint. Prefer incremental improvements over rewriting the application.

sections.text: Module 5-1 Complete

You have moved from understanding architecture to evaluating folder structures, organizing by feature, distinguishing shared from local logic, designing explicit module boundaries, and reasoning about architecture tradeoffs.
The next module moves from architecture to reusable React patterns, beginning with custom hooks.
What You Should Take Away

A strong architecture review is evidence-based and incremental. Map the current system, identify real friction, propose specific improvements, state their tradeoffs, and provide a migration path that preserves working behavior. The objective is not to prove that a particular architecture is superior; it is to show that you can improve a real codebase against real constraints.

exercises.brief: Map the current codebase and identify concrete sources of architectural friction before proposing changes.

exercises.title: Recommendation Quality Check
