quiz.question: What should you do before proposing architectural changes to an existing codebase?
options: Rewrite the folder structure immediately.
Map the current architecture and identify real sources of friction.
Delete the shared directory.
Choose the most popular architecture pattern.
quiz.explanation: The capstone requires review and diagnosis before recommendations.

quiz.question: What makes an architecture recommendation actionable?
options: It names a concrete problem, evidence, specific improvement, tradeoff, and migration path.
It uses sophisticated architecture terminology.
It proposes the largest possible rewrite.
It avoids discussing costs.
quiz.explanation: Actionable recommendations connect diagnosis to a specific incremental change.

quiz.question: Why is a full rewrite generally a weak default recommendation?
options: Existing behavior and knowledge have value, and broad rewrites introduce large simultaneous risk.
Rewrites are always technically impossible.
Folder structures cannot be changed.
Architecture never needs to evolve.
quiz.explanation: The capstone prioritizes justified incremental improvements over rewrite-everything recommendations.

quiz.question: What is a useful indicator that an architecture recommendation is working?
options: The repository has more folders.
Real feature work has clearer ownership and smaller unrelated change surfaces.
The architecture uses more abstractions.
Every feature has the same number of files.
quiz.explanation: Architecture should reduce meaningful developer friction, not merely change the directory tree.

summary: The Architecture Review Challenge is the Module 5-1 capstone. Review an existing codebase rather than designing a greenfield system, identify concrete architectural friction, and propose incremental improvements grounded in evidence and constraints. Strong recommendations address feature ownership, shared logic, module boundaries, and tradeoffs while preserving working behavior. A full rewrite is not the default solution.

title: Custom Hooks
description: Learn how to extract reusable stateful logic from React components into custom hooks, while recognizing when extraction is justified and when a one-off abstraction would add unnecessary complexity.
mastery: The learner can identify repeated stateful logic, extract it into a custom hook, preserve the original behavior, and explain why extraction is justified when the logic is genuinely reusable rather than used in only one place.
learningObjectives: Explain what a custom hook is.
Recognize stateful logic that can be extracted from a component.
Extract useState/useEffect-based logic into a reusable custom hook.
Return the state and operations a consuming component actually needs.
Preserve behavior while moving implementation into a hook.
Use a custom hook from more than one component when the logic is genuinely shared.
Recognize when extracting a custom hook is premature.
Keep single-use logic local when extraction would not improve the design.

sections.text: Extract Logic, Not Markup

A custom hook is a reusable function for React stateful logic. It lets you move logic that uses hooks such as useState or useEffect out of a component while keeping the logic reusable by other components.
The motivation should come from the logic itself. If two places genuinely need the same stateful behavior, a custom hook can give that behavior a clear reusable home.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Component = presentation and feature-specific UI. Custom hook = reusable stateful behavior that the component can consume.
Start With Inline Logic

sections.title: Stateful logic inside a component

sections.text: If this behavior is needed only by SearchBox, keeping it here is perfectly reasonable.
When Extraction Becomes Useful
Imagine a second component needs the same query state, update behavior, and clear operation. Duplicating the full stateful implementation can now create two copies of the same behavior.

sections.title: Extract the behavior

sections.text: The hook owns the reusable stateful behavior. Components decide how to present and use that behavior.
Consume the Hook

sections.title: Component using the custom hook

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not extract a custom hook just because logic exists
sections.text: A custom hook should solve a real reuse or separation problem. Extracting logic that is used only once can add indirection without improving the code.
One Use vs. Multiple Uses

sections.title: Probably keep local
sections.code:
CourseDetailsPage
→ one small piece of state
→ no other consumer
→ simple implementation

sections.title: Strong extraction candidate
sections.code:
SearchPage
ResultsPanel
SavedLessonsPage

All need:
→ query state
→ update behavior
→ clear behavior

sections.text: The important architectural signal is genuine reuse of the behavior, not simply the number of lines in the original component.
Hooks Can Encapsulate Effects Too

sections.title: Reusable state + effect logic

sections.text: This hook packages a reusable stateful interaction with an external browser event source.
A Hook Does Not Share State Between Components
Calling the same custom hook from two components gives each component its own hook state. The hook shares the logic, not automatically one shared state instance.

sections.title: Two consumers
sections.code:
Component A
→ useSearchQuery()
→ its own query state

Component B
→ useSearchQuery()
→ its own query state

sections.text: This distinction is important: custom hooks are primarily about reusable behavior, not automatically creating global state.
Interactive Practice: Extract the Hook

sections.title: Custom Hooks Playground
sections.instructions: Extract the reusable stateful logic from the component into a custom hook. Preserve the component's behavior and return only the state and operations the UI needs.

sections.text: A Good Hook API Is Small

sections.title: Prefer

sections.text: The consuming component should not need to understand every internal variable, helper, or effect used by the hook.
Don't Return the Entire Internal State Machine

sections.title: Too much implementation detail
sections.code:
return {
  query,
  submittedQuery,
  setQuery,
  setSubmittedQuery,
  normalizedQuery,
  requestState,
  internalCache,
  submit,
  clear
};

sections.text: Returning unnecessary internals makes consumers tightly coupled to the hook implementation. Return the contract the components actually need.
Hook Naming

sections.title: Names communicate behavior
sections.code:
useSearchQuery()
useOnlineStatus()
useDisclosure()
usePagination()

sections.text: A custom hook name should make its reusable behavior understandable without requiring the reader to inspect its implementation.
Hooks Should Follow Hook Rules
Custom hooks are still hooks. Their internal useState/useEffect and other hook calls follow React's hook rules.

sections.title: Keep hook calls predictable

sections.text: A Hook Is Not a Utility Function

A normal utility function calculates or transforms values without owning React hook state. A custom hook is specifically a reusable function that can compose React hooks to encapsulate stateful behavior.

sections.title: Utility
sections.code: formatCurrency(amount)

sections.title: Custom hook
sections.code:
useSearchQuery()
→ state + React behavior

sections.text: Drill: Decide Whether to Extract

sections.title: Hook Extraction Decision Drill
sections.instructions: For each scenario, decide whether to keep the logic local or extract a custom hook. Justify the choice based on actual reuse and ownership.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
One page has a 4-line useState for an accordion that no other component uses.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario B
Three pages all manage the same pagination state and behavior.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario C
Two components track online/offline browser events in identical ways.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario D
A component has 80 lines of state logic but no second consumer exists yet.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

Scenario E
Two components use similar code, but one will intentionally behave differently next month.

Choice:
____________________________
Why:
____________________________

sections.text: Extraction Should Preserve Ownership
If a hook exists only for one feature, it can still belong inside that feature. Reusable does not automatically mean application-global.

sections.title: Feature-local hook
sections.code:
features/saved-lessons/
└── hooks/
    └── useSavedLessonSelection.js

sections.text: If several Saved Lessons components use the behavior, the hook is reusable while remaining owned by the feature.
Hook Extraction and Testing

After extraction, the important behavior should remain protected. Test the hook's observable behavior and the component's user-facing behavior rather than coupling tests to the hook's internal implementation.
A Useful Refactoring Sequence

sections.title: Extract safely
sections.code:
1. Identify the stateful logic.
2. Confirm there is a real reuse/separation reason.
3. Move the logic with minimal behavior change.
4. Return a small useful API.
5. Update consumers.
6. Test the original behavior.
7. Add a second consumer only when justified.

sections.text: Avoid Premature Generalization

A first extracted hook does not need to support every future use case. Start with the reusable behavior you know exists. Generalize further only when new consumers provide evidence that the abstraction should grow.

sections.title: Prefer
sections.code: usePagination({ pageSize })

sections.title: Avoid speculative API
sections.code:
useUniversalDataController({
  strategy,
  serializer,
  adapters,
  middleware,
  cachePolicy,
  ...
})

sections.text: A hook should solve a real reusable problem, not predict every possible future requirement.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson introduces composition patterns. It moves beyond extracting behavior into a hook and explores ways to assemble components through composition rather than inheritance-style structures.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson isolates custom-hook extraction. Compound component patterns are deliberately deferred to lesson-5-2-3.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a custom hook?' A strong answer is: 'It is a reusable function that encapsulates React stateful logic so multiple components can consume the behavior without duplicating the implementation.'

A likely follow-up is: 'When should you extract one?' Extract it when the logic is genuinely reusable or the separation gives the feature a meaningful reusable stateful abstraction. Do not extract a one-off hook simply because the component has many lines.
Another follow-up is: 'Do two components calling the same hook share state?' No. Each hook call has its own state instance. The hook shares the logic, not automatically the state.
Reflect

Find a component from an earlier project that contains useState/useEffect logic. Is there a second consumer today? If not, would extracting the logic still make the code clearer, or would it simply add another layer to navigate?

sections.title: Extract because the behavior is reusable

sections.text: The strongest reason to create a custom hook is that the stateful behavior has a real reusable home. Do not let abstraction become the goal by itself.

sections.label: Complete the Custom Hooks Playground with correct behavior and pass the applied quiz item. The learner must extract reusable stateful logic into a custom hook without prematurely abstracting one-off behavior.
sections.hint: Start from inline useState/useEffect logic, extract only the reusable behavior, return a small API, and keep single-use logic local when extraction adds no value.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic from components into shareable functions. They are useful when the same behavior is genuinely needed in multiple places or when a stateful concern has a clear reusable boundary. They do not automatically share state between consumers. Keep one-off logic local, return a small API, and generalize only when real reuse justifies it.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a custom hook?
options: To share JSX markup between components.
To extract reusable stateful React logic into a shareable function.
To create global state automatically.
To replace all utility functions.
quiz.explanation: Custom hooks encapsulate reusable stateful behavior.

quiz.question: When is extracting a custom hook potentially premature?
options: When the stateful logic has multiple genuine consumers.
When the logic is used in only one place and extraction adds no clear benefit.
When the hook contains useState.
When a component returns JSX.
quiz.explanation: The source's core misconception is extracting a hook prematurely for logic that is only used once.

quiz.question: If two components call the same custom hook, what do they share?
options: The same state instance automatically.
The same reusable logic, with separate hook state for each call.
The same DOM node.
The same component props.
quiz.explanation: Custom hooks share logic; each component invocation receives its own hook state.

quiz.question: What should a custom hook generally return?
options: Every internal implementation variable.
A small API containing the state and operations consumers actually need.
The entire component tree.
Only the JSX markup.
quiz.explanation: A focused hook API reduces coupling to implementation details.

summary: Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic from React components into shareable functions. The key decision is whether the behavior is genuinely reusable; extracting one-off logic can add unnecessary indirection. A hook shares behavior rather than automatically sharing state, and a good hook exposes a small API while keeping implementation details internal.

title: Composition Patterns
description: Learn how React composition patterns let components remain flexible by receiving behavior or UI through children and render functions instead of relying on inheritance-style structures.
mastery: The learner can use children and render-prop/function-as-children composition to customize a reusable component, identify when composition is preferable to inheritance-style structures, and keep the resulting component contract clear.
learningObjectives: Explain composition as a React component design strategy.
Use children to customize a reusable component.
Use render props or function-as-children when a reusable component needs to provide data or behavior to its consumer.
Distinguish composition from inheritance-style component reuse.
Choose an appropriate composition strategy for a given UI requirement.
Keep composed component APIs understandable.
Avoid creating unnecessary wrapper abstractions when ordinary children composition is sufficient.

sections.text: React Reuse Through Composition
Composition is a way to make components reusable by allowing consumers to provide the UI or behavior that should be placed inside a reusable component.
Instead of building a rigid hierarchy and asking one component to know every possible variation, the reusable component owns the structure while the consumer supplies the parts that vary.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Reusable component owns the stable structure. Consumer supplies the variable content or behavior.
The Simplest Form: children

sections.title: Reusable layout
Compose it
sections.code:
React Foundations

Learn the basics of React.

sections.text: Card owns the container structure while the caller controls its contents. This is composition without needing a specialized component for every possible card variation.
Why Not Build a Component for Every Variation?

sections.title: Rigid approach
sections.code:
CourseCard
AdminCourseCard
SearchResultCard
ArchivedCourseCard
FeaturedCourseCard
...

sections.title: Composed approach
sections.code:
Card
+ caller-provided children/content

sections.text: Composition can keep a reusable component focused on the stable structure while callers decide which content belongs inside it.
Composition Can Also Provide Data

Sometimes the reusable component owns data or behavior that the consumer needs in order to decide how to render the UI. A render prop or function-as-children pattern can pass that information to the consumer.

sections.title: Function-as-children
Consumer controls presentation
sections.code:
{({ x, y }) => (

Mouse: {x}, {y}

)}

sections.text: MouseTracker owns the behavior; the consumer owns how that behavior is presented.
Render Props
A render prop is a function passed into a component so the component can call it with data or behavior. Function-as-children is one common form of this pattern.

sections.title: Pattern
sections.code:
Reusable component
→ owns state/behavior
        ↓
render function
        ↓
consumer decides UI

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not default to inheritance-style component hierarchies
sections.text: React's composition model generally favors passing children, elements, or functions into components rather than building rigid inheritance trees for UI reuse.
Composition vs Inheritance

sections.title: Inheritance-style thinking
sections.code:
BaseCard
  ↓
CourseCard
  ↓
FeaturedCourseCard

sections.title: Composition-style thinking
sections.code:
Card
  + Header
  + Body
  + Actions

sections.text: Composition makes variation explicit at the point where a component is used instead of requiring the reusable component to encode every possible subtype.
Named Slots Through Props

sections.title: Compose named areas
Use the layout
sections.code:
<PageLayout
  header={<CourseHeader />}
  sidebar={<LessonNavigation />}
>
  <LessonContent />
</PageLayout>

sections.text: Named content props are another composition technique when a component has several intentional insertion points.
When children Is Enough
Do not create a complicated render-prop API when ordinary children composition already expresses the variation clearly.

sections.title: Prefer simple composition
sections.code:
<Panel>
  <CourseSummary />
</Panel>

sections.title: Avoid unnecessary indirection
sections.code:
<Panel
  renderContent={() => <CourseSummary />}
/>

sections.text: Function-based composition is useful when the component needs to supply changing data or behavior to the consumer. It is unnecessary when the component only needs arbitrary child content.

sections.text: Composition With Behavior

sections.title: Reusable behavior + render function
Consumer chooses presentation
sections.code:
<Toggle>
  {({ on, toggle }) => (
    <button onClick={toggle}>
      {on ? 'On' : 'Off'}
    </button>
  )}
</Toggle>

sections.text: This pattern separates reusable interaction behavior from the visual form in which the behavior is presented.
Composition Can Improve Flexibility
A well-designed composable component can support multiple presentation contexts without needing new subclasses or a growing collection of boolean props.

sections.title: Rigid API
sections.code:
<Card
  compact
  featured
  showActions
  showBadge
  alternateHeader
  dark
/>

sections.title: Composed API
sections.code:
<Card>
  <Badge />
  <Header />
  <Body />
  <Actions />
</Card>

sections.text: Composition can reduce the number of boolean flags a component needs to understand.
But Composition Has a Contract
A reusable composed component should make its expected structure understandable. Consumers should know what children or render functions are expected and what data they receive.

sections.text: Composition and Custom Hooks
Custom hooks and composition solve different reuse problems. A hook extracts reusable stateful logic. Composition lets reusable components receive variable content or behavior.

sections.title: Different tools
sections.code:
Need reusable stateful behavior?
→ custom hook

Need reusable UI structure with variable content?
→ composition

Need both?
→ hook + composed component can work together

sections.text: A Composed Component Can Consume a Hook

sections.title: Combine the patterns

sections.text: The hook owns reusable stateful behavior while the composition API lets consumers decide how the resulting state and actions are presented.
Avoid Composition for Its Own Sake

A component does not need children functions, render props, or named slots simply because composition is considered a best practice. Use the simplest interface that gives consumers the flexibility they actually need.
Drill: Simplify the API

sections.title: Composition API Repair
sections.instructions: Simplify the overly complicated composition API. Use children where arbitrary content is sufficient, and reserve render functions for cases where the reusable component must supply changing data or behavior.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?
The next lesson introduces compound components. It builds on composition by defining a family of related components that share implicit state and operate together under a documented usage contract.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on general composition patterns, children, named content, and render functions. Compound-component contracts are deliberately deferred.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why is composition preferred in React?' A strong answer is: 'Composition lets reusable components own stable structure while consumers supply the parts that vary. It avoids rigid inheritance-style hierarchies and makes variation explicit at the point of use.'
A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use a render prop?' When the reusable component owns state or behavior and the consumer needs that data to decide how to render the UI.
Another follow-up is: 'When is a render prop unnecessary?' When the component only needs arbitrary child content and does not need to provide changing data or behavior to the consumer.
Reflect
Look at a component with many boolean props controlling different visual variations. Could some of those variations be expressed more clearly by letting the caller compose the desired content?

A reusable component should own what is stable and let consumers control what legitimately varies. Start with children, then introduce render functions only when the reusable component needs to provide data or behavior.

sections.label: Complete the Composition Patterns Playground and decision drills. The learner must use composition to make a reusable component flexible, choose between children and render-function patterns appropriately, and avoid inheritance-style UI reuse.
sections.hint: Stable structure stays in the reusable component. Variable content comes from the consumer. Use render functions when the reusable component must provide data or behavior.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Composition lets React components remain reusable without encoding every variation into one component or inheritance tree. Use children for arbitrary content, named element props for intentional insertion points, and render props/function-as-children when a reusable component owns behavior or data that the consumer needs to render. Choose the simplest composition contract that solves the actual reuse problem.

quiz.explanation: Composition lets the reusable component own stable structure and the consumer control legitimate variation.

quiz.question: When is a render prop useful?
options: When the component needs arbitrary static child content only.
When the reusable component owns data or behavior that the consumer needs to render.
When no component state exists.
Whenever a component has more than one child.
quiz.explanation: Render functions are useful when the reusable component needs to provide dynamic data or behavior to the consumer.

quiz.question: When is ordinary children composition preferable to a render prop?
options: When the consumer simply supplies arbitrary content and no dynamic data/behavior needs to be passed.
Never.
Only when the component uses useEffect.
Only for forms.
quiz.explanation: Do not add a function-based composition API when ordinary children already express the needed flexibility.

summary: Composition is React's primary way of making reusable UI flexible without inheritance-style hierarchies. Children and element props work well when consumers simply supply content, while render props or function-as-children are appropriate when a reusable component owns state or behavior that the consumer needs to turn into UI. The composition contract should stay as simple as the reuse problem allows.

title: Compound Components
description: Learn how compound components let a family of related React components share implicit state through a common parent while giving consumers a flexible, readable composition API.
mastery: The learner can build a small compound-component API, share state between related child components through a common parent, and document the contract describing how those components are intended to work together.
learningObjectives: Explain the compound-component pattern.
Recognize when several related components form one conceptual UI unit.
Share implicit state between compound component parts.
Use React context to connect related compound components when appropriate.
Create a readable compound-component API.
Document the required relationship between parent and child components.
Recognize when compound components add useful flexibility versus unnecessary complexity.
Prevent compound child components from silently being used outside their required parent.

sections.text: What Makes Components 'Compound'?
Compound components are a family of related components designed to work together as one conceptual widget.
The parent owns shared state or coordination, while child components consume that shared information and provide different parts of the UI.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: One conceptual component system → one shared state owner → multiple collaborating child components.
A Tabs Example

sections.title: Consumer-facing API
sections.code:
<Tabs>
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab value="overview">
      Overview
    </Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab value="lessons">
      Lessons
    </Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>

  <Tabs.Panel value="overview">
    Course overview
  </Tabs.Panel>

  <Tabs.Panel value="lessons">
    Lesson list
  </Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

sections.text: The API is readable because the related pieces communicate that they belong to the same Tabs system.
Where Does the Shared State Live?

sections.title: Conceptual structure
sections.code:
Tabs
 ↓
activeTab state
 ↓
context
 ├── Tabs.List
 ├── Tabs.Tab
 └── Tabs.Panel

sections.text: The parent establishes the state and context. The compound children consume the state they need.
Implicit State Sharing
The child components do not need every piece of state passed explicitly through several layers of props. Their relationship is established by belonging to the same compound component system.
A Minimal Context

sections.title: Shared context

sections.text: The context carries the state needed by the related pieces of the compound component.
A Compound Child Reads the Context

sections.title: Tabs.Tab

sections.text: The child does not receive activeTab and setActiveTab directly from its immediate parent. The compound system supplies them through its shared context.
The Contract Matters

A compound component creates an implicit relationship between its parts. That relationship must be documented clearly enough that consumers know which pieces belong together and which values are expected.

sections.title: Contract
sections.code:
Tabs
→ owns shared tab state

Tabs.Tab
→ must be inside Tabs
→ provides a tab value

Tabs.Panel
→ must be inside Tabs
→ matches a tab value

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not build compound components without documenting their usage contract
sections.text: The API may look flexible, but the parts depend on shared context and expected relationships. Consumers need to know how the family of components is intended to work together.
Fail Clearly Outside the Parent

sections.title: Guard the contract

sections.text: A clear error is preferable to allowing a compound child to fail later through an undefined context value.
Interactive Practice: Build a Compound Toggle

sections.title: Compound Components Playground
sections.instructions: Build a Toggle compound-component API where the parent owns the on/off state and the child parts consume that shared state. Preserve the consumer-facing composition style.

sections.text: Dot Notation Communicates Membership

sections.title: Compound API
sections.code:
Toggle
Toggle.Button
Toggle.Status

sections.text: The dot notation makes the relationship between the parent and child components explicit. It communicates that these pieces form one API rather than unrelated components.
Compound Components and Composition
Compound components build on the previous lesson's composition ideas. The consumer composes the parts, while the component system coordinates them through shared state.

sections.title: Composition
sections.code: Consumer chooses structure

sections.title: Compound component
sections.code:
Consumer chooses structure
+
related parts share implicit state

sections.text: When the Pattern Is Useful

sections.title: Good candidates
sections.code:
Tabs
Accordion
Menu
Select-like widgets
Disclosure systems
Multi-part form controls

sections.text: The pattern is especially useful when several UI pieces form one coordinated interaction but consumers need flexibility over their exact composition.
When Not to Use It
A single simple component does not need to become a compound component just because context exists. If there is no meaningful family of coordinated parts, the pattern can add unnecessary abstraction.

sections.title: Probably unnecessary
sections.code:
Card
Card.Title
Card.Text

when a simple Card component with children
already solves the problem.

sections.text: State Should Belong to the System
The shared state should represent the coordination contract between the compound parts. Avoid putting unrelated application-wide state into the context simply because it is available there.
Keep Context Narrow

sections.title: Focused context

sections.text: The context should contain the state and actions needed by the compound family rather than becoming a general-purpose application state container.
Drill: Design the Contract

sections.title: Compound Component Contract Drill
sections.instructions: Write the consumer contract for a compound Accordion. Identify which components belong to the family, what shared state exists, and what each part expects.

sections.text: Controlled State Can Still Be a Compound Component Concern

A compound component can expose internal coordination while still offering controlled or uncontrolled usage patterns. The detailed controlled-versus-uncontrolled distinction is intentionally deferred to the next lesson.
Compound Components and Accessibility
The pattern does not automatically make a widget accessible. The compound parts still need correct semantics, names, states, keyboard behavior, and focus management appropriate to the widget.
Testing the Contract

sections.title: Behavior-focused test

sections.text: Tests should verify the behavior the compound API promises rather than tightly coupling to its internal context implementation.
Drill: Repair a Broken Compound API

sections.title: Compound Component Repair
sections.instructions: Repair the compound component so its child parts share the parent's state safely and fail clearly when used outside the provider.

sections.text: Don't Hide the Contract

A compound component's flexibility is useful only if consumers understand the relationship between its parts. Documentation, examples, and clear runtime errors help turn the implicit relationship into an understandable contract.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson compares controlled and uncontrolled component design. It will explain when the parent should own component state versus allowing the component to manage its own internal state.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on compound components and their shared-state contract. Controlled versus uncontrolled state ownership is deliberately deferred to lesson-5-2-4.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a compound component?' A strong answer is: 'It is a family of related components that share implicit state through a common parent, allowing consumers to compose the parts while the parent coordinates their behavior.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why use this pattern instead of one giant component?' It lets consumers control composition while keeping the interaction state coordinated and the API expressive.

Another follow-up is: 'What is the danger?' The parts have an implicit contract. Without clear usage expectations and safe context handling, consumers can misuse child components or create confusing runtime failures.
Reflect

Think of a UI in one of your projects that has several related pieces—perhaps tabs, filters, or an accordion. Would consumers benefit from composing those pieces while they share one coordinated state model?
Compound components work best when the API makes it obvious which components belong together, what they share, and how consumers are expected to compose them.

sections.label: Complete the Compound Components Playground and both drills. The learner must build a working compound component with shared state, preserve a readable composition API, and document or enforce the parent-child usage contract.
sections.hint: One parent owns coordination. Related children consume the shared state. Keep the context narrow and fail clearly when a child is used outside its required parent.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Compound components are coordinated families of components that share implicit state through a common parent. They build on composition by allowing consumers to arrange the parts while the parent manages their shared interaction state. The pattern requires a clear usage contract, a focused context, and safe failure when child components are used outside the parent.

Related components share coordinated state through a common parent while consumers compose the parts.
Components inherit behavior from a base React class.

Because JSX cannot contain children.
Because context is always global.

options: Every piece of application state.

All server data in the application.

summary: Compound components coordinate a family of related React components through shared state owned by a common parent. Composition gives consumers control over structure, while context gives the related parts implicit access to the state they need. The pattern is powerful for coordinated widgets such as tabs and accordions, but it requires a clear usage contract, focused shared state, and safe handling when children are used outside their intended parent.

title: Controlled and Uncontrolled Components
description: Learn the distinction between components whose important state is driven by the parent and components that manage their own internal state, and understand when each approach is appropriate.
mastery: The learner can distinguish controlled and uncontrolled components, explain who owns the authoritative state in each pattern, choose an appropriate pattern for a given scenario, and avoid mixing controlled and uncontrolled modes for the same input.
learningObjectives: Explain what a controlled component is.
Explain what an uncontrolled component is.
Identify who owns the authoritative state in each pattern.
Compare controlled and uncontrolled forms.
Choose controlled or uncontrolled design based on application requirements.
Recognize when a component needs parent-level state visibility.
Recognize when internal state is sufficient.
Avoid switching an input between controlled and uncontrolled modes.
Explain the tradeoff between external control and component-local simplicity.

sections.text: Who Owns the State?
The key distinction between controlled and uncontrolled components is state ownership.

sections.title: Controlled
sections.code:
Parent owns the state
        ↓
passes value + change handler
        ↓
Child renders from that value

sections.title: Uncontrolled
sections.code:
Component/DOM owns the current value
        ↓
Parent does not drive every update

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Controlled = the parent is the source of truth. Uncontrolled = the component or DOM manages its own current state and the parent interacts with it through a less direct contract.
A Controlled Input

sections.title: Parent owns the value

sections.text: The input displays the value held in React state. Every change goes through the parent's state update.
Why Control an Input?

sections.title: Parent can react to every change
sections.code:
Input value changes
        ↓
React state updates
        ↓
Parent can:
→ validate
→ filter results
→ enable/disable actions
→ synchronize another control
→ persist state

sections.text: Controlled inputs are useful when other application behavior needs to respond immediately to the current value.
An Uncontrolled Input

sections.title: DOM owns the current value

sections.text: The parent does not mirror every keystroke into React state. The DOM maintains the current input value until the parent reads it.
When Uncontrolled Can Be Useful

sections.title: Possible fit
sections.code:
Simple form

Value only needed at submit time

No live validation requirement

No other component needs the current value

sections.text: An uncontrolled input can reduce the amount of React state and update logic required when the application does not need to react to every value change.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not switch the same input between controlled and uncontrolled modes
sections.text: An input should have one clear state-ownership model. Mixing modes can create warnings, ambiguous behavior, and an unclear source of truth.
The Classic Mistake

sections.title: Avoid this ambiguous pattern

sections.text: Using controlled and uncontrolled mechanisms for the same value obscures which source should be authoritative.
Controlled Is Not Automatically Better

Controlled components provide precise external control, but they also require state, change handlers, and a clear data flow. For simple forms where the value only matters at submission, that extra control may not provide enough benefit to justify the additional code.
Uncontrolled Is Not Automatically Better
Uncontrolled components can simplify simple interactions, but they are less convenient when the application needs to derive UI from the current value or synchronize that value with other state.
A Comparison

sections.title: Controlled
sections.code:
Source of truth
→ React state

Good when
→ parent needs live control
→ validation/synchronization matters
→ UI derives from current value

Cost
→ more explicit state/update plumbing

sections.title: Uncontrolled
sections.code:
Source of truth
→ DOM/component internals

Good when
→ value is only needed occasionally
→ simple interaction
→ parent does not need every update

Cost
→ less direct live control from the parent

sections.text: Controlled Components Create a Clear Data Flow

sections.title: Controlled flow
sections.code:
User input
 ↓
onChange
 ↓
Parent state
 ↓
value prop
 ↓
Input

sections.text: This explicit loop is valuable when application behavior needs a reliable source of truth.
Uncontrolled Components Reduce Synchronization

sections.title: Uncontrolled flow
sections.code:
User input
 ↓
DOM value
 ↓
Read when needed
 ↓
Submit/process

sections.text: There is less continuous synchronization between the DOM value and React state.
Default Values Belong to Uncontrolled Design

sections.title: Uncontrolled with an initial value
sections.code: <input defaultValue="React" />

sections.text: defaultValue provides an initial value without making React the ongoing source of truth.
Value Belongs to Controlled Design

sections.title: Controlled initial state

sections.text: The important distinction is not merely the syntax. It is who remains responsible for the value after initialization.
Choosing Based on Requirements

sections.title: Ask these questions
sections.code:
Does the parent need every change?

Does another part of the UI depend on the current value?

Does validation happen live?

Does the value need to synchronize with other state?

Or is the value only needed when the user submits?

sections.text: The answers indicate where the source of truth belongs.
Controlled Components and Reusable APIs
Reusable components often expose controlled APIs when consumers need to determine the current state. This lets the component remain presentational while the parent owns state.

sections.title: Reusable controlled component
sections.code:
<Toggle
  on={enabled}
  onChange={setEnabled}
/>

sections.text: The parent owns enabled. The reusable component receives the value and reports changes.
Uncontrolled Reusable APIs

sections.title: Component manages itself
sections.code: <Toggle defaultOn />

sections.text: Here the component owns subsequent state changes internally. The parent supplies an initial preference rather than controlling every update.
Controlled vs Uncontrolled Is an API Decision
For reusable components, controlled versus uncontrolled is not merely an implementation detail. It determines how consumers interact with the component and where state ownership lives.
Why Consistency Matters

sections.title: One clear model
sections.code:
Controlled
→ parent drives value
→ child reports changes

or

Uncontrolled
→ child manages value
→ parent interacts through supported API

sections.text: The key is that ownership should be explicit rather than accidentally changing based on whether a prop happened to be provided.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson is Reusable State Logic. It applies the patterns from hooks, composition, compound components, and controlled/uncontrolled design to separate what data changes from how that data is displayed.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on the conceptual controlled-versus-uncontrolled distinction. It intentionally does not introduce the next lesson's applied state-logic drills.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a controlled component?' A strong answer is: 'A controlled component is driven by state owned by its parent. The parent supplies the current value and receives changes, making the parent the source of truth.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is an uncontrolled component?' It manages its own current state internally, often through the DOM for form inputs, with the parent reading or interacting with the value only when needed.

Another follow-up is: 'When would you prefer uncontrolled?' For a simple interaction where the parent does not need to react to every change, especially when the value is only needed at submission or another discrete event.
Reflect

Look at one reusable input or form component you have built. Who currently owns its value? Does the parent actually need that level of control, or would a simpler uncontrolled API satisfy the component's requirements?

sections.title: Choose the source of truth deliberately

sections.text: The controlled-versus-uncontrolled decision is fundamentally a state-ownership decision. Choose the model that matches who actually needs to control and observe the value.

sections.label: Pass the recall checkpoint by correctly distinguishing controlled and uncontrolled components, choosing an ownership model for representative scenarios, and explaining why mixing the two patterns on one input is problematic.
sections.hint: Controlled = parent owns the value. Uncontrolled = component/DOM owns the current value. Choose based on who needs to observe or control changes.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Controlled components are driven by parent state; uncontrolled components manage their own internal state. Controlled design is useful when the parent needs live visibility, validation, synchronization, or derived UI. Uncontrolled design can be simpler when the value only matters at discrete moments. The important engineering decision is choosing one clear source of truth rather than mixing controlled and uncontrolled modes.

The parent must always store its value.
quiz.explanation: Uncontrolled inputs manage their current value outside the parent's continuously controlled React state.

quiz.question: Why is mixing controlled and uncontrolled patterns on the same input problematic?
options: It creates an unclear source of truth and can lead to React warnings or unpredictable behavior.
It always makes the input faster.
It prevents the input from receiving focus.
It disables all events.
quiz.explanation: The source specifically identifies mixing the patterns as the central misconception.

quiz.question: Which scenario is a strong candidate for controlled state?
options: The parent must disable another control whenever the input is empty.
The value is completely irrelevant until submission.
No other UI depends on the value.
The component is never observed.
quiz.explanation: The parent needs live access to the input value to drive related UI.

summary: Controlled and uncontrolled components differ primarily in state ownership. Controlled components are driven by parent state, making them useful when the application needs live visibility, validation, synchronization, or derived behavior. Uncontrolled components manage their current value internally and can be simpler when the parent only needs the value occasionally. Mixing the two patterns on the same input creates an ambiguous source of truth and should be avoided.
interviewQuestions: What is a controlled component?
What is an uncontrolled component?
Who owns the source of truth in each pattern?
When would you choose controlled state?
When can uncontrolled state be simpler?
Why should you avoid switching between controlled and uncontrolled modes?
How does this choice affect reusable component APIs?
What is the difference between value and defaultValue?

title: Reusable State Logic
description: Apply the React patterns from this module to separate what data changes from how that data is displayed, making stateful behavior reusable across components without coupling it to one component's JSX.
mastery: The learner can separate reusable stateful behavior from presentation, extract or compose that behavior appropriately, and reuse the same state logic across different UI consumers without duplicating the underlying behavior.
learningObjectives: Separate stateful behavior from presentation.
Identify logic that describes what data changes independently of how it is displayed.
Reuse state logic across multiple components or presentations.
Choose an appropriate pattern from custom hooks, composition, or compound components.
Keep state logic independent from one component's JSX structure.
Avoid duplicating the same state transition logic across different UI implementations.
Recognize when a pattern is being over-applied instead of solving a real reuse problem.

sections.text: The Goal: Separate Data Changes From Display
The module has now introduced custom hooks, composition, compound components, and controlled versus uncontrolled state. This practice lesson combines those ideas.
The central rule is simple: reusable state logic should describe what data changes and how that state behaves, without becoming tightly coupled to one component's JSX.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: State logic answers: what changes, when it changes, and what operations are available. Presentation answers: how that state is shown to the user.
Tightly Coupled Logic

sections.title: State logic mixed with one UI

sections.text: The selection behavior is embedded directly into this particular list presentation. If another component needs the same selection model, the state logic may be duplicated.
Separate the Behavior

sections.title: Reusable state logic

sections.text: Now the state machine is independent of the list markup. A list, table, or custom panel can all consume the same behavior.
Different UI, Same Logic

sections.title: Shared behavior
sections.code:
useSelection()
   ↓
 ┌───────────────┬────────────────┐
 ↓               ↓                ↓
List UI       Table UI       Detail UI

sections.text: The state logic does not need to know which of these presentations is rendering it.
Choose the Simplest Pattern

sections.title: Pattern selection
sections.code:
Reusable stateful behavior
→ custom hook

Reusable UI structure + variable content
→ composition

Coordinated family of components sharing implicit state
→ compound components

Parent must own value
→ controlled component

sections.text: These patterns solve different problems. Reusable state logic does not mean every problem should be solved with a custom hook.
The Common Failure

sections.title: Duplicated behavior
sections.code:
List
→ selection state
→ select()
→ clear()

Table
→ selection state
→ select()
→ clear()

Drawer
→ selection state
→ select()
→ clear()

sections.text: When those implementations are intended to represent the same behavior, duplicating them creates multiple places that must remain consistent.
The Opposite Failure

sections.title: Over-generalized state abstraction
sections.code:
useUniversalStateController({
  mode,
  adapters,
  serializers,
  strategies,
  renderers,
  validators,
  middleware
})

sections.text: An abstraction can become so general that consumers must understand a large API for a small problem. Reuse should simplify the system, not replace straightforward local logic with a framework of its own.
Drill 1: Extract Reusable Selection Logic

sections.title: Reusable State Logic Drill
sections.instructions: Extract the selection state and operations from the first UI and make them reusable by both a list and a summary component.

sections.text: Drill 2: Keep the State Logic Presentation-Agnostic

sections.title: State Logic Extraction Drill
sections.instructions: Refactor the provided component so the pagination behavior can be reused by a table and a card grid. The hook should know about page state and navigation, but not about the JSX used to display the results.

sections.text: Drill 3: Choose the Right Abstraction

sections.title: Pattern Selection Drill
sections.instructions: Choose the simplest reusable pattern for each problem. Do not automatically choose a custom hook.
sections.initialCode:
Scenario A
Two components need the same local pagination behavior.
Choice:
_______________________________

Scenario B
A reusable card needs arbitrary caller-provided content.
Choice:
_______________________________

Scenario C
Tabs, Tab, and Panel need to coordinate active-tab state.
Choice:
_______________________________

Scenario D
A reusable input's current value must be owned and validated by its parent.
Choice:
_______________________________

Scenario E
One component has a tiny state machine used nowhere else.
Choice:
_______________________________

sections.text: State Logic Can Be Feature-Local
Reusable state logic does not need to become global application infrastructure. A hook or state module can belong to the feature that owns the behavior.

sections.title: Feature-local reusable logic
sections.code:
features/search/
├── components/
├── hooks/
│   └── useSearchPagination.js
└── ...

Multiple search components
→ share feature logic

Other features
→ do not depend on search internals

sections.text: The API Should Describe the Behavior

sections.title: Good state-logic API

sections.text: The consumer receives state and operations rather than implementation details such as array slicing internals.
What Data Changes vs What UI Displays

sections.title: State logic
sections.code:
page changes
selected item changes
open/closed changes
query changes

sections.title: Presentation
sections.code:
table
cards
buttons
sidebar
modal
list

sections.text: The same state transition model can sometimes power multiple presentations.
Do Not Abstract Only Because Two Components Look Similar
Two UIs can look similar while representing different state semantics. Confirm that the state transitions and ownership are actually the same before extracting them into shared logic.
Keep the Contract Small

sections.title: Consumer should know
sections.code:
state it needs
+ operations it can perform

Consumer should not need to know
→ internal reducers
→ storage details
→ implementation-specific helpers

sections.text: Testing Reusable State Logic
The behavior should be tested through meaningful state transitions and the user-visible consumers that depend on them. The goal is to protect the contract, not freeze the internal implementation.
A Refactoring Checklist

sections.title: Before extracting
sections.code:
□ Is the behavior genuinely reused?
□ Is the state model actually the same?
□ Is there a clear owner?

After extracting
□ Is the API smaller than the implementation?
□ Are consumers independent of presentation details?
□ Is the behavior still correct?
□ Did abstraction reduce duplication or coupling?

sections.text: Module Capstone Preview

The next lesson is the Advanced Pattern Workshop. It combines the module's patterns—custom hooks, composition, and compound components—into a realistic UI challenge. The goal is not to use every pattern, but to select the simplest appropriate combination.

The most advanced pattern is not automatically the best pattern. A strong solution may use one custom hook and ordinary composition rather than forcing a compound-component architecture into a problem that does not require it.

sections.label: Complete all three escalating Playground drills correctly without hints. The learner must separate reusable state logic from JSX, select the simplest appropriate React pattern, and avoid over-coupling state to one presentation.
sections.hint: What data changes? What operations act on it? What part is merely presentation? Extract only the reusable behavior.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Reusable state logic separates the behavior of changing data from the UI that displays it. Custom hooks are often the simplest tool for this, while composition and compound components solve different coordination problems. Keep state abstractions feature-local when appropriate, expose a small behavior-focused API, and avoid extracting logic merely because two components look similar.

exercises.title: Reusable State Logic Drill
exercises.brief: Extract selection behavior so multiple UI consumers share the same state logic without duplicating the state machine.

exercises.title: State Logic Extraction Drill
exercises.brief: Separate pagination state and calculations from a table presentation so another UI can reuse them.

exercises.title: Pattern Selection Drill
exercises.brief: Choose between custom hooks, composition, compound components, controlled state, or local logic based on the actual reuse requirement.

quiz.question: What is the central goal of reusable state logic?
options: Make every component use the same JSX.
Separate what data changes and how it behaves from how that data is displayed.
Move all application state into global context.
Create the most abstract hook possible.
quiz.explanation: The lesson focuses on separating state behavior from presentation.

quiz.question: What should reusable state logic generally know about?
options: The exact JSX structure of every consumer.
The state and operations required by the behavior.
Only CSS classes.
Every route in the application.
quiz.explanation: Reusable state logic should be presentation-agnostic.

quiz.question: What is a sign that a state abstraction may be over-generalized?
options: Consumers get a small behavior-focused API.
The abstraction requires many configuration options for unrelated cases.
The same behavior is reused by multiple components.
Presentation remains independent.
quiz.explanation: A large speculative API can create more complexity than the reuse problem requires.

summary: Reusable state logic separates the state machine from its presentation. The strongest abstraction describes what changes and which operations are supported while remaining independent of one component's JSX. Custom hooks are often the simplest mechanism, but compound components, composition, and controlled APIs each solve different problems. The goal is not maximum abstraction; it is reusable behavior with a clear, small contract.

How do you separate state behavior from presentation?
When is a custom hook the right abstraction?
How do composition and compound components differ from reusable hooks?
Can reusable state logic remain feature-local?

How do you decide whether two similar state machines should be shared?
What should a reusable state-logic API expose?

title: Capstone: Pattern Workshop
description: Combine custom hooks, composition, compound components, and controlled/uncontrolled design into one reusable component you'd be comfortable publishing for other engineers to use.
mastery: Learning
learningObjectives: Design a component's public API before implementing it, deciding what's controlled vs. internal.
Combine a custom hook, composition, and compound-component structure in a single real component.
Extract reusable state logic so the same behavior could power more than one UI.
Evaluate a component API for ergonomics the way a reviewer or downstream consumer would.

sections.text: The Brief: Build a Reusable Combobox

You're building a searchable Combobox (a text input with a filtered dropdown of options) intended to be reused across a whole product — not a one-off. That constraint changes the design: you have to think about its public API the way a library author would, not just get one screen working.
Step 1 — Design the API Before Writing Implementation

Decide up front: should selection be controlled (value/onChange from the parent) or uncontrolled (internal state, with an optional defaultValue)? Following module-5-2's Controlled and Uncontrolled Components lesson, support both — controlled when value is provided, uncontrolled otherwise — so the component fits both a form library integration and a quick standalone use.

sections.title: The target public API

sections.text: Step 2 — Extract the Shared Logic into a Custom Hook

Filtering options by query text, tracking the highlighted option, and handling open/close state are all logic, not markup — extract them into a useCombobox hook, matching the pattern from Custom Hooks and Reusable State Logic earlier in this module. This keeps the logic testable in isolation and reusable if you ever need a different visual implementation.
Step 3 — Structure It as Compound Components

Rather than one monolithic Combobox with a dozen props for every visual detail, expose it as compound components — Combobox.Input, Combobox.Options, Combobox.Option — so consumers control layout and styling while the shared context handles the actual behavior, following the Compound Components lesson's pattern.
Reviewing Your Own API

Before calling it done, review the public surface the way a reviewer would: is there any prop whose purpose isn't obvious from its name? Does the controlled/uncontrolled behavior actually match how the rest of your form components behave, for consistency? Would a new engineer on the team be able to use this correctly without reading the implementation?

sections.label: Mastery evidence: the learner has built a Combobox component that supports both controlled and uncontrolled usage, extracts its filtering/selection logic into a custom hook separate from its markup, exposes a compound-component API rather than one prop-heavy component, and can explain each API design decision the way they would in a design review.

exercises.title: Build and Ship the Combobox
exercises.brief: Implement the full Combobox: a useCombobox hook handling filtering/open state/highlighted index, and Combobox.Input/Combobox.Options/Combobox.Option compound components consuming it via context. Support both controlled and uncontrolled value. Write a short README documenting the public API as if for other engineers on your team.

quiz.question: Why design a reusable component's public API before writing its implementation?
options: Because the API is what other engineers depend on and have to live with — implementation details are easy to change later, the public surface is not.
It's required by React.
It makes the component render faster.
It avoids needing TypeScript.
quiz.explanation: A component's public API is a much harder thing to change once other code depends on it, so it's worth deliberately designing before implementation details are locked in.

quiz.question: Why extract the Combobox's filtering and selection logic into a custom hook separate from its markup?
options: Hooks are always faster than inline logic.
It keeps the logic testable and reusable independent of any specific visual implementation.
It's required for compound components to work.
It reduces the component's bundle size automatically.
quiz.explanation: Separating stateful logic from rendering means the same behavior could power a different visual design later, and the logic can be unit-tested without rendering any UI.

quiz.question: What does supporting both controlled and uncontrolled usage in Combobox achieve?
options: It doubles the component's file size for no benefit.
It's only relevant for class components.
It fits both form-library integrations (which need controlled state) and quick standalone usage (uncontrolled), without forcing every consumer into one pattern.
It removes the need for a custom hook.
quiz.explanation: Supporting both patterns lets the same component serve different real integration needs without forcing consumers to manage state they don't want to.

summary: The Pattern Workshop capstone combines everything from this module — custom hooks for shared logic, composition and compound components for a flexible public API, and controlled/uncontrolled support for different consumption styles — into one component designed the way a real, reusable library component would be: API first, implementation second, reviewed for ergonomics before calling it done.
