Walk through how you'd design the public API for a reusable component before implementing it.
Why might a compound-component API be preferable to one component with many configuration props?

title: Reading Stack Traces
description: Learn to read a stack trace as a call path leading to an error and use it to locate the likely origin of a bug instead of stopping at the line where the error becomes visible.
mastery: The learner can reproduce a seeded error, read the stack trace from the relevant frames toward the originating call, isolate the root cause, fix the bug, and explain the difference between the visible symptom and the actual source.
learningObjectives: Explain what a stack trace represents.
Identify the useful information contained in stack-trace frames.
Read a stack trace bottom-up when that reveals the originating call.
Distinguish the location where an error becomes visible from where it originated.
Use a stack trace as part of a structured debugging process.
Reproduce and isolate a seeded stack-trace bug.
Fix the root cause rather than only changing the line that throws.

sections.text: A Stack Trace Is a Call Path
When an error is thrown, the stack trace shows the chain of function calls that led to the point where the error was observed.
The most visible frame is not necessarily the true origin of the problem. A useful debugging habit is to inspect the call path rather than simply reading the first line and editing the nearest code.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Error appears here → inspect the call path → trace toward the originating application code → identify the bad assumption or input → fix the source.
A Simple Example

sections.title: Example stack trace
sections.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
    at renderLesson (LessonCard.jsx:18)
    at LessonCard (LessonCard.jsx:42)
    at CourseList (CourseList.jsx:27)
    at CoursePage (CoursePage.jsx:15)

sections.text: The error becomes visible inside renderLesson, but the path shows that CoursePage led to CourseList, which rendered LessonCard, which eventually called renderLesson.
Read the Frames

sections.title: A frame commonly tells you
sections.code:
function name
file
line number
column number
call order

sections.text: The exact formatting varies by browser and runtime, but these details help you move from the error message to the relevant source code.
Why Bottom-Up Can Help

The source specifically emphasizes reading stack traces bottom-up when that reveals the true origin. In application code, lower frames can show how the problematic call was initiated, while the first visible frame may only be where the failure finally surfaced.

sections.title: Trace the path
sections.code:
CoursePage
   ↓
CourseList
   ↓
LessonCard
   ↓
renderLesson
   ↓
ERROR

sections.text: Do not mechanically assume that the bottom frame is always wrong or that every trace must be read in exactly one direction. The practical goal is to use the call path to find the earliest relevant application-level cause.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not read only the top line
sections.text: The first line tells you what failed, but not necessarily why it failed. The stack frames provide the path needed to investigate the originating cause.
Symptom vs Cause

sections.title: Symptom
sections.code: renderLesson throws because lesson.title is undefined.

sections.title: Possible cause
sections.code: CoursePage passed a malformed lesson object.

sections.text: Changing renderLesson to hide the error might suppress the symptom while leaving the invalid data path intact.
Debugging Workflow

sections.title: Use the stack trace inside a process
sections.code:
1. Reproduce the error.
2. Read the error message.
3. Inspect the relevant stack frames.
4. Trace into application code.
5. Check the assumptions at the originating call.
6. Fix the root cause.
7. Reproduce again.

sections.text: Interactive Debug Lab

sections.title: Stack Trace Debug Lab
sections.instructions: Reproduce the seeded error, inspect the stack trace, identify the originating application call, fix the underlying bug, and record the root cause in your own words.

sections.text: Do Not Patch the Error Blindly

sections.title: Weak fix

sections.text: Optional chaining may prevent the exception, but it can also hide invalid data. Whether it is a correct fix depends on the application's intended contract.

sections.title: Investigate the contract
sections.code:
Should lessons ever be undefined?

If no:
→ fix the source producing undefined.

If yes:
→ define the intended empty/loading/error behavior.

sections.text: Application Frames vs Library Frames
Modern stack traces can contain framework and library frames in addition to your own application frames. Focus first on the frames that lead into code you control.

sections.title: Useful path
sections.code:
browser/runtime
 ↓
React internals
 ↓
Your component
 ↓
Your helper
 ↓
invalid assumption

sections.text: The runtime and framework frames are context; the application frames usually contain the most actionable clues.
Line Numbers Are Starting Points
A line number tells you where execution failed, not automatically where the design problem originated. Inspect the surrounding code and the values flowing into it.
Root-Cause Explanation

sections.title: Strong explanation
sections.code:
Symptom:
formatLesson threw because lesson was undefined.

Root cause:
CoursePage constructed a lessons array containing an
undefined item, which CourseList passed to LessonCard.

Fix:
Correct the data source so CourseList receives valid lesson
objects according to its expected contract.

sections.text: What Counts as Passing?

sections.title: Debug Lab evidence
sections.code:
□ Error reproduced.
□ Stack trace inspected.
□ Relevant application frames identified.
□ Root cause traced.
□ Bug fixed.
□ Same scenario retested.
□ Root cause explained in own words.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?

The next lesson moves from reading the call path to a broader debugging skill: finding the real source of a bug when the visible failure occurs far away from where the incorrect state or data was introduced.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses specifically on using stack traces to understand call paths. The next lesson expands the symptom-versus-cause investigation beyond the trace itself.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you read a stack trace?' A strong answer is: 'I start with the error message, then inspect the stack frames to reconstruct the call path. I focus on the application frames and trace back toward the earliest relevant source of the bad value or assumption rather than fixing only the line where the exception surfaced.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why can the top frame be misleading?' Because it may identify where the invalid value was finally used, while an earlier caller introduced the invalid state or data.

Another follow-up is: 'What should you do after identifying the likely source?' Verify the hypothesis, fix the underlying cause, reproduce the original scenario, and confirm the symptom is gone without masking the real contract.
Reflect
Think of a recent runtime error you encountered. Did you change the line that threw first, or did you trace how its input became invalid? What did the call path tell you?
A stack trace is not just an error message. It is a map of how execution arrived at the failure. Use that map to find the cause rather than stopping at the symptom.

sections.label: Pass the Debug Lab by reproducing the seeded error, using the stack trace to trace the call path to the originating application problem, fixing the bug, and explaining the root cause in your own words.
sections.hint: Read the path, identify the relevant application frames, trace the bad input or assumption backward, then fix and retest.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A stack trace shows the call path leading to an error. The visible failure is not necessarily the root cause, so inspect the relevant application frames and trace backward toward the originating bad value or assumption. Reproduce, investigate, fix the underlying cause, retest, and explain what actually happened.

exercises.title: Stack Trace Debug Lab
exercises.brief: Reproduce and fix a seeded runtime error by tracing the stack toward its originating application-level cause.

quiz.question: What does a stack trace primarily show?
options: The call path leading to an error.
The application's CSS hierarchy.
The complete database schema.
Only the first line of the exception.
quiz.explanation: A stack trace provides the sequence of calls associated with the error.

quiz.question: Why can reading only the first line of a stack trace be insufficient?
options: It describes the symptom but may not identify where the bad value or assumption originated.
The first line is always invalid.
Stack traces do not contain source locations.
The first line only exists in production.
quiz.explanation: The trace frames provide the call path needed to investigate the true source.

quiz.question: What should you do after locating the line where the exception appears?
options: Immediately suppress the exception.
Trace the relevant call path and investigate the inputs and assumptions that led there.
Delete the function.
Ignore all earlier frames.
quiz.explanation: The lesson emphasizes finding the originating cause rather than patching the visible symptom.

summary: A stack trace is a call path leading to an error. Reading it effectively means using the frames to move beyond the visible symptom and toward the originating application-level cause. Focus on relevant application frames, inspect the values and assumptions flowing through them, fix the root cause, retest the original scenario, and explain the cause rather than merely naming the error message.
interviewQuestions: What is a stack trace?
How do you read a stack trace?
Why can the top line of a stack trace be misleading?
Which frames should you focus on first?
How do you distinguish a symptom from the root cause?
What should you do after identifying the likely source?
Why is blindly suppressing an exception often a weak fix?
How would you explain a stack-trace diagnosis to another engineer?

title: Finding the Real Source of a Bug
description: Learn to separate the visible symptom of a bug from the place where the incorrect state, data, or assumption actually originated, then trace and fix the root cause.
mastery: The learner can reproduce a bug, trace the symptom backward through the relevant data and control flow, identify the originating cause, fix that cause, and explain why patching the visible failure would have been insufficient.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a bug's symptom from its cause.
Trace incorrect data or state backward to its origin.
Use targeted logging, breakpoints, and call-path inspection to investigate a bug.
Form and verify a root-cause hypothesis.
Avoid fixing only the location where the bug becomes visible.
Reproduce the original scenario after fixing the cause.
Explain the root cause independently.

sections.text: Where You See the Bug Is Not Necessarily Where It Started
The previous lesson used stack traces to follow a call path. This lesson extends that idea to bugs whose symptoms may appear far away from the code that introduced the bad state or data.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Visible symptom → trace the value/state backward → find where the invalid condition was introduced → fix that source → verify the symptom disappears.
A Classic Example

sections.title: Visible symptom
sections.code:
Profile page crashes:
Cannot read properties of undefined

sections.title: Possible path
sections.code:
ProfilePage
 ↓
ProfileCard
 ↓
user.name
 ↓
user is undefined
 ↓
API adapter returned the wrong shape

sections.text: ProfileCard is where the problem becomes visible. It is not necessarily the place where the bug began.
Trace the Value

sections.title: A useful debugging question
sections.code:
Where did this value come from?

Where was it transformed?

Where was it validated?

Where could it have become invalid?

sections.text: Following the value backward often reveals the root cause more quickly than staring at the line that throws.
Trace State the Same Way

sections.title: State path
sections.code:
Rendered UI is wrong
 ↓
state value is wrong
 ↓
setter received unexpected input
 ↓
handler created that input
 ↓
upstream event/data was wrong

sections.text: The UI is often the last stage of a longer data or state flow.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not fix the symptom at the point where you notice it
sections.text: Adding guards, defaults, or visual workarounds can hide the visible failure while leaving the invalid state or data source unchanged.
Symptom vs Root Cause

sections.title: Symptom
sections.code: The button is disabled unexpectedly.

sections.title: Root cause
sections.code:
The validation state was set to 'invalid'
from a stale response belonging to a previous request.

sections.text: The button is behaving according to the state it received. The investigation must continue backward until the incorrect state transition is found.
Use a Hypothesis

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Hypothesis:
The button is disabled because validationState is stale.

Evidence needed:
Where is validationState changed?
Which request produced the value?
Does the state update belong to the current input?

sections.text: A hypothesis keeps debugging focused. It should be verified with evidence rather than treated as fact.
Debugging With Breakpoints

sections.title: Investigate the transition
sections.code:
1. Pause where the symptom occurs.
2. Inspect the invalid value.
3. Find where that value was assigned.
4. Move the breakpoint upstream.
5. Repeat until the invalid value is first introduced.

sections.text: Targeted Logging

sections.title: Log transitions, not everything

sections.text: Targeted diagnostic information is usually more useful than filling the console with unrelated values.
Debug Lab

sections.title: Finding the Real Source Debug Lab
sections.instructions: Reproduce the seeded UI bug, identify the incorrect value at the point of failure, then trace that value backward until you find where it was introduced incorrectly. Fix the source and retest the original scenario.

sections.text: The Value's Journey

sections.title: Trace it
sections.code:
API-like response
 ↓
normalizeUser()
 ↓
setUser()
 ↓
ProfilePage render
 ↓
ProfileCard
 ↓
user.name

sections.text: Inspect each boundary until you find the first place where the value stops matching the expected contract.
Contract Violations
Many bugs become easier to diagnose when you identify the contract that was violated: an expected object shape, state invariant, input range, or ordering assumption.

sections.title: Example contract

sections.text: The investigation then asks which boundary produced the incorrect shape.
Do Not Add a Default Automatically

sections.title: Potential symptom patch
sections.code: {user.name ?? 'Unknown user'}

sections.text: That may be the correct product behavior in some applications, but it should not be used automatically to hide a violated data contract.
Find the Earliest Wrong Value

sections.title: Strong heuristic
sections.code:
Correct
 ↓
Correct
 ↓
WRONG  ← investigate here
 ↓
Wrong
 ↓
Wrong

sections.text: The first point at which the value becomes incorrect is often much closer to the root cause than the place where the failure finally appears.
Not Every Upstream Difference Is the Cause
Trace far enough to explain the bug, but do not assume the earliest unusual value is automatically responsible. Verify the causal connection.
Root-Cause Explanation

sections.title: Strong explanation
sections.code:
Symptom:
ProfileCard displayed no user name.

Root cause:
The response uses full_name, but normalizeUser()
reads fullName. The mapping created an invalid user
shape before the component rendered.

Fix:
Correct the normalization mapping to match the response
contract.

sections.text: What Counts as Passing?

sections.title: Debug Lab evidence
sections.code:
□ Symptom reproduced.
□ Invalid value identified.
□ Value traced upstream.
□ First incorrect transition identified.
□ Root cause fixed.
□ Original scenario retested.
□ Root cause explained separately from symptom.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?

The next lesson focuses on async debugging, where tracing the source of an incorrect value becomes harder because timing, race conditions, unhandled rejections, and stale closures can change which result reaches the UI.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on general symptom-versus-cause tracing. Async timing problems are deliberately deferred to the next lesson.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you find the real source of a bug?' A strong answer is: 'I reproduce the symptom, inspect the incorrect state or data at the failure point, then trace that value backward through the relevant transformations and state updates until I find the first place where it becomes invalid. I verify the hypothesis before fixing it.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why isn't adding a guard always the right fix?' Because a guard can hide a violated contract. First determine whether the unexpected value is actually valid according to the application's requirements.

Another follow-up is: 'What is a useful debugging heuristic?' Find the earliest point where the value or state becomes wrong, then verify that transition is causally responsible for the visible symptom.
Reflect
Recall a bug where the visible error appeared inside a UI component. What upstream data, state transition, or transformation actually created the invalid condition?

sections.title: Trace the value, not just the line

sections.text: When a value is wrong, follow its journey backward. The first place where it becomes wrong is often far more useful than the place where the UI finally complains.

sections.label: Pass the Debug Lab by reproducing the seeded bug, tracing the incorrect value/state back to its originating cause, fixing that cause, and explaining why a symptom-level patch would be insufficient.
sections.hint: Inspect the bad value where it fails, then trace it backward through transformations and state updates until you find the first incorrect transition.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The visible symptom of a bug is often only the final link in a longer chain. Find the real source by tracing incorrect data or state backward, identifying the first point where the contract becomes invalid, verifying that hypothesis, and fixing the originating cause. Avoid masking the problem with symptom-level patches unless that behavior is actually part of the product contract.

exercises.title: Finding the Real Source Debug Lab
exercises.brief: Trace an invalid UI value backward through the application's data flow and fix the originating mapping or state problem.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a symptom and a root cause?
options: The symptom is where the problem becomes visible; the root cause is where the invalid condition was introduced.
They are always the same location.
The root cause is always the last stack-frame line.
The symptom is always more important than the cause.
quiz.explanation: Debugging requires separating where a problem appears from where it originated.

quiz.question: What is a useful debugging heuristic for an incorrect value?
options: Find the earliest point where the value becomes incorrect and verify that transition.
Change the component that displays it.
Add a default value immediately.
Ignore upstream transformations.
quiz.explanation: The earliest incorrect transition is often closer to the root cause.

quiz.question: Why can a defensive fallback be a poor first response?
options: It can hide a violated data or state contract instead of fixing its source.
Fallbacks never work in React.
Fallbacks always make performance worse.
Fallbacks remove stack traces.
quiz.explanation: A fallback is appropriate only when the unexpected condition is actually part of the intended product behavior.

summary: Finding the real source of a bug means separating where the symptom appears from where the invalid condition began. Trace the relevant data or state backward through transformations and updates, find the first incorrect transition, verify the causal hypothesis, and fix the source. Symptom-level guards may be appropriate when the product contract allows the condition, but they should not automatically replace root-cause investigation.

How would you trace an invalid value backward through an application?
What is the earliest incorrect transition?
Why can adding a guard be a poor debugging fix?
How do breakpoints help with root-cause analysis?
What makes a good root-cause hypothesis?
How do you verify that the identified cause is actually causal?
How would you explain your debugging process to another engineer?

title: Debugging Async Problems
description: Diagnose asynchronous bugs involving race conditions, unhandled rejections, and stale closures across await boundaries by reproducing the failure, tracing the timing and data flow, and fixing the underlying sequencing or state issue.
mastery: The learner can reproduce an asynchronous bug, determine whether the failure comes from ordering, error handling, or stale state, implement a deterministic fix, and explain why arbitrary timing delays are not a reliable solution.
learningObjectives: Recognize common asynchronous bug categories.
Diagnose race conditions caused by out-of-order completion.
Identify unhandled promise rejections.
Recognize stale closures across asynchronous boundaries.
Trace asynchronous control flow through promises and async/await.
Use request identity or cancellation strategies when appropriate.
Handle asynchronous failures explicitly.
Avoid arbitrary delays as a substitute for correct sequencing or synchronization.
Verify that the original asynchronous failure is fixed rather than merely hidden.

sections.text: Async Bugs Are Often Timing Bugs
Asynchronous code introduces another dimension to debugging: order. Two operations that begin in one order do not necessarily finish in that same order.
That means a result can be logically valid on its own while still being wrong for the current application state because it arrived too late.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Start order ≠ completion order. Debug asynchronous bugs by tracing when each operation starts, when it finishes, what state it observes, and whether its result is still relevant.
The Classic Race Condition

sections.title: Two searches
sections.code:
User types: react
→ request A starts

User types: react hooks
→ request B starts

B finishes first
→ UI shows React Hooks

A finishes later
→ UI shows older React results

sections.text: Both requests may succeed. The bug is that the older result is allowed to overwrite the newer state.
Start Time vs Completion Time

sections.title: Timeline
sections.code:
t0  Request A starts
 t1 Request B starts
 t2 Request B finishes
 t3 Request A finishes

sections.text: The application needs a rule for which result is authoritative. Without that rule, the final state depends on timing.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not add arbitrary delays to fix a race condition
sections.text: Adding setTimeout or an arbitrary wait changes timing but does not establish which result is valid. A correct fix should explicitly control sequencing, cancellation, or result ownership.
Request Identity

sections.title: One useful strategy
sections.code:
Request A → id 1
Request B → id 2

A finishes:
id 1 !== latest id 2
→ ignore A

B finishes:
id 2 === latest id 2
→ apply B

sections.text: The important idea is not the exact implementation. It is that each result must be checked against the current operation before it changes the UI.
Another Strategy: Cancellation

sections.title: Conceptual flow
sections.code:
Start A
 ↓
Start B
 ↓
Cancel A
 ↓
Only B remains relevant

sections.text: Cancellation can prevent unnecessary work and make stale results less likely to affect application state, but the correct mechanism depends on the API and architecture.
Unhandled Promise Rejections

sections.title: Failure without handling

sections.text: If loadProfile rejects and nobody handles that rejection, the failure can surface later as an unhandled promise rejection rather than at the point where the operation was initiated.
Handle the Failure Deliberately

sections.title: Explicit handling

sections.text: Whether you catch and rethrow, convert the failure into state, or handle it at a higher boundary depends on the application's error contract. The important part is that the rejection has an intentional owner.
Stale Closures Across await

sections.title: Potential stale state

sections.text: An asynchronous function closes over the values from the render in which it was created. After an await boundary, the surrounding application may have changed, but the function's captured values do not magically update.
Ask What Value the Async Function Captured

sections.title: Debugging question
sections.code:
What did this function know when it started?

What changed while it was waiting?

Which value should determine the result after await?

sections.text: This is especially important in React because rendering creates function closures over the state and props of that render.
Debug Lab

sections.title: Async Race Debug Lab
sections.instructions: Reproduce the seeded search bug. Make the application deterministic so an older asynchronous result cannot overwrite a newer search. Do not solve the problem with an arbitrary timeout. Then explain the race condition.

sections.text: Trace Async Operations

sections.title: Useful debug log

sections.text: Logging operation identity, inputs, start time, completion, and whether the result was accepted can make timing bugs much easier to reason about.
Race Conditions Are About Ownership

sections.title: Wrong rule
sections.code: Last result to finish wins.

sections.title: Better rule
sections.code: Latest relevant operation wins.

sections.text: The application needs a semantic rule for which asynchronous result should control the current state.
Async Effects in React

A common pattern is triggering asynchronous work in an Effect when a dependency changes. That creates the same race-condition considerations: multiple effects may start over time while older work remains in flight.

sections.title: Illustrative pattern

sections.text: This is one way to prevent a stale asynchronous result from updating state after the effect that initiated it is no longer current. The exact strategy should match the application's data-fetching architecture.
Unhandled Rejections Need an Owner

sections.title: Decide where failure belongs
sections.code:
Request
 ↓
Who owns failure?
 ├── component state
 ├── feature-level error boundary
 ├── data layer
 └── higher application boundary

sections.text: The answer depends on whether the failure is local to one interaction or should affect a wider application boundary.
Async Debugging Checklist

sections.title: Before fixing
sections.code:
□ What operations are running concurrently?
□ In what order did they start?
□ In what order did they finish?
□ Which operation's result is currently authoritative?
□ Can an older result still update state?
□ Who handles rejection?
□ What state/props were captured across await?

sections.text: Do Not Assume Await Means 'Nothing Else Can Happen'

await pauses the current async function until its awaited operation settles. It does not freeze the rest of the application, prevent other requests, or guarantee that the surrounding state remains unchanged.
Root-Cause Explanation

sections.title: Strong explanation
sections.code:
Symptom:
Search results sometimes show the previous query.

Root cause:
Each keystroke starts a new request, but results are applied
whenever each request finishes. A slower older request can
therefore overwrite the newer result.

Fix:
Associate the response with the latest relevant request and
ignore stale results.

Why not setTimeout?
A delay changes timing but does not establish result ownership.

sections.text: What Counts as Passing?

sections.title: Debug Lab evidence
sections.code:
□ Race condition reproduced.
□ Start/finish ordering understood.
□ Async result ownership identified.
□ Stale result prevented.
□ No arbitrary timing patch used.
□ Rejection behavior considered where relevant.
□ Original scenario retested.
□ Root cause explained in own words.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?
The next lesson focuses on state bugs, especially stale closures, unexpected mutation, and state updates whose timing or identity causes the UI to behave differently from what the developer expects.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on asynchronous timing, promise failure, and stale values across async boundaries. State-update bugs are handled separately next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you debug a race condition?' A strong answer is: 'I would reproduce the ordering, log or inspect when each operation starts and finishes, determine which result is authoritative, and prevent stale results from updating current state through cancellation, request identity, or another explicit sequencing strategy.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why doesn't setTimeout reliably fix a race condition?' Because it changes timing but does not guarantee which asynchronous operation finishes first or define which result is valid.

Another follow-up is: 'What happens to state across an await?' The async function retains the values it closed over from the relevant render or invocation; meanwhile, the application can continue changing.
Reflect
Think of an async feature you have built. What happens if the user triggers the operation twice before the first one finishes? Which result should win, and where is that rule enforced?
When asynchronous operations can overlap, do not rely on luck or timing. Define which result is current, how stale work is handled, and who owns failures.

sections.label: Pass the Async Race Debug Lab by reproducing the seeded race condition, fixing result ownership/sequencing without arbitrary delays, and explaining the asynchronous root cause.
sections.hint: Compare operation start and completion order. The latest relevant operation—not simply the last one to finish—should determine current state.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Async bugs often come from race conditions, unhandled rejections, or stale values crossing await boundaries. Debug them by making operation timing visible, identifying which result is authoritative, handling failures intentionally, and preventing stale work from overwriting current state. Arbitrary delays do not establish correctness; explicit ownership and sequencing do.

exercises.title: Async Race Debug Lab
exercises.brief: Reproduce and fix an out-of-order asynchronous search result without using arbitrary timing delays.

quiz.question: What makes an asynchronous race condition possible?
options: Operations can complete in a different order from the order in which they started.
Promises always execute synchronously.
await freezes the whole application.
Only one request can ever be active.
quiz.explanation: Concurrent asynchronous operations can finish out of order.

quiz.question: Why is adding an arbitrary setTimeout delay a poor race-condition fix?
options: It changes timing but does not establish which result is authoritative.
Timers cannot run in browsers.
It automatically cancels all promises.
It guarantees the oldest request wins.
quiz.explanation: A delay does not provide deterministic result ownership.

quiz.question: What should an async result check before updating current UI state?
options: Whether the result still belongs to the latest relevant operation.
Whether it was the first request started.
Whether at least 500ms passed.
Whether the user has stopped typing forever.
quiz.explanation: Current state should only be updated by results that are still relevant.

summary: Asynchronous bugs often arise because operations overlap in time. Race conditions occur when requests finish out of order, unhandled rejections occur when failures have no intentional owner, and stale closures occur when async functions retain values from an earlier invocation or render. Debug these problems by tracing start and completion order, defining result ownership, handling failures explicitly, and avoiding timing-based patches.

How do you diagnose out-of-order async results?
Why is setTimeout not a reliable race-condition fix?
How can request identity prevent stale results?
When might cancellation be useful?
What is an unhandled promise rejection?
How can stale closures affect async code?
How do you decide which asynchronous result is authoritative?

title: Debugging State Problems
description: Diagnose React state bugs caused by stale closures, unexpected mutation, and incorrect assumptions about when state updates become visible.
mastery: The learner can reproduce a state-related bug, determine whether the cause is stale state, mutation, or update timing, apply the correct state-update pattern, and explain why the original implementation behaved incorrectly.
learningObjectives: Recognize common React state bug patterns.
Diagnose stale closures involving state values.
Identify mutation that prevents the expected state transition or UI update.
Explain why a state setter does not immediately change the current render's state variable.
Use functional state updates when the next state depends on previous state.
Trace state changes to determine where an incorrect value was introduced.
Avoid relying on immediate state mutation assumptions.
Verify a state bug fix by reproducing the original interaction.

sections.text: State Bugs Often Start With a Wrong Mental Model
React state bugs frequently come from assumptions about when state changes, what value a callback has captured, or whether an object or array was actually changed immutably.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A state setter schedules the next state. The current render keeps its existing state values. Debug the transition and the data used to calculate the next state instead of assuming the setter mutates the current variable immediately.
The Classic 'It Didn't Update' Bug

sections.title: Reading state immediately after setting it

sections.text: The log prints the value from the current render. Calling setCount does not mutate the count variable that this particular invocation of handleClick closed over.
State Belongs to a Render Snapshot

sections.title: Conceptual timeline
sections.code:
Render A
count = 0
   ↓
click handler from Render A
   ↓
setCount(1)
   ↓
Render A still sees count = 0
   ↓
React renders again
   ↓
Render B sees count = 1

sections.text: This is why debugging state often requires asking which render created the callback that is currently running.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not assume a state setter applies immediately
sections.text: Calling a state setter does not update the current render's state variable in place. Code that immediately reads the old variable is still observing the current render's value.
When the Next State Depends on the Previous State

sections.title: Use the functional updater
sections.code: setCount((current) => current + 1);

sections.text: The functional form explicitly calculates the next value from the previous state supplied by React.
Why Multiple Updates Can Surprise You

sections.title: Same snapshot, repeated update

sections.text: All three expressions read the same count value from the current render. When the updates depend on the previous state, the functional form avoids that stale calculation.

sections.title: Functional updates

sections.text: Each updater receives the most recent pending state for the update sequence.
Stale Closures

sections.title: A callback captures a render's state

sections.text: The timeout callback captures count from the render in which handleSave was created. Updating state later does not rewrite that closure.
Debug the Captured Value

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
Which render created this callback?

What was the state value at that time?

What changed while the callback was waiting?

Should this callback use the captured value or current state?

sections.text: Unexpected Mutation

sections.title: Mutating an object

sections.text: The object is mutated in place. The state value's identity remains the same, which violates the intended immutable update model and can prevent React from treating the update as a meaningful state change.
Create a New Value

sections.title: Immutable update

sections.text: The new object represents the next state without mutating the previous state value.
Arrays Have the Same Problem

sections.title: Avoid in-place mutation
sections.code:
items.push(newItem);
setItems(items);

sections.title: Create a new array

sections.text: Debugging state bugs means checking not only what value changed, but whether the state value was changed in the way React expects.
Debug Lab

sections.title: State Debug Lab
sections.instructions: Reproduce the seeded state bug, determine whether stale state or mutation is responsible, fix the underlying state transition, and retest the original interaction.

sections.text: Trace the State Transition

sections.title: State investigation
sections.code:
Current state
 ↓
Which event fired?
 ↓
Which state value did the handler read?
 ↓
How was the next value calculated?
 ↓
Was the previous state mutated?
 ↓
What value should the next render receive?

sections.text: This sequence turns a vague statement such as 'React didn't update' into a specific investigation of the state transition.
Don't Blame Batching Automatically
Multiple updates being processed together is not itself the bug. The important question is whether each update expresses the intended relationship to the previous state.

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
Does this update depend on previous state?

If yes:
→ can the functional updater express it safely?

Is an object or array being mutated?

Which render created the callback?

sections.text: State Bugs in Effects
Effects can also expose stale state when a callback captures values from an earlier render or when dependencies do not reflect the values the effect actually uses.

sections.title: Debug the captured value

sections.text: The callback captures the value available when the effect was created. The dependency and effect design must match the desired behavior rather than assuming the closure will see future state automatically.
State Invariants
A useful debugging technique is to state what must always be true about the state, then identify which update broke that invariant.

sections.title: Example invariant
sections.code:
Selected item must either be null
or correspond to an item in the current list.

sections.text: When debugging, inspect which state transition allowed the invariant to become false.
Root-Cause Explanation

sections.title: Example
sections.code:
Symptom:
Clicking 'Add 3 points' increased the score by only 1.

Root cause:
All three updates calculated from the same score value
captured by the current render.

Fix:
Use functional state updates so each increment is based
on the previous pending state.

sections.text: Second Root Cause

sections.title: Mutation example
sections.code:
Symptom:
Updating a player's score does not reliably produce
the expected state transition.

Root cause:
The existing players array/object was mutated in place
and then passed back as the same state reference.

Fix:
Create new array/object values during the update.

sections.text: What Counts as Passing?

sections.title: Debug Lab evidence
sections.code:
□ Original state bug reproduced.
□ Cause classified correctly.
□ State update fixed.
□ Mutation removed where relevant.
□ Original scenario retested.
□ No unrelated workaround added.
□ Root cause explained in own words.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?
The next lesson turns to performance debugging. Instead of diagnosing incorrect state, you will diagnose excessive work using profiling evidence and determine what is actually slow before optimizing.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on state correctness and state-update reasoning. Performance profiling and bottleneck diagnosis are handled next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why doesn't a state setter immediately change the state variable?' A strong answer is: 'The current render is a snapshot. Calling the setter schedules a new state value; the current callback still sees the state value from the render that created it.'
A likely follow-up is: 'When should you use the functional updater?' When the next state depends on the previous state, especially when multiple updates may be queued from the same render.

Another follow-up is: 'Why is mutating state a problem?' It changes an existing state object or array in place instead of producing a new state value, which can break React's expected update semantics and make changes difficult to reason about.
Reflect
Think of a state bug you have encountered. Was the mistake about timing, stale state, mutation, or misunderstanding which render produced a callback? What would you inspect first today?

When state behaves unexpectedly, do not ask only 'Why didn't React update?' Ask which render supplied the value, how the next state was calculated, whether anything was mutated, and what state the next render should receive.

sections.label: Pass the State Debug Lab by reproducing the seeded state bugs, correctly identifying stale-snapshot and mutation causes, fixing both transitions, and explaining the underlying causes.
sections.hint: A state setter does not change the current render's variable. When next state depends on previous state, use a functional updater; never mutate the existing object or array in place.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

React state is tied to render snapshots, so a setter does not mutate the current render's state variable immediately. Bugs often result from stale closures, calculating multiple updates from the same snapshot, or mutating objects and arrays in place. Debug by tracing the state transition, identifying the render and values involved, fixing the update model, and reproducing the original interaction.

exercises.title: State Debug Lab
exercises.brief: Diagnose and repair seeded bugs involving stale state snapshots and in-place state mutation.

quiz.question: What does a state setter do to the current render's state variable?
options: It mutates the variable immediately.
It schedules the next state; the current render still observes its existing snapshot.
It clears the variable.
It changes every closure immediately.
quiz.explanation: The current render retains its state snapshot until React produces a new render.

quiz.question: When should you prefer a functional state update?
options: When the next state depends on the previous state.
Only when rendering text.
Only when using refs.
Never.
quiz.explanation: The functional updater receives the previous state and is appropriate for derived next-state calculations.

quiz.question: What is wrong with mutating a state object and passing the same object back?
options: It changes state through a new immutable value.
It mutates the existing state reference instead of producing a new state value.
It always creates two renders.
It automatically resets all state.
quiz.explanation: State should be updated through new values rather than mutating the existing object or array.

summary: React state should be understood through render snapshots. A state setter schedules a new value but does not mutate the current render's variable, so callbacks can observe stale values. When next state depends on previous state, functional updates provide the correct calculation model. State objects and arrays should also be updated immutably rather than mutated in place.

What is a render snapshot?

Why should state objects and arrays not be mutated in place?
