title: Planning the Architecture
description: Translate the feature backlog into a high-level frontend architecture by defining data flow, component boundaries, routing, and responsibility before implementation begins.
mastery: The learner can produce a practical frontend architecture plan that maps the feature backlog to data flow, component boundaries, routing, and ownership, while identifying decisions that should be made before implementation to reduce rework.
learningObjectives: Translate a feature backlog into an architectural structure.
Define high-level data flow between the relevant parts of the application.
Identify component boundaries based on responsibility and cohesion.
Plan routing for the required user flows.
Decide where important state and data ownership should live.
Identify major dependencies between architectural decisions.
Document enough architecture to guide implementation without over-designing the system.
Identify risky architectural decisions before coding begins.

sections.text: Plan the Shape Before You Build
The feature backlog tells you what should be built and in what sequence. Architecture planning decides how the application will support those features.

The goal is not to produce a perfect architecture diagram or predict every future requirement. It is to make the important structural decisions visible before implementation creates expensive constraints.

sections.title: The project rule
sections.text: Do not start implementation while major data-flow, component-boundary, or routing decisions are still unresolved. Discovering those structural problems halfway through the build creates avoidable rework.
Start From the Features

sections.title: Saved Lessons backlog
sections.code:
View saved lessons
Search saved lessons
Filter by category
Open a lesson
Remove a lesson

sections.text: Architecture should emerge from these product behaviors rather than being designed independently of them.
Map the User Flow

sections.title: Example flow
sections.code:
Saved Lessons page
        ↓
Load saved lessons
        ↓
Display list
   ↙           ↘
Search        Filter
   ↓             ↓
Filtered results
        ↓
Open lesson
        ↓
Lesson detail

sections.text: The flow helps reveal which parts need data, which parts own interaction state, and where navigation occurs.
Plan Data Flow

sections.title: High-level data flow
sections.code:
Lessons API
 ↓
Data/loading/error state
 ↓
Saved Lessons feature
 ├── search/filter state
 ├── lesson collection
 └── selected/navigation data
 ↓
UI components

sections.text: The architecture should make it understandable where data enters the feature, where it is transformed, who owns state, and which components consume it.
Component Boundaries

sections.title: Possible structure
sections.code:
SavedLessonsPage
├── SavedLessonsToolbar
│   ├── SearchInput
│   └── CategoryFilter
├── SavedLessonList
│   └── SavedLessonCard
└── SavedLessonEmptyState

sections.text: The exact component tree is not the architecture by itself. The important question is why responsibilities are separated where they are.
Boundary by Responsibility

sections.title: Useful responsibility boundaries
sections.code:
Page/container
→ feature coordination

Toolbar
→ search/filter controls

List
→ collection presentation

Card
→ one lesson's presentation and actions

Data layer
→ communication with the API

sections.text: A component boundary should reduce meaningful coupling or clarify responsibility. Splitting a component simply because it has many lines is not automatically useful.
State Ownership

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
Who needs the current search query?

Who needs the selected category?

Who needs the lesson collection?

Does another route need the selected lesson?

Does the state need to survive navigation?

sections.text: State should live at the lowest useful owner, while shared state should move upward only when multiple consumers genuinely need it.
Routing

sections.title: Example route plan
sections.code:
/saved-lessons

/saved-lessons/:lessonId

sections.text: Routing decisions should reflect actual product flows. Decide which experiences are separate routes and which are local UI state.
Do Not Route Everything
A search query, open menu, or temporary filter does not automatically need its own route. Route boundaries should correspond to meaningful navigable product states.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not discover major architecture problems halfway through the build
sections.text: Starting implementation before deciding high-level data flow, boundaries, and routing can force expensive rewrites when those decisions turn out to conflict with the feature requirements.
Architecture Does Not Mean Over-Engineering
Planning architecture is not an invitation to build a framework for hypothetical future requirements. Decide the structure required by the known feature backlog and leave speculative complexity out.

sections.title: Avoid
sections.code:
Global state system
for a feature used by one page

Generic repository layer
for one API endpoint

Five abstraction layers
before the first feature works

sections.text: Architecture Planning Exercise

sections.title: Saved Lessons Architecture Plan
sections.instructions: Using the backlog from the previous lesson, create a high-level architecture plan. Define the primary route(s), data flow, state ownership, component responsibilities, API boundary, and the first implementation slice. Do not write production code.

sections.text: Architecture Decisions Should Trace Back to Requirements

sections.title: Traceability
sections.code:
Requirement
 ↓
Feature
 ↓
Architectural decision
 ↓
Implementation
 ↓
Verification

sections.text: If you cannot explain which requirement motivated an architectural decision, reconsider whether that decision belongs in the initial design.
Identify High-Risk Decisions Early

sections.title: Possible risks
sections.code:
Unclear API response shape

Large data set

Complex navigation requirements

Cross-feature state ownership

Accessibility-sensitive interaction

Performance-sensitive rendering

sections.text: Risk does not always mean a problem. It means an area where an incorrect assumption could create expensive rework.
Decide What Must Be Known Before Coding

sections.title: Must resolve
sections.code:
Where data comes from

Who owns shared state

Which routes exist

Major component responsibilities

Critical API assumptions

sections.title: Can usually evolve later
sections.code:
Exact component filenames

Internal helper naming

Small CSS organization details

Minor implementation utilities

sections.text: The architecture plan should resolve structural questions without pretending every implementation detail needs to be finalized upfront.
A Good Architecture Plan Is Changeable

Architecture planning reduces uncertainty; it does not eliminate the need to learn during implementation. When new evidence invalidates an assumption, update the architecture deliberately rather than preserving a bad design for consistency's sake.
Review the Plan Against the Backlog

sections.title: Final check
sections.code:
Does every feature have a place?

Is every shared state owner clear?

Are routes sufficient for required flows?

Can the first vertical slice be implemented without major unknowns?

Are high-risk assumptions visible?

sections.text: What Will Come Next?
The next lesson begins implementation. You will build the interface incrementally from static structure to interactive components, keeping progress visible and testable at each stage.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson plans the high-level architecture. The next lesson uses that plan to build the interface incrementally rather than attempting the fully connected application in one pass.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you plan a frontend architecture for a new product?' A strong answer is: 'I start from the feature backlog and map the user flows, data sources, state ownership, component responsibilities, and routes. I resolve the high-risk structural decisions first, but avoid over-designing details that can evolve during implementation.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you decide where a component boundary belongs?' Look for a cohesive responsibility, meaningful reuse or separation, and a boundary that reduces coupling rather than creating wrappers without a clear purpose.
Reflect
Take the feature backlog you just created and sketch the smallest architecture that could support it. Which decision would be most expensive to change after implementation begins?
Architecture planning is most valuable where a wrong assumption would force substantial rework. Resolve those decisions early and leave low-cost details flexible.

sections.label: Submit the architecture plan as a project artifact. It must map the backlog to data flow, state ownership, component boundaries, routing, API boundaries, and identified risks well enough to begin incremental implementation.
sections.hint: Plan from the backlog. Resolve high-risk structural decisions first, but do not over-design filenames, helpers, or other details that can evolve safely.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Architecture planning translates the feature backlog into a practical application structure. Define the major data flow, state ownership, component responsibilities, routes, and API boundaries before implementation creates constraints. The objective is not perfect prediction; it is reducing expensive uncertainty while keeping the design simple enough to evolve.

exercises.title: Saved Lessons Architecture Plan
exercises.brief: Translate the feature backlog into a high-level architecture covering data flow, state ownership, component boundaries, routing, API boundaries, and risks.

quiz.question: What should architecture planning begin with?
options: The feature backlog and required user flows.
File naming conventions.
A global state library.
The deepest implementation details.
quiz.explanation: Architecture should support the features and flows already identified.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of deciding state ownership during architecture planning?
options: To make it clear where shared state lives and which components are responsible for it.
To ensure every value becomes global state.
To eliminate component props.
To avoid using local state.
quiz.explanation: Clear state ownership prevents unnecessary coupling and later structural rework.

quiz.question: What should architecture planning avoid?
options: Resolving high-risk structural decisions.
Over-designing hypothetical future requirements before the current feature needs them.
Mapping data flow.
Identifying routes.
quiz.explanation: The lesson emphasizes resolving important structure without creating speculative complexity.

summary: Planning the architecture means translating the feature backlog into a practical structure for data flow, state ownership, component responsibilities, routing, and API boundaries. Resolve high-risk structural decisions before implementation, but keep low-cost details flexible and avoid designing for hypothetical requirements. The architecture should make incremental implementation straightforward and trace directly back to the product backlog.
interviewQuestions: How do you plan frontend architecture for a new product?
How do you decide where state should live?
How do you choose component boundaries?
How do you decide which states deserve routes?
How do you identify high-risk architecture decisions?
How do you avoid over-engineering an initial architecture?
How should architecture relate to the feature backlog?
What architectural decisions are expensive to change later?

title: Building the Interface
description: Build the project interface incrementally, moving from static structure to interactive components while keeping each stage visible, testable, and aligned with the architecture and feature backlog.
mastery: The learner can implement the project interface incrementally from the planned architecture, establish the static structure first, add interaction in coherent slices, and demonstrate working progress without attempting the entire data-connected experience in one pass.
learningObjectives: Translate the architecture plan into an initial interface structure.
Build static page and component structure before wiring complex behavior.
Implement interface pieces according to the feature backlog.
Add interaction incrementally after the underlying structure is stable.
Keep each implementation slice observable and testable.
Use the planned component boundaries without creating unnecessary abstractions.
Compare implementation progress against the original requirements.
Avoid building the entire interactive application in one pass.

sections.text: Build in Layers
The previous lessons established what the product needs, how the work is divided, and how the application should be structured. This lesson turns that plan into the first working interface.
The goal is not to finish every feature immediately. The goal is to create a stable interface foundation and then extend it in small, visible, testable steps.

sections.title: The project rule
sections.text: Do not try to build the fully interactive, data-connected application in one pass. Establish the structure first, then add behavior incrementally.
The Implementation Progression

sections.title: Build sequence
sections.code:
Static structure
 ↓
Component composition
 ↓
Basic interaction
 ↓
Stateful behavior
 ↓
Data integration
 ↓
Edge cases and polish

sections.text: This sequence is not an absolute rule for every project, but it is a useful way to avoid creating too many unknowns at the same time.
Start With the Page Structure

sections.title: Initial interface skeleton

sections.text: At this stage, the goal is to establish the page's major regions and component relationships rather than implementing every interaction.
Then Add Real Components

sections.title: Component structure

sections.text: The component boundaries should follow the architecture plan, but they can evolve when implementation reveals a better boundary.
Build the First Vertical Slice

sections.title: First slice
sections.code:
Saved Lessons route
 ↓
Page shell
 ↓
Static lesson list
 ↓
Lesson card
 ↓
Open lesson action
 ↓
Verify user flow

sections.text: A vertical slice proves that the product can support one meaningful user path from the interface down to the required interaction.
Static Data Is Useful Early

sections.title: Temporary development data

sections.text: Using representative local data can let you validate layout and interaction before adding network behavior. The temporary source should be clearly separated so it can be replaced without rewriting the UI.
Do Not Fake the Architecture
Temporary data is useful for interface construction, but it should still match the expected domain shape closely enough that the eventual integration does not require a complete rewrite.
Add Interaction One Piece at a Time

sections.title: Example sequence
sections.code:
Step 1
Render lessons.

Step 2
Select a lesson.

Step 3
Open the selected lesson.

Step 4
Add remove behavior.

Step 5
Add search.

Step 6
Add category filtering.

sections.text: After each meaningful step, verify the feature still behaves correctly before introducing the next layer.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not build everything at once
sections.text: Combining layout, state, API integration, routing, loading states, search, filtering, and persistence in one pass makes failures difficult to isolate and hides progress until very late.
Build From Known to Unknown

sections.title: Implementation strategy
sections.code:
Known layout
 ↓
Known data shape
 ↓
Known interaction
 ↓
Unknown integration
 ↓
Validate
 ↓
Continue

sections.text: This reduces the number of simultaneous variables when something does not work.
Interface Build Workshop

sections.title: Saved Lessons Interface Build
sections.instructions: Build the Saved Lessons interface from the architecture plan. Work incrementally: first establish the static page structure, then render representative lesson data, then add selection/open behavior, and only after that prepare the interface for later data integration.

sections.text: Verify Each Slice

sections.title: After each slice
sections.code:
Does the feature render?

Does the intended interaction work?

Are important states still visible?

Did the new change break an earlier path?

Can the next developer step start from a stable point?

sections.text: The purpose of incremental work is not simply smaller commits. It is maintaining a sequence of states where the application remains understandable and testable.
Keep the First Version Simple

The first implementation does not need every refinement. Establish the core user path, then improve it as the backlog calls for search, filtering, error handling, accessibility, performance, and other requirements.
Do Not Hide Missing Requirements
A placeholder is acceptable during an intentional intermediate step. It is not acceptable when it hides work that the current feature slice is supposed to deliver.
Use the Backlog as the Control Surface

sections.title: Before each slice
sections.code:
Feature
 ↓
Acceptance criteria
 ↓
Implementation
 ↓
Verification
 ↓
Mark progress

sections.text: The backlog prevents implementation from drifting into unrelated improvements while the planned feature work remains unfinished.
When to Refactor

If implementation reveals a repeated responsibility, an awkward boundary, or unnecessary coupling, refactor at the smallest useful point rather than allowing a known structural problem to spread across the remaining slices.
Architecture Can Evolve

The architecture plan is a guide, not a prison. New implementation evidence may justify changing a component boundary or moving state. Make that change deliberately and update the plan so the project remains coherent.
What Counts as Progress?

sections.title: Strong progress
sections.code:
A working route
+
A visible interface
+
A complete narrow user interaction
+
Verified behavior
+
A clear next slice

sections.text: Avoid Big-Bang Integration

sections.title: Big bang
sections.code:
UI + state + API + routing + search + filtering
+ loading + errors + persistence
→ integrate everything
→ discover failures

sections.title: Incremental
sections.code:
UI shell
→ verify
→ representative data
→ verify
→ one interaction
→ verify
→ next feature

sections.text: The incremental sequence gives you multiple opportunities to catch wrong assumptions before they become expensive.
Project Checkpoint

sections.title: Evidence
sections.code:
□ Page structure implemented.
□ Planned component boundaries represented.
□ Representative data renders correctly.
□ First vertical slice works end-to-end.
□ Progress verified before the next slice.
□ No attempt was made to finish all integrations in one pass.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?

The next lesson connects the interface to real data and interactions. The stable UI built here becomes the foundation for wiring state, API calls, and user actions without simultaneously discovering the page structure.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson establishes the interface and first working slices. Real data integration and broader interaction wiring are handled in the next lesson.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you start building a new frontend project?' A strong answer is: 'I would establish the planned page and component structure first, get a narrow vertical slice working with representative data, verify it, and then add interactions and real data incrementally. That keeps the system testable and makes integration failures easier to isolate.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why not wire the API immediately?' You can, when the first slice requires it, but delaying unrelated complexity can make structural problems easier to diagnose. The important principle is to keep each implementation step observable and controlled.
Reflect

Think of a project you built where everything was wired at once. Which failure would have been easier to diagnose if the interface, data, and interactions had been introduced in separate verified slices?
A professional build should always have a clear answer to: 'What works right now, and what is the next smallest verified step?'

sections.label: Submit the current project build for rubric review. The interface must follow the planned architecture, include the first working vertical slice, and demonstrate incremental, testable progress rather than a single large integration attempt.
sections.hint: Build the shell, render representative data, complete one narrow interaction, verify it, then continue. Do not wire everything at once.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Building the interface is an incremental process. Establish static structure, create meaningful component boundaries, use representative data to validate the UI, then add interactions one slice at a time. Each slice should produce visible, testable progress and leave the project in a stable state for the next feature.

exercises.title: Saved Lessons Interface Build
exercises.brief: Implement the project interface incrementally from the architecture plan, establishing the page structure, rendering representative data, and completing the first working interaction.

quiz.question: What is the recommended progression for the project interface?
options: Static structure → component composition → basic interaction → state/data integration → polish.
API integration → all state → all components → first render.
Build every feature simultaneously.
Optimize before the first interface exists.
quiz.explanation: The lesson emphasizes incremental construction from known structure toward more complex behavior.

quiz.question: Why is representative local data useful during early interface development?
options: It lets you validate structure and interaction without introducing every integration dependency at once.
It removes the need for the real API permanently.
It guarantees the final data shape is correct.
It eliminates the need for testing.
quiz.explanation: Temporary representative data reduces simultaneous unknowns during early implementation.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of incremental implementation?
options: To keep progress visible and testable and make failures easier to isolate.
To maximize the number of commits.
To avoid ever integrating data.
To prevent architectural changes.
quiz.explanation: Incremental work creates stable checkpoints and reduces big-bang integration risk.

summary: The interface should be built incrementally from the architecture plan: establish static structure, create meaningful component boundaries, use representative data, implement a narrow vertical slice, and verify each step before adding more complexity. The goal is visible, testable progress rather than a single fully integrated build that hides failures until the end.
interviewQuestions: How do you start implementing a new frontend project?
Why build a static structure before wiring everything?
What is a vertical slice?
Why can representative local data be useful during early development?
How do you keep implementation progress testable?
When would you refactor a component boundary during a build?
Why is big-bang integration risky?
How do you decide what to build next?

title: Connecting Data and Interactions
description: Wire the project interface to real state, APIs, and user actions while preserving the component boundaries established during planning and keeping the UI independent from one specific data-source shape.
mastery: The learner can connect the implemented interface to real data and interactions, handle the relevant loading, success, empty, and error states, and keep the UI separated from the raw data-source contract through an appropriate boundary.
learningObjectives: Connect the existing interface to a real data source.
Wire user interactions to application state and data operations.
Preserve the architecture and component boundaries established earlier.
Normalize or adapt external data before it reaches presentation components when appropriate.
Handle loading, success, empty, and error states.
Keep API-specific details out of unrelated presentation components.
Verify complete user flows after integration.
Avoid coupling the UI directly to one external data source's response shape.

sections.text: Now Connect the Real System
The previous lesson established a stable interface and first vertical slice using representative data. This lesson replaces the temporary data path with the real state, API, and interaction flow.

The important constraint is that integration should not erase the architecture established earlier. The UI should not suddenly become responsible for understanding every detail of the external data source.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: External data → integration boundary → application-shaped data/state → presentation components.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not couple UI components directly to one data source's shape
sections.text: When presentation components know every field name and quirk of an external API, changing the API can force changes throughout the UI. Keep external contracts at a boundary.
External Shape vs Application Shape

sections.title: External response
Application shape

sections.text: An adapter or normalization step can translate the external contract into the shape the rest of the application expects.
Create a Data Boundary

sections.title: Normalize external data

sections.text: The exact transformation belongs at the integration boundary rather than being repeated inside every component that displays a lesson.
Keep the UI Focused

sections.title: Presentation consumes application data

sections.text: The card does not need to know whether the lesson came from an API, local storage, a mock, or another feature.
Connect the Data Flow

sections.title: Integration path
sections.code:
API
 ↓
fetch/data layer
 ↓
normalization
 ↓
feature state
 ↓
components
 ↓
user interaction
 ↓
state/data operation

sections.text: This makes the direction of data and actions explicit and gives each layer a clear responsibility.
Loading Is Part of the Feature

sections.title: Initial state
sections.code:
loading
 ↓
request
 ↓
 ┌───────────────┬───────────────┐
 ↓               ↓               ↓
success         empty           error

sections.text: A real data integration introduces states that did not exist with local placeholder data. They should be represented explicitly rather than treated as afterthoughts.
The Four Core Data States

sections.title: State model
sections.code:
Loading
→ request is in progress

Success with data
→ results available

Success with no data
→ empty state

Error
→ request failed

sections.text: These are product states, not merely implementation details. The interface needs a deliberate response to each.
Handle User Actions Through the Same Boundary

sections.title: Remove flow
sections.code:
User clicks Remove
 ↓
UI action handler
 ↓
feature operation
 ↓
API/data operation
 ↓
state update
 ↓
UI reflects new collection

sections.text: The component should not need to understand transport details to request that a lesson be removed.
Optimistic vs Confirmed Updates

sections.title: Confirmed update
sections.code:
Click Remove
 ↓
Request
 ↓
Success
 ↓
Update visible list

sections.title: Optimistic update
sections.code:
Click Remove
 ↓
Update visible list immediately
 ↓
Request
 ↓
Success → keep change
Error → recover

sections.text: The appropriate strategy depends on the product behavior, failure cost, and ability to recover. Do not introduce optimistic updates merely because they appear faster.
Integration Workshop

sections.title: Saved Lessons Data Integration
sections.instructions: Replace the previous lesson's representative data with the provided API-like data layer. Keep presentation components dependent on the application lesson shape rather than the external response. Add loading, success, empty, and error states, then wire the remove interaction through the integration boundary.

sections.text: Do Not Let API Errors Leak Everywhere
External data may contain naming conventions, nesting, optional fields, or transport-specific details that are useful at the data boundary but unnecessary for the rest of the feature.

sections.title: Boundary principle
sections.code:
External contract
→ adapt once
→ stable feature contract
→ reuse across UI

sections.text: API Failure Is Not the Only Failure

sections.title: Think through
sections.code:
Network failure

Malformed response

Empty response

Partial data

Duplicate action

Slow response

Remove failure

sections.text: The exact handling depends on the product specification. The important practice is to decide what each supported failure means for the feature rather than letting arbitrary exceptions define the UX.
Keep User Actions Predictable

sections.title: Remove action
sections.code:
idle
 ↓
submitting
 ↓
 ┌─────────────┬─────────────┐
 ↓             ↓
success       error
 ↓             ↓
updated UI    recoverable UI state

sections.text: Even when the implementation is simple, thinking in states helps prevent duplicate actions and inconsistent UI.
Keep Server State and UI State Distinct

sections.title: Example distinction
sections.code:
Server data
→ saved lessons collection

UI state
→ search query
→ selected filter
→ active interaction
→ local submission status

sections.text: Not every value returned by the server belongs in the same state model as transient UI interaction state.
Verify End-to-End Flows

sections.title: Minimum verification
sections.code:
Page opens
→ loading state appears
→ data appears

No data
→ empty state appears

Request fails
→ error state appears

Remove item
→ operation succeeds
→ item disappears

sections.text: Integration is complete only when the user flow works, not merely when the API request returns successfully.
Watch for Data Shape Drift

A useful integration boundary protects the rest of the application if the external response changes. Keep the mapping logic localized enough that an API contract adjustment does not require editing every presentation component.
Do Not Hide Integration Logic in Presentational Components

sections.title: Avoid

sections.text: The card now knows about the external contract. That coupling spreads integration concerns into the UI.
Prefer an Application Contract

sections.title: Prefer

sections.text: The presentation component now depends on the feature's stable model rather than the transport's field names.
What Will Come Next?

The next lesson is Testing and Debugging. After real data and interactions are connected, the project needs systematic testing of expected behavior, edge cases, failure states, and defects before it can be considered production-ready.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson wires real data and interactions into the feature. The next lesson evaluates the integrated build through testing and debugging rather than adding another major feature.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you prevent an API response shape from leaking into your entire frontend?' A strong answer is: 'I keep the external contract at a data or integration boundary and normalize it into the application's domain shape. Presentation components consume that stable shape instead of reading transport-specific field names directly.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you handle loading and errors?' Treat them as explicit feature states. The UI should intentionally represent loading, successful data, empty results, and failure rather than relying on accidental behavior.
Reflect
Look at an API response from a project you have built. Which fields are transport-specific, and where would you place the transformation that turns them into the shape the UI actually needs?

sections.title: Protect the UI from the outside world

sections.text: Integration is a boundary. Keep external contracts, failure behavior, and transport details contained so the rest of the application can work with a stable model.

sections.label: Submit the integrated project build for rubric review. The implementation must connect real data and user actions, handle required data states, and preserve a boundary between the external data contract and presentation components.
sections.hint: Normalize external data at the boundary, keep UI components working with application-shaped data, and verify loading, success, empty, error, and mutation flows.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Connecting data and interactions means integrating real APIs and state without collapsing the application's boundaries. Keep external data contracts at an integration layer, normalize them into a stable application shape, represent loading/success/empty/error states intentionally, and route user actions through clear data operations. Verify complete user flows rather than treating a successful network request as proof that the feature works.

exercises.title: Saved Lessons Data Integration
exercises.brief: Replace representative data with a real integration boundary, normalize the response shape, handle data states, and wire the remove interaction.

quiz.question: Why should external API data usually be adapted at a boundary?
options: To keep transport-specific details from coupling every presentation component to one external contract.
To make API calls faster.
To eliminate the need for state.
To prevent all errors.
quiz.explanation: A boundary creates a stable application-facing shape and limits coupling to the external contract.

quiz.question: Which states should a typical data-driven feature intentionally consider?
options: Loading, success with data, success with no data, and error.
Only success.
Only loading and success.
Only the network error.
quiz.explanation: The product UI needs intentional behavior for the main outcomes of a data request.

quiz.question: What is a sign that the UI is too tightly coupled to the API?
options: Presentation components directly read transport-specific field names such as lesson_title.
The API has a dedicated integration boundary.
The UI consumes normalized domain objects.
Data mapping happens once.
quiz.explanation: Transport-specific field names leaking into presentation create unnecessary coupling.

summary: Real data integration should preserve the project's architecture rather than bypass it. Keep external contracts at a clear boundary, normalize data into an application shape, represent loading/success/empty/error states, and connect user actions through explicit feature operations. The UI should remain focused on presentation and interaction rather than transport-specific details.
interviewQuestions: How do you prevent API response shapes from leaking into the UI?
Where should external data normalization happen?
How do you model loading, success, empty, and error states?
How do you connect user actions to server operations?
What is the difference between server state and UI state?
When would you use optimistic updates?
How do you handle API contract changes?
How do you verify a data-driven feature end to end?

title: Testing and Debugging
description: Test the integrated project feature against expected behavior, edge cases, and failure states, then use the resulting evidence to identify and fix defects before the feature is considered complete.
mastery: The learner can systematically test the completed feature against its acceptance criteria and meaningful edge cases, diagnose failures, fix the underlying defects, and demonstrate that the original feature remains correct after the fixes.
learningObjectives: Turn acceptance criteria into concrete test cases.
Test the primary user flow and important edge cases.
Verify loading, success, empty, and error states where relevant.
Reproduce defects before attempting to fix them.
Use evidence to isolate the cause of a failure.
Fix defects without introducing unrelated changes.
Retest the original failure after making a fix.
Perform regression checks on nearby behavior.
Recognize when a feature is not actually complete despite appearing to work on the happy path.

sections.text: Working Once Is Not the Same as Finished
The project is now connected to real data and interactions. The next step is to prove that the feature behaves correctly beyond the single successful path used during implementation.
Testing is not a final formality. It is how you discover whether the implementation actually satisfies the requirements under the conditions users will encounter.

sections.title: The project rule
sections.text: Do not consider the feature done after the first successful run. Test the acceptance criteria, important edge cases, failure states, and the surrounding behavior that could regress.
Start From the Requirements

sections.title: Requirement → test
sections.code:
Requirement:
Users can search saved lessons.

Test:
Enter a known title and verify matching lessons appear.

Requirement:
No matches show an empty state.

Test:
Enter a value with no matches and verify the empty state.

sections.text: The specification and acceptance criteria provide the first test cases. You should not have to invent the entire testing strategy from scratch after implementation.
Test the Happy Path First

sections.title: Primary flow
sections.code:
Open Saved Lessons
 ↓
Data loads
 ↓
Lessons appear
 ↓
Search works
 ↓
Open a lesson
 ↓
Remove a lesson
 ↓
UI reflects the result

sections.text: The happy path verifies that the core feature works as designed before you move into less common conditions.
Then Test the Boundaries

sections.title: Edge cases
sections.code:
No saved lessons

No search matches

Very long search input

Rapid repeated actions

Slow response

Request failure

Remove the final item

Unexpected or incomplete data

sections.text: Edge cases are not random torture tests. Choose cases that follow naturally from the requirements, data model, and likely failure modes of the feature.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not stop at the first successful run
sections.text: A feature can work perfectly for the happy path while still failing for empty data, network errors, repeated actions, boundary values, or alternate navigation flows.
Test States, Not Just Actions

sections.title: Data-driven feature
sections.code:
Loading
 ↓
Success with data

Loading
 ↓
Success with no data

Loading
 ↓
Error

sections.text: Each state is part of the product behavior and needs a corresponding verification path.
Reproduce Before You Fix

sections.title: Defect workflow
sections.code:
Observed failure
 ↓
Reproduce
 ↓
Isolate
 ↓
Hypothesis
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Reproduce again

sections.text: This keeps the debugging process grounded in evidence and provides a clear way to verify that the change actually solved the problem.
Build a Test Matrix

sections.title: Saved Lessons example
sections.code:
Scenario                     Expected result
-------------------------------------------------
Normal data                  List appears
Empty collection             Empty state
Search match                 Matching items
No search match              No-results state
API failure                  Error state
Slow API                     Loading state
Remove item                  Item disappears
Remove final item            Empty state
Open lesson                  Correct lesson route

sections.text: A small test matrix makes coverage visible and helps prevent forgetting important paths.
Debug the First Failure

sections.title: Investigation questions
sections.code:
What exactly failed?

Can I reproduce it consistently?

What value or state was unexpected?

Where did that value come from?

What contract was violated?

What is the smallest fix?

sections.text: Use the debugging methods from Module 5-3 rather than treating testing failures as a separate discipline.
Do Not Fix Tests by Weakening the Requirement

When a test exposes a failure, the first question is whether the implementation is wrong or the test expectation is inconsistent with the specification. Do not simply loosen the test because the implementation is inconvenient.
Regression Testing

sections.title: After fixing a defect
sections.code:
Original failing case
 ↓
Expected behavior restored
 ↓
Nearby related feature
 ↓
No regression introduced

sections.text: A change to filtering could affect the empty state. A removal change could affect list rendering. Test the nearby path when the same state or data flow is involved.
Testing Workshop

sections.text: Test the User's Journey, Not Just Individual Functions
A function can return the expected value while the feature still fails because state, navigation, rendering, or integration between functions is incorrect.

sections.title: End-to-end question
sections.code:
Can a real user complete the intended journey
from start to finish under the expected conditions?

sections.text: Check the Console and Network

sections.title: Useful signals
sections.code:
Unexpected runtime errors

Unhandled promise rejections

Failed network requests

Repeated requests

Malformed responses

sections.text: A user-visible feature can appear to work while still producing errors or unstable behavior underneath.
Do Not Create a False Sense of Coverage
Ten tests that all exercise the same happy path are not stronger than a smaller matrix that covers the important states and failure modes.
Prioritize Tests

sections.title: Test first
sections.code:
Core user journey

Highest-risk integration

Failure states

Boundary cases

Recently changed behavior

sections.text: The exact order can vary, but risk and user impact should influence where you spend testing effort.
A Defect Log Is Useful

sections.title: Record
sections.code:
Symptom

Reproduction steps

Expected behavior

Actual behavior

Root cause

Fix

Verification

sections.text: Recording this information prevents the same issue from being rediscovered and provides a useful explanation for later review.
Do Not Assume Every Failure Is a Code Bug
A failing check can reveal an incorrect requirement assumption, bad test data, a broken environment, or an implementation defect. Investigate the evidence before labeling the cause.
Definition of Done

sections.title: Before calling the feature done
sections.code:
□ Acceptance criteria verified
□ Primary flow works
□ Important edge cases checked
□ Loading/error/empty states verified
□ Known defects resolved
□ Fixed defects retested
□ Related regressions checked
□ Console/network behavior reviewed

sections.text: What Will Come Next?

The next lesson is Performance and Accessibility Review. Once functional behavior is stable, the finished build must be audited against measurable performance and accessibility expectations rather than relying on the feature simply appearing to work.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on functional testing and debugging. Performance and accessibility standards are audited separately in the next lesson.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you know a feature is ready?' A strong answer is: 'I trace the acceptance criteria into a test matrix, verify the primary user flow, test important edge and failure states, investigate any defects systematically, and rerun the original scenario after fixes. I also check nearby behavior for regressions.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What's an example of an important edge case?' For a data-driven feature it could be empty data, a failed request, a slow response, or removing the final item, depending on the product contract.
Reflect
Think about the last feature you called finished. Which acceptance criterion did you verify, which edge case did you test, and which important scenario did you simply assume would work?
A feature is finished when the important behavior has been demonstrated, not merely when the code runs once.

sections.label: Submit the test and debugging record with the current project build. The submission must demonstrate coverage of acceptance criteria, important edge cases, failure states, defect investigation, fixes, and regression verification.
sections.hint: Build your tests from the specification. For each failure, reproduce it, identify the cause, fix it, and rerun the original case plus related behavior.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Testing and debugging turn an apparently working feature into a verified feature. Start from the acceptance criteria, exercise the primary path and meaningful edge cases, deliberately test failure states, reproduce defects before fixing them, and perform regression checks afterward. The first successful run is only the beginning of verification.

exercises.title: Saved Lessons Test and Debug Pass
exercises.brief: Run a structured functional test pass, diagnose seeded or discovered defects, fix them, and verify the original and related scenarios.

quiz.question: What should testing begin from?
options: The feature's acceptance criteria and intended user behavior.
Whatever is easiest to click.
Only the implementation details.
Only known bugs.
quiz.explanation: Acceptance criteria provide the primary basis for verifying that the feature meets its requirements.

quiz.question: What should you do when a test exposes a defect?
options: Reproduce it, investigate the cause, fix it, and retest the original scenario.
Delete the test.
Immediately assume the test is wrong.
Make unrelated changes until the test passes.
quiz.explanation: The lesson applies the structured debugging process to testing failures.

quiz.question: Why is the happy path insufficient for feature verification?
options: Important failures can occur in empty, error, boundary, and repeated-interaction states.
Happy paths never work.
Edge cases are always more important than requirements.
Testing only matters for APIs.
quiz.explanation: A working primary flow does not establish correctness across meaningful conditions.

summary: Testing and debugging establish whether the integrated feature actually satisfies its requirements. Build a test matrix from acceptance criteria, verify the primary journey, exercise important edge and failure states, investigate defects using evidence, and rerun the original and related scenarios after fixes. A feature is not done merely because it works once.
interviewQuestions: How do you decide what to test for a new frontend feature?
How do acceptance criteria translate into tests?
What edge cases would you look for in a data-driven feature?
How do you debug a failing test or user scenario?
What is regression testing?
How do you avoid false confidence from a small test suite?
How do you decide which tests to prioritize?
What does 'done' mean for a frontend feature?

title: Performance and Accessibility Review
description: Audit the finished project against measurable performance and accessibility expectations, identify issues systematically, remediate the highest-impact problems, and document the evidence that the final build meets the review standard.
mastery: The learner can independently audit the finished application for performance and accessibility issues, prioritize findings by impact and evidence, remediate the important defects, and submit an audit record showing the checks performed and changes made.
learningObjectives: Run a structured performance review against the finished build.
Run a structured accessibility review against the finished build.
Use measurable evidence rather than visual intuition alone.
Test keyboard operation and focus behavior.
Check semantic structure, accessible names, and interactive states.
Inspect performance bottlenecks and avoid optimizing without evidence.
Prioritize audit findings by user impact and severity.
Remediate high-value issues and verify the fixes.
Document audit findings and evidence in a reusable review artifact.

sections.text: A Finished Feature Needs More Than Functional Correctness

The feature has now been built, connected, tested, and debugged. Before shipping, review two qualities that are easy to miss during feature development: how efficiently the application performs and how usable it is for people who interact with it through different input and assistive technologies.
This is an audit, not a general code review. The goal is to evaluate the finished artifact against explicit checks, record evidence, fix important findings, and verify the result.

sections.title: The audit model
sections.text: Check → record evidence → prioritize → remediate → recheck.
Performance and Accessibility Are Evidence Problems

sections.title: Weak review
sections.code:
The page feels fast.

The buttons look accessible.

I do not see any obvious issues.

sections.title: Stronger review
sections.code:
Measured interaction cost

Keyboard navigation result

Accessible-name inspection

Observed focus behavior

Recorded audit findings

sections.text: A useful audit replaces intuition with repeatable checks and evidence.
Performance Review

sections.title: Review areas
sections.code:
Initial loading cost

Large JavaScript or assets

Slow interactions

Expensive rendering or computation

Network behavior

Long main-thread tasks

sections.text: The exact bottleneck depends on the application. Start with the user journeys that matter most and collect evidence before deciding what needs optimization.
Performance Evidence

sections.title: Ask
sections.code:
What user action feels slow?

What measurement confirms the slowdown?

Where is the time actually spent?

What change would address that measured cost?

Did the same measurement improve after the fix?

sections.text: The previous debugging module established the profiling process. This audit applies it to the completed product.
Accessibility Review

sections.title: Review areas
sections.code:
Keyboard operation

Focus visibility and order

Accessible names and labels

Semantic HTML

Interactive states

Form feedback

Content and heading structure

Contrast and visual clarity

sections.text: WCAG 2.2 includes a Level A requirement that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface, and also requires that keyboard users not become trapped within a component. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Keyboard Audit

sections.title: Manual check
sections.code:
Start with a clean page.

Use Tab / Shift+Tab.

Can every interactive control receive focus?

Is the focus location visible?

Does focus move in a sensible order?

Can every opened interaction be exited with the keyboard?

sections.text: Keyboard operability should be tested directly rather than inferred from the presence of standard HTML elements. WCAG 2.2 explicitly requires keyboard operation for functionality at Level A. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Accessible Names

sections.title: Check interactive elements
sections.code:
What is this control?

What does it do?

Can assistive technology determine that?

Does the visible label match the accessible name?

sections.text: Inputs and controls need meaningful accessible names. Do not assume placeholder text alone is a sufficient long-term labeling strategy.
Semantic Structure

sections.title: Inspect
sections.code:
Heading hierarchy

Landmarks

Buttons vs links

Form labels

Lists

Tables where appropriate

Native controls before custom ARIA

sections.text: Prefer native semantic elements when they already provide the required behavior rather than recreating that behavior with generic elements and custom event handling.
Accessibility Automation Is Not the Whole Audit

Automated tools can identify useful classes of issues, but a complete review still requires manual interaction checks. In particular, keyboard behavior, focus flow, and whether the experience makes sense to a user cannot be reduced to one automated score.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not treat an automated score as proof that the interface is accessible or performant
sections.text: Automated checks are evidence, not the entire audit. Review the user journeys manually, especially keyboard operation, focus behavior, interaction states, and the real performance bottlenecks of the application.
Audit Severity

sections.title: Prioritize
sections.code:
High impact
→ blocks a user or critical path

Medium impact
→ meaningfully harms usability or robustness

Low impact
→ polish or non-critical improvement

sections.text: The goal is not to create the largest possible issue list. Prioritize problems by their effect on users, product requirements, and the confidence of the final build.
Audit Workshop

sections.title: Performance and Accessibility Audit
sections.instructions: Audit the finished project systematically. Record evidence for performance and accessibility checks, classify findings by severity, fix the highest-impact issues, and repeat the relevant checks after remediation.

sections.text: Use the Actual Product
The audit should target the finished project, not a hypothetical example. Use the same primary user flows that the specification and backlog established.
Performance Review Sequence

sections.title: Run this sequence
sections.code:
Choose important flow
 ↓
Reproduce
 ↓
Measure
 ↓
Identify bottleneck
 ↓
Make targeted change
 ↓
Measure again

sections.text: Accessibility Review Sequence

sections.title: Run this sequence
sections.code:
Choose important flow
 ↓
Navigate with keyboard
 ↓
Inspect focus and labels
 ↓
Check semantic structure
 ↓
Run automated checks where useful
 ↓
Fix issues
 ↓
Repeat manual checks

sections.text: Manual testing remains important even when automated tools are available. W3C's WCAG guidance explicitly frames keyboard operability as a user-facing requirement, not merely a code property. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Do Not Optimize the Wrong Thing
A performance review should lead to targeted changes. Do not add memoization, split components, or restructure data simply because those techniques are familiar.
Do Not Fix Only What the Tool Flags

An automated accessibility scan might miss a poor focus sequence or an interaction that is confusing when performed entirely from the keyboard. Conversely, an automated finding still deserves investigation rather than being dismissed because the UI looks visually acceptable.
Document the Remaining Risks

sections.title: Good audit conclusion
sections.code:
Resolved:
Keyboard navigation through the primary flow.

Resolved:
Slow search calculation identified and optimized.

Remaining:
Minor visual polish issue on a secondary screen.

Reason:
Does not block the primary user journey and is scheduled
for a later iteration.

sections.text: A professional audit does not pretend that every possible issue has disappeared. It records what was checked, what was fixed, and what remains.
Review Against the Standard

For accessibility, use an explicit standard as the audit reference. WCAG 2.2 is the current W3C Recommendation and provides testable success criteria such as keyboard operation and no keyboard trap. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
Do Not Treat Compliance as a Vibe

sections.title: Evidence-based statement
sections.code:
The primary flow is keyboard operable.
Focus remains visible.
The controls have identifiable accessible names.
The remaining performance issue is outside the critical path.

sections.title: Weak statement
sections.code: It seems accessible enough.

sections.text: What Will Come Next?

The next lesson moves from auditing the finished build to shipping it. You will prepare the application for release by reviewing the production build, environment configuration, deployment path, and release checklist.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson audits performance and accessibility. Shipping, deployment, and release readiness are handled in the next lesson.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you audit a finished frontend application?' A strong answer is: 'I would choose the critical user journeys, measure performance rather than guessing, and run a structured accessibility review that includes keyboard navigation, focus behavior, semantic structure, and accessible names. I would record evidence, prioritize the highest-impact findings, remediate them, and repeat the relevant checks.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Is running Lighthouse or another automated checker enough?' No. Automated checks are valuable, but they do not replace manual interaction testing, especially for keyboard operation and focus behavior.
Reflect
Take your current project and navigate its primary flow using only the keyboard. Where does focus go, what receives focus, and can every action be completed without a pointer?
A review is valuable when it measures the real product experience. Use tools to gather evidence, but always return to the user's actual path through the interface.

sections.label: Submit the completed performance and accessibility audit. The artifact must contain evidence from the finished project, prioritized findings, remediation where appropriate, and a final recheck demonstrating that important issues were addressed.
sections.hint: Do not submit a generic checklist. Audit the actual project, record what you observed, fix high-impact findings, and show the evidence after remediation.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A professional audit evaluates the finished product against measurable performance and accessibility expectations. Measure important flows, identify actual bottlenecks, test keyboard operation and focus behavior, inspect semantic structure and accessible names, prioritize findings by impact, fix the important issues, and document the final evidence. Automated tools are useful inputs, not substitutes for manual review.

exercises.title: Performance and Accessibility Audit
exercises.brief: Audit the finished project using measurable performance checks and a structured accessibility review, then remediate and recheck the important findings.

quiz.question: What should a performance audit do before recommending an optimization?
options: Measure the important user flow and identify the actual bottleneck.
Memoize every component.
Rewrite the largest component.
Optimize whichever function looks complicated.
quiz.explanation: Performance work should be evidence-driven.

quiz.question: Why is manual keyboard testing important during an accessibility audit?
options: Because keyboard operability and focus behavior must be experienced and verified as user-facing interactions.
Because automated tools never detect anything.
Because mouse interactions are not allowed.
Because WCAG only applies to keyboards.
quiz.explanation: Keyboard accessibility is an explicit WCAG requirement, and manual navigation reveals interaction behavior that automated checks may not fully capture.

quiz.question: What should the final audit artifact contain?
options: Only an accessibility/performance score.
Evidence of checks, prioritized findings, remediation, and final verification.
Only screenshots of the application.
A list of every possible WCAG criterion regardless of relevance.
quiz.explanation: The audit is intended to document what was actually checked, what was fixed, and what remains.

summary: Performance and accessibility review is a systematic audit of the finished product. Performance findings should come from measured user journeys and identified bottlenecks. Accessibility review should include manual keyboard and focus testing alongside semantic and automated checks. Prioritize findings by impact, remediate important issues, and record evidence from the actual project before declaring the review complete.
interviewQuestions: How would you audit a finished frontend application?
Why should performance optimization begin with measurement?
What would you manually test for accessibility?
Why is keyboard navigation important?
What can automated accessibility tools miss?
How do you prioritize performance and accessibility findings?
How do you verify that an audit fix actually worked?
What evidence would you include in a professional audit report?

title: Ship It
description: Prepare the completed project for release by verifying the production build, deployment configuration, environment assumptions, and real deployed behavior rather than treating the final commit as the end of the work.
mastery: The learner can prepare a production-ready build, verify the deployment configuration, deploy the application to a real environment, inspect the deployed result against the critical user flows, and document any remaining release issues.
learningObjectives: Prepare the project for a production build.
Identify configuration and environment assumptions required for deployment.
Verify that production-only behavior works as expected.
Deploy the project to a real environment.
Test critical user flows against the deployed application.
Identify deployment-specific failures that were not visible locally.
Confirm that assets, routing, API configuration, and environment variables behave correctly after deployment.
Document release readiness and any remaining known issues.
Understand why shipping is a verification stage rather than simply the final commit.

sections.text: The Project Is Not Finished at the Last Commit
The application has been implemented, tested, and audited. The final step before presentation is making sure the build actually works in the environment where users will access it.
Local development can hide problems involving production configuration, routing, asset paths, environment variables, API URLs, or build behavior.

sections.title: The shipping rule
sections.text: A project is not considered shipped merely because the source code is complete. Verify the actual deployed application in a real environment.
The Shipping Sequence

sections.title: Release flow
sections.code:
Production build
 ↓
Configuration check
 ↓
Deploy
 ↓
Open deployed application
 ↓
Verify critical flows
 ↓
Fix release issues
 ↓
Redeploy
 ↓
Final verification

sections.text: The exact deployment platform may vary, but the verification loop remains the same.
Production Build

sections.title: Check
sections.code:
Does the production build complete?

Are there build-time errors or warnings that matter?

Are the expected assets generated?

Are routes included correctly?

Are environment values configured?

sections.text: A successful local development server does not prove that the production build behaves correctly.
Environment Configuration

sections.title: Typical concerns
sections.code:
API base URL

Public configuration values

Authentication configuration

Feature flags

Build mode

Environment-specific services

sections.text: Anything that differs between development and production should be identified deliberately rather than discovered after deployment.
Do Not Ship Secrets
Production configuration may contain sensitive credentials or tokens. Only values intentionally designed for client exposure belong in a browser-delivered application.
Routing in Production

sections.title: Verify
sections.code:
Open root route
 ↓
Navigate internally
 ↓
Open a deep route directly
 ↓
Reload the page
 ↓
Confirm the route still resolves

sections.text: Single-page applications can appear correct during client-side navigation while still failing when a deep URL is loaded directly in the deployed environment.
Assets and Network Requests

sections.title: Inspect
sections.code:
JavaScript bundles

CSS

Images

Fonts

API requests

Source maps if intentionally deployed

sections.text: A deployment can succeed while individual assets or API requests fail because their URLs, paths, headers, or environment configuration differ from development.
The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not treat code completion as shipping
sections.text: The final commit only tells you that the source changed. Shipping means the real deployed artifact works for the intended user flows.
Verify the Critical User Journey

sections.title: Saved Lessons release check
sections.code:
Open application
 ↓
Open Saved Lessons
 ↓
Load data
 ↓
Search
 ↓
Open a lesson
 ↓
Remove a lesson
 ↓
Verify resulting state

sections.text: Run the most important product journey against the deployed application, not just the development version.
Shipping Workshop

sections.title: Ship It Release Checklist
sections.instructions: Prepare the finished project for deployment and document the release verification. Treat the deployed application as the source of truth. Record build status, configuration, routing, assets, API behavior, critical user-flow verification, and any remaining release issues.

sections.text: Local Success vs Deployment Success

sections.title: Local
sections.code:
localhost
→ development server
→ development environment
→ local routing
→ local API/configuration

sections.title: Deployed
sections.code:
real domain/origin
→ production build
→ production configuration
→ real routing
→ deployed API/configuration

sections.text: The second environment is the one that determines whether the application has actually shipped.
Deployment Failures Are Still Bugs
A route that works locally but returns a production error is a real defect. A missing production environment value is a real defect. An API request pointing to the wrong origin is a real defect.
Fix, Redeploy, Verify

sections.title: Release loop
sections.code:
Find issue
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Deploy
 ↓
Repeat the failing scenario

sections.text: Do not assume that a local fix automatically applies to the deployed artifact. Recheck the actual release.
Release Readiness

sections.title: Before calling it shipped
sections.code:
□ Production build succeeds
□ Required configuration is present
□ No client secrets are exposed
□ Critical routes work
□ Deep routes survive reload
□ Assets load
□ API requests use the correct environment
□ Critical user journey passes
□ Known issues documented

sections.text: Known Issues Can Be Acceptable
A professional release does not require pretending that no issue exists. A known issue can be acceptable when its impact is understood, documented, and consistent with the project's release decision.
Do Not Hide Release Risks
A strong shipping record makes remaining risks explicit. This gives reviewers and future maintainers a clear understanding of what was verified and what remains.
Production Verification Evidence

sections.title: Useful evidence
sections.code:
Deployed URL

Build output

Critical flow verification

Network inspection

Route verification

Known issue list

sections.text: The evidence should make it possible for another person to understand what was actually shipped and how it was verified.
What Will Come Next?

The next lesson is Present and Defend Your Project. You will switch from shipping the product to presenting its technical decisions, tradeoffs, implementation choices, and one improvement you would make next.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson establishes release readiness and deployment verification. The next lesson evaluates how well you can explain and defend the finished project.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What do you check before shipping a frontend application?' A strong answer is: 'I verify the production build and environment configuration, deploy it to a real environment, test critical routes and user flows there, inspect assets and API requests, and document any known release issues. I do not treat the final source commit as proof that the deployed application works.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What deployment-only problems have you seen?' Examples include incorrect environment configuration, deep-route failures, missing assets, wrong API origins, and differences between development and production builds.
Reflect
Think of the last application you deployed. Which issue could only have been discovered by testing the actual deployed artifact rather than the local development server?

sections.title: Ship the artifact, not the repository

sections.text: The user's experience is determined by the deployed application. Treat that artifact as the final source of truth during release verification.

sections.label: Submit the release checklist and deployed project evidence. The project must demonstrate a successful production build, deployment verification, working critical routes and user flows, and documented remaining release issues.
sections.hint: Verify the real deployment. Check the build, configuration, routes, assets, API behavior, and the primary user journey rather than relying on local success.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Shipping is the process of turning a finished codebase into a verified deployed product. Build for production, verify configuration, deploy to a real environment, test critical routes and user journeys, inspect assets and API behavior, fix deployment-specific issues, and document any remaining risks. The final commit is not the same thing as a shipped application.

exercises.title: Ship It Release Checklist
exercises.brief: Prepare the finished project for deployment and verify the real production artifact across build, configuration, routing, assets, data, and critical user flows.

quiz.question: What does it mean for a frontend project to be shipped?
options: The final source commit exists.
The production artifact is deployed and the critical user flows have been verified in the real environment.
The development server runs successfully.
The code has no TODO comments.
quiz.explanation: The lesson explicitly treats deployment and real-environment verification as part of shipping.

quiz.question: Why test deep routes after deployment?
options: A route can work during client-side navigation while failing when loaded or reloaded directly in the deployed environment.
Deep routes never work locally.
Routing only affects CSS.
Deep routes are unrelated to deployment.
quiz.explanation: Production hosting configuration can expose routing failures that are not visible during local navigation.

quiz.question: What should you do when a deployment-specific issue is discovered?
options: Fix it locally, redeploy, and repeat the failing verification against the deployed artifact.
Ignore it because local development works.
Delete the release checklist.
Assume the hosting provider will resolve it.
quiz.explanation: Release problems must be verified against the actual shipped artifact.

summary: Shipping is a verification stage, not merely the final commit. Prepare the production build, check environment configuration, deploy to a real environment, verify routes and assets, test the critical user journey, inspect API behavior, and document known issues. The deployed application—not the local development server—is the final source of truth.
